sections.heading: Reading companion
sections.content:
# Guide to Major Biblical Manuscripts & Canons of Textual Criticism

## I. Landmark Hebrew Bible & Old Testament Witnesses
- **Dead Sea Biblical Scrolls (c. 250 BC – 68 AD):** Earliest Hebrew witnesses (1QIsa-a, 4QSam-a, 4QDeut-q).
- **Aleppo Codex (כֶּתֶר אֲרַם צוֹבָא, c. 920 AD):** Scribal text of Solomon ben Buya'a pointed by Aaron ben
  Moses ben Asher in Tiberias; crown witness to the Masoretic Text (partially damaged in 1947).
- **Leningrad Codex (Firkovich B 19A, 1008/1009 AD):** Oldest complete dated Hebrew Bible manuscript;
  diplomatic base text of *Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia* (BHS) and *Biblia Hebraica Quinta* (BHQ).

## II. Early New Testament Papyri (2nd – 3rd Centuries AD)
| Gregory-Aland | Name / Repository | Date | Contents & Textual Significance |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **P52** | Rylands Papyrus 457 (Manchester) | c. 125–150 AD | John 18:31–33, 37–38; earliest extant NT fragment |
| **P46** | Chester Beatty II (Dublin/Ann Arbor) | c. 175–225 AD | Pauline Epistles + Hebrews; early Alexandrian witness |
| **P66** | Bodmer II (Cologny) | c. 200 AD | Nearly complete John 1–14 + fragments of 15–21 |
| **P75** | Bodmer XIV–XV (Vatican Library) | c. 175–225 AD | Luke & John; striking proto-Alexandrian affinity with B (03) |

## III. Great Majuscule (Uncial) Pandect Codices (4th – 5th Centuries AD)
- **Codex Sinaiticus (א / 01, c. 330–360 AD):** Discovered by Tischendorf at St. Catherine's Monastery;
  contains LXX, complete 27-book NT, plus Epistle of Barnabas and Shepherd of Hermas.
- **Codex Vaticanus (B / 03, c. 300–325 AD):** Housed in Vatican Library; premier Alexandrian witness
  to LXX and NT (breaks off at Hebrews 9:14; lacks Pastoral Epistles, Philemon, Revelation).
- **Codex Alexandrinus (A / 02, 5th c. AD):** British Library; early Byzantine witness in Gospels,
  Alexandrian in Acts/Epistles/Revelation; includes 1–2 Clement.

## IV. Core Canons of Reasoned Eclecticism
1. **External Evidence:** Weigh manuscripts (*ponderanda non numeranda*) by date, geographical
   distribution (Alexandrian, Western, Caesarean, Byzantine), and genealogical coherence.
2. **Transcriptional Probability (*Internal*):**
   - *Lectio difficilior potior*: Prefer the harder reading scribes would tend to smooth or harmonize.
   - *Lectio brevior potior*: Prefer the shorter reading unless homoeoteleuton/parablepsis occurred.
3. **Intrinsic Probability (*Internal*):** Prefer the reading most consistent with the author's
   documented vocabulary, syntax, and theological argument.
4. **Fundamental Principle:** Prefer the reading that best explains the origin of all rival variants.

questions.prompt: What was the structure and philological purpose of Origen of Alexandria's third-century Hexapla?
options: A harmony weaving the four canonical Gospels and two apocryphal Gospels into a single Syriac narrative.
A six-volume defense of allegorical exegesis directed against the literalists of Antioch.

A six-column synopsis aligning the Hebrew text, Greek vocalic transliteration, Aquila, Symmachus, the Septuagint (marked with obeli and asterisks), and Theodotion to assess quantitative differences between Greek and Hebrew witnesses.
A Latin revision of the Old Testament commissioned by Pope Damasus from Hebrew scrolls in Bethlehem.
questions.explanation: Compiled at Caesarea (c. 230–245 AD), Origen's Hexapla arranged six parallel columns—Hebrew, Hebrew transliterated into Greek letters, Aquila, Symmachus, the LXX, and Theodotion—using Aristarchian signs (obeli and asterisks) in the fifth column to show where the received Septuagint exceeded or lacked material present in the contemporary Hebrew text.
questions.sourceReference: Origen, Commentary on Matthew 15.14; Epistle to Africanus 4–5

questions.prompt: How did the publication of Bodmer Papyrus P75 (dated c. 175–225 AD, containing Luke and John) reshape twentieth-century debates over the Alexandrian text-type?
options: Its extraordinary verbal agreement with fourth-century Codex Vaticanus (B / 03) refuted claims that the Alexandrian text was a fourth-century scholarly recension invented under Constantine, proving instead its faithful transmission from at least the second century.
It demonstrated that the Byzantine Majority Text dominated Egyptian churches prior to 200 AD.
It provided the earliest extant witness to the Pericope Adulterae (John 7:53–8:11) in the Gospel of John.
It proved that early Christians wrote New Testament Gospels exclusively on papyrus rolls rather than codices.
questions.explanation: Prior to the discovery of the Bodmer papyri, some critics conjectured that Codex Vaticanus (B / 03) represented an artificial fourth-century editorial revision. P75 (c. 175–225 AD), a codex containing large portions of Luke and John (and omitting John 7:53–8:11), agrees so closely with Vaticanus that it established the second-century antiquity and strict copying discipline behind the proto-Alexandrian text.
questions.sourceReference: C. M. Martini, Il problema della recensionalità del codice B alla luce del papiro Bodmer XIV (1966)

questions.prompt: Which patristic scholar penned this famous observation regarding manuscript variation when commissioned to revise the Old Latin Gospels against ancient Greek exemplars?
questions.excerptContext: "You urge me to revise the old Latin version, and, as it were, to sit in judgment on the copies of the Scriptures which are now scattered throughout the whole world; and, inasmuch as they differ from one another, you would have me decide which of them agree with the Greek original... For if we are to pin our faith to the Latin texts, it is for our opponents to tell us which; for there are almost as many forms of texts as there are copies."
options: Augustine of Hippo, De Doctrina Christiana (Book II)
Tatian the Assyrian, Preface to the Diatessaron
Eusebius of Caesarea, Epistle to Carpianus
Jerome of Stridon, Epistle to Pope Damasus (Preface to the Four Gospels)
questions.explanation: In 383 AD, Jerome addressed his Preface to the Four Gospels (Novum Opus) to Pope Damasus I, justifying his fresh revision of the chaotic Vetus Latina manuscripts (*tot paene exemplaria quot codices*—"almost as many forms of texts as there are copies") by appealing to ancient Greek codices.
questions.sourceReference: Jerome of Stridon, Epistula ad Damasum (Preface to the Vulgate Gospels), 383 AD

questions.prompt: In New Testament textual criticism, the canon lectio difficilior potior ("the harder reading is preferable") instructs scholars to prefer grammatically smoother, harmonized readings because the Apostles wrote in polished classical Attic Greek.
questions.explanation: False. Formulated by Johann Albrecht Bengel (1725), lectio difficilior potior holds the exact opposite: because conscientious scribes naturally tended to smooth awkward Koine syntax, resolve apparent tensions, or harmonize parallel Gospel accounts, a rougher or seemingly harder reading (short of sheer scribal nonsense) is more likely to represent the earlier text from which smoother variants arose.
questions.sourceReference: Johann Albrecht Bengel, Prodromus Novi Testamenti Graeci (1725); Bruce M. Metzger & Bart D. Ehrman, The Text of the New Testament (4th ed.), pp. 302–303

topics.title: Formation of the Biblical Canon
topics.subtitle: The Tripartite Hebrew TaNaKh, Apostolic Recognition, Patristic Criteria, and Conciliar Lists
topics.summary: Investigates how the covenant community recognized the authoritative boundaries of the Old and New Testaments—tracing the tripartite Hebrew TaNaKh, Deuterocanonical debates, patristic criteria of apostolicity, orthodoxy, and catholicity, Eusebius's taxonomy, and Athanasius's 367 AD Festal Letter.
topics.era: 2nd Century BC – 4th Century AD (Confessional Codification 16th–17th c.)

sections.heading: The Tripartite Hebrew TaNaKh and the Question of the Alexandrian Deuterocanon
sections.body:
Derived from the Semitic word for a measuring reed (*qaneh*) and Greek *kanōn* ('rule, standard, or authoritative list'), the biblical canon denotes the closed corpus of divinely inspired books recognized by the people of God as the norming rule of faith and life. Long before the Christian era, Israel's Scriptures coalesced into the threefold architecture later abbreviated as *TaNaKh*: the *Torah* (Law of Moses), *Nevi'im* (Former and Latter Prophets), and *Ketuvim* (Writings). Around 132 BC, the Greek Prologue to the Wisdom of Jesus ben Sira already referred three times to 'the Law and the Prophets and the others that followed them,' a tripartite structure echoed by the risen Christ in Luke 24:44 ('everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms') and attested by Flavius Josephus in *Against Apion* (1.38–41), who numbered Israel's sacred library at twenty-two books (equivalent to the thirty-nine books of modern Protestant Old Testaments when Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, Ezra-Nehemiah, Ruth-Judges, Lamentations-Jeremiah, and the Twelve Minor Prophets are grouped as combined scrolls). While older scholarship hypothesized a formal 'Council of Jamnia' (Yavneh, c. 90 AD) closing the Hebrew canon, modern historians recognize that rabbinic sages at Yavneh merely reaffirmed the existing canonical status of Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes against minor scruples.

A lasting divergence emerged, however, because Hellenistic Jewish and early Gentile Christian communities read Greek Septuagint codices that circulated additional Second Temple books—including Tobit, Judith, Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach (Ecclesiasticus), Baruch, and 1–2 Maccabees, plus expansions to Esther and Daniel. In the late fourth century, Jerome—having learned Hebrew from Jewish tutors to translate the Latin Vulgate directly from the *Hebraica veritas*—argued in his *Prologus Galeatus* (c. 391 AD) that books absent from the Hebrew canon belonged among the *apocrypha*, profitable for edification of morals but incapable of establishing ecclesiastical dogma. Conversely, Augustine of Hippo and the North African synods defended the broader Septuagintal canon used in Western liturgy, presaging the sixteenth-century divide wherein the Council of Trent (1546) dogmatized these 'Deuterocanonical' books while the Lutheran, Reformed, and Anglican confessions reverted to the Hebrew Old Testament canon.

sections.heading: Apostolic Authority, Heretical Catalysts, and Early Christian Recognition
sections.body:
From its inception, the apostolic church possessed a written Old Testament canon alongside the living voice and authoritative writings of Christ's commissioned Apostles. Internal New Testament indicators already display incipient canonical consciousness: Paul directs public liturgical exchange of his epistles among congregations (Colossians 4:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:27), 1 Timothy 5:18 pairs Deuteronomy 25:4 alongside a saying of Jesus recorded in Luke 10:7 under the single formula 'For the Scripture (*hē graphē*) says,' and 2 Peter 3:15–16 ranks Paul's letters beside 'the other Scriptures' (*tas loipas graphas*). Among the Apostolic Fathers of the early second century—Clement of Rome, Ignatius of Antioch, and Polycarp of Smyrna—collections of Pauline epistles and synoptic Gospel traditions functioned authoritatively in catechesis and worship.

Second-century heterodox movements did not invent the New Testament canon, as sometimes alleged, yet they compelled the catholic Church to delineate explicitly what she already received in public worship. Around 140 AD at Rome, Marcion of Sinope severed the Creator God of Israel from the Father of Jesus, jettisoning the entire Old Testament and promulgating a truncated canon consisting solely of an expurgated Gospel of Luke and ten edited Pauline epistles (*Apostolikon*); conversely, Gnostic sects proliferated esoteric pseudepigrapha (such as the mid-second-century *Gospel of Thomas*), while Montanism claimed new ecstatic prophecies. Responding around 180 AD, Irenaeus of Lyons championed the irreducible *Tetramorphon*—the Fourfold Gospel of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John—alongside Acts, thirteen Pauline letters, 1 Peter, 1–2 John, and Revelation, a core closely mirrored in the Latin *Muratorian Fragment* (traditionally dated c. 170–200 AD), which enumerates twenty-two of the twenty-seven New Testament books while explicitly excluding Gnostic and Marcionite forgeries.

sections.heading: Patristic Criteria, Eusebian Classification, and Fourth-Century Consolidation
sections.body:
Rather than conferring inspiration by episcopal fiat, patristic theologians understood the Church as discerning and receiving self-authenticating apostolic books through three interlocking historical and doctrinal touchstones: *apostolicity* (authorship by an Apostle or immediate apostolic companion, such as Mark writing Peter's preaching and Luke accompanying Paul), *orthodoxy* (harmony with the *regula fidei*, the apostolic Rule of Faith confessed across baptismal churches), and *catholicity* (continuous, widespread public liturgical reading—*lectio publica*—across Eastern and Western sees). In his *Ecclesiastical History* (3.25, c. 324 AD), Bishop Eusebius of Caesarea surveyed universal church reception by grouping extant writings into four tiers: the universally acknowledged *homologoumena* (Four Gospels, Acts, fourteen Pauline letters, 1 John, 1 Peter, and conditionally Revelation); the *antilegomena* ('spoken against' or debated by some, yet known to most: James, Jude, 2 Peter, 2–3 John); the uncanonical *notha* ('spurious,' edifying yet non-apostolic works like *Shepherd of Hermas*, *Didache*, *Barnabas*, and *Acts of Paul*); and impious Gnostic fabrications to be cast out altogether.

Whereas the West temporarily hesitated over Hebrews' anonymous authorship and parts of the Greek East hesitated over chiliasm in Revelation, fourth-century communication resolved remaining regional doubts concerning the smaller Catholic Epistles and Apocalypse. For Easter 367 AD, Bishop Athanasius of Alexandria issued his landmark *Thirty-Ninth Festal Letter*, providing the earliest surviving catalog that lists the exact twenty-seven books of our New Testament—no more and no less—as 'fountains of salvation,' cleanly separating them both from catechetical *anagignōskomena* ('books to be read' to catechumens) and from heretical *apokrypha*. Within three decades, Western provincial synods—including the Synod of Rome under Damasus (382) and the North African Councils of Hippo Regius (393) and Third Carthage (397, confirmed 419)—ratified the identical twenty-seven-book New Testament canon confessed across Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, and Protestant communions to this day.

excerpts.quote: For we have not an innumerable multitude of books among us, disagreeing from and contradicting one another, as the Greeks have, but only twenty-two books, which contain the records of all the past times; which are justly believed to be divine... From Artaxerxes until our own time every event has been recorded, but this is not judged worthy of the like credit with what preceded it, because the exact succession of the prophets ceased.
excerpts.author: Flavius Josephus
excerpts.work: Against Apion, Book I, 8 (§§38, 41)

# Primary Source Study: Athanasius of Alexandria, 39th Festal Letter (367 AD)

## I. Historical Context
Written from Alexandria for Easter 367 AD to the bishops and churches of Egypt, Athanasius's
Thirty-Ninth Festal Epistle counters Melitian and Gnostic circulation of apocryphal books by
delineating the canonical Scriptures — providing the earliest extant list of the exact 27 books
of the New Testament without addition or omission.

## II. Translated Excerpt (Festal Letter 39, §§4–7, NPNF2-04)
> 'Forasmuch as some have taken in hand to reduce into order for themselves the books termed
> apocryphal, and to mix them up with the divinely inspired Scripture, concerning which we have
> been fully persuaded, as they who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the
> Word delivered to the fathers; it seemed good to me also, having been urged thereto by true
> brethren, and having learned from the beginning, to set before you the books included in the
> Canon, and handed down, and accredited as Divine...'
>
> 'Again it is not tedious to speak of the books of the New Testament. These are, the four
> Gospels, according to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Afterwards, the Acts of the Apostles
> and Epistles (called Catholic), seven, viz. of James, one; of Peter, two; of John, three;
> after these, one of Jude. In addition, there are fourteen Epistles of Paul, written in this
> order. The first, to the Romans; then two to the Corinthians; after these, to the Galatians;
> next, to the Ephesians; then to the Philippians; then to the Colossians; after these, two to
> the Thessalonians, and that to the Hebrews; and again, two to Timothy; one to Titus; and
> lastly, that to Philemon. And besides, the Revelation of John.'
>
> 'These are fountains of salvation, that they who thirst may be satisfied with the living
> words they contain. In these alone is proclaimed the doctrine of godliness. Let no man add
> to these, neither let him take ought from these.'

## III. Athanasius's Threefold Pastoral Distinction (§7)
1. **Kanonizomena (Canonized Books):** 22 Hebrew-counted OT books + 27 NT books ('fountains of salvation').
2. **Anagignōskomena (Books to be Read):** Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach, Esther, Judith, Tobit, Didache,
   and Shepherd of Hermas — appointed by the Fathers for catechetical instruction of converts.
3. **Apokrypha (Apocryphal Fabrications):** Heretical pseudepigrapha forged under ancient names, to be rejected.

sections.content:
# Eusebius's Canonical Classification (Historia Ecclesiastica 3.25) & Canon Timeline

## I. Eusebius of Caesarea's Fourfold Taxonomy (c. 324 AD)
| Category | Greek Term | Status in Ecclesiastical Usage | Books Assigned by Eusebius |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Recognized** | *Homologoumena* (Ὁμολογούμενα) | Universally acknowledged as Apostolic & canonical | Four Gospels, Acts, 14 Pauline Epistles, 1 John, 1 Peter, (Revelation 'if it seem proper') |
| **2. Disputed** | *Antilegomena* (Ἀντιλεγόμενα) | Known to most churches, yet debated by some | James, Jude, 2 Peter, 2 John, 3 John |
| **3. Spurious / Uncanonical** | *Notha* (Νόθα) | Orthodox or edifying, but non-Apostolic / non-canonical | Acts of Paul, Shepherd of Hermas, Apocalypse of Peter, Barnabas, Didache, (Revelation per some) |
| **4. Heretical** | *Atopa kai dyssebē* | Absurd & impious Gnostic forgeries; wholly rejected | Gospels of Peter, Thomas, Matthias; Acts of Andrew and John |

## II. Criteria of Canonical Recognition in the Patristic Church
- **Apostolicity:** Authored by an Apostle or an immediate apostolic associate (Mark with Peter; Luke with Paul).
- **Orthodoxy (*Regula Fidei*):** Conformity to the apostolic Rule of Faith handed down in the churches.
- **Catholicity (Ecumenical Reception):** Continuous public liturgical reading (*lectio publica*) across East and West.

## III. Chronological Milestones in Biblical Canonization
- **c. 132 BC — Prologue to Sirach:** Attests tripartite Hebrew Scriptures ('the Law, the Prophets, and the others').
- **c. 90–95 AD — Flavius Josephus (*Against Apion* 1.38–41):** Enumerates 22 sacred Hebrew books closed since Artaxerxes.
- **c. 90–100 AD — Rabbinic Academy at Yavneh (Jamnia):** Debates liturgical defilement of Song of Songs & Ecclesiastes.
- **c. 140 AD — Marcion of Sinope:** Truncates Scripture to edited Luke + 10 Pauline letters, catalyzing orthodox lists.
- **c. 180 AD — Irenaeus of Lyons (*Adv. Haer.* 3.11.8):** Defends the irreducible Fourfold Gospel (*Tetramorphon*).
- **c. 170–200 AD — Muratorian Fragment:** Earliest surviving Latin canon catalog (recognizes 22 of 27 NT books).
- **c. 240 AD — Origen of Alexandria:** Distinguishes undisputed books from debated epistles (Homilies on Joshua 7.1).
- **367 AD — Athanasius (*Festal Letter 39*):** First exact catalog of all 27 New Testament books.
- **382–405 AD — Jerome (*Prologus Galeatus* & Vulgate):** Translates OT from *Hebraica veritas*; distinguishes
  protocanonical Hebrew books from ecclesiastical *apocrypha*.
- **393 & 397 AD — North African Councils of Hippo & Carthage III:** Western provincial synods ratify the 27-book
  NT alongside the broader Septuagintal Old Testament read in Latin Africa (Augustine present).
- **1546 — Council of Trent (Session IV) vs. Reformed Confessions:** Rome dogmatizes Deuterocanon; Westminster
  Confession (1647, I.2–3) restricts OT canon to the 39 Hebrew books while affirming the identical 27-book NT.

questions.prompt: In Book III, Chapter 25 of his Ecclesiastical History (c. 324 AD), which five books did Eusebius of Caesarea classify as the antilegomena—writings "nevertheless recognized by most" yet still debated in certain regions?
options: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, and the Acts of the Apostles
James, Jude, 2 Peter, 2 John, and 3 John
Gospel of Thomas, Gospel of Peter, Gospel of Matthias, Acts of Andrew, and Acts of John
questions.explanation: Eusebius distinguished the universally received homologoumena from the disputed yet widely known antilegomena (James, Jude, 2 Peter, 2 John, and 3 John), separating both from uncanonical orthodox works (notha, such as Shepherd of Hermas and Didache) and heretical Gnostic fabrications.

questions.prompt: How did Athanasius of Alexandria classify works such as the Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach, Didache, and Shepherd of Hermas in his Thirty-Ninth Festal Letter (367 AD)?
options: As canonical "fountains of salvation" equal in doctrinal authority to the twenty-seven books of the New Testament.
As impious Gnostic apokrypha forged by heretics and forbidden to Christians under pain of excommunication.
As non-canonical anagignōskomena ("books to be read"), appointed by the Fathers for the catechetical edification of new converts while distinct from the canonized Scriptures.
As lost prophetic books known only through Origen's Hexapla.
questions.explanation: After listing the exact 27 books of the New Testament ("fountains of salvation"), Athanasius drew a nuanced three-part distinction: (1) kanonizomena (canonical books alone establishing doctrine), (2) anagignōskomena (non-canonical books profitable for catechumens, including Wisdom, Sirach, Tobit, Judith, Didache, and Hermas), and (3) heretical apokrypha to be wholly rejected.

questions.prompt: The First Ecumenical Council of Nicaea (325 AD), convened by Emperor Constantine, formally voted upon and promulgated the first official twenty-seven-book list of the New Testament canon.
questions.explanation: False. Despite persistent popular myth, the Council of Nicaea (325 AD) addressed the Arian Christological controversy, the date of Pascha, and twenty disciplinary canons without issuing any catalog of biblical books. The earliest extant exact 27-book New Testament list appears in Athanasius's 39th Festal Letter (367 AD), followed by Western provincial synods at Hippo (393) and Carthage (397).
questions.sourceReference: Canons of the First Council of Nicaea (325 AD); Bruce M. Metzger, The Canon of the New Testament (1987), pp. 210–212

topics.title: The Apostolic Fathers: Clement, Ignatius, Polycarp & the Didache
topics.subtitle: Sub-Apostolic Witnesses to Ecclesial Concord, Catechetical Liturgy, Eucharistic Realism, and Martyrdom (c. 70–155 AD)
topics.summary: Bridging the apostolic generation and the mid-second-century Greek Apologists, the Apostolic Fathers preserve the earliest post-New Testament witness to Christian worship, ministry, and Christological orthodoxy. From Rome's appeal to orderly presbyteral succession in 1 Clement and the Syrian catechetical-liturgical manual of the Didache to Ignatius of Antioch's seven epistles defending incarnational realism, Eucharistic unity, and the monarchical episcopate, and Polycarp of Smyrna's Johannine memory and martyrdom, these texts illuminate how sub-apostolic communities safeguarded the apostolic rule of faith across the Mediterranean.

sections.heading: Ecclesial Concord and Catechetical Liturgy: 1 Clement and the Didache
sections.body:
The designation "Apostolic Fathers" (Patres Apostolici, coined in 1672 by Jean-Baptiste Cotelier) gathers a diverse sub-apostolic corpus composed roughly between 70 and 155 AD by pastors and catechists who either knew the Apostles personally or led congregations founded directly by them. Two earliest monuments reveal how sub-apostolic churches ordered communal life and worship as living apostolic presence receded. Written around 95–96 AD on behalf of the Church of Rome to the Church of Corinth, 1 Clement (traditionally attributed to Clement, presiding presbyter-bishop in Rome) addresses a youthful Corinthian faction that had unseated duly appointed, blameless presbyters. Drawing richly upon the Septuagint, Pauline epistles, and Hebrews, Clement weaves cosmic harmony and Old Testament Levitical order into an urgent plea for ecclesial concord (homonoia) and humility, articulating the earliest extant theology of orderly apostolic succession (1 Clem. 42–44): just as God sent Christ and Christ sent the Apostles, the Apostles appointed tested firstfruits as overseers (episkopoi) and deacons, stipulating that upon their death other approved men should succeed to their liturgy so that the flock would not be fractured by partisan rivalry.

Complementing Rome's institutional sobriety is the Didache ("The Teaching of the Lord through the Twelve Apostles to the Nations," c. 50–90 AD), a Syrian or Palestinian church-order manual rediscovered in 1873 by Metropolitan Philotheos Bryennios within the eleventh-century Codex Hierosolymitanus in Constantinople. Chapters 1–6 induct gentile catechumens through a Jewish-Christian "Two Ways" moral catechesis—contrasting the Way of Life shaped by the Sermon on the Mount with the Way of Death—before moving in Chapters 7–10 to foundational liturgical rubrics. Catechumens are baptized after fasting in "living" (running) water "into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Did. 7.1), with thrice-poured water expressly permitted where running or cold immersion water is lacking. Believers fast on Wednesdays and Fridays, pray the Lord's Prayer three times daily, and offer thanksgiving prayers over the cup ("the holy vine of David") and broken bread ("scattered upon the mountains and gathered together to become one," Did. 9.4), assembling every Lord's Day (kyriakē) to confess transgressions and break bread so that their sacrifice may be pure (Did. 14.1, citing Malachi 1:11).

Crucially, both 1 Clement and the Didache capture an organic institutional transition still closely aligned with New Testament terminology. In 1 Clement 42–44 and Didache 15.1 ("Appoint therefore for yourselves bishops and deacons worthy of the Lord, men meek and not lovers of money"), local oversight remains collegiate, with episkopoi and presbyteroi functioning as coordinate titles alongside itinerant teachers and prophets tested strictly by moral conduct and fidelity to received teaching (Did. 11–13). Together they demonstrate that liturgical prayer, ethical discipline, and accountable pastoral succession formed a unified catechumenal matrix decades before formal conciliar creeds.

sections.heading: Ignatius of Antioch: Anti-Docetic Christology, Eucharistic Realism, and the Catholic Church
sections.body:
Around 107–115 AD under Emperor Trajan, Ignatius—called Theophorus ("God-bearer") and Bishop of Antioch in Syria—was transported in chains across Asia Minor under a guard of ten Roman soldiers ("ten leopards," Rom. 5.1) to face wild beasts in the Flavian Amphitheatre. Along the route at Smyrna and Troas, Ignatius dictated seven urgent letters: five to churches of Asia Minor (Ephesians, Magnesians, Trallians, Philadelphians, Smyrnaeans), one to the Church of Rome pleading with believers not to use political influence to rob him of martyrdom ("Allow me to be bread for the wild beasts, through whom I may attain to God; I am God's wheat," Rom. 4.1), and a personal pastoral letter to Bishop Polycarp of Smyrna. Authenticated in their "Middle Recension" by Archbishop James Ussher (1644), Isaac Voss (1646), J. B. Lightfoot, and Theodor Zahn against later fourth-century Arianizing interpolations, these seven epistles articulate a passionate synthesis of incarnational Christology, Eucharistic realism, and episcopal unity.

At the theological center of Ignatius's correspondence stands his uncompromising polemic against Judaizing separatists and especially Docetists (from dokein, "to seem" or "to appear")—early heterodox teachers who recoiled from divine passibility by claiming that Christ's flesh, birth, and crucifixion were mere phantasmal appearances. Against them, Ignatius hammers home the adverb alēthōs ("truly"): Jesus Christ, our God, was truly born of the Virgin Mary from the seed of David, truly ate and drank, was truly nailed to the cross in the flesh under Pontius Pilate, and truly raised Himself bodily so that after the Resurrection the Apostles touched Him (Trall. 9–10; Smyrn. 1–3). For Ignatius, Docetism instantly evacuates both martyrdom and the Eucharist of meaning: "If, as some atheists—that is, unbelievers—say, He only seemed to suffer (they themselves only seeming to exist), why then am I in chains?" (Trall. 10.1).

Because salvation hinges on union with Christ's true flesh and blood, Ignatius binds Christology directly to liturgy and the threefold ministry. Docetists abstain from the common Eucharist because they refuse to confess it to be "the flesh of our Saviour Jesus Christ, which suffered for our sins, and which the Father, of His goodness, raised up again" (Smyrn. 7.1), whereas for the faithful the one bread broken with the bishop is "the medicine of immortality (pharmakon athanasias), the antidote that we should not die, but live forever in Jesus Christ" (Eph. 20.2). Ignatius provides the earliest unmistakable witness to the monarchical episcopate—a single bishop (episkopos) surrounded by a harmonious spiritual crown of presbyters (presbyterion) and deacons (diakonoi)—not as autocratic Prelacy, but as the visible sacramental icon of concord. In Smyrnaeans 8.2, this vision yields the earliest extant occurrence of the phrase "the Catholic Church" (hē katholikē ekklēsia): wherever the bishop appears, there let the congregation gather, just as wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the universal, whole Church.

sections.heading: Polycarp of Smyrna: Johannine Living Memory and Martyrdom According to the Gospel
sections.body:
If Ignatius embodies prophetic fire, his younger friend Polycarp, Bishop of Smyrna (c. 69–155 AD), embodies living apostolic memory. According to Irenaeus of Lyons—who grew up in Smyrna and listened attentively to the aged bishop in his youth (Adversus Haereses 3.3.4; Epistle to Florinus in Eusebius, Hist. eccl. 5.20.6)—Polycarp had been instructed by Apostles, conversed with many who had seen Christ, and recounted from memory how John the disciple of the Lord taught concerning Jesus's miracles and doctrine. Polycarp thus forms the decisive historical chain connecting the Johannine circle of Asia Minor to Irenaeus's anti-Gnostic theology in Gaul, a role confirmed late in Polycarp's life when he traveled to Rome (c. 154 AD) to confer peacefully with Bishop Anicetus over the Quartodeciman Paschal date—and, per Irenaeus, confronted Marcion of Sinope face-to-face as "the firstborn of Satan."

Polycarp's lone surviving letter, his Epistle to the Philippians (written shortly after Ignatius passed through Philippi en route to Rome, forwarding copies of Ignatius's epistles at the Philippians' request), reads as a rich mosaic of New Testament Scripture. Within fourteen brief chapters, Polycarp weaves scores of allusions and citations from the Pauline corpus, 1 Peter, and 1 John, counseling presbyters toward compassionate pastoral care over a fallen elder (Valens) while warning sharply against avarice and Christological heresy. Echoing 1 John 4:2–3, Polycarp declares in Philippians 7.1 that "whosoever does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is antichrist; and whosoever does not confess the testimony of the cross is of the devil; and whosoever perverts the oracles (logia) of the Lord to his own lusts, and says that there is neither a resurrection nor a judgment, he is the firstborn of Satan," urging believers to return "to the word handed down to us from the beginning."

Around 155–156 AD, Polycarp sealed that witness in the stadium of Smyrna, commemorated in the Martyrdom of Polycarp—an encyclical letter from the Church of Smyrna to Philomelium that stands as the earliest surviving Christian martyr passio outside the New Testament. Explicitly contrasting Polycarp's "martyrdom according to the Gospel" with the rash Phrygian volunteer Quintus (who turned himself in only to apostatize in terror when he saw the beasts, Mart. Pol. 4), the narrative portrays Polycarp waiting calmly until betrayed, offering hospitality and unhurried prayer before his arrest, and answering Proconsul Statius Quadratus's demand to revile Christ with serene fidelity. Offering a Eucharistic-styled prayer of praise over the unnailed pyre, Polycarp dies pierced by a dagger, after which the Smyrnaeans gather his bones "more precious than costly stones" to celebrate the birthday (natalis) of his martyrdom—while formulating the classic patristic boundary between latria and veneration: "Him indeed we worship (sebomen) as being the Son of God, whereas the martyrs we love (agapōmen) worthily as disciples and imitators of the Lord" (Mart. Pol. 17.3).

# Primary Excerpt: Ignatius of Antioch, Epistle to the Smyrnaeans (c. 110 AD)

> **Archival Source:** *Ante-Nicene Fathers*, Vol. 1 (Roberts & Donaldson, eds.) — Authentic Middle Greek Recension

## Chapters 1–2: Confession of the Truly Incarnate and Crucified Lord Against Docetism

I glorify Jesus Christ, the God who has thus given you wisdom; for I have observed that ye are perfected in an
immovable faith, as if ye were nailed to the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, both in the flesh and in the spirit,
and are established in love through the blood of Christ, being fully persuaded with respect to our Lord, that He
was truly of the seed of David according to the flesh, and the Son of God according to the will and power of God;
that He was truly born of a virgin, was baptized by John, in order that all righteousness might be fulfilled by Him;
and was truly, under Pontius Pilate and Herod the tetrarch, nailed to the cross for us in His flesh.

Now, He suffered all these things for our sakes, that we might be saved. And He suffered truly, even as also He
truly raised up Himself, not, as certain unbelievers maintain, that He only seemed to suffer (τὸ δοκεῖν), as they
themselves only seem to be [Christians].

## Chapters 6–7: Eucharistic Realism and Separation from Heresy

They abstain from the Eucharist and from prayer, because they confess not the Eucharist to be the flesh of our
Saviour Jesus Christ, which suffered for our sins, and which the Father, of His goodness, raised up again. Those,
therefore, who speak against this gift of God, incur death in the midst of their disputes. It were better for them
to treat it with respect, that they also might rise again.

## Chapter 8: The Bishop, the Valid Eucharist, and the Catholic Church (Καθολικὴ Ἐκκλησία)

See that ye all follow the bishop, even as Jesus Christ does the Father, and the presbytery as ye would the
apostles; and reverence the deacons, as being the institution of God. Let no man do anything connected with the
Church without the bishop. Let that be deemed a proper (βεβαία) Eucharist, which is administered either by the
bishop, or by one to whom he has entrusted it. Wherever the bishop shall appear, there let the multitude [of the
people] also be; even as, wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the Catholic Church (ἡ καθολικὴ ἐκκλησία). It is not
lawful without the bishop either to baptize or to celebrate a love-feast; but whatsoever he shall approve of, that
is also pleasing to God, so that everything that is done may be secure and valid.

**Patristic Note:** *Smyrnaeans* 8.2 preserves the earliest extant occurrence of *katholikē ekklēsia* in Christian literature.

sections.heading: Reading companion
sections.content:
# Corpus Guide to the Apostolic Fathers (c. 70–155 AD)

The title *Patres Apostolici* (coined by Jean-Baptiste Cotelier in 1672) designates sub-apostolic Christian writings
whose authors knew the Apostles personally or stood in the immediate generation bridging New Testament proclamation
and the mid-second-century Greek Apologists.

| Text / Corpus | Approximate Date | Provenance | Literary Genre | Central Theological & Ecclesial Themes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Didache** (*Teaching of the Twelve Apostles*) | c. 50–90 AD | Syria / Palestine | Church Order Manual | Two Ways ethical catechesis; triune baptismal rubric; Eucharistic prayers (*Did.* 9–10); testing itinerant prophets. |
| **1 Clement** (*Rome to the Corinthians*) | c. 95–96 AD | Rome | Ecclesial Epistle | Concord (*homonoia*); orderly presbyteral succession from the apostles (*1 Clem.* 42–44); Old Testament exempla. |
| **Seven Epistles of Ignatius** | c. 107–115 AD | Antioch (en route to Rome) | Pastoral Epistles | Anti-Docetic incarnational realism; threefold ministry (bishop, presbyters, deacons); Eucharistic unity; martyrdom. |
| **Polycarp, Epistle to the Philippians** | c. 110–135 AD | Smyrna (Asia Minor) | Paraenetic Epistle | Dense weave of Pauline & Petrine citations; warning against Docetic/Marcionite denial of the flesh (*Phil.* 7.1). |
| **Fragments of Papias of Hierapolis** | c. 110–130 AD | Phrygia (Asia Minor) | Exegetical Exposition | Oral traditions of the elders on Mark (interpreter of Peter) and Matthew's Hebrew *logia* (preserved in Eusebius). |
| **Epistle of Barnabas** | c. 100–132 AD | Alexandria | Typological Treatise | Christological typology of Mosaic sacrifices and covenant ritual; Two Ways moral instruction (*Barn.* 18–20). |
| **Shepherd of Hermas** | c. 110–145 AD | Rome | Apocalyptic Visions | Post-baptismal repentance (*metanoia*); ecclesiology of the Church as a tower under construction; moral renewal. |
| **2 Clement** | c. 130–150 AD | Rome or Corinth | Extant Homily | Earliest surviving non-canonical Christian sermon; continence, almsgiving, and the pre-existent spiritual Church. |
| **Epistle to Diognetus** | c. 130–180 AD | Alexandria or Smyrna | Apologetic Protreptic | Christians as the "soul in the world" (*Diogn.* 6); the wondrous divine exchange (*antallagma*, *Diogn.* 9.2–5). |
| **Martyrdom of Polycarp** | c. 155–156 AD | Smyrna | Martyr Acta Epistle | Earliest narrative *passio*; martyrdom according to the Gospel vs. rash voluntarism; loving martyrs vs. worshipping Christ. |

## Textual Transmission Milestones

- **Codex Sinaiticus (4th c.):** Preserves the *Epistle of Barnabas* and opening chapters of the *Shepherd of Hermas*.
- **Codex Alexandrinus (5th c.):** Preserves *1 Clement* and *2 Clement* bound immediately after the New Testament.
- **Codex Hierosolymitanus (1056 AD):** Discovered by Philotheos Bryennios in Constantinople (1873), restoring the complete Greek *Didache*, *1 Clement*, and *2 Clement*.
- **Middle Recension of Ignatius:** Authenticated by James Ussher (1644), Isaac Voss (1646), J. B. Lightfoot (1885), and Theodor Zahn against the fourth-century interpolated Long Recension.

## Synthesis of Sub-Apostolic Continuity

1. **Christological Realism:** Confession that Jesus Christ came truly "in the flesh" (*en sarki*) against incipient Docetism.
2. **Liturgical Anchor:** Triune baptism (*Did.* 7.1) and Eucharistic gathering on the Lord's Day (*kyriakē*, *Did.* 14.1; Ign. *Magn.* 9.1).
3. **Institutional Coherence:** Progression from collegiate presbyter-bishops (*1 Clement*) to the monarchical episcopate (*Ignatius*) safeguarding unity.
4. **Scriptural Reception:** Reverent use of the Septuagint alongside Pauline epistles and Synoptic Gospel traditions.

questions.prompt: Where does the exact Greek phrase hē katholikē ekklēsia ("the Catholic Church") make its earliest extant appearance in Christian literature, and in what theological context?
options: Clement of Rome, 1 Clement 44, defending Rome's universal appellate jurisdiction over deposed Corinthian presbyters
Ignatius of Antioch, Epistle to the Smyrnaeans 8.2, connecting the local Eucharistic congregation gathered around its bishop with the universal presence of Jesus Christ
The Didache 9.4, describing the baptized nations gathered from the ends of the earth into one liturgical table
The Martyrdom of Polycarp 17.3, distinguishing universal Christian worship of Christ from local Smyrnaean commemoration of martyrs
questions.explanation: Ignatius of Antioch's Epistle to the Smyrnaeans 8.2 (c. 110 AD) contains the earliest surviving occurrence of hē katholikē ekklēsia: "Wherever the bishop shall appear, there let the multitude also be; even as, wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the Catholic Church." Ignatius pairs local Eucharistic unity around the bishop with the wholeness and universality of the Church centered in Christ.
questions.sourceReference: Ignatius of Antioch, Epistle to the Smyrnaeans 8.2 (c. 110 AD)

questions.prompt: What concrete ecclesial crisis prompted the Church of Rome to compose 1 Clement (c. 95–96 AD), and what principle did Clement invoke to resolve it?
options: A Docetic schism in Smyrna denying Christ's bodily resurrection, answered by defining the Eucharist as the medicine of immortality
Disputes over Quartodeciman Paschal fasting dates, resolved by appealing to the Petrine and Johannine liturgical calendars
The irregular deposition of blameless Corinthian presbyters by a younger faction, answered by appealing to ecclesial concord (homonoia) and orderly apostolic succession
Widespread apostasy during the Decian persecution, answered by instituting a graded system of public canonical penance
questions.explanation: 1 Clement was written around 95–96 AD because a faction in Corinth had deposed duly appointed, blameless presbyters. In response, Rome appealed to cosmic and biblical harmony (homonoia) and articulated the principle of orderly apostolic succession (1 Clem. 42–44), noting that the Apostles appointed tested overseers and provided that approved men should succeed them upon their death.

questions.prompt: Identify the sub-apostolic document from which this early Eucharistic prayer over the broken bread is drawn:
questions.excerptContext: Even as this broken bread was scattered over the hills, and was gathered together and became one, so let Thy Church be gathered together from the ends of the earth into Thy kingdom; for Thine is the glory and the power through Jesus Christ for ever.
options: The Didache (Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 9
Ignatius of Antioch, Epistle to the Ephesians, Chapter 20
Polycarp of Smyrna, Epistle to the Philippians, Chapter 7
questions.explanation: This liturgical thanksgiving prayer over the broken bread (klasma) comes verbatim from Didache 9.4 (c. 50–90 AD), preserved in the Codex Hierosolymitanus discovered by Philotheos Bryennios in 1873. Alongside the prayer over the cup as "the holy vine of David Thy servant," it represents one of the oldest surviving post-New Testament Eucharistic prayers.
questions.sourceReference: Didache (Teaching of the Twelve Apostles) 9.4 (c. 50–90 AD)

questions.prompt: In 1 Clement 42–44, Clement of Rome already distinguishes sharply between a single monarchical bishop (episkopos) and a subordinate college of presbyters (presbyteroi) in Corinth, matching the threefold hierarchy taught by Ignatius of Antioch.
questions.explanation: False. In 1 Clement 42–44 (as in Philippians 1:1, Acts 20:17/28, and Didache 15.1), episkopoi ("overseers/bishops") and presbyteroi ("elders/presbyters") still function interchangeably for collegiate presbyter-bishops assisted by deacons. It is Ignatius of Antioch (c. 110 AD) in Asia Minor and Syria who provides our earliest clear witness to the distinct threefold monarchical episcopate of one bishop, a college of presbyters, and deacons.

topics.title: Athanasius of Alexandria and the Cappadocian Fathers
topics.subtitle: Nicene Consubstantiality, Soteriological Theosis, Anti-Apollinarianism, and the One Ousia / Three Hypostaseis Settlement
topics.summary: Across the turbulent half-century between Nicaea (325) and Constantinople I (381), Athanasius of Alexandria and the three Cappadocian Fathers—Basil the Great of Caesarea, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Gregory of Nyssa—vindicated the full consubstantial deity of the Son and the Holy Spirit. Grounding Trinitarian dogma in soteriology ("He became human that we might become divine" and "What is not assumed is not healed"), they forged the enduring catholic grammar of one simple, infinite divine essence (ousia) eternally subsisting in three distinct persons (hypostaseis) differentiated solely by their relational properties of origin (idiōmata).

sections.heading: Athanasius Contra Mundum: Consubstantiality, Theosis, and the Deity of the Spirit
sections.body:
Present at the First Council of Nicaea (325 AD) as theological secretary and deacon to Bishop Alexander of Alexandria, Athanasius (c. 296–373 AD) succeeded to the Alexandrian patriarchate in 328 and spent forty-five years defending Nicene orthodoxy across five imperial exiles totaling seventeen years under Constantine, Constantius II, Julian the Apostate, and Valens—immortalized in Jerome's and Richard Hooker's adage Athanasius contra mundum ("Athanasius against the world"). Already in his early twin apologetic treatise Contra Gentes and On the Incarnation of the Word (De Incarnatione Verbi Dei), Athanasius articulated the redemptive logic that governed his entire career. Created out of nothing (ex ouk ontōn) through the divine Word (Logos) to abide in incorruption by participating in the image of God, humanity plunged by transgression back toward mortal non-existence and corruption (phthora). Mere repentance could neither annul divine truthfulness regarding death nor heal inward ontological decay; only the Creator Word Himself, assuming a mortal human body from the Virgin, could surrender His own temple to death on behalf of all, exhaust death's dominion from within by His incorruptible life, and restore the defaced image.

In his monumental Orations Against the Arians (Contra Arianos I–III) and De Decretis, Athanasius deployed this exact soteriological imperative to defend the Nicene watchword homoousios ("of one essence" with the Father) against Arius's claim that the Logos was a sublime creature brought into being out of nothing ("there was once when He was not," ēn pote hote ouk ēn). Distinguishing scriptural texts spoken of the Word's eternal divine generation from texts spoken economically of His incarnate servanthood (such as Proverbs 8:22 LXX and Philippians 2:7), Athanasius exposed Arianism as spiritually fatal: a created mediator would itself need grace to know God, could never unite estranged creatures directly to the Creator, and would turn Christian worship of Christ into idolatry. Salvation as deification by grace (theopoiēsis / theosis)—summed up in De Incarnatione 54.3, "He was made man that we might be made divine"—requires that the Incarnate Son possess the very numerical divine nature of the Father.

During his third exile in the Egyptian desert alongside Coptic monks (whose patriarch Anthony the Great he memorialized in the Vita Antonii), Athanasius extended identical pro-Nicene reasoning to the Holy Spirit in his four Letters to Serapion of Thmuis (c. 358–360 AD). Answering the Tropici—Egyptian Christians who confessed the Nicene Son yet treated the Holy Spirit as a high ministering angel created out of nothing by tropes of metaphor—Athanasius demonstrated that the Spirit belongs on the Creator side of the ontological divide. Because the Spirit vivifies, sanctifies, seals, and makes believers "partakers of the divine nature" (2 Peter 1:4), the Spirit cannot be a creature: creatures partake of holiness, whereas the Spirit is Holiness and Life by essence with the Son and Father, operating in one indivisible divine activity from the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit.

sections.heading: The Cappadocian Settlement: One Ousia, Three Hypostaseis, and Hypostatic Idiōmata
sections.body:
By the late 350s, Nicene theology faced both imperial Homoian compromises ("the Son is like the Father according to the Scriptures," banning essence-language altogether) and the razor-sharp Neo-Arian ("Heteroousian" or Anomoean) dialectic of Aëtius and Eunomius of Cyzicus. Eunomius argued from absolute divine simplicity that "unbegottenness" (agennēsia) is not merely a negative attribute but the exhaustive definition of God's essence itself; consequently, a begotten Son must by definition be unlike (anomoios) the Father in essence. At the same time, many Eastern bishops deeply opposed to Arius hesitated over Nicaea because the Nicene anathema of 325 had treated ousia and hypostasis as synonyms—raising legitimate fears that "one hypostasis" collapsed Father, Son, and Spirit into the modalist heresy of Sabellius or Marcellus of Ancyra. Beginning at Athanasius's conciliatory Council of Alexandria (362), three towering figures from Cappadocia in central Asia Minor—Basil the Great of Caesarea (c. 330–379), his close friend Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390), and Basil's younger brother Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335–395)—crafted the terminological settlement that secured the triumph of Constantinople I (381).

The Cappadocians unlocked the impasse by systematically distinguishing ousia (οὐσία) from hypostasis (ὑπόστασις). Ousia designates what is common (to koinon)—the one simple, infinite, incomprehensible divine essence shared wholly and identically by Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—whereas hypostasis (aligned with prosōpon, person, freed from modalist connotations of a theatrical mask) designates what is proper and particular (to idion)—the three concrete, irreducible personal subsistences. Against Eunomius, Basil (Contra Eunomium) and the two Gregories proved that God's infinite essence remains transcendentally unknowable in itself, known truly through divine operations while never exhausted by human concepts; "unbegottenness" (agennēsia) does not define what God is, but states how the Father exists in relation to the Son. The Three are distinguished solely by their incommunicable hypostatic properties or modes of origin (idiōmata / tropoi hyparxeōs): Paternity or Unbegottenness (agennēsia) proper to the Father as sole unoriginate fountainhead of deity (monarchia), Eternal Generation (gennēsis) proper to the Son, and Procession (ekporeusis, John 15:26; Greg. Naz., Or. 31.8) proper to the Holy Spirit.

As Metropolitan of Caesarea, Basil integrated dogmatic precision with ascetical renewal and concrete mercy—authoring the Longer and Shorter Rules that permanently anchored Eastern cenobitic monasticism within ecclesial charity and constructing the Basiliad, a vast complex of hospital, hospice, and poorhouse outside Caesarea. In On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto, 375 AD), dedicated to Amphilochius of Iconium against Eustathius of Sebaste's Pneumatomachians ("Spirit-fighters"), Basil practiced pastoral oikonomia by refraining from the bare unscriptural slogan "the Spirit is God" while proving the Spirit's full divine majesty from Scripture and unwritten apostolic liturgy (paradosis): baptized into one Name with Father and Son, the Spirit is co-numbered (synarithmeisthai) and receives equal honor and worship (homotimia) in the ancient doxology "Glory to the Father with (meta) the Son together with (syn) the Holy Spirit."

sections.heading: Nazianzen and Nyssen: Anti-Apollinarian Christology and Divine Infinity (Epéktasis)
sections.body:
Summoned to imperial Constantinople in 379 AD when Arians controlled every basilica in the capital, Gregory of Nazianzus ("the Theologian") gathered a tiny Nicene remnant inside a domestic chapel aptly named the Anastasis ("Resurrection"), where in 380 he delivered his celebrated Five Theological Orations (Orations 27–31). Moving from spiritual purification as the prerequisite for theology (Or. 27) and the awe-inspiring incomprehensibility of God (Or. 28) to the eternal consubstantiality of the Son (Or. 29–30), Nazianzen went directly beyond Basil's cautious reserve in Oration 31 (On the Holy Spirit): "What then? Is the Spirit God? Most certainly! Is He then consubstantial (homoousios)? Yes, if He is God!" (Or. 31.10), explaining Old-to-New-Covenant progressive revelation as pedagogical divine condescension so human eyes would not be blinded before grasping the Father's deity and the Son's deity.

Equally decisive for Chalcedonian orthodoxy was Gregory of Nazianzus's refutation of Apollinaris of Laodicea, a veteran Nicene ally who tried to safeguard Christ's substantial unity and sinlessness by teaching that in the Incarnation the divine Logos replaced the human rational mind (nous) in Jesus. In Epistle 101 (To Cledonius, c. 382 AD), Nazianzen exposed Apollinarianism's fatal soteriological defect with a lapidary axiom: "For that which He has not assumed He has not healed; but that which is united to His Godhead is also saved" (Τὸ γὰρ ἀπρόσληπτον, ἀθεράπευτον). Because Adam's rational intellect transgressed God's command first, a Savior lacking a complete human mind would leave humanity's noblest and most wounded faculty unredeemed—establishing the classic boundary between Trinitarian grammar ("one what, three whos"—allo kai allo, non alius et alius) and Christological grammar ("one who in two whats," Ep. 101.20–21).

Meanwhile, Gregory of Nyssa—hailed as "Father of Fathers" after Constantinople I—brought Cappadocian speculative depth to its zenith in Contra Eunomium, the Catechetical Oration, Ad Ablabium (That There Are Not Three Gods), and The Life of Moses. Answering charges of tritheism in Ad Ablabium, Nyssen argued that while Peter, James, and John are loosely called three men because finite human individuals act separately in fragmented space and time, the Three Divine Hypostaseis are strictly One God because the simple divine nature executes every ad extra work in one indivisible movement of will and operation (mia energeia) originating from the Father, advancing through the Son, and perfected in the Holy Spirit. Furthermore, overturning classical Greek metaphysics—which equated perfection with determinate limit (peras) and treated infinity as chaotic imperfection—Nyssen grounded God's transcendence in strict ontological infinity (apeiria). Because the Infinite Good has no boundary at which desire could stall in satiety (koros), beatitude consists in epéktasis (stretching ever forward, Phil. 3:13): an eternal, joyful ascent from glory to glory within the luminous darkness of God.

sections.heading: Reading companion
sections.content:
# Nicene & Cappadocian Trinitarian Lexicon (4th Century AD)

> **Primary Anchors:** Gregory of Nazianzus, *Orations* 27–31 & *Epistle* 101; Basil of Caesarea, *De Spiritu Sancto*; Gregory of Nyssa, *Ad Ablabium*; Athanasius, *De Incarnatione* & *Ad Serapionem*.

## I. Technical Ontological & Relational Vocabulary

- **Οὐσία (*Ousia* — Essence / Being / Substance):** What God is in common (*to koinon*). Denotes the one simple, infinite, indivisible divine nature shared wholly and equally by Father, Son, and Holy Spirit without partition or diminution.
- **Ὑπόστασις (*Hypostasis* — Concrete Subsistence / Person):** Who each of the Three distinctly is (*to idion*). Distinguished from *ousia* at Alexandria (362) and by the Cappadocians to confess **μία οὐσία, τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις** (one essence, three persons), steering between Sabellian modalism and Arian subordinationism.
- **Ὁμοούσιος (*Homoousios* — Consubstantial / Of One Essence):** Nicene watchword (325 AD) affirming that the Son is generated from the Father's own essence rather than created out of nothing (*ex ouk ontōn*) or merely similar in essence (*homoiousios*).
- **Πρόσωπον (*Prosōpon* — Person / Countenance):** Anchored to ontological *hypostasis* by Basil and Nazianzen so it could never be reduced to a transient Sabellian theatrical mask.
- **Ἰδιώματα (*Idiōmata* / *Gnōrismata* — Incommunicable Hypostatic Properties):** The eternal relational modes of origin (*tropoi hyparxeōs*) distinguishing the Three without dividing the one *ousia*:
  1. **Ἀγεννησία (*Agennēsia* — Unbegottenness / Paternity):** Proper solely to the **Father** as *archē anarchos* (unoriginate principle), refuting Eunomius's claim that unbegottenness defines the divine essence itself.
  2. **Γέννησις (*Gennēsis* — Eternal Generation / Filiation):** Proper solely to the **Son**, eternally begotten of the Father before all ages apart from passion, temporal beginning, or division.
  3. **Ἐκπόρευσις (*Ekporeusis* — Procession):** Proper solely to the **Holy Spirit**, who proceeds from the Father (*John 15:26*; Greg. Naz., *Or.* 31.8) and receives co-equal worship and glory (*homotimia*).

## II. Canonical Soteriological & Dogmatic Axioms

1. **Athanasius of Alexandria — Soteriological Logic of *Theosis* (*De Incarnatione* 54.3):**
   *"Αὐτὸς γὰρ ἐνηνθρώπησεν, ἵνα ἡμεῖς θεοποιηθῶμεν"* — "For He was made man that we might be made divine."
   **Implication:** No creature can deify another creature or abolish corruption from within; if the Logos is less than true God by nature, salvation is impossible.

2. **Athanasius of Alexandria — Deity of the Holy Spirit (*Ad Serapionem* 1.24–28):**
   Against the *Tropici*, because the Spirit sanctifies, vivifies, and seals believers into communion with the divine nature, the Spirit cannot be a creature (*ktisma*), angel, or ministering spirit, but belongs intrinsically to the undivided Triad.

3. **Gregory of Nazianzus — Anti-Apollinarian Christological Axiom (*Epistle* 101.32):**
   *"Τὸ γὰρ ἀπρόσληπτον, ἀθεράπευτον· ὃ δὲ ἥνωται τῷ Θεῷ, τοῦτο καὶ σῴζεται"* — "For that which He has not assumed He has not healed; but that which is united to His Godhead is also saved."
   **Implication:** Against Apollinaris of Laodicea, the Incarnate Word assumed a complete human rational intellect (*nous*) as well as flesh and animate soul.

4. **Basil the Great — Doxological *Homotimia* (*De Spiritu Sancto* 10.26; 27.66):**
   Baptizing into one Name (*Matt. 28:19*) and glorifying the Father "with (*meta*) the Son together with (*syn*) the Holy Spirit" prove from Scripture and apostolic liturgical *paradosis* that the Spirit is ranked with God, never with creation.

5. **Gregory of Nyssa — Single Operation & *Epéktasis* (*Ad Ablabium*; *De Vita Moysis*):**
   Every divine operation (*energeia*) originates from the Father, advances through the Son, and is perfected in the Holy Spirit; because God's essence is strictly infinite (*apeiron*), the glorified soul eternally stretches forward (*epéktasis*, Phil. 3:13) in beatific desire.

questions.prompt: How did Basil the Great and the two Gregories dismantle Eunomius of Cyzicus's Heteroousian syllogism that because "unbegottenness" (agennēsia) exhaustively defines God's simple essence, the begotten Son must be unlike (anomoios) the Father in essence?
options: They conceded that unbegottenness defines the divine essence, but argued that the Logos was unbegotten prior to Bethlehem and became begotten only in the Incarnation

They distinguished the transcendent, incomprehensible divine essence (ousia) from the incommunicable hypostatic properties (idiōmata), showing that agennēsia denotes the Father's personal relation of origin rather than the common divine essence
They abandoned divine simplicity in favor of three separate divine essences united solely by moral agreement and shared title
They argued that agennēsia and gennēsis are merely temporary Sabellian titles adopted by one single hypostasis in salvation history
questions.explanation: Against Eunomius's rationalist claim to comprehend God's essence under the single concept of agennēsia ("unbegottenness"), the Cappadocians upheld both apophatic incomprehensibility of the divine ousia and the crucial distinction between common essence (ousia) and relational personal property (idiōma). Unbegottenness states how the Father exists as unoriginate Father in relation to the eternally begotten Son—not what deity is in itself.
questions.sourceReference: Basil of Caesarea, Contra Eunomium 1.5–14; Gregory of Nazianzus, Orations 28.4 & 29.10–12

questions.prompt: Why did Basil of Caesarea in On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto, 375 AD) exercise pastoral reserve (oikonomia) by avoiding the bare creedal declaration "the Holy Spirit is God," and how did he establish the Spirit's full deity instead?
options: Because Basil believed the Holy Spirit was an intermediate creature superior to angels yet ontologically subordinate to the Son

Because Emperor Valens's Pneumatomachian opponents waited to seize upon non-scriptural slogans to expel him from Caesarea, so Basil proved the Spirit's full divine nature from Scripture, baptismal union, and liturgical co-glorification (homotimia) with Father and Son
Because the First Council of Nicaea (325) had explicitly forbidden any theological treatise from discussing the third article of the Creed
Because Basil held that the Holy Spirit's consubstantiality would only come into existence eschatologically at the General Resurrection
questions.explanation: As Gregory of Nazianzus explicitly praised in his funeral panegyric for Basil (Oration 43.68–69), Basil practiced wise pastoral oikonomia so hostile imperial and Pneumatomachian surveillance could not depose him over naked verbal formulas and hand Caesarea to Arians. Instead, De Spiritu Sancto proved the substantive reality of the Spirit's deity by showing from Scripture and ancient baptismal/doxological paradosis that the Spirit sanctifies, deifies, and receives identical worship and honor (homotimia) with Father and Son.
questions.sourceReference: Basil of Caesarea, De Spiritu Sancto 10.26, 27.66; cf. Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43.68

questions.prompt: Identify the fourth-century patristic author and treatise from which this foundational argument for the full deity of the Holy Spirit is drawn:
questions.excerptContext: If the Holy Spirit were a creature, we should have no participation in God in Him; indeed, we should be united to a creature and alienated from the divine nature, insofar as we did not partake of it. ... But since we are called partakers of Christ and partakers of God, the unction and seal that is in us belongs not to the nature of created things, but to the nature of the Son, who through the Spirit who is in Him unites us to the Father.
options: Athanasius of Alexandria, First Epistle to Serapion of Thmuis (c. 358–360 AD)
Eusebius of Caesarea, Ecclesiastical Theology Against Marcellus (c. 337 AD)
Apollinaris of Laodicea, On the Union in Christ of the Body with the Godhead (c. 375 AD)
Cyril of Jerusalem, Procatechesis to Catechumens (c. 350 AD)
questions.explanation: This passage comes from Athanasius of Alexandria's First Epistle to Serapion of Thmuis (1.24), written from Egyptian desert exile around 358–360 AD against the Tropici. Notice how Athanasius applies the identical soteriological logic of participation and theosis (2 Peter 1:4) that he used against Arius on behalf of the Son to prove that the Holy Spirit cannot be a creature.
questions.sourceReference: Athanasius of Alexandria, Epistulae ad Serapionem 1.24 (c. 358–360 AD)

questions.prompt: In Ad Ablabium (That There Are Not Three Gods), Gregory of Nyssa argues that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are strictly One God rather than three gods not merely by generic comparison to human nature, but because the indivisible divine essence executes every outward divine work in a single operation (mia energeia) originating from the Father, progressing through the Son, and perfected in the Holy Spirit.
questions.explanation: True. In Ad Ablabium, Gregory of Nyssa carefully qualifies the social analogy of Peter, James, and John: whereas finite human beings act independently in divided places and wills, the infinite divine nature is strictly simple and indivisible, and every ad extra divine work (creation, life, providence, salvation) is one single motion of will and operation (mia energeia) from the Father, through the Son, and perfected in the Holy Spirit—establishing inseparable operations as proof of numerical unity of essence.
questions.sourceReference: Gregory of Nyssa, Ad Ablabium: Quod non sint tres dei (c. 375–385 AD)

topics.title: Augustine of Hippo: Sovereign Grace, Ecclesiology, and the Triune God
topics.subtitle: From the Restless Heart of the Confessions to De Trinitate, the Two Cities, and the Anti-Donatist & Pelagian Controversies
topics.summary: Aurelius Augustinus of Hippo (354–430 AD) stands as the towering architect of Western Latin theology, shaping both medieval scholasticism and the Protestant Reformation. Tracing his conversion from Manichaean dualism and Neoplatonism to catholic baptism in the Confessions, interpreting world history through the two loves of The City of God, formulating relational and psychological Trinitarianism in On the Trinity, defending objective sacramental validity against the Donatists, and championing original sin and prevenient sovereign grace against Pelagianism, Augustine forged the grammar of Western soteriology, ecclesiology, and Trinitarian contemplation.

sections.heading: The Restless Heart and the Two Loves: Confessions and The City of God
sections.body:
Born in 354 AD at Thagaste in Roman Numidia to the pagan curial official Patricius and the fervently Christian Monica, Aurelius Augustinus rose as a brilliant professor of Latin rhetoric from Carthage to Rome and finally to the imperial court at Milan. In his thirteen-book spiritual masterpiece, the Confessions (Confessiones, c. 397–400 AD)—framed from first page to last as a liturgical prayer of praise, confession, and scriptural meditation—Augustine narrates his restless odyssey through Cicero's Hortensius, nine years as a Manichaean "Hearer" (auditor), Academic skepticism, and Milanese Neoplatonism. Manichaeism initially seduced him by offering a materialist dualism of Light and Darkness that absolved his own moral agency of blame while mocking anthropomorphic Old Testament narratives. In Milan, two providential instruments shattered those barriers: Bishop Ambrose's spiritual-figural preaching unlocked the coherence of the Old Testament, while "the books of the Platonists" (Plotinus and Porphyry in Marius Victorinus's Latin translation, Conf. VII.9.13–21.27) taught him to conceive of God as wholly incorporeal Spirit and of evil not as a rival material substance, but as privatio boni—the parasitic privation or corruption of created good caused by a defecting creaturely will.

Yet Neoplatonism showed the homeland from afar without revealing the humble Way: in those books Augustine read that in the beginning was the Word, "but that the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, I did not read there" (Conf. VII.9.14). Paralysed in Book VIII by the agonizing division of his own habituated will ("Give me chastity and continency, only not yet," Conf. VIII.7.17), Augustine wept in a Milanese garden in late summer 386 AD until a child's chant—"Tolle, lege; tolle, lege" ("Take up and read")—sent him to Romans 13:13–14 ("Put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh"), flooding his heart with serene light. Baptized by Ambrose at Easter 387, bereaved of Monica at Ostia after their shared ascent of mystical contemplation (Conf. IX.10), and ordained priest (391) and Bishop of Hippo Regius (395–430), Augustine anchored human anthropology in ordered love (ordo amoris): "Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless until it repose in Thee" (Conf. I.1.1).

That same psychology of love ("My weight is my love; by it am I borne whithersoever I am borne," Conf. XIII.9.10) structured Augustine's monumental twenty-two-book apologetic and theology of history, The City of God (De Civitate Dei, 413–426 AD). Composed after Alaric's Visigoths sacked Rome in August 410 and aristocratic pagans blamed Rome's abandonment of ancestral gods for the catastrophe, Books I–X dismantle pagan polytheism and philosophical theurgy, while Books XI–XXII trace the origin, historical pilgrimage, and eschatological destiny of two invisible societies intermingled throughout earthly time until final judgment. Refusing both Eusebian triumphalism (identifying God's kingdom with the Christianized Roman Empire) and pagan cyclical fatalism, Augustine defines every commonwealth by the shared object of its supreme love (De Civ. Dei XIX.24): the Earthly City (civitas terrena) is generated by love of self even to the contempt of God, seeking domination (libido dominandi), whereas the City of God (civitas Dei) is a pilgrim community generated by love of God even to the contempt of self, using earthly peace gratefully on its way to eternal sabbath rest.

sections.heading: Relational Trinitarianism (De Trinitate) and Objective Sacramental Grace Against the Donatists
sections.body:
Over two decades (c. 399–419 AD), Augustine composed On the Trinity (De Trinitate, Books I–XV), uniting rigorous biblical exegesis, Nicene metaphysics, and contemplative spiritual exercise. Contrary to older caricatures claiming Augustine privileged an abstract divine essence over the Three Persons, Books I–IV begin squarely from Scripture's witness to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—demonstrating full substantial equality, inseparable outward operations (opera Trinitatis ad extra indivisa sunt), and how the temporal missions (missiones) of the Incarnate Son and Pentecostal Spirit reveal Their eternal intra-Trinitarian processions. In Books V–VII, Augustine answers the Arian logical dilemma—that every statement about God must predicate either substance (making Father and Son one Person) or accident (introducing change into God)—by articulating predication according to eternal relation (ad aliquid / relatio): in God's utterly simple essence nothing is accidental, yet "Father" and "Son" are predicated eternally and really by relation. Moreover, Augustine meditates profoundly on the Holy Spirit as the ineffable mutual communion and consubstantial bond of charity (communio / caritas) of Father and Son, teaching that the Spirit proceeds "principally" (principaliter) from the Father, who in timeless generation bestows upon the Son also that the Spirit proceeds from Them both in common (communiter, De Trin. XV.17.29, XV.26.47)—the patristic fountainhead of Western Filioque theology.

In Books VIII–XV, seeking how finite believers summoned to love a Trinity they cannot see may rise by faith toward contemplation, Augustine explores created traces and above all the imago Dei within the rational human mind (mens): first the triad of lover, beloved, and love, and then the interior coinherent triad of memory, understanding, and will/love (memoria, intelligentia, voluntas/amor)—acts distinct in relation yet substantially one life and one mind. Crucially, Book XIV.12.15 insists that this image reaches its true renewal not in narcissistic self-reflexivity, but when the human mind remembers, understands, and loves God by whom it was made, while Book XV stresses that between Creator and creature the dissimilitude always exceeds the similitude.

Concurrently in North Africa, Augustine labored for twenty-five years to heal the century-old Donatist schism. Originating during Diocletian's Great Persecution (303–305 AD) when rigorist bishops refused to recognize Caecilian of Carthage because one of his consecrators (Felix of Aptunga) was accused of being a traditor ("hander-over" of sacred Scriptures to Roman magistrates), the Donatists claimed to be the sole spotless Church of the martyrs and rebaptized catholic Christians wholesale. Against Parmenian and Petilian of Cirta, Augustine articulated two enduring catholic principles: first, in earthly history the visible Church is a corpus permixtum—a mixed body of wheat and tares, good and bad fish within one net until Christ's final judgment (Matt. 13:24–30, 47–50); second, sacraments derive their objective validity (sacramentum / character) not from the fluctuating holiness of the human minister, but from Jesus Christ Himself, the invisible High Priest ("If Peter baptizes, Christ baptizes; if Judas baptizes, Christ baptizes," In Ioan. Ev. 6.7), laying the patristic foundation for ex opere operato while maintaining that schismatics lack the sacrament's saving fruit (res sacramenti)—the Holy Spirit's unifying charity (Rom. 5:5)—until restored to catholic peace.

sections.heading: The Pelagian Controversy: Original Sin, Disordered Will, and Prevenient Grace
sections.body:
Around 405 AD in Rome, the British ascetic teacher Pelagius reacted with indignation upon hearing a bishop quote Augustine's prayer from Confessions X.29.40: "Da quod iubes et iube quod vis" ("Give what Thou commandest, and command what Thou wilt"). Fearing such reliance on interior grace fostered moral laxity, Pelagius, his associate Caelestius, and later the brilliant Italian bishop Julian of Eclanum championed an autonomous moral anthropology. In the Pelagian view, mortality was natural to Adam's creation; Adam's transgression harmed his descendants not by inherited corruption, but solely by bad social example (imitatio); newborn infants enter the world in the exact unfallen state of Adam before sin; human nature possesses an indestructible, neutral capacity of free choice (posse) fully sufficient to keep every divine commandment without sin; and "grace" consists essentially in our created endowment of free will, the external instruction of the Mosaic Law, forgiveness of past sins, and the inspiring moral example of Christ.

From 411 until his death as Vandal armies besieged Hippo in August 430 AD, Augustine dismantled Pelagianism across scores of treatises—including On the Spirit and the Letter (De Spiritu et Littera, 412), On Nature and Grace (De Natura et Gratia, 415), Against Julian, and On Rebuke and Grace—citing Romans 5:12–19, 1 Corinthians 4:7 ("What hast thou that thou didst not receive?"), John 15:5, and the universal Church's immemorial practice of baptizing infants truly "for the remission of sins" rather than out of legal fiction. Humanity stood solidarily in Adam as its covenantal and seminal head; Adam's primal pride wounded human nature with peccatum originale—entailing both inherited liability to guilt (reatus) and an inward congenital disorder of desire (concupiscentia) that curves human loves away from God toward self. Fallen humanity still exercises psychological choice (liberum arbitrium) uncoerced from outside, yet because we freely choose only what we delight in, the unregenerate will lies in spiritual bondage (non posse non peccare), incapable of healing its own diseased loves.

Salvation therefore depends from start to finish upon unmerited sovereign grace: not merely external law—which without the Spirit remains "the letter that kills" by exposing covetousness without curing it (2 Cor. 3:6; Rom. 7:7–13)—but interior gratia praeveniens (prevenient grace) and gratia operans, whereby the Holy Spirit pours the love of God directly into our hearts (Rom. 5:5), kindling a triumphant spiritual delight (delectatio) in supreme goodness that heals liberum arbitrium into true moral freedom (libertas). Condemned at the Council of Carthage (418 AD) and Ephesus (431 AD), Pelagianism gave way in Southern Gaul to monastic anxieties ("Semi-Pelagianism," associated with John Cassian and Faustus of Riez) claiming that at least the initial movement of faith or cry for help (initium fidei) originated from unaided human will. At the historic Second Council of Orange (529 AD) under Caesarius of Arles, confirmed by Pope Boniface II in 531, Western Christendom canonized Augustine's doctrine of prevenient grace—affirming that even the beginning of faith is the Holy Spirit's gift, while explicitly anathematizing any notion of divine predestination to evil.

# Primary Excerpts: Augustine of Hippo on Restless Desire, Sovereign Grace & Healed Freedom

> **Archival Source:** *Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers*, First Series, Vols. 1 & 5 (Philip Schaff, ed.) — Key Latin phrases from *Corpus Christianorum Series Latina*.

## 1. *Confessiones* I.1.1 (c. 397–400 AD): Creation, Praise, and the Restless Heart

"Great art Thou, O Lord, and greatly to be praised; great is Thy power, and Thy wisdom infinite. And Thee would man
praise; man, but a particle of Thy creation; man, that bears about him his mortality, the witness of his sin, the
witness that Thou resistest the proud: yet would man praise Thee; he, but a particle of Thy creation. Thou awakest us
to delight in Thy praise; for Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless until it repose in Thee
(*fecisti nos ad te et inquietum est cor nostrum, donec requiescat in te*)."

## 2. *Confessiones* X.29.40: The Prayer That Provoked Pelagius at Rome

"My whole hope is nowhere but in Thy exceeding great mercy. Give what Thou commandest, and command what Thou wilt
(*da quod iubes et iube quod vis*). Thou enjoinest us continency; and when I knew, saith one, that no man can be
continent, unless God give it, this also was a point of wisdom to know whose gift she is (Wisdom 8:21). By continency
verily are we bound up and brought back into One, whence we were dissipated into many. For too little doth he love
Thee, who loves anything with Thee, which he loveth not for Thee."

## 3. *De Natura et Gratia* (*On Nature and Grace*, 415 AD), Ch. 3: Fallen Nature Requires the Physician

"Man's nature, indeed, was created at first faultless and without any sin; nevertheless, that nature of man in which
every one is born from Adam, now wants the Physician, because it is not sound (*non est sana*). All good qualities, no
doubt, which it still possesses in its make, life, senses, intellect, it has from the Most High God, its Creator and
Maker. But the flaw (*vitium*), which darkens and weakens all those natural goods, so that it has need of illumination
and healing, it has not contracted from its blameless Author, but from original sin, which it committed by free will."

## 4. *Enchiridion ad Laurentium* (c. 421 AD), Chs. 30 & 32: *Liberum Arbitrium* Healed by *Gratia Praeveniens*

"By the evil use of his free will, man destroyed both it and himself. For, as a man who kills himself must, of course,
be alive when he kills himself, but after he has killed himself ceases to live, and cannot restore himself to life; so,
when man by his own free will sinned, then sin being victorious over him, the freedom of his will was lost. ... God
therefore goes before (*praevenit*) the unwilling that he may will; He follows (*subsequitur*) the willing that he may not will in vain."
