questions.prompt: Which theologian wrote this classic metaphysical account of evil as privatio boni ("privation of good") rather than a created substance?
questions.excerptContext: For what is that which we call evil but the absence of good? In the bodies of animals, disease and wounds mean nothing but the absence of health... Wherefore all natures are good simply because they exist.
questions.explanation: Breaking away from Manichaean dualism, Augustine argued in his Enchiridion (ch. 11) and Confessions (Book VII) that all created being is good as God’s creature, while evil is a parasitic corruption or privation of due good.
questions.sourceReference: Augustine of Hippo, Enchiridion, ch. 11 (c. AD 420)

questions.prompt: In philosophy of religion, how does Alvin Plantinga’s "Free-Will Defense" differ in aim from a full "Theodicy"?
options: A defense denies that evil actually exists, whereas a theodicy affirms Manichaean dualism
A defense shows there is no logical contradiction between God and evil by offering a possible reason, without claiming to know God’s actual reasons in every instance
A defense argues God is finite in power, whereas a theodicy argues God causally determines sin
A defense addresses only natural disasters, whereas a theodicy addresses only human moral choices
questions.explanation: To defeat the Logical Problem of Evil (J.L. Mackie), Plantinga showed one need only establish a logically possible proposition—such as transworld depravity among genuinely free creatures—consistent with God’s omnipotence, omniscience, and goodness.
questions.sourceReference: Alvin Plantinga, God, Freedom, and Evil (1974)

topics.title: Models & Mysteries of the Atonement
topics.subtitle: Christus Victor, Ransom, Anselmian Satisfaction, Penal Substitution, and Moral Exemplar.
topics.summary: Explores the rich tapestry of biblical metaphors and historical models explaining how Christ’s life, death, and resurrection reconcile sinners and the cosmos to God.

sections.heading: Biblical Kaleidoscope of Saving Metaphors
sections.body: New Testament soteriology employs multiple Old Testament and Greco-Roman domains to describe the Cross: temple sacrifice and propitiation/expiation (hilasterion, Romans 3:25), marketplace emancipation and ransom (lytron, Mark 10:45), courtroom justification (dikaiōsis, Romans 5:1), relational reconciliation (katallagē, 2 Corinthians 5:18–19), and cosmic military triumph over spiritual principalities (Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14–15). Notably, the ecumenical church never restricted orthodoxy to a single atonement mechanism, treating biblical facets as mutually illuminating.

sections.heading: Patristic Recapitulation & Christus Victor
sections.body: In the early church, Irenaeus emphasized Recapitulation (anakephalaiōsis): Christ retraced every stage of Adam’s humanity in obedience, reversing Adam’s disobedience. Alongside this stood the dramatic Christus Victor / Ransom motif (Gregory of Nyssa, Augustine, retrieved in the 20th century by Gustaf Aulén): through his death and resurrection, Christ liberated captive humanity from the tyranny of sin, death, and the devil.

sections.heading: Satisfaction, Penal Substitution & Moral Influence
sections.body: In Cur Deus Homo (1098), Anselm of Canterbury critiqued crude ransom-to-Satan metaphors and formulated the Satisfaction theory: human sin dishonors God’s infinite majesty, creating an infinite debt only God can pay and humanity owes—hence the necessity of the God-Man. Reformers such as Luther and Calvin reframed this in forensic courtroom categories as Penal Substitution: Christ voluntarily bore the covenantal curse and penalty of God’s righteous law in the place of sinners (2 Corinthians 5:21; Galatians 3:13; Isaiah 53:5). Meanwhile, Peter Abelard accented the subjective Moral Influence of Christ’s self-giving love awakening grateful love in hardened human hearts.

excerpts.title: Why Only the God-Man Could Make Satisfaction
excerpts.author: Anselm of Canterbury
excerpts.work: Cur Deus Homo, Book II, Ch. 6
excerpts.quote: None therefore can make this satisfaction except God, and none ought to make it except man: it is needful that a God-Man should make it.
excerpts.citation: Cur Deus Homo, Book II, Ch. 6

excerpts.title: The Joyous Exchange
excerpts.author: Martin Luther
excerpts.work: On the Freedom of a Christian
excerpts.quote: Lord Jesus, you are my righteousness, just as I am your sin. You have taken upon yourself what is mine and have given to me what is yours.
excerpts.citation: On the Freedom of a Christian

perspectives.summary: Prioritizes ontological healing, Recapitulation, and Christus Victor—viewing sin primarily as spiritual sickness and mortality overcome by Christ’s life-giving death and Resurrection ("trampling down death by death").
Draws deeply on Anselmian and Thomistic satisfaction and sacrificial offering, emphasizing Christ’s superabundant love and filial obedience offered to the Father on behalf of the mystical Body.

Places Penal Substitution at the hub alongside Christus Victor, highlighting how divine justice and mercy meet at Golgotha so God is "just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus" (Rom 3:26).

keyTerms.definition: Mercy seat / atoning sacrifice (Rom 3:25; LXX Lev 16), uniting the removal of guilt (expiation) and turning away of righteous wrath (propitiation).
Redemption price paid to emancipate captives or slaves (Mark 10:45: "to give his life as a ransom for many").
"Christ the Victor": the classic patristic view of the Cross and Resurrection as decisive triumph over sin, death, and demonic powers.

sources.author: Anselm of Canterbury

questions.prompt: Which medieval theologian wrote this dialogue arguing that because humanity owes obedience to God and only God possesses infinite worth, only the God-Man can make satisfaction?
questions.excerptContext: None therefore can make this satisfaction except God, and none ought to make it except man: it is needful that a God-Man should make it.
options: Peter Abelard in Sic et Non
Anselm of Canterbury in Cur Deus Homo
Bernard of Clairvaux in On Loving God
William of Ockham in Summa Logicae
questions.explanation: In Cur Deus Homo ("Why God Became Man", AD 1098), Anselm replaced earlier ransom-paid-to-the-devil folklore with the Satisfaction model grounded in divine honor and cosmic rectitude.
questions.sourceReference: Anselm of Canterbury, Cur Deus Homo II.6 (AD 1098)

questions.prompt: Which model of the Atonement—prominent in the Church Fathers and retrieved in the 20th century by Gustaf Aulén—portrays Christ’s Cross and Resurrection primarily as a cosmic triumph liberating humanity from bondage to sin, death, and the devil?
questions.explanation: Christus Victor ("Christ the Victor") highlights passages such as Colossians 2:15 and Hebrews 2:14–15, depicting the Incarnation, Passion, and Resurrection as God’s decisive victory over hostile spiritual powers and mortality.
questions.sourceReference: Gustaf Aulén, Christus Victor (1931); cf. Colossians 2:15

topics.title: Grace, Justification, Sanctification & Theosis
topics.subtitle: Augustine vs. Pelagius, Imputed vs. Infused Righteousness, Ordo Salutis, and Deification.
topics.summary: Traces the great soteriological debates over human fallenness, divine grace, forensic justification, inward transformation, and participation in the divine nature.

sections.heading: The Pelagian Controversy & Priority of Grace
sections.body: In the early fifth century, the British monk Pelagius taught that human moral capacity remained intact after Adam, enabling believers to fulfill God’s commands by natural free will assisted externally by law and example. Augustine of Hippo countered that humanity’s will is bound in sin apart from interior liberating grace. Confirmed at the Council of Carthage (418) and the Second Council of Orange (529), historic Western orthodoxy rejected both Pelagianism (self-salvation) and Semi-Pelagianism (claiming humans initiate faith unaided by prevenient grace).

sections.heading: Reformation Debates: Imputed vs. Transformative Justification
sections.body: During the sixteenth century, Protestants distinguished strictly between Justification (God’s forensic declaration counting the believer righteous solely on account of Christ’s imputed righteousness received through faith alone, sola fide—simul iustus et peccator) and Sanctification (lifelong progressive renewal by the Spirit). The Roman Catholic Council of Trent (Session VI, 1547) likewise affirmed that initial grace is wholly unmerited, but defined justification as encompassing both the forgiveness of sins and the interior infusion of sanctifying charity, maintained and increased through faith working through love (Galatians 5:6; James 2:24).

sections.heading: Reformed vs. Arminian/Wesleyan & Eastern Theosis
sections.body: Within Protestantism, Reformed theology (Synod of Dort, 1618–1619) emphasizes unconditional election and monergistic regeneration, whereas Arminian and Wesleyan theology teaches universal prevenient grace enabling all people to respond freely to the Gospel. Meanwhile, Eastern Orthodoxy centers soteriology on Theosis (deification, 2 Peter 1:4): through sacramental and ascetic synergy with uncreated divine energies—never confusing creature with divine essence—believers become by grace what Christ is by nature.

excerpts.title: Command What Thou Wilt
excerpts.author: Augustine of Hippo
excerpts.work: Confessions, Book X, Ch. 29
excerpts.quote: My whole hope is nowhere except in Thy exceeding great mercy. Give what Thou commandest, and command what Thou wilt (Da quod iubes et iube quod vis).
excerpts.citation: Confessions, Book X, Ch. 29

perspectives.summary: Insists on forensic justification by grace alone through faith alone on account of Christ alone, grounding assurance in Christ’s finished alien righteousness (iustitia aliena) while holding that living faith inevitably bears good fruit.
Affirms justification by faith alone enabled by universal prevenient grace that restores moral agency, joined with vigorous pursuit of entire sanctification (Christian perfection in love).
Teaches that God’s unmerited prevenient grace initiates conversion, and justification genuinely makes—not merely declares—the believer inwardly righteous through infused grace and charity.
Frames salvation as union with Christ and Theosis: healing the shattered icon of God and sharing in God’s uncreated light and energies.

keyTerms.definition: "Simultaneously righteous and a sinner": Luther’s formula for the Christian who is completely righteous in Christ before God’s judgment seat while still battling indwelling sin in this life.
Deification or divinization: transformative union with God by grace in Christ through the Holy Spirit (cf. 2 Peter 1:4), preserving the Creator–creature distinction.
"Order of salvation": the logical and theological sequence of aspects of redemption (calling, regeneration, faith, justification, adoption, sanctification, glorification; cf. Rom 8:29–30).

questions.prompt: What does Martin Luther’s Latin soteriological phrase simul iustus et peccator mean?
options: Grace perfects nature without destroying human free choice
Simultaneously righteous (by Christ’s imputed righteousness) and yet a sinner (in ongoing earthly struggle against indwelling sin)
Justification occurs only after complete moral sinlessness is attained
Salvation belongs equally to those who keep the Mosaic ceremonial law
questions.explanation: Luther taught that before God’s judgment seat (coram Deo) the believer is counted completely righteous in Christ through faith alone, even while progressive sanctification battles remaining sin throughout earthly life.

questions.prompt: What position was condemned at the Council of Carthage (418) and the Second Council of Orange (529) during the Pelagian controversies?
options: That human beings possess unfallen moral ability to initiate faith and fulfill God’s law without interior prevenient grace
That baptism should be administered in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit
That Christ rose bodily from the tomb on the third day
That God created the material world out of nothing (ex nihilo)
questions.explanation: Carthage (418) condemned Pelagianism’s denial of original sin and interior grace, and Orange II (529) further rejected Semi-Pelagianism by affirming that even the beginning of faith (initium fidei) is a gift of prevenient grace.
questions.sourceReference: Canons of the Second Council of Orange (AD 529)

questions.prompt: In Eastern Orthodox soteriology, what does the term Theosis (θέωσις) signify?
options: The pantheistic absorption of human persons into the divine essence (ousia)
Transformative union with God by grace—participating in the divine life and uncreated energies while remaining creatures
A purely legal pardon that leaves the human heart inwardly unchanged
The replacement of the Old Testament by philosophical stoicism
questions.explanation: Grounded in 2 Peter 1:4 and Athanasius (De Incarnatione 54.3), Theosis denotes becoming by grace what God is by nature through union with Christ in the Holy Spirit, without ever erasing the Creator–creature distinction.
questions.sourceReference: Athanasius, On the Incarnation 54.3; Gregory Palamas, Triads

questions.prompt: How did Session VI of the Council of Trent (1547) define justification in contrast to the Protestant doctrine of forensic imputation alone?
options: Trent taught Pelagianism—that humans earn initial grace strictly by natural works apart from Christ
Trent affirmed unmerited prevenient grace, but defined justification as comprising both forgiveness of sins and the inward infusion of sanctifying grace and charity
Trent taught universalism without need of faith, baptism, or repentance
Trent denied that Christ’s Passion merited human salvation
questions.explanation: Trent explicitly anathematized Pelagianism (Canons 1–3) while defining justification as not merely forensic imputation, but also interior renewal and sanctification through infused grace.
questions.sourceReference: Council of Trent, Session VI, Ch. 7 (AD 1547)

topics.title: The Doctrine of the Trinity: Ousia, Hypostases & Perichoresis
topics.subtitle: Biblical foundations, Monarchian and Arian crises, and the Nicene-Cappadocian synthesis.
topics.summary: Articulates how historic Christianity confesses one undivided divine essence (ousia) eternally subsisting in three co-equal, co-eternal Persons (hypostases): Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

sections.heading: Monotheism & Triadic Revelation in Scripture
sections.body: Christian Trinitarianism arose directly from loyalty to Jewish monotheism (Deuteronomy 6:4, the Shema) alongside the historical revelation that Jesus the Son shares divine identity, creation, and worship (John 1:1–3; 20:28; Philippians 2:6–11; Hebrews 1:1–8) and that the Holy Spirit acts personally as Lord and Giver of life (Acts 5:3–4; 1 Corinthians 12:4–11). The Baptismal Mandate (Matthew 28:19) commands disciples to be baptized into the singular "name" (onoma) of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

sections.heading: Rejecting Modalism (Sabellianism) & Arian Subordinationism
sections.body: Early theology navigated between two opposite errors: (1) Modalistic Monarchianism (Sabellianism), which collapsed the three Persons into temporary masks or modes worn successively by a unipersonal God; and (2) Arianism, championed by the Alexandrian presbyter Arius (c. 318), who argued that because the Son was "begotten," there "was when He was not" (ēn pote hote ouk ēn), making the Logos the highest created mediator rather than truly God. At the First Council of Nicaea (325), Athanasius and the council fathers confessed the Son to be "eternally begotten of the Father... true God from true God, begotten, not made, of one substance (homoousios) with the Father."

sections.heading: The Cappadocian Settlement & Perichoresis
sections.body: In the late fourth century, Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Gregory of Nyssa clarified technical Greek terminology, distinguishing ousia (what God is: the one undivided divine essence, will, and power) from hypostasis (who each Person is: Father unbegotten, Son eternally begotten, Spirit eternally proceeding). Later summarized by John of Damascus as Perichoresis (mutual coinherence), the three Persons indwell one another without separation or confusion, and every external work of God toward creation is undivided (opera Trinitatis ad extra indivisa sunt).

excerpts.title: No Sooner Do I Conceive of the One Than I Am Illumined by the Splendor of the Three
excerpts.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
excerpts.work: Oration 40 (On Holy Baptism), §41
excerpts.quote: No sooner do I conceive of the One than I am illumined by the splendor of the Three; no sooner do I distinguish Them than I am carried back to the One.
excerpts.citation: Oration 40 (On Holy Baptism), §41

perspectives.summary: Shared across Orthodox, Catholic, and Protestant confessions: one God in Trinity and Trinity in Unity, neither confounding the Persons nor dividing the Substance.
Accents the monarchy of the Father as sole eternal font (pēgē) of deity, from whom the Son is eternally begotten and the Spirit eternally proceeds.
Highlights the sheer simplicity of the divine essence and psychological analogies of memory, understanding, and love, viewing the Spirit as proceeding from Father and Son as mutual bond of love.

keyTerms.definition: "Of the same essence/being": the decisive Nicene watchword affirming that the Son shares the exact undivided divine nature of the Father, contrasted with homoiousios ("of similar essence").
Distinct personal subsistence; in Cappadocian Trinitarian grammar, God is mia ousia, treis hypostaseis (one essence, three persons).
Mutual indwelling, interpenetration, and communion of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (cf. John 14:10–11).

sections.content:
# Cappadocian Trinitarian Grammar: *Mia Ousia, Treis Hypostaseis*

**Attached to Online Source:** Gregory of Nyssa, *On "Not Three Gods" (Ad Ablabium)* (c. AD 375)

---

## Core Conceptual Distinctions

| Greek Term | Latin Equivalent | Theological Meaning |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Ousia** (οὐσία) | *Essentia / Substantia* | The one, simple, undivided divine Being, nature, power, and will shared identically by Father, Son, and Spirit. |
| **Hypostasis** (ὑπόστασις) | *Persona / Subsistentia* | Distinct personal subsistence answering *who* rather than *what*. |
| **Homoousios** (ὁμοούσιος) | *Consubstantialis* | Sharing the exact numerical divine essence—rejecting Arianism and Semi-Arianism (*homoiousios*). |
| **Perichoresis** (περιχώρησις) | *Circumincessio* | Mutual coinherence and indwelling of the Three Persons without separation or blending. |

## Distinguishing Hypostatic Properties (*Idiomata*)
In Gregory of Nyssa and Gregory of Nazianzus, the Three Persons share *every* essential attribute (eternity, omnipotence, wisdom, goodness) and are distinguished solely by their relations of origin:
1. **The Father:** *Agennētos* (Unbegotten / Unoriginate source)
2. **The Son:** *Gennētos* (Eternally Begotten of the Father before all ages)
3. **The Holy Spirit:** *Ekporueton* (Eternally Proceeding from the Father)

## Why Not Three Gods?
In Gregory's letter to Ablabius, human beings are loosely called "three men" because their acts are separated in space, time, and will. By contrast, every divine operation toward creation originates from the Father, acts through the Son, and is perfected in the Holy Spirit as **one single, indivisible action**.

questions.prompt: Why did Nicene orthodoxy insist on homoousios ("of the same essence") rather than homoiousios ("of similar essence") to describe the Son’s relation to the Father?
options: Because homoiousios left open the Arian/Semi-Arian claim that the Son was merely a supreme creature similar to, yet ontologically below, the true God
Because homoousios meant the Father, Son, and Spirit are one single Person wearing three temporary masks
Because homoousios denied that Jesus possessed a real human body
Because homoiousios was a Latin word unknown in the Greek East
questions.explanation: A single Greek letter (iota) separated full deity from creaturehood: only homoousios confessed that the Son possesses the exact, undivided divine nature of the Father rather than being a glorious creature.
questions.sourceReference: First Council of Nicaea (AD 325); Athanasius, De Decretis

questions.prompt: Which ancient Trinitarian error taught that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three eternal Persons, but sequential modes or masks assumed by a single divine Person?
questions.explanation: Named after Sabellius (3rd century), Modalistic Monarchianism collapsed the personal distinctions of Father, Son, and Spirit, rendering Jesus’s prayers to the Father in the Gospels incoherent.

questions.prompt: In Cappadocian Trinitarian theology, how is ousia distinguished from hypostasis?
options: Ousia refers to Christ’s humanity, while hypostasis refers to Christ’s deity
Ousia denotes the one undivided divine essence ("what" God is), while hypostasis denotes each distinct Person ("who" Father, Son, or Spirit is)
Ousia denotes God’s temporal actions, while hypostasis denotes created angels
The Cappadocians rejected both terms as unbiblical
questions.explanation: Basil the Great, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Gregory of Nyssa standardized mia ousia, treis hypostaseis—one shared essence, three distinct personal subsistences distinguished by relations of origin.
questions.sourceReference: Basil of Caesarea, Epistle 236; Gregory of Nyssa, Ad Ablabium

topics.title: Christology & the Hypostatic Union
topics.subtitle: True God and True Man: Overcoming Docetism, Apollinarianism, Nestorianism, and Eutychianism.
topics.summary: Explores the mystery of the Incarnation—how the eternal Person of the Son assumed a complete human nature (body, rational mind, and human will) in one undivided Person.

sections.heading: Why Both Full Deity and Full Humanity Matter
sections.body: Early Christology operated on two soteriological axioms: first, only God can save from death and bestow divine life; second, as Gregory of Nazianzus formulated against Apollinarius, "What has not been assumed has not been healed" (to gar aproslepton, atherapeuton). If Christ were merely an exalted creature, worshiping him would be idolatry and salvation impossible; if Christ lacked a genuine human body (Docetism), rational human mind (Apollinarianism), or human will (Monothelitism), then real humanity was never redeemed from within.

sections.heading: Alexandrian Unity vs. Antiochene Distinction
sections.body: In the fifth century, Cyril of Alexandria championed the unity of the single divine-human subject, defending Mary’s title Theotokos ("God-bearer") not because Mary originated Christ’s deity, but because the Child born of her was personally the eternal Word. Conversely, Nestorius, Patriarch of Constantinople, feared mingling divinity with passible humanity and separated the two natures so sharply that critics saw "two sons" joined merely morally. Conversely, Eutyches erred in the opposite extreme (Monophysitism/Eutychianism), claiming Christ’s human nature was swallowed up into divinity like a drop of honey in the ocean.

sections.heading: The Four Chalcedonian Adverbs & Communicatio Idiomatum
sections.body: Synthesizing Cyril’s letters and Pope Leo I’s Tome, the Council of Chalcedon (451) confessed one and the same Person (prosōpon / hypostasis) made known in two complete natures (physeis): "without confusion, without change" (guarding against Eutychianism) and "without division, without separation" (guarding against Nestorianism). Through the communication of attributes (communicatio idiomatum), properties of either nature are truly predicated of the one Person of the Son—allowing Paul to speak of "the Lord of glory" being crucified (1 Cor 2:8). Later, Constantinople III (680–681) confirmed two harmonious wills (dyothelitism), illuminating Christ’s agony in Gethsemane ("not my will, but yours be done").

excerpts.title: The Unassumed Is the Unhealed
excerpts.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
excerpts.work: Epistle 101 (To Cledonius the Presbyter)
excerpts.quote: For that which He has not assumed He has not healed; but that which is united to His Godhead is also saved. If only half Adam fell, then that which Christ assumes and saves may be half also; but if the whole of his nature fell, it must be united to the whole nature of Him that was begotten, and so be saved as a whole.
excerpts.citation: Epistle 101 (To Cledonius the Presbyter)

perspectives.summary: Uphold one divine Person subsisting in two distinct, complete natures—divine and human—each retaining its proper attributes and operations.

Retain Cyril of Alexandria’s formula mia physis tou Theou Logou sesarkōmenē ("one united divine-human nature of God the Word incarnate") while also anathematizing Eutyches and affirming full humanity and deity—leading to modern ecumenical christological convergence.

keyTerms.definition: "God-bearer" or "Mother of God," affirmed at the Council of Ephesus (431) to safeguard the personal unity of the incarnate Word from conception.
Personal union of Christ’s complete divine and human natures in the one eternal Hypostasis of God the Son.
Communication of proper attributes: attributing predicates of both the divine and human natures to the single Person of Christ.

PAIDEIA CONCILIAR ATTACHMENT: THE DEFINITION OF CHALCEDON (OCTOBER 25, AD 451)
================================================================================
Attached to: Leo I's Tome & Fourth Ecumenical Council Records

ENGLISH TRANSLATION:
"Following, then, the holy Fathers, we all unanimously teach that our Lord Jesus
Christ is to us One and the same Son, the Self-same Perfect in Godhead, the
Self-same Perfect in Manhood; truly God and truly Man; the Self-same of a
rational soul and body; consubstantial [homoousion] with the Father according
to the Godhead, the Self-same consubstantial [homoousion] with us according to
the Manhood; like us in all things, sin apart [choris hamartias]; before the
ages begotten of the Father as to the Godhead, but in the last days, the
Self-same, for us and for our salvation, born of Mary the Virgin Theotokos as
to the Manhood;

One and the Same Christ, Son, Lord, Only-begotten; acknowledged in TWO NATURES
[en dyo physesin]:
  1. asynchytos   -- WITHOUT CONFUSION   (against Eutychianism / Monophysitism)
  2. atreptos     -- WITHOUT CHANGE      (against Eutychianism / mutation of Logos)
  3. adiairetos   -- WITHOUT DIVISION    (against Nestorianism)
  4. achoristos   -- WITHOUT SEPARATION  (against Nestorianism)

the distinction of natures being in no way annulled by the union, but rather the
characteristics of each nature being preserved and concurring into one Person
[prosopon] and one Subsistence [hypostasis]."

questions.prompt: Which Cappadocian Father articulated this classic Christological axiom against Apollinarius’s claim that the divine Logos replaced Jesus’s human rational mind?
questions.excerptContext: For that which He has not assumed He has not healed; but that which is united to His Godhead is also saved.
questions.explanation: In Epistle 101 to Cledonius (AD 382), Gregory of Nazianzus demonstrated that if Christ did not assume a rational human mind (nous), then the fallen human mind remains unredeemed.

questions.prompt: What was the theological purpose of affirming Mary as Theotokos ("God-bearer") at the Council of Ephesus (AD 431)?
options: To teach that Mary existed eternally prior to creation and originated the divine nature
To safeguard the personal unity of Christ—affirming that the One born of Mary according to the flesh is personally the eternal Son of God
To replace Christ’s mediation with Marian priesthood
To deny that Jesus possessed a real physical body
questions.explanation: Against Nestorius’s reluctance to predicate human birth of God the Word, Cyril of Alexandria and Ephesus affirmed Theotokos strictly as a Christological safeguard of the single Person (hypostasis) of the Incarnate Son.
questions.sourceReference: Cyril of Alexandria, Second Letter to Nestorius; Council of Ephesus (AD 431)

questions.prompt: What doctrinal principle allows Scripture to say "they crucified the Lord of glory" (1 Cor 2:8), predicating human suffering of the divine Person?
questions.explanation: Because Christ’s divine and human natures concur in one Person without confusion, attributes proper to either nature may be truly predicated of that single Person (communicatio idiomatum), even though the divine nature itself remains impassible.
questions.sourceReference: Leo I, Tome (Epistle 28); Definition of Chalcedon (AD 451)

topics.title: Patristic Exegesis & the Medieval Quadriga
topics.subtitle: Alexandrian allegory, Antiochene theoria/typology, and the fourfold sense of Scripture.
topics.summary: Charts how early and medieval Christian interpreters read the Old and New Testaments together through literal history, Christological typology, moral formation, and eschatological hope.

sections.heading: Apostolic Christological Reading of the Old Testament
sections.body: On the road to Emmaus, the risen Jesus interpreted to his disciples "in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself" (Luke 24:27). The New Testament writers read Israel’s Scriptures—Passover lamb, Exodus, bronze serpent, Davidic kingship, Suffering Servant—as finding historical and prophetic fulfillment in Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 10:1–11; Hebrews 8–10). The interpretive challenge for the post-apostolic church was establishing disciplined principles for discerning spiritual fulfillment while honoring historical reality.

sections.heading: The School of Alexandria vs. the School of Antioch
sections.body: Two great catechetical centers developed distinct hermeneutical emphases: (1) Alexandria (Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Didymus the Blind), influenced by Philo’s philosophical exegesis, distinguished bodily (literal), soulish (moral), and spiritual (allegorical) senses, seeking deep mystical correspondences beneath every detail of the text; and (2) Antioch (Diodore of Tarsus, Theodore of Mopsuestia, John Chrysostom), which warned that unrestrained allegory dissolved historical anchoring, championing philological, rhetorical, and historical rigor alongside theōria—a higher prophetic/typological contemplation organically rooted in the literal event.

sections.heading: The Medieval Fourfold Sense (Quadriga)
sections.body: John Cassian, Augustine, and later medieval scholastics synthesized patristic exegesis into the Quadriga (four-horse chariot): (1) Literal/Historical (what happened), (2) Allegorical/Christological (what you are to believe concerning Christ and the Church), (3) Tropological/Moral (what you are to do in charity), and (4) Anagogical/Eschatological (whither you are tending in heavenly glory). Crucially, Thomas Aquinas insisted in Summa Theologiae I, q. 1, a. 10 that all spiritual senses must rest firmly upon the literal sense, and doctrinal arguments can be drawn strictly from the literal sense alone.

excerpts.title: All Senses Are Founded on One—the Literal
excerpts.author: Thomas Aquinas
excerpts.work: Summa Theologiae I, q. 1, a. 10
excerpts.quote: That first signification whereby words signify things belongs to the first sense, the historical or literal... Thus in Holy Writ no confusion results, for all the senses are founded on one—the literal—from which alone can any argument be drawn.
excerpts.citation: Summa Theologiae I, q. 1, a. 10

perspectives.summary: Values spiritual/typological reading within the Church’s Rule of Faith (Regula Fidei), holding that the same Divine Author who inspired ancient history also embedded Christological patterns across salvation history.
Rejected speculative allegory detached from authorial grammar and context, while retaining biblical typology explicitly warranted by canonical patterns.

keyTerms.definition: Medieval fourfold method of biblical interpretation summarized by the couplet: Littera gesta docet, quid credas allegoria, moralis quid agas, quo tendas anagogia.
"Pattern, stamp, or mold" (Rom 5:14): real historical persons, institutions, or events in Israel’s history divinely designed to foreshadow heightened fulfillment (antitype) in Christ.
Antiochene "contemplative insight" perceiving both the immediate historical referent and the deeper Messianic horizon without erasing literal history.

sources.title: De Principiis (On First Principles), Book IV — On the Inspiration and Interpretation of Scripture
sources.author: Origen of Alexandria
sources.citation: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 4
sources.summary: First systematic treatise on biblical hermeneutics in Christian history, articulating Origen’s threefold spiritual exegesis.

sources.title: On Christian Doctrine (De Doctrina Christiana)
sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.citation: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series, Vol. 2
sources.summary: Augustine’s influential manual on signs, literal vs. figurative expressions, the Rule of Faith, and the double commandment of love as the goal of all interpretation.

sections.heading: Reading companion
sections.content:
# Hermeneutics Workbook: The *Quadriga* & Augustine's *De Doctrina Christiana*

**Attached to Online Source:** Augustine of Hippo, *On Christian Doctrine* (CCEL, AD 397/426)

---

## 1. The Mnemonic Latin Couplet (Nicholas of Lyra / John Cassian)
> *Littera gesta docet, quid credas allegoria,*  
> *Moralis quid agas, quo tendas anagogia.*

- **Literal (*Littera*):** Teaches what occurred in history and grammar.
- **Allegorical (*Allegoria*):** Shows how the event points forward to Christ and His Body.
- **Moral / Tropological (*Moralis*):** Forms the believer's ethical life of love.
- **Anagogical (*Anagogia*):** Lifts hope toward final eschatological glory.

## 2. Classic Worked Example: "Jerusalem" (John Cassian, *Conferences* 14.8)
1. **Literal / Historical:** The historic walled capital city of Judah and Israel on Mount Zion.
2. **Allegorical / Christological:** The universal Church gathered around Christ the true Temple.
3. **Tropological / Moral:** The faithful human soul ordered in peace and worship toward God.
4. **Anagogical / Eschatological:** The heavenly New Jerusalem descending from God (Gal 4:26; Rev 21:2).

## 3. Hermeneutical Guardrails
- **Augustine's Rule of Charity (*De Doctrina* I.36):** Whoever thinks they understand the Scriptures, yet builds up neither love of God nor love of neighbor, has not yet understood them rightly.
- **Aquinas's Foundational Rule (*ST* I, q.1, a.10):** Spiritual senses never float free of the text; doctrinal proof may be drawn **solely from the literal sense**.

questions.prompt: How did the Antiochene school of exegesis (e.g., John Chrysostom, Theodore of Mopsuestia) characteristically differ from the Alexandrian school (e.g., Origen)?
options: Antioch rejected the Old Testament entirely, whereas Alexandria accepted it
Antioch emphasized historical-grammatical anchoring and organic typology (theoria), cautioning against detached allegory
Antioch insisted every Old Testament narrative was unhistorical myth
Antioch forbade preaching verse-by-verse homilies to congregations
questions.explanation: While Alexandria frequently sought hidden allegorical meanings beneath every detail, Antioch insisted that spiritual insight (theoria) must remain anchored in real historical events and rhetorical context.
questions.sourceReference: John Chrysostom, Homilies; Diodore of Tarsus

questions.prompt: In the medieval Quadriga (fourfold sense of Scripture), interpreting "Jerusalem" as the heavenly city of final eschatological glory toward which believers journey exemplifies which sense?
questions.explanation: Per John Cassian’s famous example (Conferences 14.8): Literally Jerusalem is the city of the Jews; Allegorically the Church of Christ; Tropologically the faithful soul; Anagogically ("quo tendas anagogia") the heavenly Jerusalem.
questions.sourceReference: John Cassian, Conferences 14.8; Thomas Aquinas, ST I, q. 1, a. 10

questions.prompt: Which theologian established the hermeneutical rule that all spiritual senses rest upon the literal sense and that doctrinal arguments can be drawn from the literal sense alone?
questions.excerptContext: Thus in Holy Writ no confusion results, for all the senses are founded on one—the literal—from which alone can any argument be drawn.
questions.explanation: In Summa Theologiae I, q. 1, a. 10, Aquinas disciplined medieval spiritual interpretation by insisting that theology proves doctrine solely from the literal sense intended by the author.
questions.sourceReference: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 1, a. 10

topics.title: Grammatical-Historical & Canonical Hermeneutics
topics.subtitle: Exegesis vs. Eisegesis, Analogia Fidei, literary genres, and redemptive-historical context.
topics.summary: Establishes rigorous principles for drawing meaning out of the biblical text (exegesis) through original languages, historical background, literary genre, and canonical synthesis.

sections.heading: Exegesis vs. Eisegesis & Ad Fontes
sections.body: Sound hermeneutics distinguishes sharply between Exegesis ("leading out" the meaning intended by the human and divine authors in context) and Eisegesis ("reading into" the text modern assumptions, proof-texting fragments detached from surrounding argument, or etymological fallacies such as root fallacy and illegitimate totality transfer). Stimulated by Renaissance humanism’s cry Ad Fontes ("back to the sources," Erasmus, Reuchlin), the Reformers insisted on interpreting Scripture directly from Hebrew, Aramaic, and Koine Greek.

sections.heading: Literary Genres & Special Hermeneutics
sections.body: Because God spoke through diverse literary forms (Hebrews 1:1), faithful interpretation honors genre conventions: (1) Historical Narrative reveals theology through plot, characterization, and narrator evaluation rather than treating every descriptive action as prescriptive command; (2) Hebrew Poetry & Wisdom Literature employ parallelism, metaphor, and general proverbs (not unconditional mechanical promises, contrast Proverbs with Job and Ecclesiastes); (3) Epistles are occasional letters addressing concrete congregational crises; and (4) Apocalyptic Literature (Daniel, Revelation) communicates cosmic hope through vivid symbolic visions rather than woodenly literal newspaper codes.

sections.heading: Analogia Scripturae & Canonical Hermeneutics
sections.body: Known as the Analogy of Scripture (Scriptura sui ipsius interpres—"Scripture is its own interpreter"), clearer passages illuminate more obscure ones because the whole canon ultimately shares one Divine Author. Contemporary Canonical and Theological Interpretation (Brevard Childs, Kevin Vanhoozer) pairs rigorous grammatical-historical work with attention to a passage’s final canonical placement and trajectory within redemptive history.

excerpts.title: The Infallible Rule of Interpretation
excerpts.author: Westminster Assembly
excerpts.work: Westminster Confession of Faith, Ch. 1.9
excerpts.quote: The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture itself: and therefore, when there is a question about the true and full sense of any Scripture (which is not manifold, but one), it must be searched and known by other places that speak more clearly.
excerpts.citation: Westminster Confession of Faith, Ch. 1.9

perspectives.summary: Affirms that the meaning of any text is anchored in the communicative act of the inspired human author within his linguistic, cultural, and historical setting.
Integrates historical philology with the unity of the two-testament canon, reading with the Communion of Saints and the Nicene Rule of Faith.

keyTerms.definition: Critical, disciplined drawing out of a text’s meaning from its grammar, syntax, historical setting, and literary flow (cf. John 1:18, exēgēsato).
Importing foreign presuppositions or subjective agendas into a text without contextual warrant.
"Analogy of faith" (cf. Rom 12:6): interpreting individual texts in harmony with the coherent teaching of the whole canon.

sources.title: Dedicatory Epistle to Simon Grynaeus — On Lucid Brevity in Exegesis
sources.author: John Calvin
sources.citation: Commentaries on the Epistle of Paul to the Romans (CCEL)
sources.summary: Calvin’s celebrated manifesto on grammatical-historical exegesis, arguing that the commentator’s chief virtue is "lucid brevity" disclosing the author’s mind.

sources.title: Dogmatic Constitution on Divine Revelation (Dei Verbum, Ch. III)
sources.author: Second Vatican Council
sources.citation: Vatican Archive Official Documents
sources.summary: Landmark modern conciliar synthesis uniting attention to ancient literary genres and authorial intention with reading Scripture in the same Spirit in whom it was written.

questions.prompt: What is the fundamental contrast between exegesis and eisegesis?
options: Exegesis studies only the Old Testament, whereas eisegesis studies only the New Testament
Exegesis draws out the text’s intended contextual meaning, whereas eisegesis reads external assumptions into the text
Exegesis uses Latin translations, whereas eisegesis uses Greek manuscripts
Exegesis applies to poetry, whereas eisegesis applies to epistles
questions.explanation: From Greek ex-hēgeomai ("to lead out") vs. eis-hēgeomai ("to lead into"), exegesis submits to the author’s grammar, historical context, and literary argument rather than importing presuppositions.

questions.prompt: A preacher claims the English word "dynamite" defines the Greek noun dynamis ("power") in Romans 1:16 ("the gospel is the power of God"), even though Alfred Nobel invented dynamite in 1867. What hermeneutical error is this?
questions.explanation: Reading a nineteenth-century invention backward into first-century Koine Greek commits semantic anachronism: word meaning is determined by synchronic usage in the author’s era and sentence, not later English derivatives.

questions.prompt: What principle is expressed by Analogia Scripturae / Scriptura sui ipsius interpres?
options: Every proverb in Wisdom Literature is an unconditional mechanical guarantee
Scripture interprets Scripture—obscure or disputed passages must be illuminated by clearer passages across the canon
Private subjective intuition overrides grammatical syntax
Apocalyptic symbols must always be decoded using modern geopolitical headlines
questions.explanation: Because Scripture forms a unified canonical witness under divine inspiration, ambiguous passages are rightly interpreted in light of clearer, fuller passages addressing the same theme.
questions.sourceReference: Augustine, De Doctrina Christiana II–III; Westminster Confession 1.9

topics.title: Martyrs, Empire & the Rise of Monasticism
topics.subtitle: From sporadic Roman persecutions and the Edict of Milan (313) to Desert Fathers and Mothers.
topics.summary: Examines how an underground persecuted fellowship endured Roman imperial trials, navigated legalization under Constantine, and birthed desert monasticism as a "white martyrdom."

sections.heading: Witness unto Blood in the Pre-Constantinian Church
sections.body: Refusing to offer pinch-incense to the Roman genius imperatoris or traditional civic gods, early Christians were labeled atheoi ("atheists") and suspected of sedition. From Nero’s scapegoating after the Great Fire of Rome (AD 64) and Pliny the Younger’s correspondence with Trajan (c. AD 112) to empire-wide persecutions under Decius (250) and Diocletian (303–311), martyrs such as Polycarp of Smyrna, Blandina of Lyons, and Perpetua and Felicity in Carthage bore courageous witness. As Tertullian famously wrote in Apologeticus 50: "The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church."

sections.heading: The Edict of Milan (313) & Imperial Patronage
sections.body: Following Constantine’s victory at the Milvian Bridge (312), emperors Constantine and Licinius issued the Edict of Milan (313), granting religious toleration across the Roman Empire and restoring confiscated church property (Christianity later became the official imperial religion under Theodosius I’s Edict of Thessalonica in 380). Legalization enabled public basilicas, ecumenical councils, and charitable hospitals (basileias), while also introducing new temptations of political coercion and nominalism.

sections.heading: Desert Asceticism & Benedictine Rule
sections.body: Precisely as imperial favor cooled the danger of physical martyrdom, thousands fled cities for the Egyptian, Syrian, and Palestinian deserts seeking radical fidelity to the Gospel. Antony the Great (c. 251–356) pioneered eremitic (solitary) monasticism, Pachomius organized cenobitic (communal) monasteries, Macrina and Basil integrated ascetic life with scholarship and poor relief, and Benedict of Nursia (c. 480–547) composed his balanced Latin Rule (Ora et Labora—"Pray and Work") that preserved classical and biblical learning across Western Europe.

excerpts.title: Eighty and Six Years Have I Served Him
excerpts.author: Church of Smyrna
excerpts.work: Martyrdom of Polycarp, Ch. 9
excerpts.quote: Eighty and six years have I served Him, and He never did me any injury: how then can I blaspheme my King and my Savior?
excerpts.citation: Martyrdom of Polycarp, Ch. 9

perspectives.summary: Honors both the martyrs’ cult of witness and monasticism as Spirit-led prophetic renewal preserving contemplative prayer, liturgy, and scriptural manuscripts.
Celebrates early martyr courage while evaluating the fourth-century Constantinian shift critically for entangling church discipline with state power.

keyTerms.definition: Originally a legal "witness" (Acts 1:8); came to designate one who seals testimony to Christ by laying down their life.
From koinos bios ("common life"): communal monasticism lived under a shared rule and abbot/abbess, contrasted with eremitic solitude.

sources.title: Ecclesiastical History (Historia Ecclesiastica, Books I–X)
sources.author: Eusebius of Caesarea
sources.citation: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, Vol. 1
sources.summary: Indispensable primary chronicle of apostolic succession, persecutions, canon lists, and Constantine’s rise.

sources.title: Life of St. Antony (Vita Antonii)
sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.citation: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, Vol. 4
sources.summary: Biography of Antony of Egypt that galvanized monasticism East and West and helped catalyze Augustine’s conversion in Milan.

questions.prompt: What did the Edict of Milan (AD 313), issued jointly by Emperors Constantine and Licinius, actually enact?
options: It outlawed all non-Christian religions and made Christianity mandatory across the Empire
It granted legal religious toleration to Christians (and all religions) and restored confiscated church property
It divided the Roman Empire permanently into Catholic and Protestant realms
It convened the Council of Trent
questions.explanation: A common misconception confuses the Edict of Milan (313), which established religious toleration and ended Roman persecution, with Theodosius I’s later Edict of Thessalonica (380), which made Nicene Christianity the official imperial religion.
questions.sourceReference: Lactantius, De Mortibus Persecutorum 48; Eusebius, Hist. Eccl. X.5

questions.prompt: Which second-century bishop and disciple of the Apostle John spoke these words in the Smyrnaean arena when ordered by the Roman proconsul to revile Christ?
questions.excerptContext: Eighty and six years have I served Him, and He never did me any injury: how then can I blaspheme my King and my Savior?
questions.explanation: Recorded in the Martyrdom of Polycarp (ch. 9, c. AD 155), the aged bishop of Smyrna chose burning at the stake rather than deny Christ—becoming the earliest detailed post-canonical martyrdom chronicle.

questions.prompt: In the history of Christian monasticism, what distinguishes cenobitic monasticism (pioneered by Pachomius and Basil) from eremitic monasticism (exemplified by Antony)?
options: Cenobitic monks lived in structured communal monasteries under a shared rule, whereas eremitic monks lived as solitary desert hermits
Cenobitic monks served as armed crusader knights, whereas eremitic monks taught in medieval universities
Cenobitic monasticism rejected prayer, whereas eremitic monasticism rejected fasting
Cenobitic monasticism existed only in Ireland, whereas eremitic monasticism existed only in Rome
questions.explanation: Derived from Greek koinos bios ("common life") vs. erēmos ("desert/solitude"), cenobitic monasticism organized ascetics into communities of shared liturgy, labor, and mutual accountability.
questions.sourceReference: Athanasius, Life of Antony; Rule of St. Pachomius; Rule of St. Benedict

topics.title: The East–West Schism of 1054
topics.subtitle: Filioque, papal primacy vs. conciliarity, cultural divergence, and the Fourth Crusade.
topics.summary: Unpacks the centuries-long linguistic, political, liturgical, ecclesiological, and Trinitarian estrangement between Greek-speaking Eastern Orthodoxy and Latin Western Christendom.

sections.heading: Cultural, Linguistic & Political Drift
sections.body: Long before 1054, the Latin West and Greek East grew apart in language, political alignment, and liturgical custom (such as unleavened vs. leavened Eucharistic bread and clerical celibacy rules). After Charlemagne’s coronation in 800 by Pope Leo III rivaled the Byzantine emperor in Constantinople, and Photius clashed with Pope Nicholas I in the ninth century, mutual incomprehension deepened.

sections.heading: Theological Flashpoints: Filioque & Papal Jurisdiction
sections.body: Two theological issues stood at the center: (1) Ecclesiology—Rome claimed universal papal jurisdiction by Petrine succession over all patriarchates, whereas Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem held to a pentarchy of sister patriarchates in which Rome held a primacy of honor (primus inter pares) subject to ecumenical councils; and (2) The Filioque ("and the Son")—added to the Latin Nicene Creed at the Third Council of Toledo (589) and eventually adopted at Rome (1014) without an ecumenical council. Eastern theologians objected both to unilateral alteration of an ecumenical symbol and to risking compromising the Father’s unique monarchy as sole fountainhead of the Spirit.

sections.heading: 1054 Mutual Excommunications & 1204 Rupture
sections.body: In July 1054, papal legate Cardinal Humbert laid a bull of excommunication upon the altar of Hagia Sophia against Patriarch Michael Cerularius, who reciprocated with his synod. Even then, lay communion persisted in places until the tragic sack of Constantinople by Western Crusaders in 1204 hardened the breach into lasting institutional division—though the mutual anathemas of 1054 were jointly lifted in 1965 by Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras I.

excerpts.title: Joint Catholic–Orthodox Declaration of 1965
excerpts.author: Pope Paul VI & Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras I
excerpts.work: Joint Declaration Removing the Sentences of Excommunication of 1054
excerpts.quote: They regret the offensive words, the reproaches without foundation, and the reprehensible gestures which, on both sides, marked or accompanied the sad events of this period... and consign them to oblivion.
excerpts.citation: Joint Declaration Removing the Sentences of Excommunication of 1054

perspectives.summary: Maintains conciliar ecclesiology and the unaltered 381 Creed ("who proceeds from the Father"), distinguishing eternal hypostatic procession from temporal mission through the Son.

Affirms Petrine primacy as visible principle of unity and explains Filioque as expressing the Spirit’s eternal procession from Father and Son as from a single principle (tanquam ex uno principio), while omitting Filioque in Greek Catholic liturgies.

keyTerms.definition: Latin clause meaning "and from the Son," inserted into the Western Latin text of the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed regarding the procession of the Holy Spirit.
"First among equals": the Orthodox understanding of the Bishop of Rome’s ancient honor among the Patriarchs prior to schism.

sources.title: Documents of the Schism of 1054 (Bull of Humbert & Synodical Edict of Michael Cerularius)
sources.author: Cardinal Humbert & Patriarch Michael Cerularius
sources.citation: Fordham Internet Medieval Sourcebook
sources.summary: Primary diplomatic and ecclesiastical texts from the July 1054 crisis in Constantinople.

questions.prompt: Which pair of theological and ecclesiological disputes stood at the center of the East–West Schism of AD 1054?
options: Universal papal jurisdiction vs. conciliar pentarchy, and the Western insertion of Filioque into the Nicene Creed
questions.explanation: Alongside cultural and liturgical divergences, Greek East and Latin West clashed over Rome’s claim to universal jurisdiction over the Eastern patriarchates and the unilateral Western addition of Filioque ("and the Son").
questions.sourceReference: Documents of the Schism of 1054; Toledo III (589)

topics.title: The Reformations & Catholic Counter-Reformation
topics.subtitle: Luther, Zwingli, Calvin, Anabaptists, the English Reformation, and the Council of Trent.
topics.summary: Surveys the sixteenth-century theological and institutional transformations across Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican, Radical, and Tridentine Roman Catholic traditions.

sections.heading: Indulgences, Authority & the Five Solas
sections.body: Preceded by medieval reform movements under John Wycliffe and Jan Hus, the Protestant Reformation ignited on October 31, 1517, when Augustinian friar and Wittenberg professor Martin Luther circulated his Ninety-Five Theses questioning indulgence abuses and papal treasury claims. At the Leipzig Debate (1519) and Diet of Worms (1521), the debate crystallized around ultimate religious authority and salvation, later summarized in the Five Solas: Sola Scriptura (Scripture alone as supreme norming norm, norma normans), Sola Gratia (grace alone), Sola Fide (faith alone), Solus Christus (Christ alone), and Soli Deo Gloria (glory to God alone).

sections.heading: Four Streams of Protestantism
sections.body: Protestant renewal branched into four distinct streams: (1) Lutheranism (Luther, Philipp Melanchthon; Augsburg Confession, 1530), retaining liturgical continuity and Christ’s sacramental bodily presence "in, with, and under" bread and wine; (2) Reformed Protestantism (Huldrych Zwingli in Zurich, John Calvin in Geneva, John Knox in Scotland), emphasizing divine sovereignty, covenantal unity, and spiritual nourishment by Christ in the Eucharist through the Spirit; (3) The Radical Reformation / Anabaptists (Conrad Grebel, Menno Simons; Schleitheim Confession, 1527), advocating regenerate believers’ baptism, nonviolence, and separation of church and magistrate; and (4) Anglicanism (Thomas Cranmer, Book of Common Prayer, Thirty-Nine Articles), forging a reformed catholic via media.

sections.heading: Catholic Renewal & the Council of Trent (1545–1563)
sections.body: Simultaneously, the Roman Catholic Church underwent vigorous internal renewal (often called both Catholic Reform and Counter-Reformation): new religious orders such as the Society of Jesus (Ignatius of Loyola) and Discalced Carmelites (Teresa of Ávila, John of the Cross) flourished, while the Council of Trent reformed seminary education, curbed financial abuses, reaffirmed the Deuterocanonical books and Sacred Tradition alongside Scripture, defined the seven sacraments and transubstantiation, and articulated Tridentine soteriology.

excerpts.title: Conscience Captive to the Word of God
excerpts.author: Martin Luther
excerpts.work: Speech at the Diet of Worms
excerpts.quote: Unless I am convinced by the testimony of the Scriptures or by clear reason... my conscience is captive to the Word of God. I cannot and I will not recant anything, since it is neither safe nor right to go against conscience.
excerpts.citation: Speech at the Diet of Worms

perspectives.summary: Views the Reformation as a recovery of apostolic Gospel clarity, vernacular Scripture, and the priesthood of all believers—not the invention of a new church, but the reform of the church catholic according to the Word.

Acknowledges late-medieval pastoral abuses needing reform while defending visible sacramental and magisterial continuity at Trent, and engaging today in constructive dialogues such as the 1999 Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification.

keyTerms.definition: Principle that Holy Scripture, as inspired Word of God, is the sole infallible rule of faith and practice—respecting, yet testing, creeds and councils.

Dogma affirmed at Lateran IV (1215) and Trent (1551) that in the Eucharist the whole substance of bread and wine is changed into Christ’s body and blood while outward appearances (accidents/species) remain.

sources.author: Martin Luther
sources.citation: Project Wittenberg / CCEL
sources.summary: Luther’s 95 Latin propositions on repentance, papal indulgences, and the true treasure of the Church—the most holy Gospel.

sections.heading: Reading companion
sections.content:
# Sixteenth-Century Confessional Comparison

**Attached to Online Source:** Martin Luther, *The 95 Theses* (CCEL, AD 1517)

---

## Comparative Loci Across 16th-Century Traditions

| Locus | Lutheran (1530) | Reformed (1559/1563) | Anabaptist (1527) | Tridentine Catholic (1545–63) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Supreme Authority** | *Sola Scriptura* (respecting creeds & fathers) | *Sola Scriptura* (regulative principle in worship) | Scripture centered on Sermon on the Mount | Scripture + Sacred Tradition interpreted by Magisterium |
| **Justification** | Forensic imputation by grace through faith alone | Forensic imputation in union with Christ | New birth & discipleship obedience | Infused sanctifying grace & forgiveness; faith formed by charity |
| **Eucharist** | Corporeal presence "in, with, and under" elements | Real spiritual presence received by faith through the Spirit | Memorial communion of covenanted believers | Transubstantiation & propitiatory sacrifice of the Mass |
| **Baptism** | Infant & adult; regenerative promise | Infant & adult; covenantal sign & seal | Believers' baptism only upon profession | Infant & adult; instrumental regeneration (*ex opere operato*) |

questions.prompt: At the Marburg Colloquy of 1529, Martin Luther and Huldrych Zwingli agreed on fourteen out of fifteen theological articles, dividing sharply over which fifteenth issue?
options: The mode of Christ’s presence in the Lord’s Supper (Eucharist)
Whether the Apostle Paul wrote Romans
Whether Latin should remain the sole language of worship
questions.explanation: Writing Hoc est corpus meum ("This is my body") in chalk on the table, Luther insisted on Christ’s bodily presence "in, with, and under" the bread and wine, while Zwingli argued "is" meant "signifies."

questions.prompt: Which distinctive commitments characterized the sixteenth-century Anabaptist ("Radical Reformation") movement reflected in the Schleitheim Confession (1527)?
options: Believers’ baptism upon personal profession of faith, nonviolence, and separation of the covenanted church from civil coercion
Restoration of papal indulgences and Latin monasticism
Rejection of the New Testament in favor of classical Aristotelian philosophy
questions.explanation: Leaders such as Conrad Grebel, Michael Sattler, and Menno Simons critiqued both Catholic and magisterial Protestant state-churches, practicing regenerate believers’ baptism and pacifist discipleship.

topics.title: The Hebrew Bible, Septuagint & Dead Sea Scrolls
topics.subtitle: Torah, Nevi’im, Ketuvim, Alexandrian Greek translation, Masoretic scribes, and Qumran.
topics.summary: Traces the composition, tripartite arrangement, translation into Greek (LXX), Qumran manuscript witnesses, and Masoretic vocalization of the Old Testament.

sections.heading: Tripartite Structure of the Hebrew Tanakh
sections.body: In Jewish tradition and Jesus’s own words in Luke 24:44 ("the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms"), the Hebrew Scriptures are organized into three divisions forming the acronym TaNaKh: Torah (Law/Instruction: Genesis–Deuteronomy), Nevi’im (Former and Latter Prophets), and Ketuvim (Writings). Although counted as 24 books in traditional Jewish reckoning (combining Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, Ezra–Nehemiah, and the Twelve Minor Prophets into single scrolls), its exact consonantal contents correspond to the 39 books of the Protestant Old Testament.

sections.heading: The Septuagint (LXX) & Deuterocanonical Books
sections.body: Beginning in third-century BC Alexandria under Ptolemy II Philadelphus, Jewish scholars translated the Hebrew Scriptures into Koine Greek—known as the Septuagint (LXX, "Seventy"). The Septuagint became the primary Bible of the Greek-speaking Jewish diaspora and of the New Testament apostles. Greek codices also included additional Second Temple Jewish works (Tobit, Judith, Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach, Baruch, 1–2 Maccabees, and additions to Esther and Daniel), received as Deuterocanonical by Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches and regarded by Protestants (following Jerome’s Hebraica veritas principle) as valuable edifying Apocrypha rather than canonical rule of faith.

sections.heading: The Dead Sea Scrolls (1947) & the Masoretic Text
sections.body: Prior to 1947, the oldest complete Hebrew Bible manuscript was the Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), meticulously copied and vocalized by the Masoretes of Tiberias. Between 1947 and 1956, over 900 manuscripts dating from c. 250 BC to AD 68 were discovered in eleven caves near Qumran by the Dead Sea—containing fragments of every Hebrew Bible book except Esther, including the complete Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, c. 125 BC). The scrolls leaped back over a thousand years, confirming extraordinary scribal fidelity in proto-Masoretic texts while also illuminating ancient readings preserved in the Septuagint.

excerpts.title: Twenty-Two Books Strictly Preserved
excerpts.author: Flavius Josephus
excerpts.work: Against Apion, Book I, §8
excerpts.quote: For we have not an innumerable multitude of books among us, disagreeing from and contradicting one another, [as the Greeks have,] but only twenty-two books, which contain the records of all the past times; which are justly believed to be divine.
excerpts.citation: Against Apion, Book I, §8

perspectives.summary: Aligns the Old Testament strictly with the Hebrew Tanakh entrusted to ancient Israel (Romans 3:2) and recognized in first-century Judea (cf. Josephus, Against Apion 1.8).
Receives the broader Alexandrian/Septuagint heritage used liturgically by early Greek and Latin Fathers and confirmed at regional synods (Hippo 393, Carthage 397) and Trent.

"Tradition/transmission": the system of vowel points, accents, and marginal textual tallies created by Jewish Masoretic scholars to safeguard the exact pronunciation and consonantal integrity of the Hebrew text.

questions.prompt: What three divisions of the Hebrew Bible form the Hebrew acronym TaNaKh?
questions.explanation: Reflected in Luke 24:44 ("the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms"), TaNaKh combines Torah, Nevi’im, and Ketuvim—comprising 24 scrolls identical in consonantal content to the 39 Protestant Old Testament books.

questions.prompt: Why was the discovery of the Dead Sea Scrolls at Qumran (beginning in 1947) a watershed event for Old Testament textual scholarship?
options: They contained autographs of all twenty-seven New Testament books signed by the Apostles
They provided Hebrew biblical manuscripts over 1,000 years older than the Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), including the complete Great Isaiah Scroll
They proved the Hebrew language was invented in the Middle Ages
They contained minutes from the First Council of Nicaea
questions.explanation: Dating from c. 250 BC to AD 68, the Qumran scrolls included fragments of every Hebrew Bible book except Esther, demonstrating remarkable textual stability alongside illuminating variants shared with the Septuagint.

questions.prompt: What is the Septuagint (abbreviated LXX)?
options: Jerome’s fourth-century Latin translation of the Bible
The pre-Christian Koine Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures begun in Alexandria in the third century BC
A sixteenth-century German Bible printed by Johannes Gutenberg
A collection of seventy medieval papal bulls
questions.explanation: Begun in third-century BC Alexandria for Greek-speaking Jews, the Septuagint served as the primary Old Testament text quoted by New Testament authors and early Greek Church Fathers.
questions.sourceReference: Letter of Aristeas; Alexandrian Jewish Tradition

topics.title: New Testament Canon & Textual Criticism
topics.subtitle: Apostolicity, papyri and uncial codices, Athanasius’s 39th Festal Letter, and critical editions.
topics.summary: Examines how the 27 New Testament books were recognized rather than invented by the early church, and how modern textual criticism evaluates over 5,800 Greek manuscripts.

sections.heading: Criteria of Canonicity: Recognition, Not Invention
sections.body: Contrary to popular myths claiming the Council of Nicaea (325) voted on the Bible, Nicaea passed no canon of Scripture at all. Rather, a core collection of Four Gospels (Irenaeus’s fourfold Gospel, c. 180) and thirteen Pauline Epistles functioned authoritatively across the Mediterranean by the mid-second century (cf. the Muratorian Fragment, c. 170–200), spurred further by rejecting Marcion’s truncated canon (c. 140). Early churches applied three intertwined criteria to disputed books (antilegomena): (1) Apostolicity (written by an apostle or close apostolic associate), (2) Orthodoxy (conformity to the apostolic Rule of Faith), and (3) Catholicity (widespread, continuous liturgical reading across churches East and West). In AD 367, Athanasius’s 39th Festal Letter listed the exact 27 New Testament books received universally today, echoed at Rome (382), Hippo (393), and Carthage (397).

sections.heading: Papyri, Uncials, Minuscules & Ancient Versions
sections.body: The New Testament possesses unmatched manuscript attestation among ancient Greco-Roman literature: over 5,800 Greek manuscripts (from early papyri such as P52—the Rylands fragment of John 18 from c. AD 125–150—and P46, P66, P75, to fourth-century parchment uncials Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, plus thousands of medieval minuscules), alongside over 10,000 Latin manuscripts and early Syriac, Coptic, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions, plus tens of thousands of patristic citations.

sections.heading: Principles of Textual Criticism
sections.body: Because hand-copying inevitably introduced spelling shifts, accidental skips (haplography/homoeoteleuton), or harmonizations, textual critics weigh both External Evidence (age, geographical distribution, and genealogical quality of witnesses—Alexandrian, Western, Byzantine text-types) and Internal Evidence (lectio difficilior potior—"the more difficult reading is preferable," and lectio brevior—scribes tended to clarify or expand rather than omit). Well over 99% of textual variants involve spelling, word order, or minor synonyms; no cardinal Christian doctrine hangs on a disputed textual variant.

excerpts.title: In These Alone Is Proclaimed the Doctrine of Godliness
excerpts.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
excerpts.work: 39th Festal Letter
excerpts.quote: These are fountains of salvation, that they who thirst may be satisfied with the living words they contain. In these alone is proclaimed the doctrine of godliness. Let no man add to these, neither let him take ought from these.
excerpts.citation: 39th Festal Letter

perspectives.summary: Combines earliest Alexandrian papyri and uncials with internal transcriptional probabilities to reconstruct the initial text (Ausgangstext) underlying modern translations.
Values the broad consensus of Greek liturgical manuscripts copied continuously across the Greek-speaking East.

keyTerms.definition: Literally a "measuring reed" or straight rod (Gal 6:16); applied to the authoritative rule of faith and the closed list of inspired books measuring all teaching.

Eusebius’s distinction between universally acknowledged NT books (Four Gospels, Acts, Paul’s Epistles, 1 Peter, 1 John) and temporarily debated books (e.g., Hebrews, James, 2 Peter, 2–3 John, Jude, Revelation) prior to final consensus.
"The more difficult reading is stronger": textual-critical principle recognizing that copyists were far more likely to smooth out awkward grammar or apparent tensions than to create them.

questions.explanation: Contrary to popular legends about the Council of Nicaea (325)—which did not vote on the biblical canon—Athanasius’s Easter letter of AD 367 enumerates the exact 27-book New Testament canon recognized across all Christian traditions.

questions.prompt: In New Testament textual criticism, what does the internal canon lectio difficilior potior state?
options: The longest medieval manuscript reading is always original
Other factors being equal, the more difficult reading is more likely original because scribes tended to smooth out awkward expressions rather than introduce them
Latin translations always take precedence over Greek papyri
Only manuscripts copied after AD 1000 should be consulted
questions.explanation: Copyists encountering an unusual grammatical construction or apparent difficulty between parallel Gospels often harmonized or simplified the text; hence a harder reading that explains the rise of smoother readings is preferred.
questions.sourceReference: Bruce M. Metzger & Bart D. Ehrman, The Text of the New Testament

questions.prompt: What is the significance of John Rylands Papyrus P52 (containing verses from John 18)?
options: It is widely dated to c. AD 125–150 in Egypt, refuting nineteenth-century claims that the Gospel of John was composed late in the late second century
It is the earliest printed edition of Erasmus’s Greek New Testament
It contains the complete Hebrew text of Deuteronomy
It records the canons of the Council of Chalcedon
questions.explanation: Discovered in Egypt and published by C.H. Roberts in 1935, P52 demonstrated that the Fourth Gospel was already circulating in provincial Egypt within decades of its composition in Asia Minor.
questions.sourceReference: P. Rylands Greek 457 (P52), John Rylands University Library

topics.title: The Apostolic Fathers & Irenaeus of Lyons
topics.subtitle: Clement of Rome, Ignatius of Antioch, the Didache, and Irenaeus’s Recapitulation against Gnosticism.
topics.summary: Introduces the earliest generation of Christian pastors who knew or succeeded the Apostles, culminating in Irenaeus’s biblical-historical refutation of second-century Gnosticism.

sections.heading: Clement, the Didache & Ignatius on the Road to Rome
sections.body: The "Apostolic Fathers" comprise writings from c. AD 70–150 bridging the New Testament and the apologists: (1) 1 Clement (c. AD 96), written from the church at Rome to Corinth urging humility, peace, and orderly pastoral succession; (2) The Didache ("Teaching of the Twelve"), an early manual of ethical catechesis ("Two Ways"), baptism, fasting, and Eucharist; and (3) The Seven Letters of Ignatius of Antioch (c. AD 107–110), dictated while chained en route to martyrdom in the Roman amphitheater. Ignatius combated Docetism (the claim that Christ only "seemed" to have flesh and suffer), championed Eucharistic realism, and articulated the threefold ministry of bishop, presbyters, and deacons—recording the earliest surviving use of the phrase "the catholic [universal] church" (Smyrnaeans 8.2).

sections.heading: The Gnostic Crisis & Marcion
sections.body: In the second century, esoteric Gnostic teachers (Valentinus, Basilides) posited radical cosmic dualism: the material world and Old Testament Creator (the Demiurge) were flawed or evil, and salvation meant escaping matter through secret knowledge (gnōsis) imparted only to spiritual elites. Similarly, Marcion severed the Old Testament Creator God of justice from Jesus’s Father of love.

sections.heading: Irenaeus: Creation’s Goodness, Apostolic Succession & Recapitulation
sections.body: Born in Smyrna where he heard the aged Polycarp (himself a disciple of the Apostle John) and later serving as Bishop of Lyons in Gaul, Irenaeus penned Against Heresies (c. AD 180). Against Gnosticism, Irenaeus defended the goodness of material creation and bodily resurrection, pointed to public apostolic teaching openly preserved in churches founded by apostles (as opposed to "secret" Gnostic traditions), affirmed the unity of Old and New Covenants, and unfolded Recapitulation (anakephalaiōsis, Eph 1:10): Christ summed up all human life in himself to heal and glorify our humanity.

excerpts.title: The Glory of God Is a Living Human Being
excerpts.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
excerpts.work: Against Heresies, Book IV, Ch. 20.7
excerpts.quote: For the glory of God is a living man; and the life of man consists in beholding God (Gloria Dei vivens homo, vita autem hominis visio Dei).
excerpts.citation: Against Heresies, Book IV, Ch. 20.7

excerpts.title: Wherever Jesus Christ Is, There Is the Catholic Church
excerpts.author: Ignatius of Antioch
excerpts.work: Epistle to the Smyrnaeans, Ch. 8
excerpts.quote: Wherever the bishop shall appear, there let the multitude also be; even as, wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the Catholic Church.
excerpts.citation: Epistle to the Smyrnaeans, Ch. 8

perspectives.summary: Reveres the Apostolic Fathers and Irenaeus not as adding new revelation beyond Scripture, but as crucial first-hand witnesses to how the churches planted by the Apostles worshiped, governed, and read the Gospel.

keyTerms.definition: "Summing up under one head" (Eph 1:10): Irenaeus’s teaching that Christ retraced Adam’s story in faithful obedience to undo the Fall and bring creation to maturity.
Early heresy claiming Christ’s physical body, hunger, and crucifixion were mere phantoms or appearances rather than true human flesh (cf. 1 John 4:2–3).
"Rule of Faith": the concise Trinitarian summary of apostolic preaching taught to catechumens and used by Irenaeus and Tertullian to test Gnostic distortions.
