sections.heading: Reading companion
sections.content:
# Irenaeus of Lyons: *Adversus Haereses* Study Guide

**Attached to Online Source:** Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* (CCEL, c. AD 180)

---

## Spiritual Lineage
**Apostle John** (Ephesus) $\rightarrow$ **Polycarp of Smyrna** (Martyred c. 155) $\rightarrow$ **Irenaeus of Lyons** (c. 130–202).

## Valentinian Gnosticism vs. Irenaean Orthodoxy

| Theme | Valentinian Gnosticism | Irenaeus of Lyons |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Creator God** | Inferior/ignorant *Demiurge* distinct from supreme Father | One Almighty Father who created all things through His two "hands": Son and Spirit |
| **Material Body** | Prison to be escaped by pneumatic sparks | Good workmanship of God destined for resurrection glory |
| **Salvation** | Esoteric *gnosis* reserved for spiritual elites | Public apostolic Gospel accessible to all believers across the world |
| **Christology** | Heavenly Aeon descended on human Jesus at baptism and left before Cross | True Incarnation: the Eternal Word became real flesh, sanctified every stage of life, and rose bodily |

## Key Passage (Against Heresies III.18.1)
> "When He became incarnate and was made man, He commenced afresh the long line of human beings (*longam hominum expositionem in seipso recapitulavit*), and furnished us, in a brief, comprehensive manner, with salvation; so that what we had lost in Adam—namely, to be according to the image and likeness of God—that we might recover in Christ Jesus."

questions.prompt: Which first-century catechetical manual—rediscovered in 1873—begins with "There are two ways, one of life and one of death" and gives early instructions on baptism, fasting, and the Eucharist?
options: The Didache (Teaching of the Twelve Apostles)
questions.explanation: Dating to c. AD 50–100, the Didache offers a priceless window into Jewish-Christian moral instruction, baptismal practice, thrice-daily praying of the Lord’s Prayer, and Eucharistic thanksgiving.

questions.prompt: Against second-century Gnosticism, what did Irenaeus of Lyons teach under the concept of Recapitulation (anakephalaiōsis)?
options: That salvation requires escaping the physical body created by an inferior Demiurge
That the incarnate Son summed up and retraced every stage of Adam’s human life in obedience, reversing Adam’s fall and healing creation
That human souls reincarnate across successive cosmic cycles
That the Old Testament God of justice was abolished by Jesus
questions.explanation: Expounding Ephesians 1:10 and Romans 5:12–19 in Against Heresies, Irenaeus showed that the same Creator Word who fashioned Adam took real flesh to untie the knot of disobedience and bring humanity to maturity.
questions.sourceReference: Irenaeus of Lyons, Against Heresies III.18, V.1 (c. AD 180)

questions.prompt: En route to martyrdom in Rome (c. AD 110), Ignatius of Antioch urgently warned Asia Minor churches against Docetism—what did Docetists claim?
options: That Jesus was merely a political revolutionary who never claimed divine authority
That Christ only "seemed" (dokeō) to possess a physical body and suffer on the Cross, denying the reality of His flesh
That Christians must observe Levitical animal sacrifices
That bishops, presbyters, and deacons should be abolished
questions.explanation: Influenced by Hellenistic contempt for matter, Docetists denied that the divine Christ truly hungered, bled, died, and rose in the flesh—prompting Ignatius to insist that Christ was "truly born, truly crucified, and truly raised."
questions.sourceReference: Ignatius of Antioch, Epistle to the Trallians 9–10; Smyrnaeans 1–7

topics.title: Golden Age of the Fathers: East & West
topics.subtitle: Athanasius contra mundum, the Cappadocians, John Chrysostom, Jerome, and Augustine of Hippo.
topics.summary: Profiles the fourth- and fifth-century doctors of the Eastern and Western Church whose exegesis, preaching, translations, and treatises shaped all subsequent Christian thought.

sections.heading: Athanasius & the Cappadocian Fathers in the Greek East
sections.body: Exiled five times by emperors for refusing to compromise Nicene Christology ("Athanasius contra mundum"), Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373) anchored orthodoxy in soteriology: if the Son is not true God, he cannot unite us to God. Following him, the Cappadocian trio—Basil the Great (bishop, liturgical reformer, founder of charitable hospitals, author of On the Holy Spirit), his friend Gregory of Nazianzus ("the Theologian," master of the Five Theological Orations), and Basil’s younger brother Gregory of Nyssa (mystical philosopher of epektasis—infinite growth into the infinite God)—perfected Trinitarian theology. Alongside them, John Chrysostom ("Golden-Mouthed," c. 347–407) delivered peerless verse-by-verse homilies uniting Antiochene exegesis with prophetic care for the poor.

sections.heading: Ambrose, Jerome & Syriac Poetic Theology
sections.body: In the Latin West, Ambrose of Milan championed church independence from imperial tyranny and mentored a brilliant young rhetorician named Augustine, while Jerome of Stridon labored in Bethlehem learning Hebrew from Jewish scholars to translate the Latin Vulgate directly from the Hebraica veritas. Further east in Nisibis and Edessa, Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306–373), "Harp of the Spirit," demonstrated that profound Nicene theology could be sung through luminous Semitic hymnody (madrashe) and biblical paradox.

sections.heading: Augustine of Hippo: Architect of Western Theology
sections.body: Converted in a Milanese garden in AD 386 upon reading Romans 13:13–14, Augustine of Hippo (354–430) left an incomparable literary legacy: Confessions (inventing inward spiritual autobiography), On the Trinity, anti-Donatist writings (affirming that the validity of sacraments depends on Christ’s faithfulness rather than the minister’s moral perfection), anti-Pelagian treatises on sovereign grace, and The City of God (De Civitate Dei)—written after Alaric’s sack of Rome (410) to contrast the earthly city driven by self-love (amor sui) with the heavenly city ordered by love of God (amor Dei).

excerpts.title: If You Cannot Clothe Christ in the Poor, Why Adorn His Altar with Gold?
excerpts.author: John Chrysostom
excerpts.work: Homily 50 on the Gospel of Matthew, §3–4
excerpts.quote: Do you wish to honor the body of Christ? Do not ignore him when he is naked. Do not pay him homage in the temple clad in silk, only then to neglect him outside where he is cold and ill-clad.
excerpts.citation: Homily 50 on the Gospel of Matthew, §3–4

excerpts.title: Two Cities Formed by Two Loves
excerpts.author: Augustine of Hippo
excerpts.work: City of God, Book XIV, Ch. 28
excerpts.quote: Accordingly, two cities have been formed by two loves: the earthly by the love of self, even to the contempt of God; the heavenly by the love of God, even to the contempt of self.
excerpts.citation: City of God, Book XIV, Ch. 28

perspectives.summary: Venerates Basil the Great, Gregory the Theologian, and John Chrysostom liturgically as the "Three Holy Hierarchs," while engaging Augustine respectfully yet critically on Filioque and inherited guilt.

Both Thomas Aquinas and the sixteenth-century Reformers (Luther, Calvin) drew overwhelmingly on Augustine—making the Reformation in many respects an internal debate over Augustine’s doctrines of the Church and of Grace.

keyTerms.definition: "Against the world": proverb honoring Athanasius’s steadfast defense of Nicene orthodoxy during decades of imperial Arian dominance.
Love of God vs. disordered self-love—Augustine’s diagnostic key to human history, ethics, and politics in De Civitate Dei.

options: Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Gregory of Nyssa

questions.excerptContext: Accordingly, two cities have been formed by two loves: the earthly by the love of self, even to the contempt of God; the heavenly by the love of God, even to the contempt of self.
questions.explanation: Augustine labored from AD 413 to 426 on his twenty-two-book City of God to answer pagan charges that Christianity caused Rome’s fall and to distinguish transient earthly empires from God’s eternal Kingdom.

Learning Hebrew in Bethlehem and translating the Latin Vulgate directly from the Hebrew (Hebraica veritas) and Greek
Presiding over the Second Council of Nicaea in 787
Writing the Greek Ecclesiastical History of Constantine
questions.explanation: Commissioned by Pope Damasus I, Jerome revised the Old Latin Gospels and broke new ground among Western Fathers by studying Hebrew to translate the Old Testament directly rather than relying solely on the Greek Septuagint.
questions.sourceReference: Jerome, Prologus Galeatus & Letters from Bethlehem

topics.title: The Apostles’ & Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creeds
topics.subtitle: Baptismal symbols, Nicaea I (325), Constantinople I (381), and ecumenical liturgical unity.
topics.summary: Studies the origin, structure, and theological precision of Christianity’s most universally confessed statement of faith.

sections.heading: From Baptismal Interrogations to the Apostles’ Creed
sections.body: In the second and third centuries, candidates entering the baptismal waters answered three Trinitarian questions ("Do you believe in God the Father Almighty?... in Jesus Christ, His only Son?... in the Holy Spirit?"). In Rome, the Old Roman Symbol (c. AD 180–200) developed into the Western Apostles’ Creed, compactly narrating creation, Christ’s virginal conception, historical suffering under Pontius Pilate, resurrection, ascension, future judgment, the holy catholic Church, the communion of saints, forgiveness of sins, bodily resurrection, and life everlasting.

sections.heading: From Nicaea (325) to Constantinople (381)
sections.body: Convoked in 325 at Nicaea in Bithynia to resolve the Arian controversy, approximately 300 bishops adopted a creed declaring the Son "Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, of one substance (homoousios) with the Father," appending explicit anathemas against anyone claiming "there was when He was not." When Pneumatomachians ("Spirit-fighters" or Macedonians) subsequently denied the deity of the Holy Spirit, the First Council of Constantinople (381) expanded the third article, confessing the Holy Spirit as "the Lord, the Giver of Life, who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son together is worshiped and glorified, who spoke by the prophets."

sections.heading: Enduring Function of Creeds as Norma Normata
sections.body: Across Eastern Orthodox, Roman Catholic, Oriental Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran, Reformed, and Methodist worship, the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed serves as the shared ecumenical grammar of Christian identity—never replacing Scripture, but functioning as a faithful, tested summary (norma normata, "a ruled rule") guarding the biblical witness against recurring distortions.

topics.subtitle: From Ephesus (431) and Chalcedon (451) through Nicaea II (787) to Catechisms.
topics.summary: Charts the doctrinal arc of all Seven Ecumenical Councils alongside the great sixteenth- and seventeenth-century Protestant confessions and catechisms.

sections.heading: The First Four Councils: Trinity & Incarnation
sections.body: Pope Gregory the Great famously revered the first four ecumenical councils alongside the four Gospels: (1) Nicaea I (325) condemned Arius and confessed the Son homoousios with the Father; (2) Constantinople I (381) condemned Apollinarianism and Macedonians, affirming the Spirit’s deity; (3) Ephesus (431) condemned Nestorius (and Pelagianism), upholding Cyril’s Christology and Mary as Theotokos; and (4) Chalcedon (451) condemned Eutychian monophysitism, defining one Person in two complete natures without confusion, change, division, or separation.

sections.heading: Councils Five Through Seven: Neo-Chalcedonianism, Two Wills & Icons
sections.body: Three further councils completed the patristic conciliar cycle: (5) Constantinople II (553) interpreted Chalcedon in continuity with Cyril of Alexandria ("Three Chapters" debate); (6) Constantinople III (680–681), drawing on Maximus the Confessor, rejected Monothelitism ("one will") and affirmed that Christ possesses both a divine will and a free human will acting in unforced harmony; and (7) Nicaea II (787), drawing on John of Damascus during the Iconoclastic Controversy, distinguished veneration/honor (proskynēsis/dulia) offered through sacred icons to their prototype from supreme worship (latria) owed to God alone, grounding Christian art in the reality of the Incarnation.

sections.heading: Confessional Standards & Catechetical Paideia
sections.body: In the Reformation and Post-Reformation eras, churches reaffirmed the ancient Trinitarian and Christological councils while articulating detailed confessional standards and pedagogical catechisms (paideia): Luther’s Small and Large Catechisms (1529), the Augsburg Confession (1530), the Belgic Confession (1561), the warm pastoral Heidelberg Catechism (1563), the Thirty-Nine Articles (1563/1571), the Canons of Dort (1619), the Westminster Confession & Shorter/Larger Catechisms (1646–1647), the Second London Baptist Confession (1689), and the Roman Catechism of Trent (1566) alongside Eastern Orthodox confessions such as Dositheus (1672).

topics.title: What Is Apologetics?
topics.subtitle: Apologetics
topics.summary: The reasoned defense of the Christian faith: its biblical mandate, its history, and the main schools of method from classical to presuppositional.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: *Apologetics* is the branch of theology concerned with giving reasons for the truth of the Christian faith and answering objections to it. The word comes from the Greek *apologia*, a legal term for a speech of defense in court. It does not mean apologizing in the modern sense of expressing regret.

sections.heading: The Biblical Mandate
sections.body:
The classic text is 1 Peter 3:15, which in the King James Version reads:

> But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear.

The word translated "answer" is *apologia*. The verse joins two things: being ready with reasons, and giving them with gentleness and respect. Other passages show the apostles reasoning in public. Paul debated in the synagogue and marketplace at Athens and addressed the Areopagus (Acts 17:16-34), and Jude 3 urges believers to "earnestly contend for the faith."

sections.heading: A Brief History
sections.body: In the second century, writers such as **Justin Martyr** addressed "apologies" to Roman emperors, defending Christians against charges of atheism and immorality. Augustine's *City of God* answered pagan claims that Christianity caused the fall of Rome. In the Middle Ages, Anselm and Thomas Aquinas developed arguments for God's existence. The modern period brought responses to Deism, to Hume's critique of miracles, and to Darwinism. In the twentieth century, C. S. Lewis popularized apologetics, and analytic philosophers of religion such as Alvin Plantinga and Richard Swinburne gave it new academic standing.

sections.heading: Schools of Method
sections.body:
Apologists agree that Christianity is reasonable, but they disagree about where to begin. Five approaches are commonly distinguished:

1. **Classical apologetics** proceeds in two steps: first establish theism through natural theology (for example the cosmological argument), then argue from historical evidence that the God so established has revealed himself in Christ. R. C. Sproul and Norman Geisler are representatives.
2. **Evidential apologetics** argues that historical evidence, especially for the resurrection, can itself support both God's existence and Christianity in one step. Gary Habermas and John Warwick Montgomery are associated with it.
3. **Presuppositional apologetics**, developed by **Cornelius Van Til** and popularized by Greg Bahnsen, holds that there is no neutral ground between believer and unbeliever. Rather than reasoning toward God from shared premises, it argues that only the Christian worldview supplies the preconditions of logic, science, and morality (the "transcendental argument").
4. **Cumulative-case apologetics** compares worldviews the way a lawyer or historian weighs a case: no single argument is decisive, but many lines of evidence together make Christianity the best explanation. Basil Mitchell and C. S. Lewis are often cited.
5. **Reformed epistemology**, associated with **Alvin Plantinga** and Nicholas Wolterstorff, argues that belief in God can be *properly basic*: rational without being inferred from arguments, much as belief in other minds or the reality of the past is rational without proof.

These schools overlap in practice, and many apologists combine them.

sections.heading: Criticisms and Cautions
sections.body: Critics from outside the faith argue that apologetics starts with its conclusion and works backward. Some theologians also raise concerns from within. Karl Barth worried that natural theology lets human reason sit in judgment over revelation, and Kierkegaard thought that defending Christianity with probabilities misunderstands faith. Apologists reply that Scripture itself appeals to evidence (1 Corinthians 15:3-8) and that reasons can remove obstacles to faith without replacing it.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: Apologetics serves three audiences: skeptics who want reasons, believers whose faith is shaken by doubt, and the wider culture in which Christian claims are debated. Its best practitioners treat it as an act of love and honesty as much as of argument, in line with the "meekness and fear" of 1 Peter 3:15.

keyTerms.definition: Greek term for a formal speech of defense, especially in a law court; the root of "apologetics."

In Reformed epistemology, a belief that is rational to hold without being inferred from other beliefs or arguments.
An approach that weighs many lines of evidence together, arguing that Christianity is the best overall explanation.

topics.title: The Cosmological Argument
topics.subtitle: Apologetics
topics.summary: Arguments from the existence of the world to a first cause or necessary being, in Thomistic, Leibnizian, and kalam forms.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: The *cosmological argument* reasons from the existence of the universe, or of things within it, to a cause or explanation that lies beyond it. It is not one argument but a family. Three versions dominate the discussion: the **Thomistic**, the **Leibnizian**, and the **kalam**. Scripture does not set out a formal argument, but it does affirm that God's "eternal power and Godhead" are understood "by the things that are made" (Romans 1:20).

sections.heading: The Thomistic Version
sections.body:
In his *Summa Theologiae* (part I, question 2, article 3), Thomas Aquinas (1225-1274) offered "Five Ways" of showing that God exists. The first three are cosmological: from motion (change), from efficient causation, and from contingency. The Third Way concludes:

> Therefore we cannot but postulate the existence of some being having of itself its own necessity, and not receiving it from another, but rather causing in others their necessity. This all men speak of as God.

A key point is often missed. Aquinas did **not** think reason could prove that the world had a beginning in time; he accepted that on the authority of revelation. His arguments target an *essentially ordered* series of causes, in which each member depends on a prior one *here and now* (as a hand moves a stick that moves a stone). Such a series, he argued, cannot regress infinitely without a first cause that is itself uncaused, even if the universe were eternal.

sections.heading: The Leibnizian Contingency Argument
sections.body: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646-1716) built his argument on the **principle of sufficient reason**: for every fact there is a reason why it is so and not otherwise. In *Principles of Nature and Grace* he asked the famous question, "Why is there something rather than nothing?" Every contingent thing (something that could have failed to exist) has its explanation in something else. But the whole collection of contingent things is itself contingent, so its explanation must lie in a *necessary being* that exists by the necessity of its own nature.

sections.heading: The Kalam Argument
sections.body:
The *kalam* argument takes its name from medieval Islamic theology (*kalam*), where al-Ghazali (died 1111) defended it; the Christian philosopher John Philoponus had argued similarly in the sixth century. William Lane Craig revived it in *The Kalam Cosmological Argument* (1979):

1. Whatever begins to exist has a cause.
2. The universe began to exist.
3. Therefore, the universe has a cause.

Craig defends the second premise philosophically (an actually infinite series of past events is impossible) and scientifically (Big Bang cosmology and the second law of thermodynamics). He then argues that the cause must be timeless, spaceless, immensely powerful, and personal.

sections.heading: Objections
sections.body:
- **Who caused God?** Defenders reply that the arguments claim only that *contingent* things, or things that *begin to exist*, need causes; God is held to be neither.
- **Fallacy of composition.** David Hume, and Bertrand Russell in his 1948 radio debate with Frederick Copleston, objected that explaining each member of a series does not require explaining the whole; the universe might be a "brute fact."
- **The principle of sufficient reason** is denied by many philosophers, who see no reason it must hold universally.
- **Physics.** Critics question whether Big Bang cosmology proves an absolute beginning, and point to quantum events that seem to lack deterministic causes. Defenders reply that quantum events still occur within a physical framework rather than from nothing.
- **The gap problem.** Even if a first cause exists, further argument is needed to show it is the personal God of theism.

sections.heading: Assessment
sections.body: The cosmological argument remains one of the most debated topics in philosophy of religion. Its strongest forms do not claim to prove the God of Christian revelation; they aim to show that the existence of a contingent world points beyond itself to a necessary ground, leaving other arguments and revelation to say more about who that ground is.

keyTerms.definition: The property of existing but being able not to have existed; a contingent being depends on something else for its existence.
A being that exists by the necessity of its own nature and cannot fail to exist.
Leibniz's principle that for every fact there is a reason why it is so and not otherwise.
Medieval Islamic dialectical theology; the source of the argument that whatever begins to exist has a cause.
A causal series in which each member depends on a prior member here and now, as opposed to a series stretching back in time.

topics.title: The Teleological (Design) Argument
topics.subtitle: Apologetics
topics.summary: Arguments from order, purpose, and the fine-tuning of the universe to an intelligent designer, with the classic objections of Hume and Darwin.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: The *teleological argument* (from Greek *telos*, "end" or "purpose") infers an intelligent designer from features of the world that appear purposeful. Versions go back to Plato, the Stoics, and Aquinas's Fifth Way, and the theme is biblical: "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork" (Psalm 19:1). The argument has passed through two main forms: the biological design argument associated with William Paley, and the modern **fine-tuning** argument from physics.

sections.heading: Paley's Watchmaker
sections.body:
William Paley (1743-1805) opened his *Natural Theology* (1802) with a famous illustration:

> In crossing a heath, suppose I pitched my foot against a stone, and were asked how the stone came to be there; I might possibly answer, that, for anything I knew to the contrary, it had lain there for ever.

But if he found a watch, he could not give the same answer. Its parts are arranged so as to serve a purpose, telling time, and this arrangement points to a watchmaker. Paley then argued that living things, such as the eye, show far greater contrivance than any watch, and so point to a far greater designer.

sections.heading: Hume's Objections
sections.body:
David Hume's *Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion*, published posthumously in 1779 (before Paley wrote), had already put pressure on design reasoning through the character Philo:

- **Weak analogy.** The universe is not very much like a machine; it may resemble an animal or a vegetable as much as a watch.
- **Limited conclusion.** At most the argument shows a designer proportioned to the effect. Why one designer rather than many? Why an infinite or perfect one? The world could be the crude first attempt of an "infant deity."
- **Regress.** If order requires a designer, what explains the designer's own order?

sections.heading: Darwin's Challenge
sections.body: Charles Darwin's *On the Origin of Species* (1859) offered a natural mechanism, **natural selection** acting on variation, that could produce the appearance of design in organisms without a designer. For many, this undercut Paley's biological argument. Some theists, such as the American botanist Asa Gray, responded that evolution could itself be the means of God's design. More recently, proponents of *intelligent design* such as Michael Behe have argued that some biological systems are "irreducibly complex," a claim most biologists reject.

sections.heading: The Fine-Tuning Argument
sections.body:
The most discussed modern version shifts from biology to physics. Many physical constants and initial conditions, such as the strength of gravity, the cosmological constant, and the ratio of the fundamental forces, appear to fall within narrow ranges that permit life. Had they been slightly different, stars, chemistry, or life would not be possible. Defenders such as Robin Collins argue that this is far more probable on theism than on a single, undesigned universe.

Critics respond in several ways:

- **The multiverse.** If there are vast numbers of universes with different constants, some will be life-permitting by chance. Defenders reply that the multiverse is speculative and may itself require fine-tuning.
- **The anthropic principle.** We could only observe a universe compatible with our existence, so we should not be surprised to find one. Defenders answer with John Leslie's firing-squad analogy: a man who survives a firing squad of fifty marksmen should not shrug and say he could only observe his survival; he should suspect the miss was intended.
- **Necessity or deeper laws.** Perhaps a future physical theory will show the constants could not have been otherwise.
- **Probability problems.** Some philosophers question whether we can meaningfully assign probabilities to ranges of possible constants.

sections.heading: Assessment
sections.body: Darwin weakened the biological design argument in its classic form, but the fine-tuning argument has given design reasoning renewed attention among philosophers and physicists. Like other theistic arguments, it is usually presented today as raising the probability of theism rather than as a strict proof, and it says little by itself about the designer's identity.

keyTerms.definition: The study of purposes or ends; from Greek telos, "end."
Paley's argument that, as a watch implies a watchmaker, the contrivance of living things implies a designer.
Darwin's mechanism by which heritable variations that aid survival and reproduction accumulate, producing apparent design.
The claim that physical constants and initial conditions fall within narrow ranges necessary for life.
The observation that we can only observe a universe compatible with the existence of observers.
The hypothesis that many universes exist with varying constants, offered as an alternative explanation of fine-tuning.

topics.title: The Moral Argument
topics.subtitle: Apologetics
topics.summary: Arguments that objective moral values and duties are best explained by God, along with the Euthyphro dilemma and secular alternatives.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: The *moral argument* holds that the existence of objective morality points to God. Its proponents claim that the binding force of moral obligation and the reality of moral goodness are best explained if there is a perfectly good, personal God. Paul describes Gentiles who "shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness" (Romans 2:15), and moral arguments can be read as philosophical reflections on that theme.

sections.heading: Historical Forms
sections.body:
**Immanuel Kant** (1724-1804) famously rejected the traditional proofs of God's existence, but in the *Critique of Practical Reason* (1788) he argued that morality requires us to *postulate* God. Morality commands us to pursue the highest good, a state in which virtue is matched by happiness. Since we cannot bring this about ourselves and nature does not guarantee it, rational moral agents must postulate a God who can. Kant presented this as a practical requirement rather than a theoretical proof.

**John Henry Newman** argued from conscience: the experience of guilt, shame, and accountability implies a personal lawgiver before whom we are responsible. In the twentieth century, **C. S. Lewis** opened *Mere Christianity* with an argument from the universal human sense of a moral law that we know we ought to obey but do not.

sections.heading: The Contemporary Argument
sections.body:
A widely discussed version, defended by William Lane Craig, runs:

1. If God does not exist, objective moral values and duties do not exist.
2. Objective moral values and duties do exist.
3. Therefore, God exists.

"Objective" here means valid and binding independently of whether any human being believes them. Defenders of premise 2 appeal to moral experience: we apprehend that torturing children for fun is wrong as clearly as we apprehend the external world. Defenders of premise 1 argue that on naturalism, morality is ultimately a product of evolution and culture, which may explain why we *believe* in morality but not why moral claims are *true* or why duties have authority over us. Other versions, by philosophers such as Robert Adams and C. Stephen Evans, argue more modestly that theism explains moral facts better than its rivals.

sections.heading: The Euthyphro Dilemma
sections.body:
The most famous objection comes from Plato's dialogue *Euthyphro*, where Socrates asks (in Jowett's translation) "whether the pious or holy is beloved by the gods because it is holy, or holy because it is beloved of the gods." Applied to monotheism: is something good because God commands it, or does God command it because it is good?

- If good because commanded, morality seems **arbitrary**: God could have commanded cruelty.
- If commanded because good, goodness seems **independent of God**, and God is not needed to explain it.

Theists commonly reply by rejecting the dilemma's two options. Moral **goodness** is grounded in God's own nature, which is essentially good and not arbitrary, while moral **obligations** are grounded in God's commands, which flow from that nature. This is the core of Robert Adams's modified divine command theory. Critics respond that this relocates the dilemma: is God's nature good because it is God's, or because it meets an independent standard?

sections.heading: Other Objections
sections.body:
- **Secular moral realism.** Many philosophers hold that objective moral facts exist without God, as basic, necessary truths (non-natural realism) or as facts about human flourishing. On their view premise 1 is simply false.
- **Anti-realism.** Others deny premise 2, holding that morality is constructed or expressive of attitudes, not objective.
- **Moral knowledge without belief.** Theists agree that atheists can know and do what is right; the argument concerns the *grounding* of morality, not whether unbelievers can be moral. Confusing the two is a common misunderstanding on both sides.

sections.heading: Assessment
sections.body: The moral argument has wide intuitive appeal because nearly everyone acts as though some things are really right or wrong. Its success depends on contested questions in metaethics: whether moral facts can stand on their own, and whether a theistic grounding avoids the Euthyphro problem. It is often used alongside the cosmological and teleological arguments in a cumulative case.

keyTerms.definition: The view that there are objective moral facts that hold independently of human beliefs or attitudes.
The question from Plato's Euthyphro whether something is good because God commands it or commanded because it is good.
The view that moral obligations are constituted by the commands of God.
Kant's term for something, such as God, that must be assumed for moral action to be rational, though it cannot be proven theoretically.
The branch of ethics that asks what moral claims mean and what, if anything, makes them true.

topics.title: The Ontological Argument
topics.subtitle: Apologetics
topics.summary: Anselm's argument from the concept of "that than which nothing greater can be conceived," its critics from Gaunilo to Kant, and Plantinga's modal version.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: The *ontological argument* is unique among theistic arguments because it tries to prove God's existence from the concept of God alone, without appeal to experience of the world. Admirers find it profound; critics find it a clever trick. Bertrand Russell remarked that it is easier to feel convinced it must be fallacious than to say exactly where the fallacy lies.

sections.heading: Anselm's Argument
sections.body:
Anselm of Canterbury (c. 1033-1109) set out the argument in chapter 2 of his *Proslogion* (1077-1078), a work written as a prayer. He begins from the fool of Psalm 14:1, who "hath said in his heart, There is no God." Even the fool understands the phrase "a being than which nothing greater can be conceived," so that being exists at least in the understanding. Anselm continues (Deane's translation):

> And assuredly that, than which nothing greater can be conceived, cannot exist in the understanding alone. For, suppose it exists in the understanding alone: then it can be conceived to exist in reality; which is greater.

The argument is a *reductio ad absurdum*. If the greatest conceivable being existed only in the mind, we could conceive something greater, namely that same being existing in reality. That is a contradiction, so the being must exist in reality. In chapter 3 Anselm adds a second form: a being that *cannot be conceived not to exist* is greater than one that can, so God cannot even be conceived not to exist.

sections.heading: Gaunilo's Lost Island
sections.body:
A monk named **Gaunilo of Marmoutiers** replied with *On Behalf of the Fool*. Imagine an island more excellent than all others. By Anselm's reasoning, it must exist, since an island existing in reality is more excellent than one existing only in the mind. Since that conclusion is absurd, Anselm's reasoning must be flawed. Anselm answered that his argument applies only to the greatest conceivable *being*, not to things like islands, which have no intrinsic maximum of greatness.

**Thomas Aquinas** also rejected the argument (*Summa Theologiae* I, question 2, article 1), arguing that we do not know God's essence well enough for "God exists" to be self-evident to us. **René Descartes**, by contrast, offered his own version in the fifth *Meditation*, arguing that existence can no more be separated from the idea of a supremely perfect being than the equality of its three angles to two right angles can be separated from the idea of a triangle.

sections.heading: Kant's Objection
sections.body: Immanuel Kant, in the *Critique of Pure Reason* (1781), coined the name "ontological argument" and gave the most influential objection: **existence is not a real predicate**. To say a thing exists is not to add a property to its concept, as "red" or "wise" do. A hundred real coins contain no more coins than a hundred imagined ones. If existence is not a property that makes something greater, Anselm's key step fails. Defenders debate whether Kant's point applies to *necessary* existence, which seems to be a genuine perfection.

sections.heading: Plantinga's Modal Version
sections.body:
In the twentieth century Charles Hartshorne and Norman Malcolm revived Anselm's second form. **Alvin Plantinga** gave the best-known version in *The Nature of Necessity* (1974), using possible-worlds semantics. Define a *maximally great* being as one that is omnipotent, omniscient, and morally perfect in every possible world. Then:

1. It is possible that a maximally great being exists.
2. If so, it exists in some possible world.
3. But a maximally great being, by definition, exists in every possible world.
4. So it exists in the actual world.

The argument is valid in the widely used modal system S5. Everything therefore turns on premise 1. Critics note that one could run a parallel argument: "It is possible that no maximally great being exists," which in S5 entails that none exists. Plantinga himself conceded that the argument does not prove God's existence to someone who doubts the possibility premise, but claimed it shows that belief in God is rationally acceptable.

sections.heading: Assessment
sections.body: Few philosophers think the ontological argument persuades on its own, yet it continues to draw serious attention because it raises deep questions about existence, necessity, and conceivability. For Anselm, it was also an act of devotion: faith seeking understanding of the God it already loved.

keyTerms.definition: An argument whose premises can be known independently of sense experience.
A form of argument that proves a claim by showing that its denial leads to a contradiction.
In Plantinga's argument, the property of having omnipotence, omniscience, and moral perfection in every possible world.
A complete way things could have been; used in modal logic to analyze possibility and necessity.
Kant's objection that existence does not add a property to the concept of a thing.

topics.title: The Problem of Evil
topics.subtitle: Apologetics
topics.summary: The challenge that suffering poses to belief in an all-powerful, all-good God: logical and evidential forms, defenses and theodicies.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body:
The *problem of evil* is widely regarded as the most serious objection to belief in God. It asks how an all-powerful, all-knowing, and perfectly good God could allow the vast amount of suffering in the world. Scripture does not avoid the question: Job, the lament psalms, and Habakkuk all cry out to God about unjust suffering (Habakkuk 1:2-4).

The classic formulation, traditionally credited to Epicurus, is voiced by Philo in Hume's *Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion*:

> Is he willing to prevent evil, but not able? then is he impotent. Is he able, but not willing? then is he malevolent. Is he both able and willing? whence then is evil?

Philosophers distinguish **moral evil** (wrongs done by free agents, such as murder) from **natural evil** (suffering from natural causes, such as disease and earthquakes).

sections.heading: The Logical Problem
sections.body:
The *logical problem* claims that the existence of God and the existence of evil are strictly inconsistent: they cannot both be true. J. L. Mackie pressed this in his essay "Evil and Omnipotence" (1955).

Alvin Plantinga replied with the **free-will defense** (*God, Freedom, and Evil*, 1974). He argued that it is *possible* that God could not create a world containing morally significant free creatures who never do wrong, because what free creatures do is up to them. A world with free creatures who sometimes choose evil may be better than a world with no free creatures at all. Since this is possible, God and evil are not logically incompatible. Many philosophers, including many non-theists, agree that this answers the logical problem in its strict form.

sections.heading: The Evidential Problem
sections.body:
The *evidential problem* concedes that God and evil are logically compatible but argues that the amount and kinds of evil make God's existence *improbable*. William Rowe's 1979 article described a fawn trapped in a forest fire, burned and suffering for days before dying, unseen by anyone. Such suffering seems pointless: we cannot see any greater good it serves. Rowe argued that if there is pointless suffering, there is no God.

Responses include:

- **Skeptical theism** (Stephen Wykstra and others): given the vast gap between divine and human knowledge, we should not expect to see God's reasons, so our failure to see a purpose is weak evidence that none exists. Critics worry this undermines our ability to make any moral judgment.
- **Greater-good theodicies** that try to identify the goods suffering makes possible.
- **The cumulative case:** theists argue that evidence for God from other arguments outweighs the evidence from evil.

sections.heading: Defense and Theodicy
sections.body:
A **defense** aims only to show that God and evil are compatible, offering a possible reason God might have, whether or not it is the actual one. A **theodicy** (a term coined by Leibniz) attempts to state God's actual reasons for permitting evil. Plantinga's free-will defense is a defense; the following are theodicies.

### The Augustinian Tradition

Augustine (354-430) held that evil is not a substance but a *privation of good* (*privatio boni*), like blindness as the absence of sight. God created all things good; evil entered through the free rebellion of angels and humans, and natural evil follows from the Fall. God permits evil because he can bring good even out of it.

### The Soul-Making Theodicy

John Hick, in *Evil and the God of Love* (1966), developed what he called an **Irenaean** theodicy, drawing on Irenaeus of Lyons. Humans were created immature and are meant to grow into moral and spiritual maturity. A world with real challenges, dangers, and pain is a "vale of soul-making" in which virtues like courage, compassion, and perseverance can develop. Critics ask whether the amount and intensity of suffering, especially suffering that crushes rather than builds character, can be justified this way.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: For many people the problem of evil is not an abstract puzzle but a lived crisis. Christian thinkers often add that philosophy alone is not the whole response: the Christian story tells of a God who enters suffering in Christ, and promises a future in which "God shall wipe away all tears" (Revelation 21:4). Paul wrote that present sufferings "are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us" (Romans 8:18).

keyTerms.definition: Evil caused by the free choices of moral agents, such as cruelty or murder.
Suffering arising from natural processes, such as disease, earthquakes, and famine.
An argument showing that God and evil are compatible by offering a possible reason for evil, without claiming it is God's actual reason.
An attempt to justify God by stating his actual reasons for permitting evil; a term coined by Leibniz.
Augustine's view that evil is not a thing in itself but a privation or absence of good.
The view that human inability to discern God's reasons for permitting evil is not good evidence that there are none.

topics.title: The Resurrection: The Historical Case
topics.subtitle: Apologetics
topics.summary: How apologists argue historically for the resurrection of Jesus, the "minimal facts" approach, and the rival hypotheses proposed by skeptics.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: Christianity stakes itself on a historical claim. Paul wrote, "if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain" (1 Corinthians 15:14). Because of this, many apologists, especially evidentialists, have made the resurrection of Jesus the center of their case. This article outlines the historical argument as its defenders present it and the main replies of skeptical scholars.

sections.heading: The Earliest Testimony
sections.body: The oldest written account is not in the Gospels but in Paul's first letter to the Corinthians (written in the mid-50s AD). In 1 Corinthians 15:3-8 Paul says he "delivered" what he had "received": that Christ died for our sins, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to Cephas (Peter), to the Twelve, to more than five hundred at once, to James, to all the apostles, and finally to Paul himself. The language of receiving and delivering is technical vocabulary for handing on tradition, and many scholars, including skeptical ones, think this creed dates to within a few years of the crucifixion.

sections.heading: The Minimal Facts Approach
sections.body:
Gary Habermas and Michael Licona, in *The Case for the Resurrection of Jesus* (2004), popularized the **minimal facts** method. It uses only facts that are well supported by evidence and accepted by a large majority of scholars who study the subject, including skeptics:

1. Jesus died by crucifixion.
2. His disciples sincerely believed that he rose and appeared to them.
3. Paul, a persecutor of the church, was converted after what he believed was an appearance of the risen Jesus.
4. James, the brother of Jesus and formerly a skeptic, was converted.

A fifth fact, that **the tomb was empty**, is often added, though Habermas acknowledges it is accepted by a smaller majority than the core four. The argument then asks which hypothesis best explains these facts.

sections.heading: The Empty Tomb
sections.body: Arguments for the empty tomb include its place in early tradition (Mark 16:1-8), the fact that the message was proclaimed in Jerusalem where it could easily be checked, and the early Jewish counter-claim that the disciples stole the body (Matthew 28:11-15), which presupposes the tomb was empty. Apologists also point to the *criterion of embarrassment*: all four Gospels name women as the first witnesses, although women's testimony carried little weight in that culture, so the detail is unlikely to have been invented. Skeptics such as Bart Ehrman doubt that Jesus received an honorable burial at all, and some regard the tomb story as a later development.

sections.heading: Rival Hypotheses
sections.body:
- **Theft.** The disciples stole the body. Critics note that the disciples' willingness to suffer for their claim suggests sincere belief, not fraud.
- **Swoon.** Jesus did not die but revived in the tomb. Most scholars reject this, given Roman expertise in execution; a half-dead Jesus would hardly inspire belief in a glorious resurrection.
- **Wrong tomb.** The women went to the wrong grave, as Kirsopp Lake suggested in 1907. Opponents reply that the authorities could have pointed to the right one.
- **Hallucination.** The disciples experienced grief-induced visions; Gerd Lüdemann is a prominent advocate. Defenders reply that hallucinations are private, whereas the tradition reports group appearances, and that visions would not explain an empty tomb or the conversion of a hostile Paul.
- **Legend.** The stories grew over time. Defenders answer that the 1 Corinthians 15 creed is too early for legend to have displaced the core facts.

N. T. Wright's *The Resurrection of the Son of God* (2003) adds that Jewish resurrection hope concerned the bodily raising of all the righteous at the end of history; the disciples' claim that one man had been raised in the middle of history was a striking mutation that requires explanation.

sections.heading: The Question of Miracles
sections.body: Underlying the debate is a philosophical question. David Hume argued in his *Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding* (1748) that testimony can never establish a miracle, because the evidence for the uniformity of nature will always be stronger. Many historians hold that their discipline cannot, by its methods, conclude that God acted. Dale Allison, for example, grants that the empty tomb and appearances are historically plausible but argues that history alone cannot settle what caused them. Apologists reply that if God's existence is a live possibility, a resurrection is not ruled out in advance, and that the evidence should be weighed on its merits.

sections.heading: Assessment
sections.body: The historical case does not compel belief, and much depends on one's prior view of God and miracles. But the core facts are widely accepted, and explaining them is a genuine historical problem that skeptical and believing scholars continue to debate.

keyTerms.definition: A method using only well-evidenced facts accepted by most scholars, including skeptics, to argue for the resurrection.
The tradition in 1 Corinthians 15:3-7 that Paul says he received, widely dated to within a few years of the crucifixion.
The historical principle that details awkward for the early church are unlikely to have been invented.
The theory that Jesus did not die on the cross but revived in the tomb.
The theory that the resurrection appearances were subjective visions experienced by grieving followers.

topics.title: The Old Testament Canon
topics.subtitle: Bible History
topics.summary: How the Hebrew Bible took shape, the role of the Septuagint, and why Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant Old Testaments differ.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: The word *canon* comes from a Greek term for a measuring rod or rule. Applied to Scripture, it means the list of books recognized as authoritative. Christians agree on the core of the Old Testament, but Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant Bibles differ in the number of books they include. Understanding why requires looking at both Jewish and Christian history.

sections.heading: The Hebrew Bible (Tanakh)
sections.body:
The Jewish Scriptures are called the **Tanakh**, an acronym for their three divisions:

1. **Torah** (Law): Genesis through Deuteronomy.
2. **Nevi'im** (Prophets): the Former Prophets (Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings) and the Latter Prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the Twelve).
3. **Ketuvim** (Writings): Psalms, Proverbs, Job, the five scrolls (Song of Songs, Ruth, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes, Esther), Daniel, Ezra-Nehemiah, and Chronicles.

Counted this way the Tanakh has **24 books**, since Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, Ezra-Nehemiah, and the twelve Minor Prophets are each counted as one. A threefold shape appears in Jesus' reference to "the law of Moses, and... the prophets, and... the psalms" (Luke 24:44). The Jewish historian Josephus, writing near the end of the first century AD, described a fixed collection of 22 books (*Against Apion* 1.8), probably the same books counted differently.

When and how the Jewish canon was closed is debated. An older theory held that a rabbinic "Council of Jamnia" (Yavneh) fixed the canon around AD 90. Most scholars now reject the idea of a formal council there, though discussions about books such as Ecclesiastes and Song of Songs did take place. Many date the effective closing of the Writings somewhere between the second century BC and the second century AD.

sections.heading: The Septuagint
sections.body: From the third century BC, Jews in Alexandria translated their Scriptures into Greek. This translation, the **Septuagint** (abbreviated LXX), became the Bible of Greek-speaking Jews and of the early church; most Old Testament quotations in the New Testament reflect it. The Christian manuscripts of the Septuagint that survive include additional books not in the Hebrew canon: Tobit, Judith, the Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach (Ecclesiasticus), Baruch, 1 and 2 Maccabees, and additions to Esther and Daniel. Whether the Jewish community in Alexandria regarded these as Scripture is uncertain.

sections.heading: The Christian Canons
sections.body:
**The Roman Catholic Church** includes seven additional books (Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, 1 and 2 Maccabees) plus the additions to Esther and Daniel, for a 46-book Old Testament. Catholics call them **deuterocanonical** ("second canon"), meaning recognized later, not of lesser authority. Regional councils at Hippo (393) and Carthage (397) listed them, and the Council of Trent defined the canon dogmatically in 1546.

**The Eastern Orthodox churches** accept these books and several more, such as 1 Esdras, 3 Maccabees, the Prayer of Manasseh, and an additional psalm numbered 151; the Synod of Jerusalem (1672) affirmed the broader canon. Orthodox usage is not entirely uniform, and the Ethiopian Orthodox canon is broader still, including 1 Enoch and Jubilees.

**Protestant churches** follow the Hebrew canon, though in a different order and divided into **39 books**. The Reformers appealed to Jerome, who had distinguished the Hebrew books from those the church read for edification. Luther's German Bible (1534) gathered these books into a separate section titled *Apocrypha*. The Church of England's Thirty-Nine Articles (Article VI) states:

> And the other Books (as Hierome saith) the Church doth read for example of life and instruction of manners; but yet doth it not apply them to establish any doctrine.

The Westminster Confession (1646) took a firmer line, declaring that the Apocrypha are no part of the canon. Protestants usually call these books the **Apocrypha** ("hidden" books).

sections.heading: Arguments on Each Side
sections.body: Protestants argue that the Hebrew canon was the Scripture of Jesus and the apostles, that the New Testament never explicitly quotes the deuterocanonical books as Scripture, and that Jerome and other early scholars questioned them. Catholics and Orthodox reply that the early church widely used and quoted these books, that the Septuagint was the church's Old Testament, and that the church received them through its councils and liturgy. All sides agree that the books are valuable for understanding the period between the Testaments.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: The canon question touches on authority: who recognizes Scripture, and on what basis? It also has practical effects; for example, 2 Maccabees 12 has been cited in Catholic discussions of prayer for the dead. Knowing the history helps readers understand why their neighbors' Bibles may contain different books.

topics.title: The New Testament Canon
topics.subtitle: Bible History
topics.summary: How the church came to recognize 27 books as the New Testament, from early collections and the Muratorian fragment to Athanasius and the councils.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: The 27 books of the New Testament were written in the first century, but the church's recognition of exactly these 27 as a closed collection took several centuries. The process was gradual, largely unofficial, and driven more by use in worship than by decrees.

sections.heading: Early Collections
sections.body:
From the beginning, Christians treated the Old Testament as Scripture and gave the words of Jesus supreme authority. Collections of apostolic writings formed early: 2 Peter 3:15-16 already speaks of Paul's letters alongside "the other scriptures." By the mid-second century, Justin Martyr reports that the "memoirs of the apostles" were read in Sunday worship alongside the prophets.

Challenges sharpened the question. Around 144, **Marcion** of Sinope rejected the Old Testament and accepted only an edited Gospel of Luke and ten letters of Paul. Gnostic groups produced their own gospels. In response, **Irenaeus** of Lyons (c. 180) insisted that there are four Gospels, no more and no fewer, in *Against Heresies*.

sections.heading: The Muratorian Fragment
sections.body:
The **Muratorian fragment** is a Latin list of New Testament books discovered by the Italian scholar Ludovico Antonio Muratori in a manuscript in Milan and published in 1740. Its beginning is lost; it starts by calling Luke "the third book of the Gospel." It then lists John, Acts, thirteen letters of Paul, Jude, two letters of John, and the Revelation of John, along with the Wisdom of Solomon and the Apocalypse of Peter (which, it notes, some do not want read in church). It allows the Shepherd of Hermas for private reading but not public reading as Scripture, and rejects letters forged in Paul's name to promote Marcion's views. Hebrews, James, and the letters of Peter are not mentioned.

Most scholars date the list to the late second century, partly because it describes the Shepherd as written "very recently, in our times." A minority, including Albert Sundberg and Geoffrey Hahneman, have argued for a fourth-century date.

sections.heading: Disputed Books
sections.body:
By around 200, a core of four Gospels, Acts, thirteen Pauline letters, 1 Peter, and 1 John was widely accepted. Other books were debated for longer. In his *Church History* (3.25), written in the early fourth century, **Eusebius** of Caesarea sorted writings into categories:

- **Recognized** books (*homologoumena*), such as the Gospels, Acts, and Paul's letters.
- **Disputed** books (*antilegomena*), "known to most" but questioned by some: James, Jude, 2 Peter, and 2 and 3 John.
- **Spurious** books, such as the Shepherd of Hermas and the Didache.
- **Heretical** writings, such as the Gospel of Peter.

Revelation's status was uncertain in the East; Eusebius placed it among the recognized books "if it seem proper" and also among the spurious. Hebrews was accepted early in the East but doubted in the West, partly because its authorship was uncertain.

sections.heading: Athanasius and the Councils
sections.body:
The first known list that names exactly the 27 books of our New Testament is the **39th Festal Letter** of **Athanasius**, bishop of Alexandria, written for Easter in **367**. After listing the books he wrote:

> These are fountains of salvation, that they who thirst may be satisfied with the living words they contain. In these alone is proclaimed the doctrine of godliness. Let no man add to these, neither let him take ought from these.

In the West, the North African councils of **Hippo** (393) and **Carthage** (397) also listed the 27 books, with the strong support of Augustine. These were regional, not ecumenical, councils, and they confirmed existing usage rather than inventing a canon. Some Eastern churches took longer: the Syriac Peshitta lacked 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude, and Revelation, and Revelation was not read in the Byzantine liturgy.

sections.heading: Criteria
sections.body:
The early church did not publish a formal set of criteria, but several considerations appear repeatedly:

1. **Apostolicity**: written by an apostle or a close associate (Mark with Peter, Luke with Paul).
2. **Orthodoxy**: agreement with the "rule of faith," the church's received teaching.
3. **Catholicity**: wide and long-standing use in churches across the Christian world.
4. **Antiquity**: origin in the apostolic age.

sections.heading: Interpretations of the Process
sections.body: Traditions describe the process differently. Protestants typically say the church *recognized* books that were already authoritative because they were inspired, rather than conferring authority on them. Catholic and Orthodox theology emphasizes that the church, guided by the Holy Spirit, discerned and defined the canon within its tradition. Some critical scholars stress the role of debate and church politics in excluding alternative writings. Luther, for his part, questioned the apostolic standing of Hebrews, James, Jude, and Revelation, and placed them at the end of his New Testament.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: The New Testament canon was not imposed by a single council or emperor; it emerged from the worship and discernment of churches across centuries. Knowing that history allows readers to answer popular claims that the canon was invented late, while also appreciating that some books were genuinely debated.

topics.title: Manuscripts and Textual Criticism
topics.subtitle: Bible History
topics.summary: The manuscript evidence for the Old and New Testaments, from the Masoretic Text and Dead Sea Scrolls to the great codices and early papyri, and how scholars evaluate variants.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: No original manuscript (*autograph*) of any biblical book survives. What we have are copies, and copies of copies, made by hand over many centuries. *Textual criticism* is the discipline that compares these manuscripts to reconstruct, as closely as possible, the earliest attainable form of the text. It is practiced on all ancient literature, and the Bible is by far the best-attested ancient text.

sections.heading: The Old Testament: The Masoretic Text
sections.body:
The standard Hebrew text is the **Masoretic Text** (MT), named after the **Masoretes**, Jewish scribes active roughly from the sixth to the tenth centuries AD, especially in Tiberias. Hebrew was originally written with consonants only; the Masoretes added vowel points and accent marks to preserve the traditional pronunciation and reading, along with marginal notes (the *masorah*) recording details such as word counts to safeguard the text. The most important complete manuscripts are the **Aleppo Codex** (about 930, partly lost in the twentieth century) and the **Leningrad Codex** (dated 1008 or 1009), which is the basis of modern critical editions of the Hebrew Bible.

Other witnesses include the **Septuagint**, the Greek translation made from the third century BC, and the **Samaritan Pentateuch**. These sometimes differ from the MT, as in the book of Jeremiah, whose Septuagint form is about one-eighth shorter.

sections.heading: The Dead Sea Scrolls
sections.body:
Beginning in **1947**, Bedouin shepherds and then archaeologists discovered scrolls in eleven caves near **Qumran** by the Dead Sea. Dating from about the third century BC to the first century AD, they include fragments of nearly every book of the Hebrew Bible; Esther is the notable absence. Before 1947, the oldest substantial Hebrew manuscripts dated from the ninth and tenth centuries AD, so the scrolls pushed the evidence back about a thousand years.

The **Great Isaiah Scroll** (1QIsa-a), a nearly complete copy of Isaiah from the second century BC, agrees closely with the medieval Masoretic Text apart from mostly minor differences in spelling and wording, a striking witness to careful transmission. At the same time, the scrolls show that more than one form of some books circulated in the Second Temple period: some Qumran manuscripts align with the MT, others with the Septuagint or the Samaritan Pentateuch.

sections.heading: The New Testament: Papyri and Codices
sections.body:
The New Testament survives in more than five thousand Greek manuscripts, along with early translations and quotations in the church fathers. Key witnesses include:

- **Papyrus 52** (P52, the Rylands papyrus), a small fragment containing John 18:31-33, 37-38. It is often dated to the first half of the second century, though some scholars argue for a later date in the second century. It is widely cited as the earliest known New Testament fragment.
- **The Bodmer and Chester Beatty papyri**, including P66 and P75 (Gospels) and P46 (Paul's letters), mostly dated around AD 200 or the third century.
- **Codex Sinaiticus**, a fourth-century manuscript of the whole Greek Bible, containing the oldest complete New Testament. Constantin von Tischendorf found it at St. Catherine's Monastery at Mount Sinai in the mid-nineteenth century; most of it is now in the British Library. It also contains the Epistle of Barnabas and part of the Shepherd of Hermas.
- **Codex Vaticanus**, also from the fourth century, held in the Vatican Library, and regarded by many as the single most important New Testament manuscript.

sections.heading: Types of Variants
sections.body:
Most differences between manuscripts are trivial. Scholars classify them as:

1. **Spelling and word order** differences, which in Greek often do not affect meaning. These are by far the most common.
2. **Accidental errors**, such as skipping lines when two lines end with the same letters (*homoeoteleuton*), writing a word twice (*dittography*), or omitting a repeated letter or word (*haplography*).
3. **Intentional changes**, such as harmonizing parallel Gospel passages or clarifying a difficult phrase.
4. **Meaningful and viable** variants, a small minority, including a few longer passages: the ending of Mark (Mark 16:9-20) and the story of the woman caught in adultery (John 7:53-8:11) are absent from the earliest manuscripts, and modern translations usually mark them.

sections.heading: Principles of Evaluation
sections.body:
Textual critics weigh **external evidence** (the age, quality, and geographical spread of manuscripts) and **internal evidence**, guided by principles such as:

- Prefer the reading that best explains the origin of the others.
- Prefer the **more difficult reading** (*lectio difficilior potior*), since scribes tended to smooth out difficulties.
- The shorter reading was traditionally preferred, though this rule is now debated.

Manuscripts are grouped into families or text types, commonly called Alexandrian, Western, and Byzantine. The **Textus Receptus**, based on Erasmus's Greek New Testament (1516) and late Byzantine manuscripts, underlay the King James Version; most modern translations rely on critical editions such as the Nestle-Aland *Novum Testamentum Graece*, which give greater weight to the earlier manuscripts.

sections.heading: Assessment
sections.body: Scholars differ on how much confidence the evidence warrants. Bart Ehrman's *Misquoting Jesus* (2005) emphasized the number and significance of variants; scholars such as Daniel Wallace stress that the vast majority are insignificant and that no central Christian doctrine depends on a disputed reading. Nearly all agree that the wealth of manuscripts makes the Bible's text far better attested than any other ancient work.

topics.title: The History of Bible Translation
topics.subtitle: Bible History
topics.summary: From the Septuagint and Vulgate through Wycliffe, Tyndale, Luther, and the King James Version to modern translation philosophies.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: Christianity has been a translating faith from the start. The New Testament itself was written in Greek, not in the Aramaic Jesus usually spoke, and at Pentecost the crowd heard the apostles speak "every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born" (Acts 2:8). The history of Bible translation is a story of scholarship, controversy, and sometimes martyrdom.

sections.heading: Ancient Translations
sections.body:
**The Septuagint.** The Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures was begun in Alexandria in the third century BC, starting with the Torah. The *Letter of Aristeas* tells a legend that seventy-two Jewish elders translated the Law for King Ptolemy II; the name Septuagint ("seventy") comes from this tradition. It became the Old Testament of the early church.

**Other early versions.** As the gospel spread, the Bible was translated into Syriac (the Peshitta), Coptic, Gothic (by the missionary bishop Ulfilas in the fourth century), Armenian, and later Old Church Slavonic, for which the brothers Cyril and Methodius developed an alphabet in the ninth century.

**The Vulgate.** Several uneven Old Latin translations circulated in the West. In 382 Pope Damasus asked **Jerome** to revise the Latin Gospels. Jerome went on to translate most of the Old Testament directly from Hebrew, insisting on the *Hebraica veritas* (Hebrew truth), a decision that was controversial at the time. His work, known as the **Vulgate** ("common" version), became the standard Bible of the Western church for over a thousand years, and the Council of Trent (1546) declared it authentic for public use.

sections.heading: The Medieval and Reformation Era
sections.body:
**Wycliffe.** In the 1380s, followers of the Oxford theologian **John Wycliffe** produced the first complete Bible in English, translated from the Latin Vulgate and copied by hand. In 1409 the Constitutions of Oxford forbade unauthorized English translations, and Wycliffe's followers, the Lollards, were persecuted.

**Printing and the Greek text.** Johannes Gutenberg printed the Latin Bible in the 1450s. In 1516 the humanist scholar **Erasmus** published the first printed Greek New Testament, which made the original language widely available to translators.

**Luther.** **Martin Luther** translated the New Testament into German from Erasmus's Greek while hiding at the Wartburg castle; it appeared in September 1522. The complete Luther Bible followed in 1534. Its vigorous, idiomatic German shaped the German language itself.

**Tyndale.** **William Tyndale** produced the first printed English New Testament translated from Greek (1526), working in exile in Germany and the Low Countries; he then translated the Pentateuch and other Old Testament books from Hebrew. Copies were smuggled into England and burned by authorities. Tyndale was arrested and executed near Brussels in 1536. Much of his phrasing, such as "Let there be light" and "the powers that be," passed into later English Bibles.

**From Coverdale to Geneva.** Miles Coverdale published the first complete printed English Bible in 1535. The **Great Bible** (1539) was authorized for use in English churches. The **Geneva Bible** (1560), produced by English Protestant exiles with extensive study notes, became the household Bible of Shakespeare's era and of the Puritans. Catholic exiles produced the **Douay-Rheims** translation from the Vulgate (New Testament 1582, Old Testament 1609-1610).

sections.heading: The King James Version (1611)
sections.body:
At the Hampton Court Conference of 1604, King James I commissioned a new translation. About fifty scholars, organized in six companies at Westminster, Oxford, and Cambridge, worked from the Hebrew and Greek, building on earlier English versions, especially Tyndale's. Published in 1611, the "Authorized Version" became the dominant English Bible for over three centuries. Its preface, "The Translators to the Reader," explains the purpose of translation:

> Translation it is that openeth the window, to let in the light; that breaketh the shell, that we may eat the kernel; that putteth aside the curtain, that we may look into the most Holy place.

sections.heading: Modern Translations and Philosophies
sections.body:
Nineteenth- and twentieth-century discoveries of older manuscripts and advances in linguistics led to new versions, beginning with the Revised Version (1881-1885) and continuing with the RSV, NASB, NIV, NRSV, ESV, and many others. Translations differ in their underlying philosophy:

- **Formal equivalence** ("word for word") stays as close as possible to the wording and structure of the original. Examples: KJV, NASB, ESV.
- **Dynamic or functional equivalence** ("thought for thought"), associated with the linguist **Eugene Nida**, seeks to produce the same effect on modern readers that the original had on its first readers. Examples: the Good News Bible and the New Living Translation; the NIV seeks a balance between the two approaches.
- **Paraphrase** freely restates the meaning in contemporary idiom. Examples: The Living Bible and The Message.

Each approach involves trade-offs between precision and readability; many readers use more than one translation.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: Every translation is an interpretation. Knowing the history helps readers appreciate the cost at which vernacular Bibles were won and understand why translations differ.

A translation philosophy, associated with Eugene Nida, that aims to reproduce the original's meaning and effect in natural modern language.

topics.title: Second Temple Judaism
topics.subtitle: Bible History
topics.summary: The Persian, Hellenistic, and Roman periods between the Testaments, the Maccabean revolt, the Jewish sects, and the world into which Jesus was born.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: The **Second Temple period** runs from the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile (completed around 516 BC) to its destruction by the Romans in AD 70. It covers the centuries "between the Testaments" and the setting of the New Testament itself. Without knowing this period, much of the Gospels, from the Pharisees and Sadducees to the hope for a Messiah, is hard to understand.

sections.heading: The Persian Period (539-332 BC)
sections.body: In 539 BC the Persian king **Cyrus the Great** conquered Babylon and permitted exiled peoples, including the Jews, to return home (Ezra 1:1-4). Under leaders such as Zerubbabel the temple was rebuilt, and in the following century **Ezra** the scribe taught the Law and **Nehemiah** rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem. Judah (Yehud) was a small province of the Persian Empire, governed with significant religious autonomy. Many Jews remained in Babylon and elsewhere, the beginning of a large *diaspora* (dispersion).

sections.heading: The Hellenistic Period (332-63 BC)
sections.body:
**Alexander the Great** conquered the Persian Empire, bringing Judea under Greek rule and spreading Greek language and culture (*Hellenism*). After his death in 323 BC his empire was divided. Judea was ruled first by the **Ptolemies** of Egypt and then, from about 200 BC, by the **Seleucids** of Syria. In Alexandria, Jews translated their Scriptures into Greek, producing the Septuagint.

Tension between Jewish tradition and Hellenistic culture came to a head under the Seleucid king **Antiochus IV Epiphanes**. In 167 BC he banned circumcision and Sabbath observance and set up a pagan altar in the temple, the "abomination that maketh desolate" (Daniel 11:31). A priest named Mattathias and his sons led a revolt; his son **Judas Maccabeus** ("the hammer") recaptured Jerusalem and rededicated the temple in 164 BC, an event commemorated in **Hanukkah**, the "feast of the dedication" mentioned in John 10:22. The story is told in 1 and 2 Maccabees. Mattathias's descendants, the **Hasmonean dynasty**, ruled an independent Jewish state for about a century.

sections.heading: The Roman Period (63 BC-AD 70)
sections.body: In 63 BC the Roman general **Pompey** took Jerusalem. Rome later made **Herod the Great** king of Judea; he ruled from 37 to 4 BC, and Jesus was born near the end of his reign (Matthew 2:1). Herod was a brilliant builder who greatly expanded the temple, but he was also notoriously ruthless. After him, his kingdom was divided among his sons, and Judea came under Roman governors such as **Pontius Pilate** (AD 26-36). Resentment of Roman rule grew until the **First Jewish Revolt** broke out in AD 66. In AD 70 the Roman general Titus captured Jerusalem and destroyed the temple, ending the Second Temple period.

sections.heading: Jewish Groups and Movements
sections.body:
The historian **Josephus** describes Jewish "philosophies" or schools:

- **Pharisees**: a lay movement devoted to careful observance of the Law, including the "tradition of the elders" (Mark 7:3), and to belief in the resurrection of the dead. Rabbinic Judaism grew largely out of their tradition after AD 70.
- **Sadducees**: associated with the priestly aristocracy and the temple. They rejected the Pharisees' oral traditions and denied the resurrection and angels (Acts 23:8; Mark 12:18).
- **Essenes**: a strict, communal movement emphasizing purity. Many scholars identify the community at Qumran, which produced or preserved the Dead Sea Scrolls, as Essene, though this identification is debated.
- A "**fourth philosophy**" of militant resistance to Rome, associated with Judas the Galilean, which fed into the later **Zealots**.

Other groups included the **scribes**, experts in the Law; the **Herodians**, supporters of Herod's dynasty; and the **Samaritans**, who worshiped at Mount Gerizim and accepted only the Pentateuch (John 4:20).

sections.heading: Religious Life
sections.body: The **temple** was the center of worship, sacrifice, and pilgrimage festivals. Alongside it, the **synagogue** became a place for reading and teaching Scripture and for prayer in towns throughout Judea, Galilee, and the diaspora. Its origins are debated, with some scholars tracing it to the exile and others to later centuries, but by the first century it was well established, as when Jesus read from Isaiah in the synagogue at Nazareth (Luke 4:16-21). The period also produced a rich literature, including apocalyptic works such as 1 Enoch, wisdom writings, and the Qumran texts. Messianic hopes varied: some expected a royal son of David, others a priestly figure, and some no individual messiah at all.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: The New Testament grew out of Second Temple Judaism. Jesus' debates with Pharisees and Sadducees, the expectation of a Messiah, the role of the temple, and the mission to the diaspora all make fuller sense against this background.
