topics.title: The History of Ancient Israel
topics.subtitle: Bible History
topics.summary: An overview of Israel's story from the patriarchs to the return from exile, with key archaeological evidence and the points where scholarly dating is debated.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: The Old Testament tells the story of Israel from Abraham to the return from Babylonian exile. Historians reconstruct that story by combining the biblical text with archaeology and the records of neighboring empires. For the earlier periods the evidence is sparse and the debates are sharp; from the ninth century BC onward, external sources increasingly intersect with the biblical account. This survey follows the biblical sequence and notes where scholars disagree.

sections.heading: The Patriarchs
sections.body: Genesis 12-50 recounts the lives of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph. Conservative scholars have traditionally placed the patriarchs in the early second millennium BC and pointed to customs and names that fit that period. Many critical scholars regard the patriarchal stories as traditions shaped much later, and some doubt that they preserve history at all. No extrabiblical source mentions the patriarchs, which is unsurprising for nomadic family groups, so the question turns mainly on how one evaluates the biblical narratives.

sections.heading: Exodus and Conquest
sections.body:
The book of Exodus describes Israel's slavery in Egypt and deliverance under Moses. Its date is debated. An **early date** around 1446 BC is derived from 1 Kings 6:1, which places the exodus 480 years before the fourth year of Solomon. A **late date** in the thirteenth century BC, under Ramesses II, is suggested by the store city named Raamses (Exodus 1:11) and by archaeological patterns. Many critical scholars doubt that a large-scale exodus occurred, though some think a smaller group escaping Egypt contributed the tradition. Egyptian records do not mention the event.

The **Merneptah Stele** (around 1208 BC), an Egyptian victory inscription, contains the earliest known mention of "Israel" outside the Bible, as a people in Canaan.

How Israel emerged in Canaan is also debated. The book of Joshua emphasizes military conquest, while Judges describes a more gradual and incomplete process. Scholarly models include a **conquest** model (associated with W. F. Albright), **peaceful infiltration** (Albrecht Alt), a **peasant revolt** (George Mendenhall and Norman Gottwald), and an **indigenous emergence** model, held by many archaeologists such as Israel Finkelstein and William Dever, which sees Israel arising largely from within Canaanite society in the highland villages of the early Iron Age.

sections.heading: The United Monarchy
sections.body: According to Samuel and Kings, Saul, David, and Solomon ruled a united kingdom, conventionally dated around 1050-930 BC. Here, too, scholars disagree. So-called *minimalists* (such as the Copenhagen school) once doubted that David existed. The discovery of the **Tel Dan Stele** in 1993, an Aramaic inscription of the ninth century BC referring to the "House of David," persuaded most scholars that David was a historical figure. The size of his kingdom and of Solomon's building projects remains debated: some archaeologists argue for a modest chiefdom, while others point to sites such as Khirbet Qeiyafa as evidence of a more organized early state.

sections.heading: The Divided Kingdom
sections.body:
After Solomon's death (around 930 BC) the kingdom split (1 Kings 12). The northern kingdom, **Israel**, eventually had its capital at Samaria, founded by King Omri. The southern kingdom, **Judah**, kept Jerusalem and the Davidic dynasty. From this period, external evidence becomes more abundant. The **Mesha Stele** (around 840 BC), from Moab, mentions Omri as king of Israel. Assyrian inscriptions name kings such as Ahab and Jehu.

The rising **Assyrian Empire** besieged Samaria, which fell in 722 BC; much of its population was deported (2 Kings 17). Judah survived as a vassal. In 701 BC the Assyrian king Sennacherib invaded Judah; his annals boast that he shut up Hezekiah in Jerusalem "like a bird in a cage," but they do not claim the city's capture, which agrees with the biblical account that Jerusalem was spared (2 Kings 18-19). King **Josiah** later carried out a religious reform after the discovery of the "book of the law" in the temple in 622 BC (2 Kings 22).

sections.heading: Exile and Return
sections.body:
Babylon replaced Assyria as the dominant power. King **Nebuchadnezzar** deported Judah's king and elite in 597 BC, and in 587 or 586 BC he destroyed Jerusalem and Solomon's temple (2 Kings 25). The **Babylonian exile** was a profound crisis that shaped much of the Old Testament's theology and, many scholars believe, its final editing.

In 539 BC **Cyrus** of Persia conquered Babylon. The **Cyrus Cylinder** records his policy of returning displaced peoples and restoring their sanctuaries, though it does not mention the Jews specifically. Ezra 1:1-4 records his decree allowing the Jews to return and rebuild the temple, which was completed around 516 BC (Ezra 6:15), opening the Second Temple period.

sections.heading: Assessment
sections.body: The history of ancient Israel is an area of lively debate. Scholars range from those who see the biblical narrative as broadly reliable to those who regard much of it as later theological construction. Readers should note where evidence is strong (especially from the ninth century onward), where it is debated, and how each position weighs the biblical text and the archaeological record.

topics.title: The Apostolic Fathers
topics.subtitle: Church Fathers
topics.summary: The earliest Christian writings after the New Testament: Clement, Ignatius, Polycarp, the Didache, the Shepherd of Hermas, and the Epistle to Diognetus.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: "Apostolic Fathers" is a modern label, popularized by a 1672 edition of texts by the scholar Jean-Baptiste Cotelier, for a group of early Christian writings thought to come from the generation that knew the apostles or their immediate successors. The collection is diverse: letters, a church manual, an apocalypse, and an apologetic treatise. Together these texts offer a rare window into Christian life, worship, and leadership from roughly the late first to the mid-second century.

sections.heading: Clement of Rome
sections.body: The letter known as *1 Clement* was sent from the church at Rome to the church at Corinth, traditionally around AD 96, though some scholars date it a little earlier or later. Corinthian Christians had deposed their presbyters, and the letter calls them to repentance, humility, and order. It mentions the martyrdoms of Peter and Paul (chapter 5) and argues that the apostles appointed leaders and provided for their succession (chapter 44). Later tradition identified its author as Clement, an early bishop of Rome, although the letter itself speaks in the name of the Roman church.

sections.heading: Ignatius of Antioch
sections.body:
Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, was taken under guard to Rome to be executed, traditionally in the reign of Trajan (c. 110; some scholars place it later). On the way he wrote seven letters: to the Ephesians, Magnesians, Trallians, Romans, Philadelphians, Smyrnaeans, and to Polycarp. He urges unity around the bishop, presbyters, and deacons; warns against teachers who denied that Christ truly suffered in the flesh (*docetism*); calls the Eucharist "the medicine of immortality" (*Ephesians* 20); and gives the earliest surviving use of the phrase "the catholic church" (*Smyrnaeans* 8). He begs the Roman Christians not to prevent his martyrdom:

> "I am the wheat of God, and let me be ground by the teeth of the wild beasts, that I may be found the pure bread of Christ." (*Romans* 4)

sections.heading: Polycarp of Smyrna
sections.body:
Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, is remembered as a link to the apostolic generation; Irenaeus later wrote that he had known the apostle John. His *Letter to the Philippians* is full of quotations from apostolic writings. The *Martyrdom of Polycarp*, the earliest Christian account of a martyrdom outside the New Testament, describes his death around 155-160. Urged by the proconsul to revile Christ, he replied:

> "Eighty and six years have I served Him, and He never did me any injury: how then can I blaspheme my King and my Saviour?"

sections.heading: The Didache
sections.body: The *Didache* ("Teaching of the Twelve Apostles") was known only by name until Philotheos Bryennios discovered it in a Constantinople manuscript in 1873; he published it in 1883. It begins with the "Two Ways" of life and death, then gives instructions on baptism (preferably in running water, but by pouring if necessary), fasting on Wednesdays and Fridays, praying the Lord's Prayer three times daily, Eucharistic prayers, and receiving traveling apostles and prophets. Its date is debated: many scholars place it in the late first or early second century, while some argue for an earlier date for parts of it.

sections.heading: The Shepherd of Hermas and the Epistle to Diognetus
sections.body:
The *Shepherd of Hermas*, written in Rome, records visions, commandments, and parables given to Hermas by an angelic shepherd. Its central concern is whether Christians who sin seriously after baptism may repent, and it offers one further opportunity. The Muratorian Fragment says it was written recently, while Hermas's brother Pius was bishop of Rome. The Shepherd was so widely read that some regarded it as Scripture, and it appears in the fourth-century Codex Sinaiticus.

The *Epistle to Diognetus* is an anonymous defense of Christianity of uncertain date (often placed in the second century). It portrays Christians as citizens of every land yet strangers everywhere: "What the soul is in the body, that are Christians in the world" (chapter 6).

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: The Apostolic Fathers show the church developing leadership structures, liturgy, and moral teaching while remaining close to the New Testament world. Catholic and Orthodox readers often stress their witness to episcopal order and Eucharistic realism; Protestant scholars tend to emphasize the diversity of early church structures and the gradual development of the threefold ministry. All agree on their value as the earliest Christian voices after the apostles.

topics.title: The Early Apologists
topics.subtitle: Church Fathers
topics.summary: Second-century writers such as Justin Martyr, Athenagoras, Theophilus, and Tertullian who defended Christianity against pagan accusations and engaged Greek philosophy.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: In the second century Christians faced suspicion, slander, and periodic violence. A group of educated converts responded with *apologies*, formal defenses (from the Greek *apologia*, a speech for the defense) addressed to emperors, officials, or the educated public. According to Eusebius, the earliest, by Quadratus and Aristides, were addressed to Emperor Hadrian. The apologists sought legal fairness for Christians, answered popular charges, and argued that Christianity was the true philosophy. In doing so they laid early foundations for Christian theology, especially the doctrine of the Logos.

sections.heading: The Charges Against Christians
sections.body: Pagan critics accused Christians of three crimes, which Athenagoras lists explicitly: *atheism*, since they rejected the gods; *Thyestean feasts* (cannibalism), a garbled rumor about the Eucharist; and *Oedipodean intercourse* (incest), a misunderstanding of Christians calling one another "brother" and "sister." Christians were also suspected of disloyalty because they would not sacrifice for the emperor. The apologists insisted that Christians prayed for rulers (1 Timothy 2:1-2), lived chaste and honest lives, and should be judged by their deeds, not punished for the name alone.

sections.heading: Justin Martyr
sections.body:
Justin (c. 100-c. 165) was born at Flavia Neapolis in Samaria. In his *Dialogue with Trypho* he describes passing through several philosophical schools before an old man pointed him to the Hebrew prophets, and as a Christian teacher he continued to wear the philosopher's cloak. He taught in Rome, where he wrote two *Apologies*; the first is addressed to Emperor Antoninus Pius and his sons. He was beheaded around 165 under the prefect Junius Rusticus.

Justin's most influential idea is the *logos spermatikos*, the "seminal Word." Christ, the Logos who "enlightens every man" (John 1:9), had scattered seeds of truth among all people, so philosophers like Socrates grasped truth in part. As he put it, "Whatever things were rightly said among all men, are the property of us Christians" (*Second Apology* 13). The *First Apology* also contains the earliest detailed description of Christian worship:

> "And on the day called Sunday, all who live in cities or in the country gather together to one place, and the memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read, as long as time permits." (*First Apology* 67)

sections.heading: Athenagoras and Theophilus
sections.body:
**Athenagoras of Athens** addressed *A Plea for the Christians* to Emperors Marcus Aurelius and Commodus (c. 177). In polished Greek he refutes the three charges and offers an early statement of the unity and distinction of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. A treatise *On the Resurrection* is also attributed to him, though some scholars question the attribution.

**Theophilus of Antioch** wrote *To Autolycus* (c. 180) for a pagan friend. He is the first known writer to use the Greek word *trias* ("triad") of God, speaking of "God, and His Word, and His Wisdom" (*To Autolycus* 2.15).

sections.heading: Tertullian the Apologist
sections.body:
In Latin North Africa, **Tertullian** of Carthage wrote his *Apology* (197). With a lawyer's sharpness he attacks the injustice of the trials. He criticizes Trajan's rescript as self-contradictory: if Christians are guilty, why are they not sought out; if innocent, why are they punished? He insists that persecution only spreads the faith: "the blood of Christians is seed" (*Apology* 50).

Tertullian was more suspicious of philosophy than Justin. In *The Prescription Against Heretics* he asks, "What indeed has Athens to do with Jerusalem?" warning that philosophy breeds heresy (compare Colossians 2:8). Yet he too used philosophical and legal concepts freely.

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.body: The apologists modeled a confident engagement with surrounding culture, following Paul at the Areopagus (Acts 17:22-31) and the call to give "an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you" (1 Peter 3:15). Their Logos theology helped prepare the way for later Trinitarian doctrine, though some of their formulations, which could appear to subordinate the Son, were refined in the fourth century. Christians of every tradition still debate the balance they struck between welcoming and resisting pagan wisdom.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: By the late second century the greatest challenge to the church came not only from persecution but from rival forms of Christianity. Gnostic teachers offered secret knowledge and a radically different account of God and creation; others blurred the distinction between Father and Son. Irenaeus of Lyons and Tertullian of Carthage developed enduring responses that shaped Christian theology in both East and West.

sections.heading: The Gnostic Challenge
sections.body: "Gnosticism" is a modern umbrella term for diverse movements. Many of the systems Irenaeus describes, such as that of the Valentinians, taught that the true God was remote, surrounded by a spiritual realm (the *Pleroma*) of emanations called *aeons*. The material world was the flawed work of a lesser creator, the *Demiurge*, often identified with the God of the Old Testament. Salvation meant liberation of the spirit through secret knowledge (*gnosis*) available to a spiritual elite. Marcion, though not a Gnostic in the same sense, likewise separated the Creator from the Father of Jesus and rejected the Old Testament.

sections.heading: Irenaeus of Lyons
sections.body:
Irenaeus (c. 130-c. 202) grew up in Asia Minor, where as a youth he heard Polycarp of Smyrna. He became bishop of Lyons in Gaul after the persecution of 177. Around 180 he wrote *Against Heresies* (properly, *The Detection and Overthrow of Knowledge Falsely So-Called*) in five books. A shorter work, the *Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching*, was rediscovered in an Armenian translation in 1904.

Irenaeus's arguments include:

- **The rule of faith.** The church throughout the world "has received from the apostles and their disciples this faith," in one God the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth, in one Christ Jesus, and in the Holy Spirit (*Against Heresies* 1.10.1). This public summary, confessed at baptism, gives the true sense of Scripture.
- **Apostolic succession.** Against claims of secret tradition, Irenaeus points to public lists of bishops descending from the apostles, giving the succession at Rome down to Eleutherius (3.3.3). If the apostles had secret teachings, they would have handed them to these successors. His statement that every church should agree with Rome "on account of its preeminent authority" (3.3.2) is much debated: Catholic interpreters see an early witness to Roman primacy, while others read it more narrowly.
- **The fourfold Gospel.** He defends exactly four Gospels as the church's authoritative accounts.
- **Recapitulation.** Drawing on Ephesians 1:10, Irenaeus teaches that Christ "sums up" (*recapitulates*) humanity in himself, passing through every stage of human life and reversing Adam's disobedience by his obedience (Romans 5:12-19). Mary's obedience likewise undoes Eve's.

Irenaeus affirms the goodness of creation and the body against Gnostic contempt for matter:

> "For the glory of God is a living man; and the life of man consists in beholding God." (*Against Heresies* 4.20.7)

sections.heading: Tertullian of Carthage
sections.body:
Tertullian (c. 155-c. 220) was the first major Christian author to write in Latin and coined much of Western theology's vocabulary. In *The Prescription Against Heretics* he used a legal argument: Scripture belongs to the church that received it from the apostles, so heretics have no right to appeal to it.

His *Against Praxeas* (c. 213) answered *modalism* (also called Monarchianism or Patripassianism), which so stressed God's oneness that Father, Son, and Spirit became mere modes of one person, implying that the Father suffered on the cross. Tertullian complained that Praxeas "put to flight the Paraclete, and he crucified the Father." In response he spoke of God as a *trinitas* (Trinity) and described Father, Son, and Spirit as three *personae* of one *substantia*. Although some of his formulations imply a subordination of the Son later avoided, his terms became standard in Latin theology.

sections.heading: Tertullian and Montanism
sections.body: Tertullian's later writings show sympathy with the *New Prophecy*, or Montanism, a movement from Phrygia led by Montanus and the prophetesses Priscilla and Maximilla. It emphasized ecstatic prophecy, strict fasting, and moral rigor, such as rejecting second marriage. Jerome reports that Tertullian broke with the church, but many modern scholars think the New Prophecy at Carthage may have remained a movement within the church. Unlike Irenaeus, Tertullian is not venerated as a saint.

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.body: Irenaeus is often called the first great systematic theologian of the church, admired in the East and West for his vision of salvation history. Tertullian gave the Latin church its theological vocabulary. Their appeals to Scripture, the rule of faith, and apostolic tradition remain points of discussion among Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant theologians.

topics.title: The Alexandrian Fathers
topics.subtitle: Church Fathers
topics.summary: Clement, Origen, Athanasius, and Cyril: the theologians of Alexandria who joined Christian faith to learning and defended the full divinity of Christ.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: Alexandria in Egypt was the intellectual capital of the Greek-speaking world, home of a great library, a large Jewish community that had produced the Septuagint and the philosopher Philo, and flourishing schools of philosophy. Its Christian teachers became known for engaging philosophy, for spiritual and allegorical interpretation of Scripture, and, in the fourth and fifth centuries, for fierce defense of the divinity of Christ.

sections.heading: Clement of Alexandria
sections.body: Christian instruction at Alexandria was associated with a catechetical school, whose early teachers included Pantaenus. His successor **Clement** (c. 150-c. 215) wrote a trilogy: the *Exhortation to the Heathen*, the *Instructor* (*Paedagogus*), and the *Stromata* (*Miscellanies*). Clement argued that philosophy had prepared the Greeks for Christ as the Law prepared the Jews (compare Galatians 3:24), and he described the mature believer as the true "gnostic," whose knowledge is rooted in faith and love. He left Alexandria during the persecution under Septimius Severus around 202.

sections.heading: Origen
sections.body:
**Origen** (c. 185-c. 253) was the most prolific scholar of the early church. His father Leonides was martyred in 202, and the young Origen soon led catechetical instruction in Alexandria. He compiled the *Hexapla*, a six-column edition of the Old Testament setting the Hebrew text beside a transliteration and several Greek translations. He wrote commentaries and homilies on most of the Bible, *Against Celsus*, a reply to a pagan critic, and *On First Principles*, the first systematic theology, which survives mainly in Rufinus's Latin translation.

Origen taught that Scripture has a bodily (literal), a psychic (moral), and a spiritual sense, like a human being of body, soul, and spirit. He also taught the eternal generation of the Son. After conflict with Bishop Demetrius he moved to Caesarea in Palestine in the early 230s. Tortured during the Decian persecution, he died soon afterward. Some of his speculative ideas, such as the pre-existence of souls and the final restoration of all things, were later condemned; anathemas against "Origenism" are associated with the Second Council of Constantinople (553), though the exact circumstances are debated. Many in East and West continue to admire his exegesis and spirituality.

sections.heading: Athanasius
sections.body:
The Arian controversy began around 318 when **Arius**, a presbyter of Alexandria, taught that the Son was the first and highest creature: "there was when he was not." He appealed to texts such as Proverbs 8:22 ("The Lord created me" in the Greek). Bishop Alexander opposed him, and the Council of Nicaea (325) confessed the Son *homoousios* with the Father.

**Athanasius** (c. 296-373) attended Nicaea as Alexander's deacon and became bishop of Alexandria in 328. For forty-five years he defended Nicaea against shifting imperial policies and was exiled five times, under Constantine, Constantius II, Julian, and Valens. In *On the Incarnation* he argues that only God could restore fallen humanity:

> "For He was made man that we might be made God." (*On the Incarnation* 54)

His *Discourses Against the Arians* defend the Son's eternal divinity, and his *Life of Antony* popularized monasticism. His Festal Letter of 367 is the first known list of exactly the twenty-seven books of the New Testament.

sections.heading: Cyril of Alexandria
sections.body: **Cyril** (bishop 412-444) led the opposition to Nestorius of Constantinople, who objected to calling Mary *Theotokos* ("God-bearer") and seemed to divide Christ into two subjects. Cyril insisted that the eternal Word himself was born, suffered, and died in the flesh he made his own, so Mary is truly the mother of God incarnate (compare Luke 1:43). His Twelve Anathemas and leadership at the Council of Ephesus (431) secured Nestorius's condemnation, and in 433 he reached a Formula of Reunion with John of Antioch. His phrase "one incarnate nature of God the Word" was later claimed by the non-Chalcedonian churches. His episcopate also included violent conflicts in the city, including the murder of the philosopher Hypatia by a Christian mob in 415; historians debate Cyril's responsibility.

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.body: The Alexandrians emphasized salvation as union with God, called *deification* or *theosis* (2 Peter 1:4), which remains central in Orthodox theology. Their defense of Christ's full divinity became the faith of Nicaea and Ephesus for Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant churches alike, while Origen's legacy remains contested.

topics.title: The Cappadocian Fathers
topics.subtitle: Church Fathers
topics.summary: Basil the Great, Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa, and their sister Macrina, who clarified the language of the Trinity and secured the Nicene faith.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: After Nicaea, the church spent more than fifty years debating what *homoousios* meant and whether the Holy Spirit is fully God. The decisive theological work that led to the Council of Constantinople (381) came from three bishops of Cappadocia, in central Asia Minor: Basil of Caesarea, his friend Gregory of Nazianzus, and his younger brother Gregory of Nyssa. Their eldest sister, Macrina, shaped them profoundly.

sections.heading: A Remarkable Family
sections.body:
**Macrina the Younger** (c. 327-379) turned the family estate at Annesi into an ascetic community of prayer and service. According to her brother Gregory's *Life of Macrina*, she persuaded Basil, returning proud from his studies, to embrace the ascetic life. In Gregory's dialogue *On the Soul and the Resurrection*, Macrina is the teacher, discussing death and the resurrection on her deathbed.

**Basil the Great** (c. 330-379) became bishop of Caesarea in 370. He wrote monastic rules that still guide Eastern monasticism and founded a large complex for the sick and poor outside Caesarea. His treatise *On the Holy Spirit* (c. 375) defended a doxology giving glory to the Father "with the Son, together with the Holy Spirit," arguing that the Spirit shares the honor and glory of the Father and the Son.

**Gregory of Nazianzus** (c. 329-390), known in the East as "the Theologian," delivered his *Five Theological Orations* (Orations 27-31) in Constantinople in 380, defending the Son's and the Spirit's divinity. He briefly presided over the Council of Constantinople in 381 before resigning. Against Apollinarius, who denied that Christ had a human mind, he wrote:

> "For that which He has not assumed He has not healed; but that which is united to His Godhead is also saved." (*Letter* 101, to Cledonius)

**Gregory of Nyssa** (c. 335-c. 395) was the most philosophical of the three. His works include *Against Eunomius*, the *Great Catechism*, *On the Making of Man*, and *The Life of Moses*. He stressed the infinity and incomprehensibility of God and described the spiritual life as endless progress into God (*epektasis*, from Philippians 3:13).

sections.heading: The Opponents
sections.body: The Cappadocians faced two main challenges. **Eunomius** of Cyzicus, a leader of the *Anomoeans*, argued that the Father's essence is to be unbegotten, so the begotten Son must be "unlike" (*anomoios*) the Father in essence. The **Pneumatomachians** ("Spirit-fighters") accepted the Son's divinity but denied the Spirit's. Other groups proposed compromise formulas, such as *homoiousios* ("of like substance") or simply calling the Son "like" the Father.

sections.heading: Clarifying the Vocabulary
sections.body:
A key obstacle was terminology. At Nicaea, *ousia* (essence) and *hypostasis* (subsistence) were used almost interchangeably; the Nicene anathemas condemned anyone who said the Son was of another "hypostasis or ousia." To Greek ears, "three hypostases" could sound like three gods, while "one hypostasis" could sound like modalism. A council at Alexandria in 362 began to accept that both expressions could be orthodox if properly understood.

The Cappadocians distinguished the terms:

- **Ousia** names what is common: the one divine essence shared fully by Father, Son, and Spirit.
- **Hypostasis** names what is particular: each of the three who possess that essence.

Basil compared the distinction to that between the general and the particular. The three hypostases are distinguished not by different natures but by their relations of origin: the Father is unbegotten, the Son is begotten, and the Spirit proceeds from the Father (John 15:26). The resulting formula, one *ousia* in three *hypostases*, became the classic statement of Trinitarian orthodoxy. Gregory of Nyssa's short work *On Not Three Gods* answered the charge that this amounted to tritheism by emphasizing the single divine action of the three.

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.body: The Council of Constantinople (381) vindicated the Cappadocian position, affirming the Spirit as "the Lord, the Giver of life, who with the Father and the Son is worshipped and glorified." The Orthodox Church honors Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus, with John Chrysostom, as the "Three Holy Hierarchs," and the Divine Liturgy of St. Basil is still celebrated. Western theology received their Trinitarian conclusions through translation and through the councils, though with different emphases from Augustine onward. Their insistence on the mystery of God alongside precise language continues to shape Trinitarian theology in all traditions.

topics.title: Augustine of Hippo
topics.subtitle: Church Fathers
topics.summary: The life and thought of the most influential theologian of the Latin West: the Confessions, the City of God, and the Donatist and Pelagian controversies.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: Augustine (354-430), bishop of Hippo in North Africa, is widely regarded as the most influential theologian of Western Christianity after the apostle Paul. His autobiography, his theology of grace, his account of the church, and his vision of history shaped medieval Catholicism and the Protestant Reformers alike.

sections.heading: Restless Searching
sections.body:
Augustine was born in 354 at Thagaste in Roman North Africa to Patricius, a pagan, and Monica, a devout Christian. At nineteen, reading Cicero's *Hortensius*, he was fired with a love of wisdom. He spent about nine years as a "hearer" among the Manichees, a dualist sect that taught that good and evil were two opposing powers. A brilliant teacher of rhetoric, he moved from Carthage to Rome and in 384 to Milan, where the sermons of Bishop Ambrose showed him that the Bible could be read intelligently, and books of the Neoplatonists helped him conceive of God as spiritual and evil as a privation of good.

In 386, in a garden in Milan, tormented by his inability to give up his ambitions and his sexual habits, he heard a child's voice chanting "take up and read." He opened Paul's letters at Romans 13:13-14: "not in rioting and drunkenness... but put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ." He was baptized by Ambrose at Easter 387. Monica died soon afterward at Ostia.

sections.heading: Bishop of Hippo
sections.body: Returning to Africa, Augustine formed a community of celibate men. In 391, while visiting Hippo Regius, he was pressed by the congregation into ordination as a priest, and around 395-396 he became bishop. For the rest of his life he preached, judged disputes, wrote prolifically, and defended the faith. He died on 28 August 430 as the Vandals besieged Hippo.

sections.heading: The Confessions and the City of God
sections.body:
The *Confessions* (c. 397-400), written as a prayer addressed to God, narrate his early life and conversion and end with meditations on memory, time, and creation. Its opening is famous:

> "You have made us for Yourself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in You." (*Confessions* 1.1)

The *City of God* (413-426) responded to pagans who blamed Christianity for the sack of Rome by Alaric's Visigoths in 410. Over twenty-two books Augustine traces two communities intermingled through history:

> "Two cities have been formed by two loves: the earthly by the love of self, even to the contempt of God; the heavenly by the love of God, even to the contempt of self." (*City of God* 14.28)

sections.heading: The Donatist Controversy
sections.body: The Donatists arose after the Diocletianic persecution. They refused to recognize Caecilian as bishop of Carthage because one of his consecrators was accused of being a *traditor* who had surrendered the Scriptures. Holding that sacraments performed by unworthy clergy were invalid, they rebaptized converts and saw themselves as the pure church. Augustine argued that the sacraments belong to Christ, so their validity does not depend on the minister's holiness, and that the church on earth is a mixed body of wheat and tares until the judgment (Matthew 13:24-30). After the Conference of Carthage (411), he supported imperial coercion of the Donatists, appealing to "compel them to come in" (Luke 14:23), a stance widely criticized since.

sections.heading: The Pelagian Controversy
sections.body: Pelagius, a British monk teaching in Rome, was disturbed by Augustine's prayer in the *Confessions*, "Give what You command, and command what You will." Pelagius held that God's commands imply human ability to obey them. Augustine replied that since Adam's fall all humanity inherits original sin (Romans 5:12), and that grace is not merely external help but God's inner work, necessary for every good act and for faith itself (Ephesians 2:8-9). Pelagianism was condemned at the Council of Carthage in 418. Augustine's later writings on predestination provoked further debate, partly resolved for the West at the Council of Orange (529).

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.body: Augustine's influence runs through Aquinas, Luther, Calvin, and Jansenism, and through Western thinking about the self, time, and politics. Catholics honor him as a Doctor of the Church. Protestants claim his theology of grace. Orthodox Christians venerate him as "Blessed Augustine," though some Orthodox theologians criticize aspects of his teaching on original sin and the Trinity.

keyTerms.definition: A dualist religion teaching two opposing cosmic powers of good and evil, to which Augustine belonged for about nine years.
Augustine's prayerful autobiography (c. 397-400) narrating his life and conversion.
Augustine's work (413-426) contrasting the earthly and heavenly cities, prompted by the sack of Rome in 410.
A North African schism holding that sacraments by unworthy clergy were invalid and that the true church must be pure.
The teaching that humans can obey God's commands without prior inner grace, condemned in 418.
The fallen condition inherited by all humanity from Adam, which Augustine emphasized against Pelagius.

topics.title: Chrysostom, Jerome, and the Desert Fathers
topics.subtitle: Church Fathers
topics.summary: A great preacher, a great translator, a bold bishop, and the monks of the Egyptian desert who shaped Christian spirituality in the fourth and fifth centuries.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: The fourth century, when Christianity gained imperial favor, was also the age of the desert. As the church grew comfortable, many men and women sought a more radical discipleship in the wilderness. At the same time great bishops and scholars preached, translated, and confronted the powerful. This topic introduces the founders of monasticism and three towering figures of the era: Ambrose, John Chrysostom, and Jerome.

sections.heading: Antony and the Desert
sections.body: **Antony of Egypt** (c. 251-356) heard the Gospel read in church as a young man: "If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor" (Matthew 19:21). He gave away his inheritance and withdrew in stages deeper into the desert, living as a hermit, battling temptation, and becoming a sought-after spiritual guide. The *Life of Antony*, written by Athanasius soon after Antony's death, spread the monastic ideal across the empire; Augustine's *Confessions* tells how hearing about it helped move him toward conversion.

sections.heading: Pachomius and Communal Monasticism
sections.body: Where Antony represents the *eremitic* (hermit) life, **Pachomius** (c. 292-348), a former soldier, founded *cenobitic* (communal) monasticism at Tabennisi in Upper Egypt around the 320s. His monks lived under a rule, shared work, meals, and prayer, and obeyed a superior, echoing the shared life of the Jerusalem church (Acts 2:44-45). His federation of monasteries grew to thousands of monks and nuns, and his rule influenced later monastic legislators in East and West.

sections.heading: The Sayings of the Desert Fathers
sections.body: The wisdom of the desert was preserved in the *Apophthegmata Patrum*, the *Sayings of the Desert Fathers*, compiled in Greek in the fifth century in alphabetical and thematic collections and later translated into Latin and other languages. These brief stories and sayings of abbas and ammas (desert mothers such as Amma Syncletica and Amma Sarah) emphasize humility, silence, perseverance in one's cell, refusal to judge others, and the struggle against the passions. Their influence on monastic and lay spirituality, East and West, has been immense.

sections.heading: Ambrose of Milan
sections.body: **Ambrose** (c. 339-397) was the Roman governor in Milan when, in 374, the people acclaimed him bishop, though he was still an unbaptized catechumen. He became a powerful preacher, a writer of hymns, and a defender of Nicene orthodoxy. He also confronted emperors: after Theodosius I ordered a massacre at Thessalonica in 390, Ambrose required him to do public penance. Ambrose baptized Augustine in 387.

sections.heading: John Chrysostom
sections.body:
**John** of Antioch (c. 347-407) was later called *Chrysostom*, "golden-mouthed," for his eloquence. After years of ascetic discipline he was ordained priest in Antioch in 386 and preached extended series of homilies on Genesis, Matthew, John, and Paul's letters. His interpretation followed the Antiochene emphasis on the literal and historical sense, applied to daily moral life, and he repeatedly urged the wealthy to care for the poor (1 Timothy 6:17-19). His treatise *On the Priesthood* remains a classic.

In 398 he was made archbishop of Constantinople. His reforms and his preaching against luxury offended powerful people, including Empress Eudoxia and Theophilus of Alexandria. A council known as the Synod of the Oak deposed him in 403; after a brief recall, he was exiled again and died on a forced march in 407. A sobering part of his legacy is his series of sermons *Against the Jews* (386-387), whose harsh rhetoric was later used to justify anti-Jewish hostility; modern scholars read them in their polemical context while acknowledging their harm. The Divine Liturgy most often celebrated in the Orthodox Church bears his name.

sections.heading: Jerome
sections.body: **Jerome** (c. 345-420), born at Stridon near the border of Dalmatia and Pannonia, studied in Rome, lived as an ascetic in the Syrian desert where he learned Hebrew, and served as secretary to Pope Damasus I (382-384), who commissioned him to revise the Latin Gospels. Settling in Bethlehem in 386 with the Roman noblewoman Paula and her daughter Eustochium, he translated most of the Old Testament directly from Hebrew, preferring the "Hebrew truth" to the Greek Septuagint. His work became the core of the *Vulgate*, though not every book in it is his translation. He also wrote commentaries and many letters, and is credited with the saying that "ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ" (prologue to his *Commentary on Isaiah*). The Council of Trent declared the Vulgate authentic for public use in 1546.

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.body: Monasticism became one of the main channels of Christian renewal, scholarship, and mission for the next thousand years. Chrysostom remains a model preacher, and Jerome's Vulgate was the Bible of the Western church for over a millennium. Orthodox, Catholic, and many Protestant Christians draw on the desert sayings for spiritual guidance.

topics.title: The Apostolic Age and the Persecutions
topics.subtitle: Church History
topics.summary: From Pentecost to the Great Persecution: how a Jewish messianic movement became an empire-wide church under intermittent, then systematic, Roman pressure.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: The first three centuries of Christian history run from a small community of Jesus' followers in Jerusalem to a church present in nearly every city of the Roman Empire. That growth happened without legal protection and, at times, under severe persecution. Understanding this period explains why martyrdom, the authority of the apostles, and the boundaries of the church mattered so much to later generations.

sections.heading: From Pentecost to the Gentile Mission
sections.body: The Book of Acts presents the outpouring of the Spirit at Pentecost (Acts 2:1-41) as the public beginning of the church's mission. The earliest believers were Jews who continued to worship at the Temple while confessing Jesus as Messiah. The martyrdom of Stephen (Acts 7) and the scattering that followed carried the message beyond Jerusalem, and at Antioch "the disciples were called Christians first" (Acts 11:26). Through Paul and others, congregations spread across Asia Minor, Greece, and eventually Rome.

sections.heading: The Jerusalem Council
sections.body: The influx of Gentiles raised a pressing question: must non-Jewish converts be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses to be saved? Acts 15:1-29 describes a meeting of the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, usually dated around AD 49. After testimony from Peter, Paul, and Barnabas, James proposed that Gentiles not be burdened with circumcision, asking only that they abstain from food offered to idols, from blood, from what is strangled, and from sexual immorality. The council became a model for later church assemblies resolving disputes by common deliberation.

sections.heading: Nero, Domitian, and Local Hostility
sections.body:
The first known Roman action against Christians came under Nero. According to the historian Tacitus (*Annals* 15.44), after the great fire of Rome in 64, Nero blamed the Christians and executed many of them cruelly. Early tradition places the martyrdoms of Peter and Paul in Rome in this period. Later Christian writers such as Eusebius also remembered a persecution under Domitian (81-96), the period to which many scholars date the Book of Revelation, though modern historians debate how extensive it was.

For most of the second century persecution was local and sporadic rather than imperial policy. Christians were suspected of "atheism" (refusing the gods), disloyalty, and secret crimes, and a riot or an accusation could bring them before a governor. Ignatius of Antioch, Polycarp of Smyrna, Justin Martyr, and the martyrs of Lyons (177) all died in such circumstances.

sections.heading: Pliny and Trajan
sections.body:
Around 112, Pliny the Younger, governor of Bithynia-Pontus, wrote to Emperor Trajan for guidance about Christians. He reported that they met before dawn on a fixed day and

> "sing responsively a hymn to Christ as to a god, and ... bind themselves by oath, not to some crime, but not to commit fraud, theft, or adultery." (Pliny, *Letters* 10.96)

Trajan replied that Christians "are not to be sought out," but if accused and convicted they were to be punished; anyone who denied being a Christian by worshiping the gods would be pardoned, and anonymous accusations were not to be accepted. This rescript shaped Roman practice for generations.

sections.heading: Empire-Wide Persecution
sections.body:
The third century brought the first coordinated campaigns:

- **Decius (250):** an edict required all inhabitants to sacrifice to the gods and obtain a certificate (*libellus*) proving they had done so. Many Christians complied or bought certificates, creating the painful question of how to treat the "lapsed."
- **Valerian (257-258):** targeted clergy and property; Cyprian of Carthage was martyred in 258.
- **Diocletian (from 303):** the "Great Persecution" ordered churches destroyed, Scriptures surrendered, clergy arrested, and eventually universal sacrifice. It lasted longest in the East, easing only with Galerius's edict of toleration in 311.

sections.heading: Timeline
sections.body:
1. c. 30 - Pentecost in Jerusalem
2. c. 49 - Jerusalem Council
3. 64 - Fire of Rome; Nero's persecution
4. c. 112 - Pliny's correspondence with Trajan
5. 250 - Decian edict on sacrifice
6. 303-311 - Great Persecution under Diocletian and Galerius

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.body: Persecution shaped Christian identity deeply. The memory of martyrs became central to worship, and Tertullian could boast that "the blood of Christians is seed" (*Apology* 50). At the same time, the question of how to restore those who had lapsed under pressure produced lasting controversies, including the Donatist schism in North Africa. Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant Christians alike look back to this era as a witness to faithfulness under suffering.

The systematic persecution begun by Diocletian in 303 and continued in the East under Galerius and others until 311 and beyond.
Literally "those who handed over"; Christians who surrendered Scriptures to authorities during the Diocletianic persecution.

topics.title: Constantine and the Seven Ecumenical Councils
topics.subtitle: Church History
topics.summary: From the Edict of Milan to the Second Council of Nicaea: how imperial favor and seven great councils shaped the church's doctrine of the Trinity and of Christ.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: Within a few years of the Great Persecution, the Roman emperor himself became a patron of the church. Constantine's support transformed Christianity's public position and made it possible for bishops from across the empire to meet in councils. Between 325 and 787 seven such gatherings came to be recognized, in varying degrees, as *ecumenical* (empire-wide, "of the whole inhabited world"), and their decisions still define mainstream Christian teaching about God and Christ.

sections.heading: Constantine and the Edict of Milan
sections.body:
Constantine attributed his victory over his rival Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge (312) to the God of the Christians. In 313 he and his co-emperor Licinius agreed at Milan on a policy of religious toleration and the restitution of confiscated church property. The so-called Edict of Milan survives as a letter issued by Licinius, which declares the emperors' intention

> "that we might grant to the Christians and others full authority to observe that religion which each preferred."

Historians note that this was a grant of toleration, not the establishment of Christianity as the state religion, which came only under Theodosius I in 380. Constantine nevertheless endowed churches, exempted clergy from certain obligations, and intervened in church disputes, setting a pattern of close church-state relations.

sections.heading: The Seven Councils
sections.body:
1. **Nicaea I (325):** Called by Constantine to resolve the dispute over Arius, who taught that the Son was a created being. The council confessed the Son to be *homoousios*, "of one substance," with the Father, and also addressed the date of Easter and church discipline.
2. **Constantinople I (381):** Convened by Theodosius I, it reaffirmed Nicaea against continuing Arianism, affirmed the full divinity of the Holy Spirit against the Pneumatomachians, and condemned Apollinarianism. The expanded creed associated with it is the Nicene Creed used today.
3. **Ephesus (431):** Condemned Nestorius, archbishop of Constantinople, who objected to calling Mary *Theotokos* ("God-bearer"). Led by Cyril of Alexandria, it insisted that the one born of Mary is the eternal Word made flesh.
4. **Chalcedon (451):** Responding to Eutyches, who blurred Christ's humanity into his divinity, it defined Christ as one person in two natures, drawing on the *Tome* of Pope Leo I.
5. **Constantinople II (553):** Under Emperor Justinian, it condemned the "Three Chapters," writings associated with Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret, and Ibas, interpreting Chalcedon in a way meant to reassure followers of Cyril.
6. **Constantinople III (680-681):** Rejected Monothelitism, the teaching that Christ has only one will, affirming that he has a divine and a human will in harmony.
7. **Nicaea II (787):** Ended the first phase of Iconoclasm by approving the veneration of icons, distinguishing honor (*proskynesis*) paid to images from the worship (*latreia*) due to God alone.

sections.heading: Who Receives Which Councils?
sections.body:
The councils did not produce universal agreement, and Christian traditions receive them differently:

- **Eastern Orthodox** Christians receive all seven and regard them as the definitive voice of the undivided church.
- **Roman Catholics** receive all seven as the first of twenty-one ecumenical councils, the most recent being Vatican II.
- **Oriental Orthodox** churches (Coptic, Armenian, Syriac, Ethiopian, and others) receive the first three but not Chalcedon.
- The **Church of the East** receives the first two, but not Ephesus.
- **Protestant** traditions generally accept the doctrinal decisions of the early councils, especially the first four, as faithful summaries of Scripture, while holding them subordinate to Scripture. The Church of England's Article XXI states that general councils "may err, and sometimes have erred." Many Protestants have reservations about Nicaea II's endorsement of icon veneration.

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.body: The councils gave the church its classic vocabulary for the Trinity and the person of Christ. They also raised enduring questions about the relationship between church and state, since emperors convened and enforced them. Orthodox theologians tend to stress the councils as expressions of the church's Spirit-guided consensus; Catholic theology adds the role of papal confirmation; Protestant theology emphasizes testing conciliar teaching by Scripture. All three, however, regard the Christology of Nicaea and Chalcedon as a shared inheritance.

topics.title: The Great Schism
topics.subtitle: Church History
topics.summary: How Eastern and Western Christianity drifted apart and finally divided, and why the events of 1054, 1204, and 1965 matter for Catholic-Orthodox relations.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: The division between the Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic churches is often dated to 1054, but historians increasingly describe it as a long process of estrangement rather than a single event. Language, culture, politics, and theology pulled the Greek East and Latin West apart over centuries, and later events turned a quarrel among church leaders into a lasting separation.

sections.heading: Roots of Estrangement
sections.body: By the early Middle Ages the two halves of Christendom no longer shared a common language: few Latin theologians read Greek and few Greeks read Latin. Political rivalries deepened the gap, especially after the pope crowned Charlemagne emperor in 800, a step Byzantines saw as challenging the one Roman emperor in Constantinople. In the ninth century a conflict between Patriarch Photius and Pope Nicholas I foreshadowed later disputes. Differences in practice, such as the West's use of unleavened bread in the Eucharist and its requirement of clerical celibacy, became symbols of deeper mistrust.

sections.heading: The Two Great Issues
sections.body:
**The filioque.** The Nicene Creed of 381 confesses that the Holy Spirit "proceeds from the Father," echoing John 15:26. In the West, beginning in Spain (the Third Council of Toledo in 589 is commonly cited), the Latin word *filioque*, "and the Son," was added. The practice spread in Frankish lands and was adopted in the liturgy at Rome by the early eleventh century. Orthodox Christians object both that the creed of an ecumenical council was altered without an ecumenical council and that the addition compromises the Father's role as the sole source within the Trinity. Catholic theology holds that the filioque expresses the Son's real role in the Spirit's procession, consistent with Latin fathers such as Augustine and compatible with the Greek formula "from the Father through the Son."

**Papal primacy.** Both sides honored the bishop of Rome as first among the patriarchs. Rome increasingly understood this primacy as a universal jurisdiction rooted in Peter's commission (Matthew 16:18-19). The East generally understood it as a primacy of honor within a communion of churches governed by councils.

sections.heading: The Events of 1054
sections.body: In 1054 Pope Leo IX sent legates led by Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida to Constantinople. Negotiations with Patriarch Michael Cerularius broke down, and on 16 July 1054 Humbert laid a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia. Cerularius and his synod responded by excommunicating the legates. Leo had already died, which raises questions about the legates' authority, and the excommunications were personal rather than directed at entire churches. Contacts and even shared communion continued in places for some time.

sections.heading: Hardening: The Crusades and Florence
sections.body:
What turned estrangement into enduring division was, for many historians, the Fourth Crusade. In 1204 crusaders diverted from their goal sacked Constantinople, looted its churches, and installed a Latin emperor and patriarch; the Latin Empire lasted until 1261. The memory of the sack embittered Orthodox believers for centuries.

Attempts at reunion followed. At the Council of Florence (1438-1445), the Byzantine emperor John VIII Palaiologos and Greek bishops, seeking Western aid against the Ottoman Turks, agreed to a decree of union in 1439. Mark of Ephesus refused to sign, and the union was widely rejected by clergy and people in the East. Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453.

sections.heading: Timeline
sections.body:
1. 589 - Third Council of Toledo, commonly cited for the filioque
2. 1054 - Mutual excommunications in Constantinople
3. 1204 - Sack of Constantinople in the Fourth Crusade
4. 1439 - Decree of union at Florence, later rejected in the East
5. 1965 - Excommunications of 1054 lifted

sections.heading: Toward Reconciliation
sections.body: On 7 December 1965 Pope Paul VI and Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras I issued a joint declaration in which they "regret and remove both from memory and from the midst of the Church the sentences of excommunication" of 1054. The declaration did not restore full communion, but it opened a period of theological dialogue that continues today.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: The schism remains one of Christianity's deepest wounds. Orthodox and Catholics share the sacraments, apostolic succession, and the first seven councils, yet differ on authority and on aspects of Trinitarian theology. Studying the schism shows how doctrine, culture, and politics intertwine, and why many Christians on both sides regard reconciliation as an unfinished task.

topics.title: The Medieval Church and Scholasticism
topics.subtitle: Church History
topics.summary: Monks, reforming popes, friars, and university masters: how the Western church of the Middle Ages organized its life and pursued "faith seeking understanding."

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: The medieval Western church was not a static institution but a succession of reform movements. Monasteries preserved learning and prayer, popes struggled to free the church from lay control, new orders of friars took the gospel to growing towns, and the universities produced a rigorous method of theology known as scholasticism.

sections.heading: Benedict and the Monastic Foundation
sections.body:
Benedict of Nursia (c. 480-c. 547) founded the monastery of Monte Cassino and wrote a *Rule* that became the standard for Western monasticism. It organizes life around common prayer (the Divine Office), manual work, and sacred reading, under an abbot, with vows that include stability, obedience, and conversion of life. Its prologue describes the monastery modestly:

> "And so we are going to establish a school for the service of the Lord. In founding it we hope to introduce nothing harsh or burdensome."

Pope Gregory the Great (590-604), himself a former monk, wrote the best-known early life of Benedict in his *Dialogues*. Gregory also strengthened papal administration, wrote the influential *Pastoral Rule* on the duties of bishops, and sent a mission under Augustine (later of Canterbury) that reached England in 597.

sections.heading: Cluny and the Gregorian Reform
sections.body:
In 910 Duke William of Aquitaine founded the abbey of Cluny in Burgundy and placed it directly under the protection of the pope, free from interference by local lords and bishops. Cluny became the head of a vast network of monasteries famed for elaborate liturgy, and it fostered a reforming spirit.

That spirit reached the papacy in the eleventh century. Reformers attacked *simony* (buying church offices) and clerical marriage, and above all *lay investiture*, the practice of rulers installing bishops. Pope Gregory VII (1073-1085) gave the movement its name. His *Dictatus Papae* asserted sweeping papal powers, and his clash with Emperor Henry IV led to Henry's penitent appearance at Canossa in 1077. The Investiture Controversy was settled by compromise in the Concordat of Worms (1122).

sections.heading: The Rise of Scholasticism
sections.body:
Scholasticism was a method of teaching and inquiry that applied logic to the authorities of Scripture and the fathers.

- **Anselm of Canterbury (1033-1109)** described theology as "faith seeking understanding." His *Proslogion* offered the famous "ontological" argument for God's existence, and *Cur Deus Homo* explained the incarnation in terms of satisfaction for sin.
- **Peter Abelard (1079-1142)** compiled *Sic et Non* ("Yes and No"), setting apparently conflicting authorities side by side to train students to resolve them. His bold methods drew the opposition of Bernard of Clairvaux, and he was condemned at Sens in 1140 or 1141.
- **Peter Lombard (c. 1100-1160)** organized Christian doctrine in his *Four Books of Sentences*, which became the standard theological textbook; for centuries, commenting on the *Sentences* was part of becoming a master of theology.

sections.heading: Universities and Mendicant Orders
sections.body:
From around 1200, universities at Bologna, Paris, and Oxford became the centers of learning. At the same time the *mendicant* ("begging") orders arose. Francis of Assisi (c. 1181-1226) embraced radical poverty, and his friars received papal approval around 1209-1210. Dominic founded the Order of Preachers, confirmed in 1216, to combat heresy through learned preaching. The friars quickly became leading university teachers.

The greatest of them was **Thomas Aquinas (1225-1274)**, a Dominican who integrated the newly recovered works of Aristotle with Christian theology. His unfinished *Summa Theologiae* opens with "five ways" of arguing for God's existence and proceeds through creation, ethics, Christ, and the sacraments. His Franciscan contemporary Bonaventure offered a more Augustinian synthesis.

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.body: Benedictine monasteries, reforming popes, and the universities shaped European civilization. Catholic theology has long regarded Aquinas as a preeminent teacher, especially since Leo XIII's encyclical *Aeterni Patris* (1879). Reformers such as Luther sharply criticized scholastic theology, though later Protestant theologians adopted scholastic methods of their own. Orthodox theologians have often contrasted Western scholasticism with the more mystical and liturgical character of Eastern theology.

topics.title: The Protestant Reformation
topics.subtitle: Church History
topics.summary: From Wycliffe and Hus to Luther, Zwingli, Calvin, the Anabaptists, and the English church: the sixteenth-century movements that reshaped Western Christianity.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: The Protestant Reformation of the sixteenth century divided Western Christianity and gave rise to the Lutheran, Reformed, Anabaptist, and Anglican traditions. It grew out of long-standing calls for reform, but it became a movement about the gospel itself: how sinners are made right with God and where final authority in the church lies.

sections.heading: Forerunners
sections.body: Two late-medieval figures anticipated many Reformation themes. **John Wycliffe** (c. 1330-1384), an Oxford theologian, criticized papal power and the doctrine of transubstantiation and championed the authority of Scripture; his followers, the Lollards, produced English Bible translations. **Jan Hus** (c. 1372-1415) of Prague, influenced by Wycliffe, preached reform in Czech and criticized indulgences. Summoned to the Council of Constance under a promise of safe conduct, he was condemned and burned in 1415. The same council condemned Wycliffe posthumously.

sections.heading: Luther and the German Reformation
sections.body:
Martin Luther (1483-1546), an Augustinian friar and professor at Wittenberg, struggled to find a gracious God and came to understand "the righteousness of God" (Romans 1:16-17) as a gift received by faith. In 1517 he published the *Ninety-Five Theses* against the preaching of indulgences. The first thesis reads:

> "Our Lord and Master Jesus Christ, when He said Poenitentiam agite, willed that the whole life of believers should be repentance."

In 1520 Luther wrote major treatises, including *The Freedom of a Christian*, and was excommunicated in January 1521. At the Diet of Worms in April 1521, before Emperor Charles V, he refused to recant unless convinced "by the testimony of the Scriptures or by clear reason," declaring his conscience "captive to the Word of God." (The famous words "Here I stand" appear in early printed versions, but scholars are unsure he spoke them.) Protected at the Wartburg castle, he translated the New Testament into German.

sections.heading: Zwingli and Calvin
sections.body:
In Zurich, **Huldrych Zwingli** (1484-1531) began preaching through the Gospel of Matthew in 1519 and led the city council to reform worship. At the Marburg Colloquy (1529) he and Luther agreed on much but divided over the Lord's Supper: Luther insisted on Christ's bodily presence, while Zwingli taught a spiritual, memorial understanding. Zwingli died in battle at Kappel in 1531.

**John Calvin** (1509-1564), a French humanist converted to the evangelical cause, published the first edition of his *Institutes of the Christian Religion* in 1536. Expelled from Geneva in 1538, he returned in 1541 and organized the church with four offices: pastors, teachers, elders, and deacons. Geneva became a training center for Reformed pastors across Europe, though Calvin's legacy also includes the execution of the anti-Trinitarian Michael Servetus (1553).

sections.heading: The Radical Reformation
sections.body: Some of Zwingli's associates, including Conrad Grebel and Felix Manz, concluded that baptism should follow personal confession of faith. In January 1525 they performed the first adult baptisms in Zurich, earning the label *Anabaptists* ("rebaptizers"). They sought a church of committed believers separate from state power; many practiced nonresistance. Catholics and Protestants alike persecuted them, and Manz was drowned in 1527. The violent episode at Münster (1534-1535) was not typical of the movement, which Menno Simons later helped consolidate.

sections.heading: The English Reformation
sections.body: In England, reform began with politics. When the pope would not annul Henry VIII's marriage, Parliament's Act of Supremacy (1534) declared the king supreme head of the Church of England. Under Edward VI, Archbishop Thomas Cranmer introduced the *Book of Common Prayer* (1549, 1552); Mary I restored Catholicism; and the Elizabethan Settlement (1559) and the Thirty-Nine Articles established a Protestant church retaining bishops and much traditional liturgy.

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.body: Protestants summarize the Reformation's teaching with later slogans such as *sola scriptura* and *sola fide* and the priesthood of all believers (1 Peter 2:9). Catholic historians, while acknowledging the need for reform, typically see the breach of unity as a tragedy. Recent dialogue has narrowed some differences, as in the Lutheran-Catholic *Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification* (1999).

topics.title: The Catholic Reformation
topics.subtitle: Church History
topics.summary: The Council of Trent, the Jesuits, Teresa of Ávila, global missions, and the wars of religion that ended with the Peace of Westphalia.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: The Roman Catholic Church of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries underwent a profound renewal. Historians once called it simply the "Counter-Reformation," emphasizing its response to Protestantism. Many now prefer "Catholic Reformation" or "Catholic renewal," because reforming energy was already present before Luther and because the movement included spiritual, missionary, and pastoral initiatives that went well beyond controversy. Both dimensions were real.

sections.heading: Roots of Renewal
sections.body: Calls for reform "in head and members" had echoed for over a century. In Spain, Cardinal Ximénes de Cisneros reformed religious houses and sponsored biblical scholarship. In Italy, confraternities such as the Oratory of Divine Love fostered devotion and charity, and new orders appeared: the Theatines (1524), the Capuchins (1528), and the Ursulines (1535), devoted to educating girls. Pope Paul III (1534-1549) appointed reforming cardinals and finally convoked a general council.

sections.heading: The Council of Trent (1545-1563)
sections.body:
The council met at Trent in northern Italy in three periods (1545-1547, 1551-1552, 1562-1563), interrupted by war and politics. Its work was both doctrinal and disciplinary.

**Doctrine.** Trent declared that the truths of the gospel are contained "in the written books, and the unwritten traditions," both of which the church receives with equal reverence; it listed the canon of Scripture, including the deuterocanonical books, and declared the Latin Vulgate authentic for public use. Its decree on justification (1547) taught that justification is God's gracious work, beginning with prevenient grace, but rejected justification by faith alone as the Reformers taught it, insisting on inner renewal and human cooperation with grace. It affirmed seven sacraments, transubstantiation, the sacrificial character of the Mass, purgatory, and the veneration of saints and images.

**Discipline.** Trent required bishops to reside in their dioceses, abolished the office of professional indulgence collectors, and ordered every diocese to establish a seminary for training priests. Afterwards came the Roman Catechism (1566) and a revised Roman Missal (1570).

sections.heading: The Jesuits and Spiritual Renewal
sections.body:
**Ignatius of Loyola** (1491-1556), a Basque soldier wounded at Pamplona in 1521, underwent a conversion during his convalescence. His *Spiritual Exercises* guide a retreatant through a month of meditation toward discerning God's will. With a small group of companions he founded the Society of Jesus, approved by Paul III in 1540. The Jesuits became renowned for education, founding hundreds of colleges, and for missions.

**Teresa of Ávila** (1515-1582) reformed the Carmelite order, founding the first convent of "Discalced" (barefoot) Carmelites in 1562, and wrote classics of mystical prayer such as *The Interior Castle* (1577). With John of the Cross she extended the reform to friars. In 1970 she became one of the first two women declared Doctors of the Church. Bishops such as Charles Borromeo of Milan modeled the pastoral ideals of Trent.

sections.heading: Global Missions
sections.body: Catholic missions accompanied Spanish and Portuguese expansion. Francis Xavier preached in India and reached Japan in 1549; Matteo Ricci adapted the gospel to Chinese culture and settled in Beijing in 1601. In the Americas, friars such as Bartolomé de las Casas protested the abuse of Indigenous peoples, even as missions were entangled with colonial violence. In 1622 the papacy founded the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith to coordinate missions.

sections.heading: Wars of Religion and Westphalia
sections.body:
Religious division fueled a century of conflict:

1. 1555 - Peace of Augsburg recognizes Lutheranism alongside Catholicism in the Empire
2. 1562-1598 - French Wars of Religion, including the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre (1572)
3. 1598 - Edict of Nantes grants French Protestants limited toleration
4. 1618-1648 - Thirty Years' War devastates central Europe
5. 1648 - Peace of Westphalia

The treaties of Westphalia, concluded at Osnabrück and Münster, ended the Thirty Years' War and extended legal recognition in the Empire to the Reformed as well as Lutherans and Catholics. Pope Innocent X protested the settlement, but it marked the end of efforts to restore religious unity by force in the Empire.

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.body: Trent defined Catholic teaching and practice until the Second Vatican Council, and its seminaries reshaped the priesthood. Catholics regard the period as a time of genuine holiness and missionary expansion; Protestant historians have often emphasized its polemical edge. Most scholars now see both reform and confessional rivalry at work.

topics.title: The Modern Church
topics.subtitle: Church History
topics.summary: From Pietism and the Great Awakenings to world missions, the Vatican Councils, Pentecostalism, ecumenism, and the southward shift of global Christianity.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: Since the late seventeenth century Christianity has been reshaped by revival movements, a global missionary expansion, major Catholic councils, the rise of Pentecostalism, and efforts at reunion. By the twenty-first century the typical Christian was no longer European but African, Latin American, or Asian.

sections.heading: Pietism and the Moravians
sections.body: In Lutheran Germany, Philipp Jakob Spener's *Pia Desideria* (1675) called for small groups for Bible study, lay participation, and a living faith rather than mere doctrinal correctness. August Hermann Francke made Halle a center of Pietist education and charity. Count Nikolaus von Zinzendorf sheltered Moravian refugees at Herrnhut, where a renewal in 1727 launched a remarkable missionary effort.

sections.heading: The Great Awakenings
sections.body:
Pietist influence touched the English-speaking world. In 1738 John Wesley attended a meeting in Aldersgate Street, London, where Luther's preface to Romans was being read:

> "I felt my heart strangely warmed. I felt I did trust in Christ, Christ alone, for salvation." (Wesley's *Journal*, 24 May 1738)

Wesley, his brother Charles (the hymn writer), and George Whitefield began open-air preaching. Whitefield's tours of Britain and the American colonies drew enormous crowds. In New England, Jonathan Edwards documented a revival at Northampton (1734-1735) and preached "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God" (1741); he also wrote careful analyses of authentic religious experience. Wesley's Methodist societies remained within the Church of England during his life but became separate churches afterward. A Second Great Awakening in the United States (c. 1790-1840) brought camp meetings and the rapid growth of Methodists and Baptists.

sections.heading: The Modern Missionary Movement
sections.body: William Carey (1761-1834), an English Baptist shoemaker, argued in his *Enquiry* (1792) that the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19-20) still bound Christians. He helped found the Baptist Missionary Society and sailed for India in 1793, where he and colleagues at Serampore translated the Bible into many languages. Carey is often called the father of modern Protestant missions. Others followed, including Hudson Taylor, who founded the China Inland Mission in 1865. Catholic missionary orders also expanded greatly in the nineteenth century.

sections.heading: The Vatican Councils
sections.body:
The **First Vatican Council** (1869-1870), under Pius IX, defined in *Pastor Aeternus* the pope's universal jurisdiction and infallibility when he speaks *ex cathedra* on faith and morals. The council was cut short by the Franco-Prussian War and the capture of Rome; some who rejected the definition formed the Old Catholic churches.

The **Second Vatican Council** (1962-1965), opened by John XXIII and concluded by Paul VI, sought *aggiornamento* ("updating"). Its documents permitted vernacular liturgy (*Sacrosanctum Concilium*), described the church as the people of God (*Lumen Gentium*), addressed revelation (*Dei Verbum*) and the modern world (*Gaudium et Spes*), and embraced ecumenism, religious liberty, and dialogue with other religions.

sections.heading: Pentecostalism
sections.body: Pentecostalism emphasizes the baptism of the Holy Spirit, often evidenced by speaking in tongues (Acts 2:4). Its modern beginnings are traced to Charles Parham's Bible school in Topeka (1901) and especially to the Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles (1906), led by the African American preacher William J. Seymour, where Black and white worshipers prayed together at a time of segregation. Denominations such as the Assemblies of God (1914) followed, and a charismatic renewal spread into older churches from the 1960s. Pentecostal and charismatic Christianity is now among the fastest-growing forms of the faith.

sections.heading: Ecumenism and the Global South
sections.body:
The World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh (1910) is often seen as the beginning of the modern ecumenical movement, which led to the founding of the World Council of Churches in Amsterdam in 1948. The Catholic Church entered ecumenical dialogue after Vatican II, and evangelicals organized their own global gatherings, such as the Lausanne Congress (1974).

Meanwhile, Christianity's center of gravity has moved south. Widely cited demographic studies indicate that most of the world's Christians now live in Africa, Latin America, and Asia, a shift popularized by Philip Jenkins's *The Next Christendom* (2002).

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: Modern church history explains the shape of the church today: its denominations, its missionary reach, its Catholic reforms, and its Pentecostal energy. It also raises open questions about unity, culture, and where the future leadership of world Christianity will come from.

keyTerms.definition: A seventeenth- and eighteenth-century Lutheran renewal movement stressing personal faith, Bible study, and holy living.
Waves of revival in Britain and America in the 1730s-1740s associated with Edwards, Whitefield, and the Wesleys.
The doctrine defined at Vatican I that the pope is preserved from error when he defines faith or morals ex cathedra.
Italian for "updating"; John XXIII's watchword for the renewal sought at Vatican II.
A movement emphasizing Spirit baptism, speaking in tongues, and spiritual gifts, rooted in Topeka (1901) and Azusa Street (1906).
The movement to promote unity and cooperation among divided Christian churches.
