topics.title: The Apostles' Creed
topics.subtitle: Creeds & Confessions
topics.summary: The West's most familiar baptismal creed: its legendary origins, its real roots in the Old Roman Creed, its threefold structure, and its use across traditions.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: The Apostles' Creed is the most widely used summary of Christian faith in Western churches. Catholics, Lutherans, Reformed, Anglicans, Methodists, and many others confess it at baptism, in daily prayer, and in catechesis. Although it was not written by the apostles, it preserves the shape of the faith the early Roman church confessed at baptism.

sections.heading: The Text
sections.body:
In the traditional English of the *Book of Common Prayer*:

> I believe in God the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth: And in Jesus Christ his only Son our Lord, Who was conceived by the Holy Ghost, Born of the Virgin Mary, Suffered under Pontius Pilate, Was crucified, dead, and buried: He descended into hell; The third day he rose again from the dead, He ascended into heaven, And sitteth on the right hand of God the Father Almighty; From thence he shall come to judge the quick and the dead. I believe in the Holy Ghost; The holy Catholic Church; The Communion of Saints; The Forgiveness of sins; The Resurrection of the body, And the Life everlasting. Amen.

sections.heading: Legend and History
sections.body:
Around 404, Rufinus of Aquileia recorded a tradition that the apostles, before separating to preach, composed the creed together, "each contributing his several sentence." Medieval writers went further and assigned each of twelve articles to a particular apostle. The name "Apostles' Creed" (*symbolum apostolorum*) itself appears in a letter from a synod at Milan around 390. In the fifteenth century, the humanist Lorenzo Valla challenged apostolic authorship, and at the Council of Florence the Greek bishop Mark of Ephesus noted that the Eastern churches did not know this creed at all.

Modern scholars trace the creed to the **Old Roman Creed** (or Old Roman Symbol), the baptismal creed of the church at Rome. It is attested in Greek by Marcellus of Ancyra around 340 and in Latin by Rufinus. Its roots lie in still earlier *interrogatory* creeds: candidates for baptism were asked three questions, "Do you believe in God the Father Almighty? ... in Christ Jesus, the Son of God? ... in the Holy Spirit?", and answered "I believe" before each immersion, following the baptismal command of Matthew 28:19. The church order known as the *Apostolic Tradition*, traditionally attributed to Hippolytus (both date and authorship are debated), preserves such questions.

sections.heading: From Rome to the Received Text
sections.body: The Old Roman Creed was shorter than the creed used today. Phrases such as "Maker of heaven and earth," "conceived," "suffered," "descended into hell," "catholic," and "the communion of saints" were added gradually in various regions, especially in Gaul and Spain. The earliest witness to the full received text (*textus receptus*) is the early eighth-century handbook of the missionary bishop Pirminius. Under Carolingian influence this form was adopted throughout the West, including at Rome.

sections.heading: Structure
sections.body:
The creed is **Trinitarian** in shape, with three articles following the baptismal questions:

1. **The Father**, almighty Creator.
2. **The Son**, the longest section, narrating Christ's conception, birth, suffering, death, burial, descent, resurrection, ascension, session, and return in judgment, echoing early summaries of the gospel such as 1 Corinthians 15:3-8.
3. **The Holy Spirit**, followed by the church, the communion of saints, forgiveness, resurrection, and eternal life, which are the Spirit's works.

Medieval catechesis also divided it into twelve articles, reflecting the legend of apostolic authorship.

sections.heading: Disputed Phrases
sections.body:
- **"He descended into hell"** (Latin *descendit ad inferos*, "to the lower regions") is interpreted differently. Catholic and Orthodox teaching generally understand it as Christ's descent to the realm of the dead to proclaim victory and free the righteous (compare 1 Peter 3:18-20). Calvin read it as Christ's enduring the agony of God's judgment on the cross. Some modern translations say "he descended to the dead."
- **"Catholic"** means "universal." Some Protestant versions, following Luther's German, render it "Christian church."

sections.heading: Use Across Traditions
sections.body: In the Catholic Church the creed is professed at baptism and may be used at Mass. Anglicans recite it at Morning and Evening Prayer. Luther's Small Catechism and the Heidelberg Catechism expound it article by article, as did the Roman Catechism of Trent. The Eastern Orthodox churches do not use it liturgically, confessing the Nicene Creed instead, though they find its content consistent with their faith.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: Because it grew out of baptism, the Apostles' Creed is a personal confession: "I believe." It gives a compact narrative of the gospel and has served for centuries as a common text for teaching, worship, and Christian identity across Western traditions.

keyTerms.definition: The baptismal creed of the early Roman church, attested by Marcellus (c. 340) and Rufinus, from which the Apostles' Creed developed.

topics.title: The Nicene Creed
topics.subtitle: Creeds & Confessions
topics.summary: The creed of 325, its expansion associated with Constantinople in 381, the meaning of homoousios, and the controversy over the Western addition of the filioque.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: The Nicene Creed is the most widely accepted statement of Christian faith, confessed by Orthodox, Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran, Reformed, and many other churches. What most Christians call "the Nicene Creed" is in fact the expanded form associated with the Council of Constantinople in 381, known to scholars as the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed. Its story involves two councils, one controversial word, and a later addition that still divides East and West.

sections.heading: The Creed of 325
sections.body:
Around 318 Arius, a presbyter of Alexandria, taught that the Son of God was a creature who "was not" before he was begotten. The Council of Nicaea (325), summoned by Constantine, answered with a creed based on existing baptismal creeds but sharpened with anti-Arian language. It confessed the Son as

> "the only-begotten of his Father, of the substance of the Father, God of God, Light of Light, very God of very God, begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father." (NPNF translation)

The decisive word was **homoousios**, "of one substance" or "of the same being." The creed of 325 ended abruptly with "And in the Holy Ghost," followed by anathemas condemning those who said "there was a time when he was not" or that the Son was a creature or of another substance or hypostasis.

sections.heading: The Struggle Over Homoousios
sections.body: Nicaea did not end the controversy. Many bishops disliked *homoousios* because it was not a scriptural word and seemed to some to blur the distinction between Father and Son. Alternatives circulated: *homoiousios* ("of like substance"), *homoios* ("like"), and the radical *anomoios* ("unlike"). Emperors favored different parties, and Athanasius was exiled repeatedly. Over decades, Athanasius and then the Cappadocian Fathers showed that *homoousios* safeguarded what Scripture teaches about the Son's full divinity (John 1:1-3, Colossians 1:15-17, Hebrews 1:3).

sections.heading: The Creed of 381
sections.body:
The Council of Constantinople (381) reaffirmed Nicaea. The creed associated with it differs from 325 in several ways. It adds phrases such as "maker of heaven and earth," "before all ages," "crucified for us under Pontius Pilate," and "of whose kingdom there shall be no end" (Luke 1:33), often seen as a reply to Marcellus of Ancyra. It drops the phrase "that is, of the substance of the Father" and the anathemas. Above all, it greatly expands the article on the Holy Spirit:

> "And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and Giver of life, who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified, who spoke by the prophets." (translated from the Greek)

Without calling the Spirit *homoousios*, this language affirms the Spirit's full divinity through divine titles and equal worship. Final clauses confess one holy, catholic, and apostolic church, one baptism for the remission of sins, the resurrection of the dead, and the life of the world to come.

The text is first attested in the acts of the Council of Chalcedon (451), where it was read alongside the creed of 325. Scholars debate whether the council of 381 composed it or adopted and endorsed an existing baptismal creed.

sections.heading: The Filioque
sections.body:
The Greek text says the Spirit "proceeds from the Father," echoing John 15:26. In the Latin West the words *filioque*, "and the Son," were added. The Third Council of Toledo (589) in Spain is commonly cited as the earliest official use, and the addition spread through the Frankish church. Pope Leo III (c. 810) accepted the doctrine but declined to add the phrase to the creed, and is reported to have had the creed engraved without it. Rome adopted the filioque in its liturgy in the early eleventh century.

Orthodox Christians object on two grounds: procedurally, the creed of an ecumenical council was altered without an ecumenical council (the Council of Ephesus in 431 had forbidden composing a different creed), and theologically, the addition seems to compromise the Father as the unique source of the Son and the Spirit. Catholic theology defends the doctrine as expressing the Son's role in the eternal procession of the Spirit, in continuity with Latin fathers like Augustine. In recent decades some Western churches have recommended or permitted omitting the clause in ecumenical settings, and popes have recited the creed in Greek without it alongside Orthodox patriarchs.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: The Nicene Creed is the clearest common confession of the divided churches. It is recited in the Eucharist of East and West and serves as a touchstone of Trinitarian faith. Its history shows how the church developed precise language to protect the mystery of the Trinity, and how a single phrase can carry centuries of theological and ecclesial meaning.

keyTerms.definition: Greek for "of one substance" or "of the same being"; the Nicene term affirming the Son's full divinity with the Father.
Greek for "of like substance"; a compromise term proposed by some fourth-century bishops in place of homoousios.

A formal condemnation; the creed of 325 ended with anathemas against Arian positions.
Latin for "and the Son"; the Western addition to the creed concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit.
The eternal origin of the Holy Spirit, described in John 15:26 as proceeding from the Father.

topics.title: The Chalcedonian Definition and the Athanasian Creed
topics.subtitle: Creeds & Confessions
topics.summary: Chalcedon's "one person in two natures" with its four negative adverbs, and the Quicunque Vult, a Latin creed of uncertain origin on the Trinity and the incarnation.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: Two texts from the fifth and sixth centuries complete the classic statements of Christian doctrine. The Definition of Chalcedon (451) sets the boundaries of orthodox teaching about the person of Christ, and the Athanasian Creed, despite its name a later Latin composition, summarizes both Trinitarian and Christological orthodoxy in memorable, rhythmic form.

sections.heading: The Road to Chalcedon
sections.body: After the Council of Ephesus (431) condemned Nestorius for seeming to divide Christ into two subjects, the opposite danger appeared. **Eutyches**, a monk of Constantinople, taught that after the union there was only one nature in Christ, and denied that Christ's humanity was of one substance with ours. Pope Leo I wrote his *Tome* (449) affirming two natures, each acting in communion with the other, in one person. But a council at Ephesus in 449, dominated by Dioscorus of Alexandria, vindicated Eutyches; Leo denounced it as a "robber synod" (*latrocinium*). After the death of Theodosius II, the new emperor Marcian convened a council at Chalcedon in 451, which deposed Dioscorus, received Leo's *Tome* and Cyril's letters, and issued a definition of faith.

sections.heading: The Definition
sections.body:
The Definition confesses "one and the same Son," perfect in Godhead and perfect in manhood, truly God and truly man, of a rational soul and body, consubstantial with the Father according to the Godhead and consubstantial with us according to the manhood, "in all things like unto us, without sin" (Hebrews 4:15), born of the Virgin Mary, the *Theotokos*, according to the manhood. Its heart is the confession of Christ

> "in two natures, inconfusedly, unchangeably, indivisibly, inseparably; the distinction of natures being by no means taken away by the union, but rather the property of each nature being preserved, and concurring in one Person and one Subsistence." (Schaff's translation)

sections.heading: The Four "Withouts"
sections.body:
The four Greek adverbs, often rendered "without confusion, without change, without division, without separation," work as boundary markers rather than an explanation of the mystery:

1. **Without confusion** (*asynchytos*) and
2. **Without change** (*atreptos*): against Eutyches, the natures are not mixed or transformed into a third thing.
3. **Without division** (*adiairetos*) and
4. **Without separation** (*achoristos*): against Nestorius, Christ is not two sons or two subjects.

The union is located in the one *person* (*prosopon*) and *hypostasis* of the Word, while the natures remain distinct (John 1:14, Colossians 2:9).

sections.heading: Reception and Division
sections.body: Chalcedon is received by the Eastern Orthodox, Catholic, and most Protestant churches. But the **Oriental Orthodox** churches (Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopian, Eritrean, and Malankara) rejected it, believing that "in two natures" compromised Cyril of Alexandria's teaching of "one incarnate nature of God the Word." They reject the label "monophysite" and prefer *miaphysite* ("one united nature"), and they condemn Eutyches as firmly as Chalcedonians do. Twentieth-century dialogues, including a 1973 common declaration by Pope Paul VI and Coptic Pope Shenouda III and agreed statements between Eastern and Oriental Orthodox theologians in 1989 and 1990, concluded that much of the division had been about terminology rather than substance.

sections.heading: The Athanasian Creed
sections.body:
The **Athanasian Creed** is named *Quicunque vult* from its Latin opening, "Whosoever will be saved." It has two main parts. The first sets out the Trinity:

> "That we worship one God in Trinity, and Trinity in Unity; Neither confounding the Persons: nor dividing the Substance."

It proceeds in balanced clauses: the Father is uncreated, the Son uncreated, the Holy Spirit uncreated, "and yet they are not three uncreated... but one uncreated." It states that the Spirit is "of the Father and of the Son," reflecting the Western filioque. The second part confesses Christ as perfect God and perfect man, "one, not by conversion of the Godhead into flesh, but by taking of the Manhood into God." Opening and closing *damnatory clauses* declare that those who do not hold this faith "shall perish everlastingly."

sections.heading: Date and Authorship
sections.body: Athanasius almost certainly did not write it. It was composed in Latin, not Greek; it is unknown in the East before much later; and it presupposes theological developments after his death, including Augustinian Trinitarian thought and the Christological debates of the fifth century. Most scholars place it in southern Gaul in the late fifth or early sixth century; it is quoted by Caesarius of Arles (died 542). Proposed authors have included Ambrose, Vincent of Lérins, Hilary of Arles, and Caesarius, but none commands consensus.

sections.heading: Use and Legacy
sections.body: The Athanasian Creed was traditionally recited in the Western office, appears among the three ecumenical creeds in the Lutheran Book of Concord, and is affirmed in Article VIII of the Thirty-Nine Articles. The *Book of Common Prayer* (1662) appoints it on certain feasts, though the American Episcopal Church omitted it from its prayer book in 1789, partly over the damnatory clauses. Eastern Orthodox churches do not use it liturgically. Together with Chalcedon, it remains a standard by which Western churches measure teaching on the Trinity and the incarnation.

keyTerms.definition: The union of divine and human natures in the one person (hypostasis) of the Word, as confessed at Chalcedon.

topics.title: The Reformation Confessions
topics.subtitle: Creeds & Confessions
topics.summary: The Schleitheim, Augsburg, Belgic, Heidelberg, Thirty-Nine Articles, Dort, Westminster, and 1689 Baptist confessions: what they are and what distinguishes them.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: The sixteenth and seventeenth centuries produced a remarkable body of confessional documents. Unlike the ancient creeds, which are brief and shared by most Christians, these *confessions of faith* are longer statements defining a particular church's teaching on the disputed questions of the Reformation: Scripture, justification, the sacraments, the church, and Christian life. They were written to teach congregations, to unify churches, and often to explain their beliefs to hostile rulers.

sections.heading: Timeline
sections.body:
1. 1527 - Schleitheim Confession (Swiss Anabaptists)
2. 1530 - Augsburg Confession (Lutheran)
3. 1561 - Belgic Confession (Reformed, Low Countries)
4. 1563 - Heidelberg Catechism (Reformed, Palatinate)
5. 1563/1571 - Thirty-Nine Articles (Church of England)
6. 1618-1619 - Canons of Dort (Reformed)
7. 1646-1647 - Westminster Confession and Catechisms (Presbyterian)
8. 1689 - Second London Baptist Confession (Particular Baptist)

sections.heading: The Schleitheim Confession (1527)
sections.body: The "Brotherly Union" adopted by Swiss Brethren at Schleitheim, largely the work of Michael Sattler, is one of the earliest Protestant confessions. Its seven articles address believers' baptism, the ban (church discipline), the breaking of bread, separation from the world, pastors, the sword, and the oath. It teaches that Christians should not wield the sword as magistrates and should not swear oaths (Matthew 5:33-37). Sattler was executed a few months later. Schleitheim shaped Anabaptist and Mennonite identity.

sections.heading: The Augsburg Confession (1530)
sections.body: Drafted chiefly by Philip Melanchthon and presented to Emperor Charles V at the Diet of Augsburg on 25 June 1530, this is the foundational Lutheran confession. Its first twenty-one articles state doctrine, emphasizing continuity with the catholic tradition, and the last seven address abuses the Lutherans had corrected. Article IV teaches that people "are freely justified for Christ's sake, through faith" (compare Romans 3:28). It was later included in the *Book of Concord* (1580).

sections.heading: The Reformed Confessions
sections.body:
The **Belgic Confession** (1561), written by Guido de Brès for the persecuted Reformed churches of the Low Countries and addressed to King Philip II, sets out Reformed doctrine in thirty-seven articles. De Brès was executed in 1567.

The **Heidelberg Catechism** (1563), commissioned by Elector Frederick III of the Palatinate and written chiefly by Zacharias Ursinus with Caspar Olevianus and others, is arranged in 129 questions divided into fifty-two "Lord's Days" for preaching. Its three parts treat human misery, deliverance, and gratitude. Its first question is among the most beloved in Protestantism:

> "What is your only comfort in life and in death? That I am not my own, but belong, body and soul, in life and in death, to my faithful Savior, Jesus Christ."

The **Canons of Dort** (1618-1619) were issued by an international Reformed synod at Dordrecht responding to the Remonstrants, followers of Jacobus Arminius, who had challenged Reformed teaching on predestination and grace. Its five "heads of doctrine" later inspired the popular (and much later) mnemonic "TULIP." Together the Belgic Confession, Heidelberg Catechism, and Canons of Dort are known as the **Three Forms of Unity** of continental Reformed churches.

sections.heading: The Thirty-Nine Articles
sections.body: Revised from Thomas Cranmer's Forty-Two Articles (1553), the Thirty-Nine Articles were approved in 1563 and given final form in English in 1571. They combine a broadly Reformed doctrine of Scripture, justification, and the sacraments with the retention of bishops and the *Book of Common Prayer*. Article VI affirms that Scripture contains all things necessary to salvation.

sections.heading: The Westminster Standards
sections.body: The Westminster Assembly, summoned by the English Parliament in 1643, produced the **Westminster Confession of Faith** (1646) and the Larger and Shorter Catechisms (1647). Though the Church of England did not keep them, the Church of Scotland adopted them, and they became the doctrinal standards of Presbyterian churches worldwide. The Confession opens with a chapter on Scripture as the rule of faith and life.

sections.heading: The Second London Baptist Confession (1689)
sections.body: English Particular (Calvinistic) Baptists first published this confession in 1677 and publicly endorsed it at a general assembly in 1689, after the Act of Toleration. It closely follows the Westminster Confession (and the Congregationalist Savoy Declaration), but differs on baptism, teaching the baptism of believers by immersion (Romans 6:3-4), and on church government, favoring independent congregations.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: These confessions show that the Reformation produced several traditions, not one. They agree on the supreme authority of Scripture and salvation by grace but differ on the sacraments, church order, and the relation of church and state. Many churches still require their ministers to subscribe to them, and they remain rich resources for teaching and devotion.

topics.title: Catechisms and the Function of Creeds
topics.subtitle: Creeds & Confessions
topics.summary: What creeds are for, how the church has taught the faith through catechesis, the great catechisms, and how different traditions understand creedal authority.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: Creeds and catechisms are tools the church uses to confess, teach, and guard its faith. Studying how they function helps explain why Christians have written them, why they memorize them, and why traditions disagree about how binding they are.

sections.heading: What Creeds Are For
sections.body:
Creeds serve several purposes at once:

- **Confession and worship.** A creed is first an act of faith addressed to God, often recited in the liturgy (compare Romans 10:9-10).
- **Baptismal identity.** The earliest creeds were professed at baptism, marking entry into the church.
- **Boundary and guard.** Creeds exclude teachings judged to distort the gospel, as Nicaea excluded Arianism. The Latin name *symbolum*, "token" or "password," suggests a sign of recognition among believers.
- **Summary and teaching.** A creed condenses the story of Scripture into a memorable form, a "pattern of sound words" (2 Timothy 1:13) to be handed on.
- **Unity.** A shared creed binds congregations across time and place in "the faith which was once delivered unto the saints" (Jude 1:3).

sections.heading: Catechesis in the Early Church
sections.body:
*Catechesis* comes from the Greek *katēcheō*, "to instruct orally" or "to sound down into the ear." Luke wrote so that Theophilus might know the certainty of the things in which he had been "instructed" (Luke 1:4), and Paul speaks of the one "that is taught in the word" (Galatians 6:6).

By the third and fourth centuries, converts passed through a period as *catechumens*, often lasting years. Near the end of their preparation, during Lent, the bishop "handed over" the creed (*traditio symboli*), and the candidates later "gave it back" by reciting it from memory (*redditio symboli*) before baptism at Easter. Cyril of Jerusalem's *Catechetical Lectures* (c. 350) are a series of such instructions, and Augustine's *On Catechizing the Uninstructed* offers advice to teachers. In the medieval West, basic instruction centered on the Apostles' Creed, the Lord's Prayer, and the Ten Commandments.

sections.heading: The Reformation Catechisms
sections.body:
The printing press and the Reformation produced a flood of catechisms. **Luther's Small Catechism** (1529) was written after visitations of Saxon parishes revealed widespread ignorance. Intended for heads of households to teach their families, it covers the Ten Commandments, the Creed, the Lord's Prayer, Baptism, Confession, and the Lord's Supper, repeatedly asking "What does this mean?" On the first article of the Creed it answers:

> "I believe that God has made me and all creatures; that He has given me my body and soul, eyes, ears, and all my limbs, my reason, and all my senses, and still preserves them."

Luther's Large Catechism (1529) was written for pastors. Reformed churches produced the **Heidelberg Catechism** (1563), and the Westminster Assembly the Larger and **Westminster Shorter Catechism** (1647). The Shorter Catechism's 107 questions begin: "What is the chief end of man? Man's chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him forever."

sections.heading: Catholic and Orthodox Catechisms
sections.body: The Council of Trent commissioned the *Roman Catechism* (1566) to guide parish priests. Later catechisms, such as the *Baltimore Catechism* (1885) in the United States, used question-and-answer formats for children. The **Catechism of the Catholic Church**, promulgated by Pope John Paul II in 1992 with the apostolic constitution *Fidei Depositum*, follows a fourfold structure: the Profession of Faith (the Creed), the Celebration of the Christian Mystery (the sacraments), Life in Christ (the commandments), and Christian Prayer (the Lord's Prayer). John Paul II called it "a sure norm for teaching the faith." In the Orthodox world, catechisms such as that of Metropolitan Philaret of Moscow (1823) have played a similar role.

sections.heading: How Traditions Understand Creedal Authority
sections.body:
- **Eastern Orthodox** Christians regard the creed and decisions of the ecumenical councils as expressions of Holy Tradition, guided by the Holy Spirit, and treat the Nicene Creed as unalterable.
- **Roman Catholics** receive the creeds and dogmatic definitions as authoritative teaching, with Scripture and Tradition forming one deposit of faith interpreted by the Magisterium.
- **Lutheran and Reformed** theologians call Scripture the *norma normans* (the "norming norm") and their confessions the *norma normata* (the "normed norm"), authoritative because, or insofar as, they agree with Scripture.
- **Anglicans** affirm in Article VIII of the Thirty-Nine Articles that the three creeds "ought thoroughly to be received and believed: for they may be proved by most certain warrants of holy Scripture."
- Many **Baptists, Anabaptists, and free churches** are wary of binding creeds, and a slogan associated with the Stone-Campbell Restoration Movement declared "no creed but Christ." Even so, most such groups have issued confessions as testimonies of shared belief.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: Creeds and catechisms are how the faith is passed from one generation to the next (Deuteronomy 6:4-9). They show the church thinking carefully about what is essential, and the differing views of their authority illuminate deeper questions about Scripture, tradition, and the church.

keyTerms.definition: From the Greek for oral instruction; the church's teaching of the faith, especially to those preparing for baptism or confirmation.
A person receiving instruction in preparation for baptism.
The "handing over" of the creed to catechumens before baptism, followed by its recitation (redditio symboli).
Latin for "norming norm"; in Lutheran and Reformed theology, Scripture as the supreme rule over all other standards.
Latin for "normed norm"; a confession or creed whose authority derives from and is subordinate to Scripture.

topics.title: The Doctrine of Scripture
topics.subtitle: Systematic Doctrine
topics.summary: How Christians understand revelation, the inspiration and authority of the Bible, the inerrancy debates, the sufficiency of Scripture, and its relation to Tradition.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: Every Christian tradition treats the Bible as uniquely authoritative, but traditions differ on how Scripture came to be, what kind of truthfulness it has, and how it relates to the teaching authority of the Church. The doctrine of Scripture (sometimes called *bibliology*) addresses these questions and so shapes how every other doctrine is argued.

sections.heading: General and Special Revelation
sections.body:
Theologians distinguish two modes by which God makes himself known:

- **General revelation** is God's self-disclosure through creation, conscience, and history, available to all people. "The heavens declare the glory of God" (Psalm 19:1), and God's "eternal power and divinity" are "clearly seen" in the things he has made (Romans 1:20).
- **Special revelation** is God's particular self-disclosure in redemptive history, supremely in Jesus Christ, and in the inspired Scriptures that witness to him (Hebrews 1:1-2).

How much can be known from general revelation alone is debated. The First Vatican Council (1870) taught that God can be known with certainty from created things by the natural light of reason. In 1934 Karl Barth answered Emil Brunner's defence of a "point of contact" for the gospel in human nature with a famous essay titled simply *Nein!* ("No!"), rejecting natural theology as a source of saving knowledge.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.body: The classic text is 2 Timothy 3:16: "All Scripture is given by inspiration of God." The Greek word *theopneustos* means "God-breathed." Second Peter 1:21 adds that prophets "spoke from God, being moved by the Holy Spirit." Most theologians reject a **mechanical dictation** theory, in which human authors were passive secretaries. Many evangelicals affirm **verbal plenary** inspiration: the whole of Scripture (plenary), down to its words (verbal), is inspired, through a *concursus* in which God worked through the personalities, styles, and research of human authors (Luke 1:1-4). Catholic teaching likewise holds that God is the principal author of Scripture while the human writers are "true authors."

sections.heading: Inerrancy and Infallibility
sections.body:
**Inerrancy** is the view that Scripture, in its original manuscripts (autographs), is without error in everything it affirms, including history and science. B. B. Warfield and A. A. Hodge gave it classic expression in their article *Inspiration* (1881). The **Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy** (1978), drafted by the International Council on Biblical Inerrancy, set out nineteen articles of affirmation and denial and remains a standard evangelical reference.

Other Protestants prefer **infallibility** in a narrower sense: Scripture never fails in its purpose of teaching faith and practice, but need not be free of every historical or scientific imprecision. Jack Rogers and Donald McKim argued in 1979 that this was the older Reformation view, a claim inerrantists strongly disputed. The Lausanne Covenant (1974) described Scripture as "without error in all that it affirms."

The Second Vatican Council's *Dei Verbum* (1965) teaches that the books of Scripture "must be acknowledged as teaching solidly, faithfully and without error that truth which God wanted put into sacred writings for the sake of salvation." Catholic interpreters debate whether this restricts inerrancy to salvific matters or describes the purpose of all Scripture.

sections.heading: Sufficiency and Sola Scriptura
sections.body: The Reformers taught **sola scriptura**: Scripture is the only infallible rule of faith and the supreme norm for judging all church teaching. The Westminster Confession (1.6) states that "the whole counsel of God, concerning all things necessary for His own glory, man's salvation, faith and life, is either expressly set down in Scripture, or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from Scripture." This is the doctrine of **sufficiency**. Magisterial Protestants did not reject creeds or tradition; they treated them as subordinate authorities (a *norma normata*, a "normed norm") under Scripture, the *norma normans*.

sections.heading: Scripture and Tradition
sections.body:
The **Council of Trent** (1546) taught that the truths of the gospel are contained "in the written books, and the unwritten traditions," and are to be received with equal reverence. Trent also defined the canon, including the books Protestants call the Apocrypha and Catholics the *deuterocanonical* books. *Dei Verbum* describes the relationship organically:

> Sacred tradition and Sacred Scripture form one sacred deposit of the word of God, committed to the Church.

The Magisterium (the teaching office of the bishops in communion with the pope) interprets this deposit authentically, yet "is not above the word of God, but serves it." **Eastern Orthodox** theology speaks of Scripture as the supreme expression *within* Holy Tradition, the Spirit-led life of the Church that also includes the ecumenical councils, the Fathers, and the liturgy. Orthodox Bibles include a slightly broader Old Testament canon than the Catholic one.

sections.heading: Points of Agreement and Difference
sections.body: All traditions affirm that Scripture is inspired by God and authoritative for the Church. They differ on whether Scripture alone is the final norm or is received together with Tradition and the Magisterium, on the extent of the canon, and on how to describe its truthfulness.

topics.title: The Doctrine of God
topics.subtitle: Systematic Doctrine
topics.summary: The divine attributes, including aseity, simplicity, immutability, impassibility, omnipotence, omniscience, and omnipresence, and the debate between classical theism and its critics.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body:
Before Christian theology speaks of God as Trinity, it asks what kind of being God is. The doctrine of God (*theology proper*) studies God's existence, nature, and **attributes**, or perfections. Its traditional form, called **classical theism**, was developed by the Church Fathers, Augustine, Anselm, and Thomas Aquinas, and was inherited by both Catholic and Protestant scholasticism. The Westminster Confession (2.1) summarises it:

> There is but one only, living, and true God, who is infinite in being and perfection, a most pure spirit, invisible, without body, parts, or passions; immutable, immense, eternal, incomprehensible, almighty.

sections.heading: Communicable and Incommunicable Attributes
sections.body: Reformed theologians such as Herman Bavinck and Louis Berkhof classify the attributes into two groups. **Incommunicable** attributes have no real analogue in creatures: aseity, simplicity, immutability, infinity, eternity. **Communicable** attributes are reflected, finitely, in creatures made in God's image: wisdom, goodness, love, holiness, justice. Other theologians organise the attributes differently, but nearly all insist that God possesses even the "communicable" perfections in a unique, infinite way.

sections.heading: The Classical Attributes
sections.body:
### Aseity

**Aseity** (from Latin *a se*, "from himself") means that God exists of himself and depends on nothing outside himself. Everything else exists by God's will, but God's existence is underived (Exodus 3:14; Acts 17:24-25).

### Simplicity

**Divine simplicity** holds that God is not composed of parts, whether physical parts, form and matter, or essence and existence. God does not *have* goodness or wisdom as properties distinct from himself; he *is* his goodness and wisdom. Thomas Aquinas argued in the *Summa Theologiae* (I, q. 3) that God is "altogether simple," and the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) confessed the divine essence to be entirely simple. The Eastern tradition, especially after Gregory Palamas, affirms simplicity while distinguishing God's unknowable essence from his energies.

### Immutability and Impassibility

**Immutability** means God does not change in his being, character, or purposes: "I am the LORD, I do not change" (Malachi 3:6; James 1:17). **Impassibility** means God is not subject to passions, that is, he is not acted upon or emotionally overcome by creatures. Classical theists insist this does not make God cold: his love is a perfect, unchanging act rather than a fluctuating feeling.

### Omnipotence, Omniscience, Omnipresence

- **Omnipotence**: God can do all things consistent with his nature. Classical theists note that God cannot lie (Hebrews 6:18) or do what is logically contradictory, not from weakness but because such "acts" are not genuine powers.
- **Omniscience**: God knows all things, actual and possible, past, present, and future (Psalm 139:1-6; 1 John 3:20).
- **Omnipresence**: God is present to all places with his whole being, without being spatially extended or contained (Psalm 139:7-10; Jeremiah 23:24).

Many classical theists also hold that God is **eternal** in the sense of timeless, possessing his life all at once rather than in successive moments, as Boethius put it.

sections.heading: Ways of Knowing God
sections.body: Theologians have sought knowledge of God by several routes. The **way of negation** (*via negativa*) says what God is not, as in the apophatic theology prized in the East. The **way of eminence** attributes creaturely perfections to God in a supreme degree. Anselm's description of God as "that than which nothing greater can be conceived" grounds what is now called **perfect being theology**. Aquinas taught that words applied to God and creatures are used neither univocally nor equivocally but **analogically**.

sections.heading: Classical Theism and Its Critics
sections.body:
Since the nineteenth century, several movements have challenged elements of classical theism:

- **Process theism** (Alfred North Whitehead, Charles Hartshorne) holds that God is in some respects temporal and changing, affected by the world's becoming.
- **Open theism**, set out in *The Openness of God* (1994) by Clark Pinnock and others, holds that God does not exhaustively know future free choices, because they are not yet settled.
- Theologians such as **Jürgen Moltmann** in *The Crucified God* (1972) argued that the cross reveals a God who truly suffers, rejecting impassibility.
- Some analytic philosophers of religion, including Alvin Plantinga in *Does God Have a Nature?* (1980), questioned whether divine simplicity is coherent.

Defenders of classical theism respond that these revisions make God a being among beings, compromise his sovereignty and reliability, and misunderstand the classical claims; Thomas Weinandy's *Does God Suffer?* (2000) is a prominent defence of impassibility. Recent decades have seen a significant retrieval of classical theism among Protestant and Catholic theologians alike.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: The divine attributes undergird every other doctrine: God's aseity grounds creation from nothing, his immutability grounds the reliability of his promises, his omniscience bears on predestination and providence, and his impassibility shapes how the incarnation and the cross are understood.

topics.title: The Trinity
topics.subtitle: Systematic Doctrine
topics.summary: One God in three persons: the biblical basis, the vocabulary of ousia and hypostasis, the councils of Nicaea and Constantinople, the filioque, and the classic Trinitarian heresies.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: The doctrine of the **Trinity** confesses that the one God exists eternally as three distinct persons, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, who share one undivided divine nature. It is shared by Catholic, Orthodox, and historic Protestant churches and is often regarded as the defining doctrine of Christian faith. The word "Trinity" does not appear in the Bible: the Greek *trias* is first found in Theophilus of Antioch (late second century), and Tertullian was the first known writer to use the Latin *trinitas*.

sections.heading: Biblical Basis
sections.body:
The doctrine arose from holding together several strands of biblical teaching:

- **There is one God.** The Shema declares, "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4), a confession the New Testament reaffirms (1 Corinthians 8:4-6).
- **The Son is God.** "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). Jesus receives worship and is confessed as Lord (Philippians 2:9-11; John 20:28).
- **The Spirit is God and personal.** The Spirit teaches, can be grieved, and is called "another Advocate" (John 14:16-17, 26).
- **The three are distinct and named together.** Jesus commands baptism "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19), and Paul's benediction joins the three (2 Corinthians 13:14).

sections.heading: Ousia and Hypostasis
sections.body:
Early theologians needed vocabulary to say what is one and what is three. At first the Greek terms **ousia** (being, essence) and **hypostasis** (subsistence) were often used as synonyms. In the later fourth century the **Cappadocian Fathers**, Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Gregory of Nyssa, standardised the formula *one ousia, three hypostases*. The persons are distinguished only by their relations of origin: the Father is unbegotten, the Son is eternally begotten of the Father, and the Spirit eternally proceeds. Latin theology spoke of one *substantia* and three *personae*. The Athanasian Creed, a Latin text of the fifth or sixth century not actually written by Athanasius, puts it this way:

> We worship one God in Trinity, and Trinity in Unity; neither confounding the Persons, nor dividing the Substance.

sections.heading: Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381)
sections.body:
The Alexandrian presbyter **Arius** taught that the Son was the first and highest creature: "there was when he was not." Emperor Constantine summoned the **Council of Nicaea** in 325, which confessed the Son to be "begotten, not made," and **homoousios** ("of one substance") with the Father. Athanasius of Alexandria became Nicaea's leading defender through decades of controversy and exile.

The **First Council of Constantinople** in 381, convened under Emperor Theodosius I, reaffirmed Nicaea and expanded the creed's article on the Holy Spirit, against the *Pneumatomachians* ("Spirit-fighters") who denied the Spirit's full divinity. The resulting **Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed** confesses the Spirit as "the Lord, the giver of life, who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son is worshipped and glorified."

sections.heading: The Filioque
sections.body: In the Latin West the phrase **filioque** ("and the Son") was added to the creed, so that the Spirit "proceeds from the Father *and the Son*." The addition appears at the **Third Council of Toledo** in Spain (589), spread through the Frankish church, and was adopted in the liturgy at Rome in the early eleventh century. Eastern Orthodox theologians object on two grounds: the West altered an ecumenical creed unilaterally, and the doctrine compromises the Father's role as the sole source (*monarchia*) of the Godhead. Western theologians have defended it as safeguarding the unity of Father and Son, often adding that the Spirit proceeds from the Father *through* the Son. The dispute contributed to the schism between East and West, and it remains a topic of ecumenical dialogue; some Western churches omit the phrase in ecumenical settings.

sections.heading: Trinitarian Heresies
sections.body:
- **Modalism** (also called Sabellianism, after Sabellius) teaches that Father, Son, and Spirit are successive modes or masks of one person. A form called *patripassianism* implied that the Father suffered on the cross. It denies the real distinction of persons.
- **Arianism** teaches that the Son is a created being, not eternal or fully divine. It denies the Son's consubstantiality with the Father.
- **Tritheism** treats the three persons as three separate gods, denying the unity of the divine essence. John Philoponus was accused of it in the sixth century, and Gregory of Nyssa wrote *On "Not Three Gods"* to rebut the charge against orthodox teaching.

sections.heading: Economic and Immanent Trinity
sections.body: Theologians distinguish the **economic Trinity**, God as revealed in his works of creation and redemption (the "economy" of salvation), from the **immanent Trinity**, God as he is in his own eternal life. A traditional axiom holds that the external works of the Trinity are undivided: all three persons act in every divine work. In the twentieth century **Karl Rahner** proposed his famous rule: "The 'economic' Trinity is the 'immanent' Trinity, and the 'immanent' Trinity is the 'economic' Trinity." Critics worry that overly tight readings of the rule make God's inner life dependent on history.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: For Christians, the Trinity is not an abstract puzzle but the shape of salvation: the Father sends the Son, and the Spirit unites believers to the Son so that they may call God "Abba, Father" (Galatians 4:4-6).

keyTerms.definition: Greek for 'being' or 'essence'; the one divine nature shared equally by Father, Son, and Spirit.
Greek for 'subsistence'; used from the Cappadocians onward for each of the three persons of the Trinity.
'Of one substance': the Nicene term affirming that the Son shares the same divine being as the Father.
Latin 'and the Son': the Western addition to the creed stating that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.
The heresy that Father, Son, and Spirit are successive modes or roles of a single divine person.
The Trinity as revealed in God's works of creation and redemption, as distinct from the immanent Trinity, God's eternal inner life.

topics.title: Christology
topics.subtitle: Systematic Doctrine
topics.summary: Who Jesus Christ is: the hypostatic union, the Chalcedonian Definition of 451, the heresies it excluded, monothelitism, and modern kenotic Christology.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: **Christology** is the study of the person of Jesus Christ. Once the Council of Nicaea (325) had affirmed that the Son is fully divine, a further question pressed: how are divinity and humanity related in the one Jesus? The answer developed through intense controversy is the doctrine of the **hypostatic union**: Christ is one person (*hypostasis*) in two natures, fully divine and fully human.

sections.heading: The Biblical Witness
sections.body: The New Testament presents Jesus as truly human: he was born (Galatians 4:4), grew in wisdom (Luke 2:52), hungered, wept (John 11:35), was tempted (Hebrews 4:15), and died. It also presents him as truly divine: the eternal Word who "became flesh, and dwelt among us" (John 1:14), in whom "all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily" (Colossians 2:9). Philippians 2:5-11 describes him as existing "in the form of God" and taking "the form of a servant."

sections.heading: Errors Rejected Along the Way
sections.body:
### Apollinarianism

**Apollinarius of Laodicea** (died around 390) taught that in Christ the divine Word took the place of a human rational mind (*nous*). Gregory of Nazianzus replied that "that which He has not assumed He has not healed": if Christ lacked a human mind, the human mind is not redeemed. Apollinarianism was condemned at the First Council of Constantinople (381).

### Nestorianism

**Nestorius**, who became patriarch of Constantinople in 428, objected to calling Mary **Theotokos** ("God-bearer"), preferring *Christotokos* ("Christ-bearer"). His opponents, led by **Cyril of Alexandria**, charged that he divided Christ into two persons, a divine Son and a human Jesus joined only by a moral union. The **Council of Ephesus** (431) affirmed Theotokos and condemned Nestorius. Whether Nestorius himself held the views attributed to him is debated by historians. The Assyrian Church of the East, traditionally labelled "Nestorian," rejects the label, and in 1994 its patriarch and Pope John Paul II signed a Common Christological Declaration.

### Eutychianism

**Eutyches** (around 380-456), a monk in Constantinople, reacted against Nestorianism by teaching that after the union Christ had only one nature, with his humanity absorbed into his divinity. A council at Ephesus in 449, later called the "Robber Synod," vindicated him, but Pope Leo I's **Tome** (449) insisted on two natures united in one person.

sections.heading: The Chalcedonian Definition (451)
sections.body:
The **Council of Chalcedon** (451), the fourth ecumenical council, received Leo's Tome and Cyril's letters and issued its Definition, which confesses one and the same Christ:

> acknowledged in Two Natures unconfusedly, unchangeably, indivisibly, inseparably; the difference of the Natures being in no way removed because of the Union, but rather the properties of each Nature being preserved, and (both) concurring into One Person and One Hypostasis.

The four adverbs function as guardrails: *unconfusedly* and *unchangeably* exclude Eutychianism; *indivisibly* and *inseparably* exclude Nestorianism. Chalcedon is accepted by Catholics, Eastern Orthodox, and the major Protestant traditions.

The **Oriental Orthodox** churches (Coptic, Armenian, Syriac, Ethiopian, Eritrean, and Malankara) did not accept Chalcedon. Following Cyril's formula "one incarnate nature of God the Word," they are often called *miaphysite*. They reject Eutyches and affirm Christ's full humanity; joint commissions of the Eastern and Oriental Orthodox churches have stated that the two families share the same Christological faith expressed in different terms.

sections.heading: Monothelitism
sections.body: In the seventh century, in an effort to reconcile the anti-Chalcedonian churches, Patriarch Sergius of Constantinople and Emperor Heraclius promoted the view that Christ had one "energy" (*monoenergism*) and then one will (**monothelitism**). **Maximus the Confessor** opposed it, arguing that will belongs to nature, so a Christ without a human will would lack full humanity; Christ's prayer in Gethsemane, "not my will, but yours, be done" (Luke 22:42), shows a human will freely submitting to the divine. The **Third Council of Constantinople** (680-681) affirmed two natural wills and two operations in Christ (*dyothelitism*), the human will always in harmony with the divine.

sections.heading: Communication of Properties and Kenosis
sections.body:
Because there is one person, what belongs to either nature may be attributed to that person: it is correct to say "God died" or "the man Jesus is eternal," speaking of the one subject. This principle is called the **communicatio idiomatum** (communication of properties).

**Kenosis** comes from Philippians 2:7, where Christ "emptied himself" (*heauton ekenōsen*). In the nineteenth century the German Lutheran Gottfried Thomasius and later British theologians such as Charles Gore and P. T. Forsyth developed **kenotic Christologies**, proposing that the Son laid aside or limited certain divine attributes, such as omniscience, in becoming incarnate. Critics in the classical tradition reply that the passage describes the Son's humility in *taking* the form of a servant, not in subtracting from his divinity, and that a God who ceases to be omniscient would no longer be fully God.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: The Fathers insisted on Christ's full divinity and full humanity because of salvation: only God can save, and only what is assumed is healed. Christology thus underlies the doctrines of the atonement, the sacraments, and theosis.

keyTerms.definition: The union of the divine and human natures in the one person (hypostasis) of the Son of God.

The communication of properties: attributes of either nature may be predicated of the one person of Christ.
From Philippians 2:7, Christ's 'self-emptying'; kenotic Christologies hold that the Son limited divine attributes in the incarnation.

topics.title: Pneumatology
topics.subtitle: Systematic Doctrine
topics.summary: The person and work of the Holy Spirit, the spiritual gifts, the cessationist and continuationist debate, and the rise of the Pentecostal and charismatic movements.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: **Pneumatology** (from Greek *pneuma*, "breath, wind, spirit") is the study of the Holy Spirit. Long called the "forgotten" person of the Trinity in Western theology, the Spirit has received renewed attention through the global growth of Pentecostal and charismatic Christianity, now among the largest movements in world Christianity.

sections.heading: The Person of the Spirit
sections.body:
Christian orthodoxy confesses the Spirit as a **divine person**, not an impersonal force. The Spirit speaks (Acts 13:2), teaches (John 14:26), intercedes (Romans 8:26), can be grieved (Ephesians 4:30), and is called "another Advocate" (*paraklētos*) like Jesus himself (John 14:16). Lying to the Spirit is lying to God (Acts 5:3-4).

In the fourth century the *Pneumatomachians* ("Spirit-fighters") denied the Spirit's full divinity. **Basil of Caesarea** answered in *On the Holy Spirit* (around 375), defending the doxology that glorifies the Father "with the Son together with the Holy Ghost." The **First Council of Constantinople** (381) confessed the Spirit as "the Lord, the giver of life," who "with the Father and the Son is worshipped and glorified." The later Western addition of the *filioque* concerns the Spirit's procession and remains a point of difference between Eastern and Western churches (see the topic on the Trinity).

sections.heading: The Work of the Spirit
sections.body:
Scripture attributes a wide range of works to the Spirit:

- **Creation and life**: the Spirit hovered over the waters (Genesis 1:2) and gives life (Psalm 104:30).
- **Inspiration**: prophets spoke as they were "moved by the Holy Spirit" (2 Peter 1:21).
- **The incarnation and ministry of Christ**: Jesus was conceived by the Spirit and anointed by the Spirit at his baptism (Luke 1:35; Luke 4:18).
- **Salvation**: the Spirit convicts of sin (John 16:8), regenerates (John 3:5-8), indwells believers, unites them to Christ, and assures them that they are God's children (Romans 8:15-16).
- **Sanctification**: the Spirit produces the "fruit of the Spirit": love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control (Galatians 5:22-23).
- **The Church**: the Spirit was poured out at Pentecost (Acts 2:1-4), builds up the body of Christ, and empowers its mission.

Catholic and Orthodox theology emphasise the Spirit's work in the sacraments, especially confirmation (called *chrismation* in the East) and the *epiclesis*, the prayer invoking the Spirit in the Eucharist. Orthodox theology also links the Spirit closely to theosis.

sections.heading: The Gifts of the Spirit
sections.body: Paul lists *charismata* (grace-gifts) in several places, including 1 Corinthians 12:4-11, Romans 12:6-8, and Ephesians 4:11-12. They range from teaching, service, and generosity to prophecy, healing, miracles, tongues, and interpretation of tongues. Catholic tradition also speaks of the **seven gifts of the Holy Spirit** drawn from Isaiah 11:2-3 in its Greek and Latin versions: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord.

sections.heading: Cessationism and Continuationism
sections.body:
Christians disagree about whether the more extraordinary gifts continue today.

**Cessationists** hold that the revelatory and sign gifts, such as prophecy, tongues, and miraculous healing, served to authenticate the apostles and lay the church's foundation (Ephesians 2:20; Hebrews 2:3-4), and ceased once the apostolic age ended and the canon of Scripture was complete. The Princeton theologian B. B. Warfield's *Counterfeit Miracles* (1918) is a classic statement. Cessationists usually affirm that God still answers prayer and can heal, but deny that individuals possess these gifts as ongoing endowments.

**Continuationists** hold that all the gifts remain available until Christ returns, often reading "when that which is perfect has come" (1 Corinthians 13:10) as a reference to the second coming. Some continuationists, such as Wayne Grudem, distinguish New Testament congregational prophecy, which must be tested, from the authoritative revelation of Scripture. A middle position is sometimes called "open but cautious."

sections.heading: The Pentecostal and Charismatic Movements
sections.body:
Modern **Pentecostalism** emerged from the Wesleyan Holiness movement. In January 1901, at Charles Fox Parham's Bible school in Topeka, Kansas, students reported speaking in tongues. The **Azusa Street Revival** in Los Angeles, led from 1906 by the African American preacher **William J. Seymour**, drew multiracial crowds and spread the movement worldwide. Classical Pentecostals, such as the Assemblies of God (founded 1914), teach a **baptism in the Holy Spirit** distinct from and subsequent to conversion, with speaking in tongues as its initial evidence.

The **charismatic renewal** brought similar experiences into mainline churches from about 1960, when the Episcopal priest Dennis Bennett publicly reported speaking in tongues, and into the Catholic Church from 1967 after a retreat at Duquesne University. Many charismatics interpret Spirit baptism differently from classical Pentecostals, for example as a release of grace already given in baptism. A later "third wave," associated with John Wimber and the Vineyard movement, emphasised healing and signs without requiring a second-blessing experience.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: Pneumatology bears on how Christians pray, worship, read Scripture, and understand the Christian life. Disagreements over the gifts have divided congregations, while shared confession of the Spirit as Lord and giver of life unites Christians across traditions.

keyTerms.definition: From Greek paraklētos, 'advocate' or 'helper': Jesus' title for the Holy Spirit in John 14-16.
Grace-gifts given by the Spirit for building up the church, listed in passages such as 1 Corinthians 12.

The view that all the spiritual gifts, including prophecy and tongues, remain available until Christ's return.
In classical Pentecostalism, an empowering experience subsequent to conversion, evidenced initially by speaking in tongues.

topics.title: Theological Anthropology
topics.subtitle: Systematic Doctrine
topics.summary: What it means to be human in Christian theology: the image of God, body and soul, the fall, Augustinian original sin versus Eastern 'ancestral sin', and total depravity.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: **Theological anthropology** studies human beings in relation to God: what we were created to be, what has gone wrong, and what we are destined to become. It sets the stage for soteriology, since one's account of the human problem shapes one's account of the remedy.

sections.heading: The Image of God
sections.body:
Genesis declares that God created humanity "in our image, after our likeness... male and female he created them" (Genesis 1:26-27). The **imago Dei** grounds human dignity (Genesis 9:6; James 3:9). Theologians interpret it in three main ways:

- **Substantive**: the image is a capacity or quality in human nature, especially reason and will. Thomas Aquinas located it chiefly in the intellectual nature by which humans can know and love God.
- **Relational**: the image consists in relationship with God and others. Karl Barth connected it with the creation of humanity as "male and female," mirroring relationship within God.
- **Functional**: the image is humanity's royal vocation to represent God and exercise dominion over creation (Genesis 1:28), a view widely held among Old Testament scholars.

Many Church Fathers, notably **Irenaeus**, distinguished the *image* (given in creation and retained) from the *likeness* (growth into God-likeness through the Spirit). The Reformers generally treated the two words as Hebrew parallelism for the same reality. The New Testament presents Christ as the true "image of the invisible God" (Colossians 1:15), into whose image believers are being renewed (Colossians 3:10).

sections.heading: Body and Soul
sections.body: Christian tradition has generally affirmed that a human being is a unity of body and soul. **Dichotomists** distinguish two aspects, body and soul (or spirit); **trichotomists** distinguish body, soul, and spirit, appealing to 1 Thessalonians 5:23. Following Aristotle, Aquinas taught that the soul is the *form* of the body, and the Council of Vienne (1311-1312) declared the rational soul to be the form of the body. Some contemporary theologians, such as Nancey Murphy, defend a **nonreductive physicalism** that denies a separate soul while affirming the resurrection. Against Gnostic disdain for matter, all orthodox traditions affirm the goodness of the body and look for its resurrection.

sections.heading: The Fall
sections.body: Genesis 3 narrates the first humans' disobedience, resulting in shame, alienation, toil, and death. Paul interprets it christologically: "as through one man sin entered into the world, and death through sin... so death passed to all men" (Romans 5:12), while in Christ "all shall be made alive" (1 Corinthians 15:22). Traditions differ on how Adam's sin affects his descendants.

sections.heading: Original Sin: The Augustinian Tradition
sections.body:
**Augustine** taught that all humanity was present in Adam and so shares in both his guilt and his corruption. He read Romans 5:12 in a Latin version that said "in whom (*in quo*) all sinned." In *The City of God* he wrote:

> For we all were in that one man, since we all were that one man, who fell into sin by the woman who was made from him before the sin.

Western traditions built on this foundation in different ways:

- **Catholic** teaching, defined at the Council of Trent (1546), holds that original sin is transmitted by propagation, not imitation, and is removed by baptism. The Catechism explains that it is a sin "contracted" rather than "committed," a deprivation of original holiness and justice. The inclination to sin (*concupiscence*) remains after baptism but is not itself sin.
- **Lutheran** teaching (Augsburg Confession, Article II) holds that original sin, including concupiscence, is truly sin that condemns those not born again through baptism and the Spirit.
- **Reformed** theology often explains the transmission of guilt through **federal headship**: Adam acted as the covenant representative of humanity, so his guilt is imputed to all, as Christ's righteousness is imputed to believers.

sections.heading: Total Depravity
sections.body: Reformed theologians teach **total depravity**. This does not mean humans are as wicked as possible, but that sin affects every part of human nature (mind, will, emotions, and body), leaving fallen people unable to turn to God without regenerating grace (Romans 3:10-12; Ephesians 2:1-3). Wesleyan Arminians also affirm total depravity but teach that God's prevenient grace restores to all a measure of freedom to respond to the gospel.

sections.heading: Ancestral Sin: The Eastern Tradition
sections.body: **Eastern Orthodox** theologians commonly speak of **ancestral sin** rather than original sin in the Augustinian sense. On this view, Adam's descendants inherit the *consequences* of his sin, above all mortality and corruption, together with a weakened nature prone to sin, but not his personal guilt. Many read Romans 5:12 as "because (*eph' hō*) all sinned," and stress that death itself leads to sin (Hebrews 2:14-15). John Romanides's study *The Ancestral Sin* (1957) is an influential modern statement. Orthodox churches still baptise infants, for new life and union with Christ. Orthodox writers vary, and some earlier Orthodox confessions used more Western language.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: Views of human nature shape views of grace, freedom, baptism, ethics, and human dignity. All traditions affirm that humans are created good in God's image, are truly fallen, and are restored in Christ, the second Adam.

keyTerms.definition: Latin for 'image of God': the dignity and vocation given to humanity in creation according to Genesis 1:26-27.

The Orthodox understanding that Adam's descendants inherit the consequences of his sin, chiefly mortality and corruption, but not his personal guilt.
The Reformed view that Adam acted as covenant representative of humanity, so that his guilt is imputed to all.
The teaching that sin affects every part of human nature, leaving fallen people unable to turn to God without grace.
The disordered inclination to sin; Catholics hold it remains after baptism but is not itself sin, while Lutherans call it truly sin.

topics.title: Ecclesiology and Sacraments
topics.subtitle: Systematic Doctrine
topics.summary: The nature and marks of the Church, models of church government, and the major Christian views of baptism and the Eucharist, from transubstantiation to memorialism.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: **Ecclesiology** is the study of the Church (Greek *ekklēsia*, "assembly"). It asks what the Church is, where it is found, how it is governed, and how it mediates God's grace through preaching and **sacraments**. These questions lie close to the heart of the divisions among Christians.

sections.heading: The Marks of the Church
sections.body:
The Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed (381) confesses belief in "one, holy, catholic, and apostolic Church." These four **marks** are accepted across traditions, though interpreted differently:

- **One**: the Church is united as the one body of Christ (Ephesians 4:4-6).
- **Holy**: the Church is set apart by God and sanctified by Christ (Ephesians 5:25-27), even though its members sin.
- **Catholic**: from Greek *kath' holou*, "according to the whole"; the Church is universal and possesses the fullness of the faith.
- **Apostolic**: the Church is founded on the apostles and continues their teaching and mission (Ephesians 2:20).

The **Catholic Church** teaches that the Church of Christ "subsists in the Catholic Church, which is governed by the successor of Peter and by the Bishops in communion with him," while acknowledging that "many elements of sanctification and of truth are found outside of its visible structure" (*Lumen Gentium* 8, 1964). The **Eastern Orthodox Church** understands itself to be the one Church, preserving the apostolic faith in continuity with the ecumenical councils. Catholics, Orthodox, and Anglicans emphasise **apostolic succession**, the unbroken succession of bishops from the apostles.

**Protestant** confessions locate the Church where the gospel is faithfully proclaimed. The Augsburg Confession (Article VII) defines it as "the congregation of saints, in which the Gospel is rightly taught and the Sacraments are rightly administered." The Reformed Belgic Confession (1561) adds church discipline as a third mark. Protestants commonly distinguish the **visible church** of professing members from the **invisible church** of all the elect known to God, and understand apostolicity chiefly as faithfulness to apostolic teaching.

sections.heading: Church Polity
sections.body:
Three main forms of church government have developed:

1. **Episcopal**: governance by bishops, with priests or presbyters and deacons. Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, and some Lutheran and Methodist churches follow this pattern.
2. **Presbyterian**: governance by elders (*presbyteroi*) in a hierarchy of courts, from the local session to presbyteries, synods, and a general assembly. Reformed and Presbyterian churches follow this model.
3. **Congregational**: each local congregation is self-governing under Christ. Baptists, Congregationalists, and many independent churches follow this model, often cooperating in voluntary associations.

sections.heading: Sacraments
sections.body: A definition derived from Augustine calls a sacrament a visible sign of an invisible grace. Catholic and Orthodox churches recognise **seven** sacraments (the Orthodox often say "mysteries"): baptism, confirmation or chrismation, Eucharist, penance, anointing of the sick, holy orders, and marriage. Most Protestants recognise **two**, baptism and the Lord's Supper, as instituted directly by Christ. The Council of Trent taught that sacraments confer grace *ex opere operato* ("by the work worked"), that is, by Christ's action and not by the minister's holiness, though fruitful reception requires proper disposition. Many Baptists and others prefer the term **ordinance** to emphasise obedience to Christ's command.

sections.heading: Baptism
sections.body: Most churches, including Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican, and Methodist, baptise infants as well as adult converts. Catholic, Orthodox, and Lutheran theology teach **baptismal regeneration**: through baptism God forgives sin and gives new birth (John 3:5; Titus 3:5). Reformed theology treats baptism as a sign and seal of the covenant of grace, parallel to circumcision (Colossians 2:11-12). **Baptists**, Anabaptists, and many Pentecostals practise **believer's baptism**, usually by immersion, as a public confession of faith by those old enough to profess it (Acts 2:38-41).

sections.heading: The Eucharist
sections.body:
Christians agree that Jesus said, "This is my body" (Matthew 26:26), but they understand his presence in the Lord's Supper differently:

- **Transubstantiation** (Catholic): the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) used the term, and the Council of Trent (1551) taught that by consecration the whole substance of bread and wine is converted into the body and blood of Christ, while the outward appearances remain.
- **Orthodox**: a real change (*metabolē*) of the gifts into Christ's body and blood, typically confessed as a mystery without binding itself to scholastic categories.
- **Sacramental union** (Lutheran): Christ's true body and blood are present "in, with, and under" the bread and wine, which remain. The Augsburg Confession (Article X) teaches that "the Body and Blood of Christ are truly present." Lutherans usually reject the label "consubstantiation."
- **Spiritual presence** (Reformed): following Calvin, the bread and wine remain, but by the Holy Spirit believers truly feed on Christ's body and blood, spiritually rather than physically.
- **Memorialism**: the Supper is chiefly a memorial and proclamation of Christ's death, obeying "do this in remembrance of me" (1 Corinthians 11:24-25). It is commonly associated with Ulrich Zwingli and is widespread among Baptists and other evangelicals.

At the **Marburg Colloquy** of 1529, Luther and Zwingli agreed on fourteen of fifteen articles but could not agree on Christ's presence in the Supper, a division that has shaped Protestantism ever since.

sections.heading: Points of Agreement and Difference
sections.body: All traditions confess the Church as Christ's body, practise baptism with water in the triune name, and celebrate the Lord's Supper. They differ on where the true Church is found, how it should be governed, how many sacraments there are, who should be baptised, and how Christ is present in the Eucharist.

topics.title: Eschatology
topics.subtitle: Systematic Doctrine
topics.summary: The doctrine of last things: death and the intermediate state, the return of Christ, the millennial views, resurrection, final judgment, heaven, and hell.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: **Eschatology** (from Greek *eschatos*, "last") is the doctrine of the last things. It covers both **personal eschatology**, what happens to individuals at death, and **cosmic eschatology**, the return of Christ, the resurrection, the final judgment, and the renewal of all things. The New Testament presents the "last days" as already begun with Christ's resurrection and the outpouring of the Spirit, yet awaiting consummation, a tension often described as "already and not yet."

sections.heading: Death and the Intermediate State
sections.body:
Christians confess that death is an enemy defeated by Christ (1 Corinthians 15:26). Between death and the final resurrection lies the **intermediate state**. Most Christian traditions hold that the soul survives death and is consciously with Christ or separated from him: Paul desired "to depart, and to be with Christ" (Philippians 1:23), and Jesus told the penitent thief, "Today you will be with me in Paradise" (Luke 23:43).

- **Catholic** teaching holds that those who die in God's grace but are not fully purified undergo **purgatory**, a final purification before entering heaven, defined at the Councils of Florence (1439) and Trent (1563). Pope Benedict XII's constitution *Benedictus Deus* (1336) taught that the souls of the fully purified see God's essence immediately, even before the resurrection.
- **Eastern Orthodox** Christians pray for the departed and speak of an intermediate state in which souls foretaste their destiny, but generally reject the Western doctrine of purgatory as formulated.
- **Protestants** generally reject purgatory, holding that believers at death are made perfect in holiness and pass immediately into Christ's presence.
- Some groups, including Seventh-day Adventists, teach **soul sleep** (Christian mortalism), an unconscious state until the resurrection. John Calvin wrote his *Psychopannychia* against this view.

sections.heading: The Return of Christ
sections.body: All the historic creeds confess that Christ "will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead." The New Testament describes his return (*parousia*) as personal, visible, and sudden (Acts 1:11; 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17; Matthew 24:30, 36). Christians disagree, however, about the events surrounding it.

sections.heading: The Millennial Views
sections.body:
Revelation 20:1-6 speaks of Satan bound and of saints reigning with Christ for "a thousand years." Interpretation of this passage produces four main positions:

### Historic Premillennialism

Christ returns *before* (*pre*) a literal earthly reign. Early writers such as Papias, Justin Martyr, and Irenaeus held forms of this view, often called *chiliasm* (from Greek *chilioi*, "thousand"). Historic premillennialists usually expect the church to pass through the great tribulation. George Eldon Ladd was an influential twentieth-century advocate.

### Dispensational Premillennialism

Developed by **John Nelson Darby** (1800-1882) of the Plymouth Brethren and popularised by the *Scofield Reference Bible* (1909), dispensationalism maintains a sharp distinction between Israel and the church. Most dispensationalists teach a **pretribulation rapture**, in which Christ removes the church before a seven-year tribulation, followed by his visible return and a millennial reign in which God's promises to national Israel are fulfilled.

### Amillennialism

The "thousand years" symbolises Christ's present reign, with the saints, between his first and second comings. **Augustine** gave this view classic shape in *The City of God*, Book XX:

> Therefore the Church even now is the kingdom of Christ, and the kingdom of heaven.

Amillennialism, though the label itself is modern, has been the majority position in Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, and much Reformed theology. The Catholic Catechism rejects millenarianism, the expectation of an earthly messianic kingdom before the final judgment.

### Postmillennialism

Christ returns *after* (*post*) a long period in which the gospel's spread brings widespread conversion, peace, and righteousness. Associated with the English writer Daniel Whitby and influential in eighteenth- and nineteenth-century Protestantism, including among many Puritans and American revivalists, it fed confidence in missions and social reform. It declined after the World Wars but has been revived by some Reformed theologians.

sections.heading: Resurrection and Judgment
sections.body: Christian hope centres on the **bodily resurrection**. The resurrected body will be continuous with the present one yet transformed, "raised imperishable" (1 Corinthians 15:42-44), like Christ's risen body. All people will face **final judgment** before Christ (Matthew 25:31-46; 2 Corinthians 5:10).

sections.heading: Heaven and Hell
sections.body:
**Heaven** is ultimately not merely a disembodied realm but a "new heaven and a new earth" where God dwells with his people and wipes away every tear (Revelation 21:1-4). Catholic theology describes its heart as the **beatific vision**, the direct sight of God; Orthodox theology speaks of eternal growth in theosis.

**Hell** has traditionally been understood as eternal conscious punishment, separation from God's blessing (Matthew 25:46). Two minority views have gained attention. **Annihilationism** or conditional immortality holds that the unrepentant finally cease to exist, a view defended by Edward Fudge and tentatively suggested by John Stott. **Universalism** holds that all will finally be saved; Origen's speculations in this direction were condemned in sixth-century anathemas, and the view has modern defenders such as David Bentley Hart. Hans Urs von Balthasar argued that Christians may *hope*, without asserting, that all will be saved.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: Eschatology gives Christian life its direction and urgency. Despite deep disagreements over details, the creeds unite Christians in confessing Christ's return, the resurrection of the dead, judgment, and "the life of the world to come."
