topics.title: Introduction to Hermeneutics
topics.subtitle: Hermeneutics
topics.summary: What hermeneutics is, why interpretation is necessary, and core concepts such as exegesis, eisegesis, authorial intent, and the hermeneutical spiral.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body:
*Hermeneutics* is the theory and practice of interpretation. The word comes from the Greek verb *hermēneuō*, "to interpret" or "to explain," and was associated in Greek thought with Hermes, the messenger of the gods. In biblical studies, hermeneutics asks how we move from the words of ancient texts to a faithful understanding of what they mean, and from there to what they mean for readers today.

Interpretation is as old as Scripture itself. When Ezra read the Law to the returned exiles, the Levites "read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading" (Nehemiah 8:8). On the road to Emmaus, the risen Jesus "expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself" (Luke 24:27); the Greek verb there is a compound of *hermēneuō*. When Philip asked the Ethiopian official whether he understood Isaiah, the answer was, "How can I, except some man should guide me?" (Acts 8:30-31).

sections.heading: Why Interpretation Is Needed
sections.body:
Every reader interprets; the question is whether we do it well. The Bible was written over many centuries, in Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek, in cultures far removed from ours. Interpreters speak of several kinds of *distance* between the text and the modern reader:

- **Linguistic:** the original languages, idioms, and word meanings.
- **Historical and cultural:** customs, politics, and assumptions the original audience shared.
- **Literary:** genres and conventions, such as Hebrew poetry or apocalyptic symbolism.
- **Theological:** the place of a passage within the unfolding story of the whole Bible.

sections.heading: Exegesis and Eisegesis
sections.body: **Exegesis** (from Greek, "to lead out") is the careful drawing out of a text's meaning from the text itself, attending to its language, context, and genre. **Eisegesis** ("to lead in") is reading one's own ideas into a text. A classic example of eisegesis is lifting Philippians 4:13 ("I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me") out of its context, where Paul speaks of contentment in hunger and plenty, and treating it as a promise of success in any undertaking. The goal of sound hermeneutics is to practice exegesis and guard against eisegesis, though every interpreter brings assumptions that must be acknowledged.

sections.heading: Authorial Intent and Its Critics
sections.body:
Many evangelical and traditional interpreters locate a text's meaning in what its **author intended** to communicate. The literary theorist E. D. Hirsch, in *Validity in Interpretation* (1967), defended this view and distinguished *meaning* (what the author meant, which does not change) from *significance* (the text's relation to a reader or situation, which can change). Theologians add that Scripture has a divine as well as a human author, which raises the question of whether God may intend more than the human writer grasped.

Other theorists place more weight on the text itself or on readers. Hans-Georg Gadamer, in *Truth and Method* (1960), described understanding as a "fusion of horizons" between the world of the text and the world of the interpreter. *Reader-response* approaches emphasize how communities of readers produce meaning. Most biblical interpreters today grant that readers are never neutral, while still holding that texts constrain interpretation.

sections.heading: The Hermeneutical Circle and Spiral
sections.body:
The German theologian Friedrich Schleiermacher (1768-1834), often called the father of modern hermeneutics, described the **hermeneutical circle**: we understand the parts of a text in light of the whole, but we understand the whole only through its parts. A similar circle exists between reader and text: our presuppositions shape what we see, yet the text can challenge and correct those presuppositions.

Grant Osborne's *The Hermeneutical Spiral* (1991) proposed that the image of a *spiral* is better than a circle. Interpretation does not go round in a closed loop; each pass between text and reader, part and whole, moves closer to the text's meaning.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: For Christians who hold Scripture to be the word of God, interpretation is a matter of faithfulness, not just technique. Paul urged Timothy to be "rightly dividing the word of truth" (2 Timothy 2:15). Christian traditions also stress that interpretation is a spiritual task, involving humility, prayer, the illumination of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 2:14), and the wisdom of the church across the centuries.

keyTerms.definition: The theory and practice of interpretation, from the Greek hermēneuō, "to interpret."
Drawing the meaning out of a text through careful study of its language, context, and genre.
Reading one's own ideas into a text rather than drawing out its meaning.
The view that a text's meaning is what its author intended to communicate.
The interplay by which parts of a text are understood through the whole and the whole through its parts.
Grant Osborne's image of interpretation as progressive movement closer to a text's meaning.

topics.title: The Historical-Grammatical Method
topics.subtitle: Hermeneutics
topics.summary: The interpretive method that seeks a text's plain sense through its historical setting, grammar, and literary context, and how it differs from historical criticism.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: The *historical-grammatical method* (also called the grammatico-historical method) seeks the meaning a biblical text had for its author and first readers by studying its **language** and its **historical setting**. It is the dominant method in evangelical and conservative Protestant scholarship, and its basic principles are shared by many Catholic, Orthodox, and mainline interpreters as well.

sections.heading: Origins
sections.body:
The method's roots lie in the Antiochene emphasis on the plain sense, in the medieval insistence (by Thomas Aquinas, among others) that all spiritual senses rest on the literal, and above all in the Reformation, when Luther and Calvin rejected allegorical excess and called interpreters back to the grammatical sense of Scripture. Augustine had already laid down a guiding principle in *On Christian Doctrine*: obscure passages should be explained by clearer ones, for "among the things that are plainly laid down in Scripture are to be found all matters that concern faith and the manner of life."

The phrase "grammatico-historical" is commonly associated with the eighteenth-century German scholar Johann August Ernesti, whose handbook on New Testament interpretation (1761) emphasized grammar and usage. In the English-speaking world, Milton Terry's *Biblical Hermeneutics* (1883) became a standard textbook.

sections.heading: The Steps of the Method
sections.body:
Practitioners describe the process in slightly different ways, but the core steps are these:

1. **Establish the text.** Begin with the best available original-language text, aided by textual criticism.
2. **Study the historical context.** Who wrote, to whom, when, and why? What were the political, social, and religious circumstances? Knowing that Philippians was written from imprisonment, for example, shapes how we hear its call to joy.
3. **Analyze the grammar and vocabulary.** Examine syntax, verb forms, and the meaning of key words in their contexts.
4. **Read in literary context.** Consider the surrounding paragraphs, the argument of the whole book, and the passage's genre.
5. **Relate to the whole of Scripture.** Compare related passages ("Scripture interprets Scripture") and place the text within biblical theology.
6. **Apply.** Move from what the text meant to what it means for readers today, distinguishing timeless principles from culturally specific forms.

sections.heading: Word-Study Pitfalls
sections.body:
Linguistic study has made interpreters cautious about common errors. James Barr's *The Semantics of Biblical Language* (1961) criticized theological arguments built on faulty word studies, and D. A. Carson's *Exegetical Fallacies* catalogued similar mistakes:

- **The root fallacy:** assuming a word's meaning is determined by its etymology. Meaning is determined by usage in context.
- **Illegitimate totality transfer:** reading every possible meaning of a word into a single occurrence.
- **Anachronism:** reading later meanings back into earlier texts, such as hearing modern "dynamite" in the Greek *dunamis*.

sections.heading: Historical-Grammatical vs. Historical-Critical
sections.body:
The historical-grammatical method should be distinguished from the **historical-critical method** that developed in the Enlightenment. Both study history and language, but they differ in assumptions. Historical criticism, with its tools of source, form, and redaction criticism, typically treats the Bible like any other ancient text, investigates how it was composed, and generally does not presuppose inspiration or the possibility of predictive prophecy and miracle. Historical-grammatical interpreters usually work within a commitment to Scripture's inspiration and unity, and they read the canon as a coherent whole.

The line is not always sharp. Many evangelical scholars use critical tools while rejecting naturalistic assumptions. In Catholic teaching, Pope Pius XII's encyclical *Divino Afflante Spiritu* (1943) encouraged the study of original languages, history, and literary forms, and the Second Vatican Council's *Dei Verbum* (1965) directed interpreters to attend to what the human authors intended, while also reading Scripture within the living tradition of the whole Church.

sections.heading: Assessment
sections.body: The strength of the historical-grammatical method is its discipline: it anchors interpretation in the text and protects against arbitrary readings. Its critics raise two concerns. Some argue that it can neglect the theological and Christ-centered reading practiced by the New Testament writers and the church fathers. Others, from a critical standpoint, argue that it lets doctrinal commitments decide historical questions in advance. Most interpreters today see the recovery of the original sense as the indispensable starting point, whatever else they add.

keyTerms.definition: Interpretation that seeks a text's original meaning through its grammar, vocabulary, literary context, and historical setting.
The meaning conveyed by the words of the text as the author used them, including figures of speech; not the same as wooden literalism.
The error of assuming that a word's etymology determines its meaning in a given context.
An Enlightenment-era approach that studies the Bible's composition and history like any ancient text, typically without presupposing inspiration.
The principle that Scripture should be interpreted by Scripture, with clearer passages shedding light on obscure ones.

topics.subtitle: Hermeneutics
topics.summary: How the Bible's many genres, from narrative and law to poetry, prophecy, and apocalyptic, each call for different reading strategies.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: The Bible is not one kind of book but a library of many kinds of writing. A *genre* is a category of literature with recognizable conventions, and readers interpret differently depending on the genre they recognize: we do not read a poem the way we read a legal contract. Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart's *How to Read the Bible for All Its Worth* popularized genre-sensitive reading for a general audience. This article surveys the major genres and the questions each raises.

sections.heading: Narrative
sections.body: Narrative is the most common genre in the Bible, from Genesis through Esther and from the Gospels through Acts. Biblical narrators rarely stop to moralize; they *show* rather than tell, through plot, characterization, dialogue, and repetition. A key principle is to distinguish what a narrative **describes** from what it **prescribes**. Judges records Jephthah's vow and its tragic outcome (Judges 11:29-40) without endorsing it. Interpreters also ask what role a story plays in the larger narrative of God's dealings with his people.

sections.heading: Law
sections.body: The Pentateuch contains extensive legal material. Scholars, following Albrecht Alt, distinguish **apodictic** law, which states absolute commands ("Thou shalt not kill"), from **casuistic** or case law, which takes an "if... then" form addressing particular situations (Exodus 21:28-29). Christians have long debated how Old Testament law applies after Christ. The Reformed tradition, for example, distinguished moral, ceremonial, and civil law, holding that the moral law remains binding while the ceremonial law is fulfilled in Christ; others approach the law through its fulfillment in Christ as a whole (Matthew 5:17).

sections.heading: Poetry
sections.body:
About a third of the Old Testament is poetry. Its defining feature is **parallelism**, which Robert Lowth described in his lectures on Hebrew poetry (1753). In parallelism, a second line echoes, contrasts with, or extends the first:

> The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork.

That verse (Psalm 19:1) is an example of synonymous parallelism. Poetry also relies heavily on imagery and metaphor, so readers should not press its language literally: when the psalmist says God hides him "under the shadow of thy wings" (Psalm 17:8), he is not describing God's anatomy.

sections.heading: Wisdom
sections.body: Wisdom literature (Proverbs, Job, Ecclesiastes, and in the Catholic and Orthodox canons Sirach and the Wisdom of Solomon) reflects on how to live skillfully in God's world. Proverbs are generally true observations, not unconditional promises. Proverbs 26:4-5 juxtaposes "Answer not a fool according to his folly" with "Answer a fool according to his folly," showing that wisdom requires discernment about when each applies. Job and Ecclesiastes probe the limits of conventional wisdom.

sections.heading: Prophecy
sections.body: The prophets were primarily *forthtellers*, calling Israel back to covenant faithfulness, and only secondarily *foretellers* of future events. Much prophecy concerns judgment and restoration in the prophets' own time. Some prophecy is explicitly conditional: Jeremiah 18:7-10 teaches that God may relent if a nation repents, as Nineveh did in Jonah. Prophetic language is often poetic and should be read with that in mind.

sections.heading: Gospel
sections.body: The four Gospels are narratives of Jesus' life, death, and resurrection. Many scholars, following Richard Burridge's *What Are the Gospels?* (1992), compare them to Greco-Roman *bioi* (ancient biographies), which focused on a subject's character and significance rather than giving a complete chronology. Each evangelist arranges his material to emphasize particular themes, so readers compare parallel accounts and ask why each Gospel tells a story as it does.

sections.heading: Epistle
sections.body: The New Testament letters are **occasional** documents, written to specific churches or individuals addressing particular situations. Interpreters must reconstruct the occasion, often hearing only one side of a conversation, before applying the letter's teaching. Letters follow ancient conventions: opening greeting, thanksgiving, body, and closing.

sections.heading: Apocalyptic
sections.body: Apocalyptic literature, including parts of Daniel and the book of Revelation, uses vivid symbolic visions, numbers, and cosmic imagery to reveal God's sovereignty over history and the final triumph of his kingdom. Its symbols are not meant to be read as literal descriptions; Revelation itself sometimes explains them (Revelation 1:20 says the seven candlesticks are seven churches). Interpreters differ widely on Revelation, from preterist to futurist readings, but most agree that recognizing its genre is the first step.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: Misreading genre leads to misreading the message. Recognizing genre does not settle every question, but it tells the reader what kind of truth a passage is communicating and how it communicates it.

keyTerms.definition: A category of literature with recognizable conventions that guide how a text should be read.
The defining feature of Hebrew poetry, in which a second line echoes, contrasts with, or develops the first.
Law stated as absolute commands or prohibitions, such as the Ten Commandments.
Case law in "if... then" form addressing particular situations.
A letter written to address a specific situation in a particular church or for a particular person.
A genre using symbolic visions and cosmic imagery to reveal God's purposes in history and its consummation.

topics.title: A History of Biblical Interpretation
topics.subtitle: Hermeneutics
topics.summary: From Alexandrian allegory and Antiochene literalism through the medieval fourfold sense, the Reformation, and modern historical criticism.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: Christians have read the Bible for two thousand years, and the ways they have read it have changed with the questions and tools of each era. Knowing this history helps modern readers recognize their own assumptions and learn from interpreters of the past.

sections.heading: Alexandria and Antioch
sections.body:
In the early church two broad tendencies are often contrasted, though the contrast can be overdrawn.

**Alexandria** in Egypt was a center of Platonic philosophy and of Jewish allegorical interpretation, represented by Philo of Alexandria (died c. AD 50). The great Christian scholar **Origen** (c. 185-c. 253) taught that Scripture, like a human being, has a body, a soul, and a spirit. In *On First Principles*, Book IV, he distinguished the literal sense, a moral sense, and a spiritual sense. Origen held that some passages contain things that cannot be literally true, which signal the reader to look for a deeper meaning. Allegory let Alexandrian interpreters find Christ and the spiritual life throughout the Old Testament, and Paul himself speaks of the story of Hagar and Sarah as an allegory (Galatians 4:24).

**Antioch** in Syria emphasized the historical and literal sense. Its leading figures, Diodore of Tarsus, Theodore of Mopsuestia, and John Chrysostom, criticized allegory for detaching meaning from history. They spoke instead of *theoria*, a spiritual insight grounded in the historical sense, which allowed for typology. Chrysostom's homilies on the Bible became models of practical, text-centered preaching.

Augustine (354-430) drew on both streams. In *On Christian Doctrine* he taught that interpretation must be governed by the rule of faith and by love of God and neighbor.

sections.heading: The Medieval Fourfold Sense
sections.body:
Medieval interpreters systematized these approaches into the **quadriga**, the four senses of Scripture. A thirteenth-century couplet, attributed to Augustine of Dacia, summarized it:

> The letter teaches what happened; allegory, what you should believe; the moral sense, what you should do; anagogy, where you are going.

1. The **literal** or historical sense: what the text records.
2. The **allegorical** sense: what it teaches about Christ and the Church.
3. The **tropological** or moral sense: how the believer should live.
4. The **anagogical** sense: what it reveals about final, heavenly realities.

The standard example is Jerusalem: literally the city in Judea, allegorically the Church, tropologically the faithful soul, and anagogically the heavenly city. Thomas Aquinas insisted that all the spiritual senses are founded on the literal sense, and that only the literal sense can be used to prove doctrine (*Summa Theologiae* I, question 1, article 10).

sections.heading: The Reformation
sections.body:
The Reformers called the church back to the literal or grammatical sense. Martin Luther, though he continued to read the Old Testament christologically, criticized the excesses of allegory. The principle of *sola scriptura* held that Scripture is the supreme authority over church tradition, and the principle that **Scripture interprets Scripture** meant that unclear passages should be read in light of clear ones. The Westminster Confession (1646) states: "The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture itself" (1.9). John Calvin's commentaries, with their attention to context and authorial intent, became models of Reformation exegesis.

The Roman Catholic Council of Trent (1546) responded that no one should interpret Scripture contrary to the sense held by the Church or the unanimous consent of the Fathers. Eastern Orthodox interpreters similarly read Scripture within the church's tradition and the consensus of the Fathers.

sections.heading: Modern Historical Criticism
sections.body:
The Enlightenment brought new questions. Baruch Spinoza's *Theological-Political Treatise* (1670) argued that the Bible should be studied like any natural object. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries scholars developed source criticism, culminating in Julius Wellhausen's influential documentary hypothesis about the sources of the Pentateuch. Albert Schweitzer's *The Quest of the Historical Jesus* (1906) surveyed attempts to recover a Jesus behind the Gospels. In the twentieth century, form criticism and redaction criticism examined how traditions were shaped and edited, and Rudolf Bultmann called for "demythologizing" the New Testament.

Reactions were varied. Conservative scholars defended traditional authorship and inspiration. Others, such as Karl Barth, accepted critical methods but insisted that Scripture must be heard as the word of God. In recent decades, canonical criticism (Brevard Childs) and the movement for *theological interpretation of Scripture* have sought to recover reading the Bible as the church's book, often drawing again on patristic and medieval interpreters.

sections.heading: Assessment
sections.body: Every era has seen something its predecessors missed and missed something they saw. Allegory risked arbitrariness; historical criticism risked reducing the Bible to an artifact. Many interpreters today aim to hold together careful historical reading with the theological and spiritual reading that the church has practiced from the beginning.

keyTerms.definition: Interpretation that finds a hidden spiritual meaning beneath the literal sense of a text.
In the Antiochene school, spiritual insight grounded in and controlled by the historical sense of the text.
The medieval fourfold sense of Scripture: literal, allegorical, tropological, and anagogical.
The moral sense of Scripture, concerning how the believer should live.
The sense of Scripture that points to final, heavenly realities.
The Reformation principle that Scripture is the supreme authority for faith and practice, above church tradition.

topics.title: Typology and the New Testament Use of the Old
topics.subtitle: Hermeneutics
topics.summary: How the New Testament writers read the Old Testament as fulfilled in Christ, the nature of typology, and current debates about apostolic exegesis.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: The New Testament quotes or alludes to the Old Testament on almost every page. Jesus himself taught that "all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me" (Luke 24:44). Understanding *how* the apostles read their Scriptures is one of the central questions of hermeneutics. Augustine captured the traditional Christian view in his *Questions on the Heptateuch*: the New is hidden in the Old, and the Old is made plain in the New.

sections.heading: Ways the New Testament Uses the Old
sections.body:
Scholars identify several distinct patterns:

- **Direct prophecy and fulfillment.** Matthew 2:5-6 cites Micah 5:2 to show that the Messiah would come from Bethlehem.
- **Typological fulfillment.** Matthew 2:15 applies Hosea 11:1 ("Out of Egypt have I called my son"), which in Hosea refers to Israel's exodus, to the child Jesus returning from Egypt. Jesus recapitulates Israel's story.
- **Analogy and illustration.** Paul draws lessons from Israel's wilderness experience "for our admonition" (1 Corinthians 10:11).
- **Theological argument.** Paul reasons from Genesis 15:6 that Abraham was justified by faith before circumcision (Romans 4).
- **Allusion and echo.** Many texts evoke Old Testament language without formal quotation.

sections.heading: What Is Typology?
sections.body:
The word comes from the Greek *typos*, "pattern" or "impression." Paul calls Adam "the figure of him that was to come" (Romans 5:14), and 1 Peter 3:21 calls baptism the *antitypos* of the flood. A **type** is a person, event, or institution in the Old Testament that foreshadows a greater reality in Christ, the **antitype**. Typology has several marks:

1. It is rooted in **history**: the type was a real person, event, or institution with its own meaning in its own time.
2. There is a genuine **correspondence** between type and antitype.
3. There is **escalation**: the antitype is greater than the type. Jesus is "greater than Jonas" and "greater than Solomon" (Matthew 12:41-42).

Common examples include Adam and Christ, the Passover lamb ("Christ our passover is sacrificed for us," 1 Corinthians 5:7), the manna and Jesus as the bread of life (John 6:31-35), the tabernacle and priesthood (Hebrews 8-10), and Melchizedek (Hebrews 7).

sections.heading: Typology and Allegory
sections.body: Typology is usually distinguished from **allegory**. Typology finds correspondences between *events* in redemptive history; allegory finds hidden meanings in the *details of a text*, often without regard to its history. Augustine's famous reading of the parable of the Good Samaritan, in which the inn represents the Church and the innkeeper the apostle Paul, is allegorical. The distinction is useful but not absolute. Paul describes his reading of Hagar and Sarah with a form of the Greek verb *allēgoreō* (Galatians 4:24), though many interpreters argue his method there is closer to typology.

sections.heading: Jewish Interpretive Methods
sections.body: The apostles read Scripture as first-century Jews. Contemporary methods included **midrash**, creative expository commentary; **pesher**, used in the Dead Sea Scrolls, which applied prophetic texts directly to the community's own time ("its interpretation concerns..."); and rabbinic rules such as *qal wahomer*, arguing from the lesser to the greater, which Jesus uses in Matthew 7:11.

sections.heading: Current Debates
sections.body:
Scholars disagree about whether the New Testament authors respected the original context of the passages they cited.

- **C. H. Dodd**, in *According to the Scriptures* (1952), argued that New Testament writers often cited a verse as a pointer to its whole context, drawing on a shared body of key Old Testament passages.
- **Richard Longenecker** argued that the apostles used Jewish interpretive methods of their day, and that their conclusions are authoritative even if their methods are not necessarily ours to copy.
- **G. K. Beale** and others defend the view that the apostles' interpretations, though they go beyond the human author's conscious intention, develop meaning organically present in the Old Testament context.
- **Richard Hays**, in *Echoes of Scripture in the Letters of Paul* (1989), drew attention to subtle allusions and to what he later called "figural reading," in which earlier events are read backward in light of Christ.

The related idea of a **sensus plenior** ("fuller sense"), popularized by the Catholic scholar Raymond E. Brown in the 1950s, proposes that God intended a deeper meaning in some texts than the human author clearly understood, a meaning brought to light by later revelation.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: How we understand the apostles' use of the Old Testament shapes how we read the whole Bible: as a unified story culminating in Christ, as a collection of separate witnesses, or as something in between. It also raises the practical question of whether modern interpreters may imitate apostolic exegesis, or should restrict themselves to typologies the New Testament itself identifies.

keyTerms.definition: A person, event, or institution in the Old Testament that foreshadows a greater fulfillment in Christ.
The fulfillment to which a type points, such as Christ as the true Passover lamb.
The principle that the antitype is greater than the type it fulfills.
A Qumran method of interpretation applying prophetic texts directly to the community's own time.
A "fuller sense" intended by God in a text beyond what the human author clearly understood.
A rabbinic argument from the lesser to the greater.

topics.title: Covenant Theology and Dispensationalism
topics.subtitle: Hermeneutics
topics.summary: Two Protestant frameworks for understanding the unity of the Bible and the relationship between Israel and the church, and the mediating positions between them.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: How do the Old and New Testaments fit together? How does Israel relate to the church? Protestant theology has produced two major systems for answering these questions: **covenant theology** and **dispensationalism**. Each is a framework for reading the whole Bible, and each has shaped preaching, eschatology, and church practice. Catholic and Orthodox theology address the same questions in other terms and are generally not organized around either system.

sections.heading: Covenant Theology
sections.body:
Covenant theology organizes the Bible around God's covenants. It grew out of the Reformed Reformation, with roots in Heinrich Bullinger and Zacharias Ursinus, and was developed by Johannes Cocceius in his *Doctrine of the Covenant and Testament of God* (1648) and by Herman Witsius in *The Economy of the Covenants* (1677). The Westminster Confession (1646), chapter 7, gave it confessional form.

Classic covenant theology speaks of three overarching covenants:

1. The **covenant of redemption**, an eternal agreement within the Trinity in which the Father appoints the Son to redeem the elect.
2. The **covenant of works**, made with Adam, promising life on condition of perfect obedience. Adam broke it in the Fall.
3. The **covenant of grace**, announced in Genesis 3:15 and administered through the covenants with Noah, Abraham, Moses, and David, and fulfilled in the new covenant in Christ.

Key emphases follow. There is **one people of God** throughout history; the church is the continuation and fulfillment of Israel, and Gentile believers are Abraham's seed (Galatians 3:29). Because the sign of the covenant was given to the children of believers in the Old Testament, most covenant theologians practice **infant baptism**. Reformed Baptists, following the Second London Baptist Confession (1689), hold their own form of covenant theology and baptize only believers. In eschatology, covenant theologians have most often been amillennial or postmillennial, though some are historic premillennialists.

sections.heading: Dispensationalism
sections.body:
Dispensationalism arose in the nineteenth century through **John Nelson Darby** (1800-1882), a leader of the Plymouth Brethren. It spread widely in America through Bible conferences and the **Scofield Reference Bible** (1909), and it was developed academically at Dallas Theological Seminary, founded in 1924, by Lewis Sperry Chafer and later Charles Ryrie and John Walvoord.

A *dispensation* is a distinct stewardship or administration in which God relates to humanity in a particular way. Scofield identified seven: innocence, conscience, human government, promise, law, grace, and kingdom. Charles Ryrie, in *Dispensationalism Today* (1965), argued that the essential marks (the *sine qua non*) of dispensationalism are:

1. A consistent **distinction between Israel and the church**.
2. A consistently **literal** (plain) hermeneutic, especially in prophecy.
3. The **glory of God**, rather than salvation alone, as the unifying purpose of history.

Because God's promises to ethnic Israel, including land and kingdom, are read literally, dispensationalists expect their future fulfillment. Classic dispensationalism is **premillennial**, usually holding to a **pretribulational rapture** of the church before a future tribulation and a literal thousand-year reign of Christ in which promises to Israel are fulfilled. Dispensationalists appeal to texts such as Romans 11:25-29, where Paul speaks of a future for Israel.

sections.heading: Points of Debate
sections.body:
- **Israel and the church.** Covenant theologians argue that the New Testament applies Israel's titles to the church (1 Peter 2:9) and that Christ is the true seed of Abraham. Dispensationalists reply that Romans 9-11 and the irrevocable "gifts and calling of God" (Romans 11:29) point to a distinct future for ethnic Israel.
- **Hermeneutics.** Dispensationalists charge covenant theology with spiritualizing prophecy; covenant theologians reply that they follow the New Testament's own reading of the Old.
- **Law and grace.** Older dispensationalists sometimes sharply contrasted the dispensations of law and grace, prompting critics to object that they implied different ways of salvation. Later dispensationalists affirmed that salvation has always been by grace through faith.

sections.heading: Mediating Positions
sections.body: **Progressive dispensationalism**, developed in the 1980s and 1990s by Craig Blaising, Darrell Bock, and Robert Saucy, sees the dispensations as progressive stages of a single plan, holds that Christ already reigns as Davidic king in some sense, and softens the Israel-church distinction while maintaining a future for national Israel. On the other side, **New Covenant Theology** and **progressive covenantalism** (Peter Gentry and Stephen Wellum, *Kingdom through Covenant*, 2012) affirm the unity of the covenants while emphasizing the newness of the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31-34) and generally rejecting infant baptism.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: These frameworks shape how readers interpret prophecy, relate the Mosaic law to Christians, view the modern state of Israel, and practice baptism. Knowing them helps readers recognize the assumptions behind sermons and commentaries, and to evaluate those assumptions by Scripture itself.

keyTerms.definition: In covenant theology, God's gracious arrangement to save sinners, administered through the biblical covenants and fulfilled in Christ.
In covenant theology, the covenant with Adam promising life on condition of perfect obedience.
A distinct stewardship or administration in which God relates to humanity in a particular way.
Latin for "without which not"; Charles Ryrie's term for the essential marks of dispensationalism.
The view, common in classic dispensationalism, that the church will be taken to Christ before a future tribulation.
A revision of dispensationalism that sees the dispensations as progressive stages of one plan and softens the Israel-church distinction.

topics.title: Introduction to Soteriology
topics.subtitle: Soteriology
topics.summary: What Christians mean by sin, grace, and salvation, how theologians order the steps of salvation, and where Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant frameworks part ways.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: **Soteriology** is the branch of Christian theology that studies salvation. The word comes from the Greek *sōtēria* ("deliverance, salvation") and *logos* ("word, account"). It asks what humanity needs saving from, what God has done in Christ to accomplish that rescue, and how that rescue reaches individual people. Every Christian tradition answers these questions, but they frame them in different ways.

sections.heading: The Problem: Sin
sections.body: Christian theology begins with the claim that something has gone wrong between God and humanity. Paul summarises it bluntly: "all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God" (Romans 3:23). Sin is understood both as particular wrong acts and as a deeper condition: a disordered love that turns away from God toward lesser goods. Its consequences include guilt before God, corruption of human desires, alienation from others, and death (Romans 6:23). How deep this corruption runs, and whether Adam's guilt is inherited, is debated (see the topic on theological anthropology).

sections.heading: The Remedy: Grace
sections.body:
**Grace** (Greek *charis*) is God's free and unmerited favour toward sinners. All the major traditions agree that salvation is a gift that originates with God rather than a wage earned by human effort (Ephesians 2:8-9). They differ on what grace *is* and how it works:

- **Protestant** theologians characteristically stress grace as God's favourable disposition, his pardon and acceptance of sinners for Christ's sake.
- **Catholic** teaching also speaks of grace as a gift that really transforms the soul. The Catechism describes grace as "a participation in the life of God," and distinguishes *sanctifying* (habitual) grace, which abides in the soul, from *actual* grace, God's help for particular acts.
- **Orthodox** theology speaks of grace as God's uncreated energies, his very life communicated to human beings.

sections.heading: Ordering Salvation: The Ordo Salutis
sections.body:
Protestant theologians after the Reformation developed the **ordo salutis** ("order of salvation"), a logical sequence of the aspects of salvation applied to the believer. Its classic proof text is Romans 8:29-30, sometimes called the "golden chain": those God foreknew he predestined, called, justified, and glorified. A typical Reformed ordo runs:

1. Election
2. Effectual calling
3. Regeneration
4. Faith and repentance (conversion)
5. Justification
6. Adoption
7. Sanctification
8. Perseverance
9. Glorification

The order is mostly *logical* rather than temporal. Its fine points carry real disagreements. Reformed theologians place regeneration *before* faith, holding that a spiritually dead person must be made alive in order to believe. Arminian and Wesleyan theologians hold that *prevenient grace* enables a person to respond in faith, with regeneration following faith. Lutherans emphasise the means of grace, the Word and the sacraments, through which the Spirit creates faith, and they teach that God regenerates in baptism.

sections.heading: Three Frameworks
sections.body:
### Catholic

Catholic teaching presents salvation as a lifelong process rooted in the sacraments. In baptism a person is justified: sins are forgiven and sanctifying grace is infused, so justification includes inner renewal. This grace can grow through the sacraments and good works done in grace, and it can be lost through **mortal sin**, after which it is restored through the sacrament of penance (reconciliation).

### Orthodox

Eastern Orthodox theology tends to describe salvation less in legal categories and more as healing, illumination, and union with God, summed up in the word **theosis** (deification). Salvation involves *synergy*, the cooperation of human freedom with divine grace, within the sacramental life of the Church.

### Protestant

Protestant theology distinguishes **justification**, a forensic (legal) declaration that the sinner is righteous on account of Christ's righteousness received by faith, from **sanctification**, the ongoing transformation of the believer. The two are inseparable but must not be confused; good works are the fruit of justification rather than its ground.

sections.heading: Points of Agreement and Difference
sections.body: All three traditions confess that salvation is accomplished by the Triune God through the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ, that it is received by grace, and that it culminates in the resurrection and eternal life. The disputes concern how grace operates, how human freedom relates to it, whether justification is a declaration or a transformation (or both), and what role the Church and sacraments play. The remaining topics in this section take up each of these questions in turn.

keyTerms.definition: The study of salvation, from the Greek sōtēria (salvation) and logos (word or account).
God's free and unmerited favour and help toward sinners; understood in Catholic and Orthodox theology also as a real sharing in God's life.

In Arminian and Wesleyan theology, grace that goes before conversion and enables a fallen person to respond freely to the gospel.
In Catholic teaching, a grave sin committed with full knowledge and deliberate consent that destroys sanctifying grace in the soul.

topics.title: Theories of the Atonement
topics.subtitle: Soteriology
topics.summary: Ransom, recapitulation, Christus Victor, satisfaction, moral influence, penal substitution, and governmental theories: the main Christian accounts of how Christ's death saves.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: The word **atonement** was coined in English to mean "at-one-ment," reconciliation between estranged parties. Christians have always confessed that "Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures" (1 Corinthians 15:3), but the ecumenical creeds never defined *how* his death reconciles humanity to God. Over the centuries several models, often called "theories," have been proposed. Many theologians treat them as complementary angles on one mystery rather than strict rivals.

sections.heading: Patristic Models
sections.body:
### Ransom

Jesus said that he came "to give his life as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45). Some early writers, notably **Origen** and **Gregory of Nyssa**, developed this into the idea that humanity had fallen under the power of the devil, and that Christ's life was the price that released captives. Gregory famously compared Christ's humanity to bait concealing the "fishhook" of his divinity: death swallowed him and could not hold him. Later critics objected to the suggestion that God owed the devil anything.

### Recapitulation

**Irenaeus of Lyons** (second century) taught that Christ, the second Adam, "recapitulated" (summed up and re-lived) the whole of human existence. Where Adam disobeyed, Christ obeyed at every stage of life, undoing the fall and restoring humanity's communion with God. The term echoes Ephesians 1:10, where God purposes to "sum up all things in Christ." Irenaeus's vision of the Son becoming "what we are, that He might bring us to be even what He is Himself" deeply shaped Eastern theology.

### Christus Victor

In *Christus Victor* (1931 in English), the Swedish Lutheran bishop **Gustaf Aulén** argued that the dominant view of the early church was a "classic" or dramatic theory: Christ's cross and resurrection are God's victory over sin, death, and the devil (Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14-15). Aulén's book revived interest in this theme, and it remains central in Orthodox liturgy and in much recent Protestant theology.

sections.heading: Medieval Models
sections.body:
### Satisfaction

In *Cur Deus Homo* ("Why God Became Man," completed around 1098), **Anselm of Canterbury** argued that sin robs God of the honour owed to him. Justice requires either punishment or satisfaction. Because the debt is infinite, only God can pay it; because humanity owes it, only a human being should. Hence the God-man:

> If it be necessary, therefore, as it appears, that the heavenly kingdom be made up of men, and this cannot be effected unless the aforesaid satisfaction be made, which none but God can make and none but man ought to make, it is necessary for the God-man to make it.

Christ's freely offered death, which he did not owe, makes superabundant satisfaction. Thomas Aquinas refined this view, and the Council of Trent taught that Christ "merited Justification for us by His most holy Passion on the wood of the cross, and made satisfaction for us unto God the Father."

### Moral Influence

**Peter Abelard** (1079-1142), commenting on Romans, stressed that the cross displays God's love so powerfully that it kindles answering love in sinners (Romans 5:8). Abelard did not deny other aspects of the atonement, but later liberal Protestant theologians made the "moral influence" or "moral example" theme central, sometimes to the exclusion of any objective change in God's relation to humanity.

sections.heading: Reformation and After
sections.body:
### Penal Substitution

The Protestant Reformers, especially **John Calvin**, developed a model in which Christ bore the *penalty* that sinners deserved, standing in their place under God's just judgment. Key texts include Isaiah 53:5 ("he was wounded for our transgressions"), 2 Corinthians 5:21, and Romans 3:25-26, where Christ is set forth as a **propitiation** that shows God to be both "just and the justifier." Penal substitution became the dominant view in Reformed, Lutheran, and evangelical theology. Critics have objected that it can seem to divide the Father from the Son or to make God's forgiveness depend on violence; defenders reply that the Trinity acts together and that God himself bears the cost.

### Governmental

The Dutch jurist **Hugo Grotius** (1583-1645) proposed that God acts as the moral governor of the universe. Christ's death is not the exact equivalent of the penalty owed, but a public demonstration of the seriousness of sin that upholds the moral order and allows God to forgive. This governmental theory was influential among Arminians, later New England theologians, and some Methodist writers.

sections.heading: Points of Agreement and Difference
sections.body: Catholic theology has historically emphasised satisfaction and sacrifice; Orthodox theology emphasises victory over death and the healing of human nature through the incarnation; Reformed and many evangelical theologians regard penal substitution as the heart of the atonement while affirming other themes. All agree that the cross is the act of God's love (John 3:16) and that its saving power is inseparable from Christ's resurrection.

keyTerms.definition: Reconciliation between God and humanity accomplished through Christ; the English word originally meant 'at-one-ment'.
Irenaeus's teaching that Christ, the second Adam, re-lived and summed up human existence in obedience, undoing the fall.
In Anselm's model, the payment of honour owed to God, which Christ as the God-man offers freely on behalf of humanity.
A sacrifice that turns away wrath or satisfies justice; a translation of the Greek hilastērion in Romans 3:25.
The view that Christ bore in the place of sinners the penalty their sins deserved under God's just judgment.
Hugo Grotius's view that Christ's death publicly upholds God's moral government, allowing God to forgive without being the exact penalty owed.

topics.title: Justification
topics.subtitle: Soteriology
topics.summary: How a sinner is made or declared right with God: Luther's sola fide, the Council of Trent's response, the 1999 Joint Declaration, and the New Perspective on Paul.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: **Justification** concerns how a sinner comes to stand in a right relationship with God. It was the central doctrinal dispute of the sixteenth-century Reformation, and it remains a touchstone of Protestant and Catholic identity. Key biblical texts include Romans 3:21-28, Romans 4:1-8, Galatians 2:16, and James 2:24.

sections.heading: Luther and Sola Fide
sections.body:
**Martin Luther** (1483-1546), an Augustinian friar and professor at Wittenberg, came to read Romans 1:17, "the righteous shall live by faith," as describing not God's punishing justice but the righteousness God gives freely to those who believe. From this grew the Reformation principle of **sola fide**, justification by faith alone. In his 1522 German New Testament Luther rendered Romans 3:28 as justification "by faith alone" (*allein durch den Glauben*), a translation he defended as capturing Paul's sense.

Luther and his successors taught that:

- Justification is **forensic**: God *declares* the sinner righteous, as a judge pronounces a verdict.
- The righteousness on which this verdict rests is Christ's, an "alien righteousness" **imputed** (credited) to the believer, received by faith (Romans 4:5).
- The believer is therefore *simul iustus et peccator*, "at the same time righteous and a sinner."
- Good works necessarily follow as fruit, but they contribute nothing to the ground of justification.

The **Augsburg Confession** (1530), Article IV, gave this teaching confessional form for Lutherans, and Reformed confessions such as the Westminster Confession taught substantially the same doctrine.

sections.heading: The Council of Trent
sections.body:
The Catholic **Council of Trent** issued its **Decree on Justification** in its sixth session, approved in January 1547, with sixteen chapters and thirty-three canons. Trent taught that justification is "not remission of sins merely, but also the sanctification and renewal of the inward man." Its sole formal cause is "the justice of God, not that whereby He Himself is just, but that whereby He maketh us just": righteousness is truly *infused*, not merely imputed. Faith is necessary, being "the beginning of human salvation, the foundation, and the root of all Justification," but faith must be joined with hope and charity. Justification can increase through good works and can be lost through mortal sin.

Trent also insisted that justification is a free gift:

> we are therefore said to be justified freely, because that none of those things which precede justification, whether faith or works, merit the grace itself of justification.

At the same time its canons condemned anyone who "saith, that by faith alone the impious is justified" in the sense that nothing else is required to cooperate (Canon 9).

sections.heading: The Joint Declaration (1999)
sections.body:
After decades of dialogue, the **Lutheran World Federation** and the Catholic Church signed the **Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification** in Augsburg on 31 October 1999. It claimed a "consensus in basic truths," stated in a common confession:

> By grace alone, in faith in Christ's saving work and not because of any merit on our part, we are accepted by God and receive the Holy Spirit, who renews our hearts while equipping and calling us to good works.

The Declaration holds that the remaining differences in language and emphasis are not church-dividing, and that the sixteenth-century mutual condemnations do not apply to the teaching of the other side *as presented in the Declaration*. It was later affirmed by the World Methodist Council (2006), the Anglican Consultative Council (2016), and the World Communion of Reformed Churches (2017). Some confessional Lutherans and evangelicals, and some Catholic critics, judged that it papered over real differences.

sections.heading: The New Perspective on Paul
sections.body:
In the late twentieth century, biblical scholars questioned whether the Reformation debate had read Paul correctly. **E. P. Sanders**, in *Paul and Palestinian Judaism* (1977), argued that Second Temple Judaism was not a religion of earning salvation by works but of "covenantal nomism": one enters the covenant by grace and keeps the law as a response. **James D. G. Dunn** popularised the phrase "New Perspective on Paul" and argued that "works of the law" refers especially to boundary markers such as circumcision, food laws, and Sabbath that separated Jews from Gentiles. **N. T. Wright** has argued that justification is primarily God's declaration of who belongs to his covenant people.

Defenders of the traditional Protestant reading respond that Paul's contrast between faith and works (Romans 4:4-5) concerns human achievement in general, not only ethnic markers, and that the New Perspective underplays imputation.

sections.heading: Points of Agreement and Difference
sections.body: Catholics and Protestants agree that justification is God's gracious work in Christ, received in faith, and that it issues in good works. They differ over whether justification is a declaration distinct from inner renewal or includes that renewal, whether righteousness is imputed or infused, and how James 2:24 ("by works a man is justified, and not only by faith") relates to Paul. Orthodox theology, which did not experience the Reformation debate, usually treats justification within the larger frame of theosis.

keyTerms.definition: 'Faith alone': the Reformation principle that sinners are justified through faith apart from works of the law.
The crediting of Christ's righteousness to the believer's account, as taught by Lutheran and Reformed theology.
Catholic teaching that in justification God's grace truly makes the person inwardly righteous, not merely declared so.
Luther's phrase meaning 'at the same time righteous and a sinner', describing the justified believer.
E. P. Sanders's description of Second Temple Judaism: one enters the covenant by God's grace and stays in it by keeping the law.

topics.title: Augustine and Pelagius
topics.subtitle: Soteriology
topics.summary: The fifth-century controversy over grace, free will, and original sin, from Pelagius and Augustine through the Council of Carthage (418) to the Council of Orange (529).

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: In the early fifth century a controversy erupted in the Latin West that would shape Western theology for over a millennium. Its central question was simple to state and hard to answer: can human beings obey God by their own natural powers, or do they need God's inner grace even to begin to turn toward him? The main protagonists were the British ascetic **Pelagius** and **Augustine**, bishop of Hippo in North Africa (354-430).

sections.heading: Pelagius and His Teaching
sections.body:
Pelagius (died after 418) was a respected moral teacher in Rome who urged Christians to take holiness seriously. Augustine later reported that Pelagius was disturbed by a prayer in Augustine's *Confessions*:

> Give what You command, and command what You will.

To Pelagius this seemed to excuse moral laziness, as if obedience were impossible until God acted. Pelagius and his followers, notably **Celestius** and later **Julian of Eclanum**, taught that:

- God created human nature good, and the capacity to choose good remains intact after Adam.
- Adam's sin harmed his descendants by bad *example*, not by transmitting guilt or a corrupted nature.
- Infants are born in the state Adam was in before the fall.
- Grace consists chiefly of external aids: the gift of free will itself, the law, Christ's teaching and example, and the forgiveness of past sins.

If God commands perfection (Matthew 5:48), Pelagians reasoned, perfection must be possible.

sections.heading: Augustine's Response
sections.body:
Augustine wrote a series of anti-Pelagian treatises, including *On the Spirit and the Letter* (412) and *On Nature and Grace* (415). He argued that:

- In Adam all humanity fell (Romans 5:12), inheriting both guilt and a disordered will (**original sin**).
- Fallen human beings retain free choice, but their will is in bondage to sin and cannot love God without grace.
- Grace is not merely external instruction but an **inner** gift by which God heals the will and pours love into the heart (Romans 5:5).
- Grace is **prevenient** (it comes first) and **operative**: God works in us both to will and to act (Philippians 2:13).
- Because faith itself is a gift, salvation rests on God's gracious **predestination** of the elect (1 Corinthians 4:7).

sections.heading: The Council of Carthage (418)
sections.body: After Pelagius was acquitted at a synod in Diospolis (Palestine) in 415, North African bishops pressed the issue. A council at **Carthage in 418** issued canons condemning the denial of original sin, the claim that grace is only the forgiveness of past sins, and the claim that grace only makes obedience easier rather than possible. Pope Zosimus then condemned Pelagianism in his letter known as the *Tractoria*, and the Council of Ephesus (431) also condemned Celestius's followers.

sections.heading: Semi-Pelagianism
sections.body: Augustine's strong teaching on predestination troubled monks in southern Gaul, such as **John Cassian** and later **Faustus of Riez**. They rejected Pelagius but held that the *beginning of faith* (*initium fidei*) could arise from the human will, with grace then assisting and completing it. This position was later labelled **semi-Pelagianism**, a term coined long afterwards, in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Prosper of Aquitaine defended Augustine against these critics.

sections.heading: The Council of Orange (529)
sections.body:
The regional **Second Council of Orange** in 529, led by Caesarius of Arles and later approved by Pope Boniface II, settled the matter for the Western church. Its canons taught that:

1. Original sin affects both body and soul and passes to all Adam's descendants.
2. Even the beginning of faith and the desire for it are gifts of grace, not natural achievements.
3. Free will, weakened by the fall, cannot be restored except by grace.
4. The baptised, with Christ's help, are able to fulfil what pertains to salvation.

Orange explicitly anathematised the idea that anyone is predestined to evil by divine power. It did not adopt Augustine's full doctrine of predestination, and it said nothing of irresistible grace. Its canons were little known in the Middle Ages and were rediscovered in the sixteenth century, when both Catholic and Protestant theologians appealed to them.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body: Every later Western debate over grace, including the Reformation, the Jansenist controversy, and the clash between Calvinism and Arminianism, replays themes from this controversy. Catholics, Lutherans, Reformed, and Arminians all reject Pelagianism and affirm the necessity of grace; they differ on how grace relates to human cooperation. Eastern Orthodox theology was little involved in the controversy; it speaks of *synergy* between grace and freedom and does not accept the Western label "semi-Pelagian" as a fair description of its view.

keyTerms.definition: The teaching associated with Pelagius that human nature retains the natural power to obey God, so that inner grace is not strictly necessary for righteousness.
In Augustine's teaching, the guilt and corruption inherited by all humanity from Adam's fall.
Grace that 'comes before' any human movement toward God, enabling the will to turn to him.
A later label for the view that the beginning of faith arises from the human will, with grace assisting afterwards.
Latin for 'the beginning of faith'; whether it comes from grace or from nature was the key question in the semi-Pelagian dispute.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: Within Protestantism, the most enduring debate about salvation concerns predestination: does God choose whom he will save unconditionally, or does his choice take account of human faith freely given? The debate took its classic shape in the Dutch Republic in the early seventeenth century and remains lively among evangelicals today.

sections.heading: Jacobus Arminius
sections.body: **Jacobus Arminius** (1560-1609) was a Dutch Reformed minister who had studied at Geneva under Theodore Beza, Calvin's successor. As professor of theology at Leiden from 1603, he questioned the strict predestinarian theology of colleagues such as Franciscus Gomarus. Arminius taught that God's decree of election is based on his foreknowledge of who would believe, that Christ died for all, and that God's grace, though necessary for any good, can be resisted. He died in 1609 before the controversy came to a head.

sections.heading: The Remonstrance (1610)
sections.body:
In 1610 Arminius's followers presented the States of Holland with a **Remonstrance** in five articles. They taught:

1. **Conditional election**: God decreed to save those who, through grace, believe in Christ and persevere.
2. **Universal atonement**: Christ died for all people, though only believers actually enjoy forgiveness.
3. **Necessity of grace**: fallen humanity cannot of itself think, will, or do anything truly good without regenerating grace.
4. **Resistible grace**: grace is the beginning and completion of all good, but it is not irresistible.
5. **Perseverance**: believers are empowered by grace to persevere, but whether they can fall away required further examination from Scripture.

Note that the Remonstrants affirmed human inability apart from grace; they were not Pelagians.

sections.heading: The Synod of Dort (1618-19)
sections.body:
A national synod met at **Dordrecht** from November 1618 to May 1619, with delegates from Reformed churches in Britain, the German territories, and Switzerland as well as the Netherlands. It rejected the Remonstrance and issued the **Canons of Dort**, arranged in heads of doctrine answering the five articles. Remonstrant ministers were deposed, and the political crisis surrounding the synod saw the statesman Johan van Oldenbarnevelt executed and Hugo Grotius imprisoned. The Canons define election thus:

> Election is God's unchangeable purpose by which he did the following: Before the foundation of the world, by sheer grace, according to the free good pleasure of his will, God chose in Christ to salvation a definite number of particular people out of the entire human race.

sections.heading: The "Five Points of Calvinism"
sections.body:
The Canons' replies are now often summarised by the English acronym **TULIP**, a mnemonic that appears only in the twentieth century:

- **T**otal depravity: sin affects every part of human nature, leaving people unable to turn to God unaided.
- **U**nconditional election: God's choice is not based on foreseen faith or works (Ephesians 1:4-5; Romans 9:16).
- **L**imited atonement, often called *definite* or *particular redemption*: Christ died to secure the salvation of the elect, while his death is sufficient for all.
- **I**rresistible grace, or *effectual calling*: God's regenerating grace infallibly brings the elect to faith (John 6:44).
- **P**erseverance of the saints: those truly regenerated will not finally fall away.

Many Reformed theologians caution that TULIP oversimplifies the Canons and the broader Reformed tradition.

sections.heading: Wesleyan Arminianism
sections.body: In eighteenth-century England, **John Wesley** (1703-1791) became the most influential Arminian. He named his periodical *The Arminian Magazine* (1778). Wesley affirmed total depravity but taught that God gives **prevenient grace** to all people, restoring enough freedom to accept or reject the gospel (John 1:9; Titus 2:11). He stressed universal atonement, assurance, and Christian perfection. His fellow evangelist George Whitefield, by contrast, held Calvinist views, and Methodism divided into Wesleyan and Calvinistic branches. Through Methodism, the Holiness movement, and Pentecostalism, Arminian theology came to shape a large share of global Protestantism.

sections.heading: Molinism
sections.body: A third option arose in Catholic theology. The Spanish Jesuit **Luis de Molina** (1535-1600), in his *Concordia* (1588), proposed that God has **middle knowledge** (*scientia media*): knowledge of what any free creature *would* freely do in any possible circumstance. By choosing which circumstances to actualise, God providentially ensures his purposes while creatures remain libertarianly free. Dominican theologians such as Domingo Báñez opposed Molina, and in 1607 Pope Paul V allowed both schools to teach while forbidding them to call each other heretics. Some Protestant philosophers, such as William Lane Craig, have revived Molinism in recent decades.

sections.heading: Points of Agreement and Difference
sections.body: Calvinists and Arminians agree that salvation is by grace through faith, that fallen humanity cannot save itself, and that Christ's death is the only ground of forgiveness. They differ on whether election is conditional or unconditional, on the intended scope of the atonement, on whether grace can be finally resisted, and on whether true believers can fall away. Each side accuses the other of difficulties: Arminians charge that Calvinism makes God the author of reprobation, while Calvinists charge that Arminianism makes the human decision decisive.

keyTerms.definition: The 1610 statement in five articles by followers of Arminius setting out conditional election, universal atonement, and resistible grace.
The doctrinal rulings of the Synod of Dort (1618-19), which rejected the Remonstrance and defined Reformed teaching on predestination and grace.
The Reformed teaching that God chose the elect according to his good pleasure, not on the basis of foreseen faith or works.
Also 'limited atonement' or 'particular redemption': the view that Christ died to secure the salvation of the elect specifically.
In Wesleyan theology, grace given to all people that restores the ability to accept or reject the gospel.
In Molinism, God's knowledge of what free creatures would freely do in any possible circumstances (scientia media).

topics.title: Sanctification and Theosis
topics.subtitle: Soteriology
topics.summary: How believers grow in holiness: Protestant sanctification, Wesleyan Christian perfection, Catholic infused grace, and the Orthodox vision of theosis or deification.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: Salvation in Christian teaching is not only forgiveness but transformation. Scripture calls believers to "be holy, for I am holy" (1 Peter 1:16) and speaks of being "transformed into the same image from glory to glory" (2 Corinthians 3:18) and even of becoming "partakers of the divine nature" (2 Peter 1:4). Traditions describe this transformation with different vocabularies: **sanctification** (from Latin *sanctus*, "holy") in the West, **theosis** or deification in the East.

sections.heading: Protestant Sanctification
sections.body:
Lutheran and Reformed theology distinguishes sanctification sharply from justification. Justification is a once-for-all verdict; sanctification is the lifelong renewal that inevitably follows. The Westminster Shorter Catechism (1647) defines it:

> Sanctification is the work of God's free grace, whereby we are renewed in the whole man after the image of God, and are enabled more and more to die unto sin, and live unto righteousness.

Reformed theologians describe sanctification as both *definitive* (believers are already set apart in union with Christ, 1 Corinthians 6:11) and *progressive* (they grow throughout life). The Holy Spirit is its author, yet the believer actively cooperates: "work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you" (Philippians 2:12-13). The Westminster Confession holds that sanctification remains imperfect in this life. Lutherans often describe sanctification as daily returning to one's baptism, dying to sin and rising to new life, and stress that the Christian remains *simul iustus et peccator*.

sections.heading: Wesleyan Christian Perfection
sections.body: **John Wesley** taught that believers may, in this life, receive **entire sanctification** or **Christian perfection**. In *A Plain Account of Christian Perfection* (1766) he explained this not as freedom from ignorance, mistakes, or temptation, but as a heart filled with "perfect love" for God and neighbour, so that voluntary transgression of known law no longer rules (Matthew 22:37-40; 1 John 4:18). Wesley held that this could be received by faith as a gift, often as a distinct experience after conversion, while growth continues afterward. The nineteenth-century **Holiness movement** made entire sanctification central, and it in turn influenced early Pentecostalism. Reformed critics argue that the doctrine underestimates indwelling sin (Romans 7; 1 John 1:8).

sections.heading: Catholic Teaching: Infused Grace
sections.body: In Catholic theology, sanctification is not a separate stage following justification; justification itself includes inner renewal. The Council of Trent taught that in justification God infuses **sanctifying grace** together with the theological virtues of faith, hope, and charity. This grace is a real, created quality of the soul that makes a person pleasing to God and a sharer in divine life. Trent added that the justified "increase in that justice which they have received through the grace of Christ" through cooperation with grace in good works and the sacraments, especially the Eucharist. Good works done in grace are truly meritorious, though such merit is itself God's gift. For those who die in grace but are not fully purified, **purgatory** completes the process.

sections.heading: Orthodox Theosis
sections.body:
Eastern Orthodox theology describes salvation as **theosis**, deification: union with God that transforms the whole person. The theme runs through the Greek Fathers. Irenaeus spoke of the Son becoming what we are so that we might become what he is. **Athanasius** of Alexandria wrote in *On the Incarnation*:

> For He was made man that we might be made God.

Maximus the Confessor described the goal of history as the deification of creation in Christ. In the fourteenth century **Gregory Palamas** defended the hesychast monks' prayer and the distinction between God's **essence**, which remains utterly unknowable and unshareable, and his **energies**, in which creatures truly participate. Human beings become "god" by grace and participation, never by nature: the creature-Creator distinction is not erased. Many Fathers distinguished the *image* of God (given in creation) from the *likeness* (to be attained through grace and freedom), reading Genesis 1:26. Theosis is pursued through the sacraments, prayer, ascetic struggle, and love, in **synergy** between divine grace and human freedom.

sections.heading: Points of Agreement and Difference
sections.body: All traditions agree that God intends to make his people holy and that holiness is the work of grace calling forth human response. Protestants keep sanctification distinct from the ground of justification; Catholics see inner renewal as part of justification itself; Orthodox frame the entire Christian life as participation in God. Recent scholarship has noticed convergences: the Finnish school of Luther research led by Tuomo Mannermaa argued that Luther himself spoke of union with Christ in terms close to theosis, and Wesley drew deeply on Eastern Fathers such as Macarius.

keyTerms.definition: The process (and, in some accounts, also the definitive act) by which God makes believers holy, renewing them after the image of God.
Wesley's teaching that believers may in this life be filled with perfect love so that conscious, voluntary sin no longer rules them; also called Christian perfection.
In Catholic theology, the infused, abiding gift of grace that renews the soul and makes it a sharer in divine life.
Deification: the Orthodox doctrine that human beings are united with God and share his life by grace, not by nature.
Gregory Palamas's teaching that God's essence is unknowable and unshareable, while his uncreated energies can be truly participated in.

topics.title: Assurance and Perseverance
topics.subtitle: Soteriology
topics.summary: Can believers know they are saved, and can they lose salvation? Reformed perseverance, Arminian conditional security, Lutheran and Catholic teaching, and the warning passages of Hebrews.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: Two related questions occupy this topic. **Perseverance** asks whether a truly regenerate believer can finally fall away from salvation. **Assurance** asks whether, and how, a believer can know that he or she is in a state of grace. Pastoral concerns run high here: one side worries about presumption and moral laxity, the other about anxiety and works-righteousness.

sections.heading: The Reformed Doctrine of Perseverance
sections.body:
Reformed theology teaches the **perseverance of the saints**. The fifth head of the Canons of Dort (1619) affirms that God preserves those he has regenerated so that, though they may fall into grievous sins, they will not totally or finally lose faith. The Westminster Confession (1646), chapter 17, states:

> They, whom God hath accepted in His Beloved, effectually called, and sanctified by His Spirit, can neither totally nor finally fall away from the state of grace, but shall certainly persevere therein to the end, and be eternally saved.

The ground of perseverance is not the believer's strength but God's unchangeable election, Christ's intercession, and the Spirit's indwelling (John 10:27-29; Romans 8:30; Philippians 1:6). Reformed theologians insist that perseverance includes continuing in faith and holiness; it is not a guarantee for those who profess faith and then live without it. A popular Baptist form, often called "eternal security" or "once saved, always saved," sometimes places less stress on persevering holiness.

On **assurance**, the Westminster Confession, chapter 18, teaches that believers may attain an "infallible assurance of faith," based on God's promises, the inward evidence of grace, and the testimony of the Spirit (Romans 8:16; 1 John 5:13). Yet such assurance "doth not so belong to the essence of faith" that a true believer may not wait long and struggle before attaining it.

sections.heading: Arminian Conditional Security
sections.body: The Remonstrance of 1610 left the possibility of falling away as a question requiring further study. Later Remonstrants, and above all **John Wesley**, taught that true believers *can* fall away by turning from Christ. This is often called **conditional security**: the believer is secure as long as he or she remains in faith. Arminians stress that no external power can snatch believers from Christ's hand, but that a person may freely abandon faith. Wesleyans generally hold that the fallen can be restored through repentance. **Reformed Arminians** (such as many Free Will Baptists) hold that apostasy occurs only through a decisive rejection of faith and is irremediable, citing Hebrews 6:4-6. Wesley also emphasised the **witness of the Spirit** as a present assurance of adoption.

sections.heading: Lutheran Teaching
sections.body: Lutherans affirm that salvation rests entirely on God's grace, and they offer believers strong assurance through the promise of the gospel, baptism, and the Lord's Supper. Yet the Augsburg Confession (1530), Article XII, condemns those "who deny that those once justified can lose the Holy Ghost." Lutherans thus teach both robust assurance grounded in God's promises and the real possibility of falling from grace through unbelief.

sections.heading: Catholic Teaching
sections.body: The Council of Trent (1547) taught that the justified can lose grace through mortal sin and recover it through the sacrament of penance. It rejected the claim that a believer is bound to believe with the certainty of faith that he is among the predestined, and its Canon 16 condemned anyone who claims to know "of an absolute and infallible certainty" that he will have "that great gift of perseverance unto the end," unless by special revelation. Perseverance is a gift to be hoped and prayed for. Catholics thus speak of a confident **hope** grounded in God's mercy rather than certainty about one's final state.

sections.heading: Orthodox Perspectives
sections.body: Orthodox theology views salvation as a lifelong journey of theosis. One can turn away from God, and the faithful are urged to watchfulness and repentance, while trusting in God's love. The Orthodox generally avoid systematic doctrines of assurance or perseverance.

sections.heading: The Warning Passages in Hebrews
sections.body:
The Letter to the Hebrews contains several severe warnings against drifting away and apostasy, including Hebrews 2:1-4, Hebrews 6:4-6, and Hebrews 10:26-31. Interpreters read them in different ways:

1. **Loss of salvation**: true believers are warned that they may really fall away (common in Arminian and Lutheran readings).
2. **False professors**: the passages describe those who participated in the church without being regenerate (a common Reformed reading).
3. **Means of perseverance**: the warnings are the very means God uses to keep the elect persevering, so they are real but will be heeded by true believers.
4. **Hypothetical**: the passages describe what *would* happen if falling away were possible, without implying that it occurs.

sections.heading: Points of Agreement and Difference
sections.body: All traditions agree that believers must continue in faith, that God's grace is the source of perseverance, and that warnings and promises in Scripture should both be taken seriously. They differ on whether true believers can finally fall away, and on whether believers may have certainty or only confident hope about their final salvation.

keyTerms.definition: The Reformed teaching that those truly regenerated by God will not totally or finally fall away but will be preserved to the end.
A believer's confidence that he or she is truly in a state of grace and will be saved.
The Arminian view that believers are secure in Christ as long as they continue in faith, but may fall away by abandoning it.
A decisive falling away from or rejection of the Christian faith by one who had professed it.
The inner testimony of the Holy Spirit that one is a child of God (Romans 8:16), emphasised by John Wesley.
