topics.title: The Early Church and the Roman Empire
topics.subtitle: Church History
topics.summary: From Pentecost to Theodosius: the spread of the faith, waves of persecution, the martyrs, Constantine and the Edict of Milan.

sections.heading: A movement spreads
sections.body: From Jerusalem the gospel spread along the roads and sea-lanes of the Roman Empire (Acts 1:8). By the end of the first century there were churches across Asia Minor, Greece, Italy, Egypt and Syria. Sociologist Rodney Stark estimated a growth rate of around 40 percent per decade, reaching perhaps six million Christians by AD 300.

sections.heading: Why were Christians persecuted?
sections.body: Christians refused to offer sacrifice to the gods or to the emperor's genius, which Romans saw as **atheism** and a threat to the *pax deorum* — the peace between Rome and the gods on which prosperity depended. Rumours circulated of "Thyestean feasts" (cannibalism, a distortion of the Eucharist) and "Oedipean intercourse" (incest, a distortion of "brother" and "sister" language).

sections.heading: The main phases
sections.body:
- **Nero (AD 64)** blamed Christians for the great fire of Rome; Tacitus (*Annals* 15.44) describes Christians burned as torches. Tradition places the martyrdoms of **Peter** and **Paul** in this period.
- **Pliny and Trajan (c. 112)**: Pliny, governor of Bithynia, asked the emperor how to handle Christians. Trajan replied that they were not to be sought out, but if accused and refusing to recant, punished. Pliny's letter records that Christians met before dawn and sang "a hymn to Christ as to a god."
- **Local persecutions** in the second century produced famous martyrs: **Ignatius of Antioch** (c. 110), **Polycarp of Smyrna** (c. 155), the martyrs of Lyons (177), and **Perpetua and Felicity** at Carthage (203), whose prison diary is among the earliest writings by a Christian woman.
- **Decius (250)** issued the first empire-wide order requiring sacrifice, certified by a *libellus*. Many lapsed; the question of whether to readmit the **lapsed** divided the church (Cyprian of Carthage; the Novatianist schism).
- **Valerian (257-258)** targeted clergy; **Cyprian** was beheaded in 258.
- **Diocletian's "Great Persecution" (303-311)** ordered churches destroyed, Scriptures burned and clergy arrested. Galerius issued an edict of toleration in 311.

Tertullian wrote that "the blood of Christians is seed" (*Apology* 50, paraphrasing "semen est sanguis Christianorum").

sections.heading: Constantine
sections.body: Before the **Battle of the Milvian Bridge (312)**, Constantine reportedly saw a sign — the Chi-Rho or a cross — with the words "In this sign, conquer." In **313** he and Licinius agreed the **Edict of Milan**, granting religious freedom to Christians and restoring confiscated property. Constantine favoured the church, built basilicas, summoned the **Council of Nicaea (325)** and founded **Constantinople (330)**; he was baptised near his death in 337.

sections.heading: Toward a Christian empire
sections.body: Julian "the Apostate" (361-363) tried to revive paganism. In **380** Theodosius I issued the **Edict of Thessalonica**, declaring Nicene Christianity the faith of the empire, and in 391-392 banned pagan sacrifice. The church moved from persecuted minority to imperial religion — a transition whose blessings and dangers historians still debate.

topics.title: The Seven Ecumenical Councils
topics.subtitle: Church History
topics.summary: Nicaea to Nicaea II (325–787): what each council decided, why it met, and which churches receive them.

sections.heading: What is an ecumenical council?
sections.body: An **ecumenical** (from *oikoumenē*, "the inhabited world") council is a gathering of bishops from across the whole church whose decisions are received as authoritative for all. Its precedent is the **Council of Jerusalem** in Acts 15. Seven councils between 325 and 787 are recognised by both the Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic churches.

sections.heading: The seven councils
sections.body:
1. **Nicaea I (325)** — summoned by Constantine against **Arius**. Confessed the Son *homoousios* (of one substance) with the Father, produced the original Nicene Creed, and set principles for the date of Easter.
2. **Constantinople I (381)** — summoned by Theodosius I. Affirmed the divinity of the **Holy Spirit** against the Pneumatomachi, condemned **Apollinarianism**, and produced the expanded **Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed** used in liturgy today.
3. **Ephesus (431)** — condemned **Nestorius** and affirmed Mary as **Theotokos** ("God-bearer"); led by **Cyril of Alexandria**. It also condemned Pelagianism.
4. **Chalcedon (451)** — condemned **Eutyches** and defined Christ as one person "in two natures"; Pope **Leo I's Tome** was acclaimed ("Peter has spoken through Leo").
5. **Constantinople II (553)** — under Justinian, condemned the "**Three Chapters**" (writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia and others seen as Nestorian), seeking reconciliation with miaphysites.
6. **Constantinople III (680-681)** — condemned **monothelitism**, affirming Christ's two wills, divine and human.
7. **Nicaea II (787)** — ended the first phase of **iconoclasm**, affirming that icons may be venerated (*proskynesis*), while worship (*latreia*) belongs to God alone; honour paid to the image passes to its prototype.

sections.heading: Reception
sections.body:
- **Eastern Orthodox** — the seven councils (some Orthodox also esteem councils of 879-880 and 1341-1351).
- **Roman Catholic** — the seven, plus fourteen later Western councils, for twenty-one in total, through **Vatican II (1962-1965)**.
- **Oriental Orthodox** (Coptic, Ethiopian, Armenian, Syriac, Eritrean, Malankara) — the first **three**, rejecting Chalcedon.
- **Assyrian Church of the East** — the first **two**.
- **Protestants** — generally receive the doctrinal decisions of the first four as faithful to Scripture (Luther and Calvin both did so) and value later councils variously; Lutherans and Anglicans have often been most explicit, while Reformed churches have typically rejected Nicaea II's teaching on images.

sections.heading: Why the councils matter
sections.body: The councils rarely invented new beliefs; they defined boundaries around the apostolic faith when it was disputed. Their creeds and definitions remain the common grammar of Christian teaching on the Trinity and Christ — and their fractures, especially after Chalcedon, remain visible in the map of world Christianity.

keyTerms.definition: A council of bishops from the whole church whose decisions are received as universally binding.
The movement (726-787, 815-843) that rejected and destroyed religious images.

Worship due to God alone, distinguished at Nicaea II from veneration of icons.
Churches that accept the first three councils but not Chalcedon.

# The Seven Ecumenical Councils

*A Paideia study chart.*

| # | Council | Date | Emperor | Controversy | Key figures | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Nicaea I | 325 | Constantine I | Arianism | Alexander of Alexandria, Athanasius, Arius | Son is *homoousios* with the Father; Nicene Creed; Easter dating |
| 2 | Constantinople I | 381 | Theodosius I | Pneumatomachi; Apollinarianism | Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa | Divinity of the Holy Spirit; expanded Nicene Creed |
| 3 | Ephesus | 431 | Theodosius II | Nestorianism | Cyril of Alexandria, Nestorius | Mary is *Theotokos*; Nestorius deposed |
| 4 | Chalcedon | 451 | Marcian | Eutychianism | Leo I (Tome), Eutyches, Dioscorus | Christ one person in two natures |
| 5 | Constantinople II | 553 | Justinian I | The Three Chapters | Justinian, Pope Vigilius | Condemnation of writings deemed Nestorian |
| 6 | Constantinople III | 680-681 | Constantine IV | Monothelitism | Maximus the Confessor (posthumously vindicated) | Christ has two wills and two energies |
| 7 | Nicaea II | 787 | Constantine VI & Empress Irene | Iconoclasm | Patriarch Tarasius; John of Damascus (earlier) | Icons may be venerated; worship belongs to God alone |

## Which churches receive which councils?

| Tradition | Councils received |
| --- | --- |
| Assyrian Church of the East | 1-2 |
| Oriental Orthodox (Coptic, Ethiopian, Armenian, Syriac…) | 1-3 |
| Eastern Orthodox | 1-7 |
| Roman Catholic | 1-7 plus 14 later councils (21 total) |
| Lutheran and Anglican | Doctrinal decisions of 1-4 commonly affirmed; later ones variously |
| Reformed | Doctrinal decisions of 1-4 (sometimes 1-6) affirmed; Nicaea II's teaching on images rejected |

## Memory aid

**N-C-E-C, C-C-N** — **N**icaea, **C**onstantinople, **E**phesus, **C**halcedon, **C**onstantinople, **C**onstantinople, **N**icaea: the series begins and ends at Nicaea, with Constantinople three times.

sections.heading: Reading companion
sections.content:
# The Nicene Creed

*Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed (Council of Constantinople, 381), in the traditional English of the 1662 Book of Common Prayer (public domain).*

> I believe in one God the Father Almighty,
> Maker of heaven and earth,
> And of all things visible and invisible:
>
> And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God,
> Begotten of his Father before all worlds,
> God of God, Light of Light,
> Very God of very God,
> Begotten, not made,
> Being of one substance with the Father,
> By whom all things were made:
> Who for us men, and for our salvation came down from heaven,
> And was incarnate by the Holy Ghost of the Virgin Mary,
> And was made man,
> And was crucified also for us under Pontius Pilate.
> He suffered and was buried,
> And the third day he rose again according to the Scriptures,
> And ascended into heaven,
> And sitteth on the right hand of the Father.
> And he shall come again with glory to judge both the quick and the dead:
> Whose kingdom shall have no end.
>
> And I believe in the Holy Ghost,
> The Lord and giver of life,
> Who proceedeth from the Father and the Son,
> Who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified,
> Who spake by the Prophets.
> And I believe one Catholick and Apostolick Church.
> I acknowledge one Baptism for the remission of sins.
> And I look for the Resurrection of the dead,
> And the life of the world to come. Amen.

## Study notes

**Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381).** The Council of Nicaea produced a shorter creed ending "And in the Holy Spirit," followed by anathemas against Arian teaching. The text above is the expanded form associated with the Council of Constantinople (381), which added the fuller article on the Holy Spirit and the closing articles on the Church, baptism and the resurrection. It is the most widely used creed in Christendom — recited by Orthodox, Catholics, Anglicans, Lutherans and many other Protestants.

**"Of one substance with the Father."** This renders the Greek *homoousios*, the key Nicene term affirming that the Son is fully God, of the same being as the Father, against Arius's claim that the Son was a creature.

**"Begotten, not made."** The Son's eternal generation from the Father is distinguished from creation. He is not the first creature; he is the one "by whom all things were made."

**"And the Son" (Filioque).** The words *and the Son* were not part of the Greek creed of 381, which says simply that the Spirit "proceeds from the Father." The phrase entered Latin use in Spain (Third Council of Toledo, 589), spread in the Frankish church, and was adopted in the Roman liturgy in 1014. It remains a point of dispute between Eastern and Western Christians; some Western churches now omit it in ecumenical settings.

**"Catholick."** "Catholic" means universal — the whole Church throughout the world — not only the Roman Catholic Church.

**"The quick and the dead."** "Quick" is older English for "living."

## Questions for reflection

1. Which phrases in the creed answer the Arian controversy directly?
2. Why might the creed devote so much more space to the Son than to the Father?
3. What does it mean to confess the creed *together* in worship rather than merely assent to it individually?

topics.title: Monasticism and the Medieval Church
topics.subtitle: Church History
topics.summary: Desert monks, Benedict's Rule, Cluny and Gregorian reform, scholasticism, the friars, Lateran IV, and the crises of Avignon and the Western Schism.

sections.heading: The desert and the monastery
sections.body:
When martyrdom ceased, many sought a "white martyrdom" of self-denial. **Anthony of Egypt** (c. 251-356) withdrew to the desert; Athanasius's *Life of Anthony* made him famous. **Pachomius** (c. 292-348) organised communal (*cenobitic*) monasteries, and **Basil of Caesarea** wrote rules that still shape Eastern monasticism. The sayings of the desert fathers and mothers (*Apophthegmata Patrum*) remain spiritual classics.

In the West, **Benedict of Nursia** wrote his *Rule* (c. 530) at Monte Cassino: a balanced life of prayer and work (*ora et labora*), stability, obedience and the daily round of the Divine Office. Monasteries preserved learning, copied manuscripts and evangelised Europe — Irish monks such as **Columba** and **Columbanus** and the Anglo-Saxon **Boniface** were great missionaries.

sections.heading: Popes, emperors and reform
sections.body: **Gregory the Great** (pope 590-604) sent Augustine of Canterbury to England (597). In 800 **Charlemagne** was crowned emperor by Pope Leo III. The monastery of **Cluny** (founded 910) became the centre of a reform movement free from lay control. **Pope Gregory VII** (1073-1085) championed clerical celibacy and the church's independence, leading to the **Investiture Controversy** with Emperor Henry IV (famously humbled at Canossa, 1077), settled by the **Concordat of Worms (1122)**. The **Crusades** began in 1095 at Urban II's call.

sections.heading: The schools and the friars
sections.body:
**Scholasticism** applied logic to theology in the cathedral schools and new universities (Paris, Oxford, Bologna). **Anselm** described theology as "faith seeking understanding"; **Peter Lombard**'s *Sentences* (c. 1150) became the standard textbook; **Thomas Aquinas** (1225-1274) produced the *Summa Theologiae*, integrating Aristotle with Christian doctrine. **Bernard of Clairvaux** led the reformed Cistercians and was a great preacher of mystical love.

The thirteenth century saw the **mendicant** (begging) orders: **Francis of Assisi** (Franciscans, approved 1209/1223) embraced radical poverty, and **Dominic** founded the Order of Preachers (1216) to combat heresy through learned preaching.

The **Fourth Lateran Council (1215)**, under Innocent III, used the term **transubstantiation**, required annual confession and Easter communion, and is often seen as the high-water mark of the medieval papacy.

sections.heading: Crisis and calls for reform
sections.body:
- **The Avignon Papacy (1309-1377)**: popes resided in Avignon under French influence.
- **The Western Schism (1378-1417)**: two, and later three, rival popes claimed office.
- **The Council of Constance (1414-1418)** ended the schism by electing Martin V, but also condemned and burned **Jan Hus** (1415) and condemned the teachings of **John Wycliffe**.
- **Conciliarism** argued that general councils hold authority over popes.

Mystics such as **Julian of Norwich** and **Catherine of Siena**, the *Devotio Moderna* (Thomas à Kempis, *The Imitation of Christ*), and Christian humanists such as **Erasmus** nourished piety and set the stage for the reformations of the sixteenth century.

keyTerms.definition: Communal monastic life, organised by Pachomius, as distinct from hermits (eremitic).
The sixth-century guide to monastic life that shaped Western monasticism.
The medieval method of theology using logical analysis, questions and disputation.
Religious orders living by begging, such as the Franciscans and Dominicans.
The 11th-12th century conflict over whether rulers or popes appointed bishops.
The view that a general council holds authority over the pope.

topics.title: The Great Schism of 1054
topics.subtitle: Church History
topics.summary: How the Greek East and Latin West drifted apart: the Filioque, papal primacy, the events of 1054, the Fourth Crusade, and modern rapprochement.

sections.heading: A slow estrangement
sections.body:
The division between the Eastern (Orthodox) and Western (Catholic) churches is conventionally dated to **1054**, but it was the outcome of centuries of drift:

- **Language and culture**: the West increasingly knew only Latin, the East Greek; theological traditions developed separately.
- **Political division**: after the fall of the Western empire (476), and especially after Charlemagne's coronation (800), East and West had rival emperors.
- **Ecclesiology**: Rome increasingly claimed universal jurisdiction for the pope as successor of Peter; the East understood the bishop of Rome as "first among equals" within a **pentarchy** of patriarchates (Rome, Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem) and gave final authority to ecumenical councils.
- **The Filioque**: the Western addition to the creed that the Spirit proceeds from the Father "and the Son," made without an ecumenical council. Easterners objected both to the unilateral change and, for many, to its theology.
- **Practice**: leavened (East) versus unleavened (West) bread in the Eucharist, clerical celibacy, fasting rules.

The **Photian Schism** (863-867) under Patriarch Photius of Constantinople and Pope Nicholas I was an important rehearsal of these disputes.

sections.heading: The events of 1054
sections.body: Tensions arose when Patriarch **Michael Cerularius** closed Latin churches in Constantinople. Pope Leo IX sent legates led by **Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida**. On **16 July 1054** Humbert laid a bull of excommunication on the altar of **Hagia Sophia**; Cerularius and his synod responded by anathematising the legates. Ironically, Pope Leo had died in April, so the legates' authority was questionable — and the excommunications were personal, not of whole churches.

sections.heading: Sealing the division
sections.body: What made the break decisive was not 1054 alone but later events, above all the **Fourth Crusade's sack of Constantinople (1204)** by Western crusaders, who installed a Latin patriarch. Attempts at reunion at the **Second Council of Lyons (1274)** and the **Council of Ferrara-Florence (1438-1439)** were agreed by delegates but rejected by the Eastern faithful and clergy. Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in **1453**.

sections.heading: Toward reconciliation
sections.body: On **7 December 1965**, Pope **Paul VI** and Ecumenical Patriarch **Athenagoras I** issued a joint declaration lifting the mutual excommunications of 1054 and "consigning them to oblivion." Their 1964 meeting in Jerusalem was the first between a pope and an ecumenical patriarch in over five centuries. Theological dialogue continues through the Joint International Commission (from 1980), with questions of papal primacy remaining the central issue.

keyTerms.definition: The five ancient patriarchates: Rome, Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem.
The Western creedal addition that the Spirit proceeds "and from the Son."
The authority of the bishop of Rome; disputed whether it is one of honour or universal jurisdiction.
Dispute over the use of unleavened bread (azymes) in the Eucharist.
The 9th-century conflict between Patriarch Photius and Pope Nicholas I.

topics.title: The Protestant and Catholic Reformations
topics.subtitle: Church History
topics.summary: Luther, Zwingli, Calvin, the Radical and English Reformations, the five solas, and the Catholic response at Trent.

sections.heading: Luther and the beginning
sections.body:
On **31 October 1517**, the Augustinian friar and Wittenberg professor **Martin Luther** circulated his **Ninety-Five Theses** against the sale of **indulgences**, promoted locally by Johann Tetzel to fund the rebuilding of St Peter's Basilica. Printing spread the theses across Germany within weeks. Luther's "tower experience" — his discovery that the "righteousness of God" in Romans 1:17 is the righteousness God gives by faith — reshaped his theology.

Key moments: the **Leipzig Debate** with Johann Eck (1519); three great treatises of **1520** (*To the Christian Nobility*, *The Babylonian Captivity of the Church*, *The Freedom of a Christian*); the papal bull *Exsurge Domine*, which Luther burned; and the **Diet of Worms (1521)**, where he refused to recant: "My conscience is captive to the Word of God." Hidden at the Wartburg Castle, he translated the New Testament into German (1522). The **Augsburg Confession (1530)**, drafted by **Philip Melanchthon**, became Lutheranism's defining statement.

sections.heading: The Reformed tradition
sections.body: In Zurich, **Ulrich Zwingli** began expository preaching through Matthew in 1519. He and Luther agreed on fourteen of fifteen articles at the **Marburg Colloquy (1529)** but split over Christ's presence in the Lord's Supper. **John Calvin** published the *Institutes of the Christian Religion* (1536; final edition 1559) and led the church in **Geneva**. Reformed churches spread to France (the Huguenots), the Netherlands, Hungary, and — through **John Knox** — Scotland.

sections.heading: The Radical Reformation
sections.body: **Anabaptists** ("re-baptisers") such as Conrad Grebel and Felix Manz (Zurich, 1525) insisted on **believer's baptism**, a gathered church of committed disciples and, for most, non-violence and separation from the state. The **Schleitheim Confession (1527)** summarised their convictions. Persecuted by Catholics and Protestants alike, they survive in Mennonite (after **Menno Simons**), Amish and Hutterite communities.

sections.heading: The English Reformation
sections.body: **Henry VIII** broke with Rome over his annulment; the **Act of Supremacy (1534)** declared the king Supreme Head of the Church of England. Under Edward VI, **Thomas Cranmer** produced the **Book of Common Prayer** (1549, 1552). After Mary I's Catholic restoration, **Elizabeth I** (1558) established a settlement later defined by the **Thirty-Nine Articles** (1563/1571).

sections.heading: The solas
sections.body: Later summaries describe Reformation convictions with the "five solas": ***sola Scriptura*** (Scripture alone), ***sola gratia*** (grace alone), ***sola fide*** (faith alone), ***solus Christus*** (Christ alone) and ***soli Deo gloria*** (glory to God alone). The Reformers also stressed the **priesthood of all believers** and vernacular worship.

sections.heading: The Catholic Reformation
sections.body: Catholic renewal had begun before Luther and accelerated in response. The **Society of Jesus**, founded by **Ignatius of Loyola** and approved in **1540**, became a force in education and mission (Francis Xavier in Asia). The **Council of Trent (1545-1563)** affirmed Scripture *and* Tradition, the Vulgate, the deuterocanonical books, seven sacraments and the Catholic doctrine of justification, while reforming abuses: seminaries for clergy, residence of bishops and an end to the sale of indulgences.

sections.heading: Settlements
sections.body: The **Peace of Augsburg (1555)** allowed each German prince to choose Lutheranism or Catholicism (*cuius regio, eius religio*). After the devastating **Thirty Years' War**, the **Peace of Westphalia (1648)** extended recognition to the Reformed.

Radical reformers who practised believer's baptism and separation from the state.
The teaching that all Christians have direct access to God through Christ (1 Peter 2:9).
"Whose realm, his religion" — the principle of the Peace of Augsburg (1555).

topics.title: The Old Testament Canon
topics.subtitle: Bible History
topics.summary: The Tanakh and its three divisions, the Septuagint, the deuterocanonical books, and why Protestant, Catholic and Orthodox Old Testaments differ.

sections.heading: The Hebrew Bible
sections.body:
The Jewish Scriptures are known as the **Tanakh**, an acronym of their three divisions:

- **Torah** (Law): Genesis to Deuteronomy, the five books of Moses.
- **Nevi'im** (Prophets): the Former Prophets (Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings) and the Latter Prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and the Twelve).
- **Ketuvim** (Writings): Psalms, Proverbs, Job, the five scrolls (Song of Songs, Ruth, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes, Esther), Daniel, Ezra-Nehemiah and Chronicles.

Counted the Jewish way, there are **24 books**; the same content divided differently yields the **39 books** of the Protestant Old Testament (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles and Ezra-Nehemiah are split in two; the Twelve Minor Prophets are counted individually). **Josephus** (*Against Apion* 1.8, c. AD 95) speaks of 22 books, probably the same collection counted differently. Jesus' reference to "the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms" (Luke 24:44) reflects the threefold shape.

The older theory that a "**Council of Jamnia**" (Yavneh, c. AD 90) closed the Jewish canon is now widely doubted; the discussions at Yavneh concerned whether particular books (such as Ecclesiastes and Song of Songs) "defile the hands," and many scholars think the collection was largely settled earlier.

sections.heading: The Septuagint
sections.body: The **Septuagint** (LXX, "seventy") is the Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures made in Alexandria beginning in the 3rd century BC. The legendary *Letter of Aristeas* describes 72 translators producing the Torah for Ptolemy II. The LXX was the Bible of most early Christians and is frequently quoted in the New Testament. Its manuscripts include additional books and additions not found in the Hebrew Bible.

sections.heading: The deuterocanonical books
sections.body:
The Catholic Old Testament includes seven books beyond the Hebrew canon — **Tobit, Judith, 1 and 2 Maccabees, Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) and Baruch** — plus additions to **Esther** and **Daniel** (Susanna, Bel and the Dragon, the Prayer of Azariah). Catholics call these **deuterocanonical** ("second canon"); Protestants traditionally call them the **Apocrypha**.

- The early church used these books widely. **Augustine** and the councils of **Hippo (393)** and **Carthage (397)** included them; **Jerome** preferred the Hebrew canon (the "*Hebraica veritas*"), though he translated some of them.
- **Luther** gathered them into a separate section between the Testaments in his 1534 Bible, describing them as "useful and good to read" but not equal to Scripture. Article VI of the Church of England's **Thirty-Nine Articles** says the Church reads them "for example of life and instruction of manners," but not to establish doctrine.
- The **Council of Trent (1546)** defined them as fully canonical.
- **Eastern Orthodox** Bibles include a somewhat larger set (e.g. 1 Esdras, 3 Maccabees, the Prayer of Manasseh, Psalm 151), following the Septuagint; the **Ethiopian Orthodox** canon is broader still, including **1 Enoch** and **Jubilees**.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: Canon debates touch the doctrine of Scripture's authority and how the church recognises it. Protestants generally argue that the church *recognised* rather than *created* the canon; Catholics and Orthodox emphasise the church's role in discerning and defining it.

topics.title: The New Testament Canon
topics.subtitle: Bible History
topics.summary: How the 27 books were recognised: the criteria of canonicity, Marcion, the Muratorian Fragment, Eusebius, Athanasius's Festal Letter of 367, and the disputed books.

sections.heading: From apostolic writings to canon
sections.body: The earliest Christians' Scripture was the Old Testament. Alongside it they treasured the **words of Jesus** and the **apostolic writings**. Already within the New Testament, Paul's letters were collected and compared with "the other Scriptures" (2 Peter 3:15-16), and 1 Timothy 5:18 quotes a saying found in Luke 10:7 alongside Deuteronomy as "Scripture."

sections.heading: Criteria of canonicity
sections.body:
The church did not use a formal checklist, but its discussions reveal several recurring criteria:

1. **Apostolicity** — written by an apostle or a close associate (Mark with Peter, Luke with Paul).
2. **Orthodoxy** — consistent with the **rule of faith** (*regula fidei*) received in the churches.
3. **Catholicity** — widely used and accepted across the churches, not just locally.
4. **Antiquity** — dating from the apostolic period.

Many add the **self-authenticating** character of Scripture — the church *recognising* the voice of its Lord rather than conferring authority.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.body:
- **Marcion** of Sinope (c. 140) rejected the Old Testament and accepted only an edited Luke and ten letters of Paul. His challenge helped push the church to define its own collection.
- **Irenaeus** (c. 180) insisted there are exactly **four Gospels**, no more and no fewer — the fourfold Gospel was already established.
- The **Muratorian Fragment**, a Latin list traditionally dated to the late 2nd century (some scholars argue for the 4th), names most of the New Testament books and rejects others, such as the *Shepherd of Hermas* for public reading.
- **Eusebius** (*Church History* 3.25, early 4th century) sorted books into **recognised** (*homologoumena*), **disputed** (*antilegomena* — James, Jude, 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John), and **spurious**; he noted that opinion on Revelation was divided.
- **Athanasius**, bishop of Alexandria, in his **39th Festal Letter (367)**, lists exactly the **27 books** of today's New Testament, calling them "the springs of salvation."
- The North African councils of **Hippo (393)** and **Carthage (397)** endorsed the same 27 books.

sections.heading: The disputed books
sections.body: The books whose acceptance took longest — **Hebrews, James, 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude and Revelation** — were debated over authorship, circulation or content. Revelation was long hesitated over in parts of the East. The Syriac Peshitta originally omitted 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude and Revelation. Luther, much later, placed Hebrews, James, Jude and Revelation at the end of his New Testament, questioning their apostolic status, though he did not remove them.

sections.heading: Gospels outside the canon
sections.body: Works such as the **Gospel of Thomas** (a sayings collection discovered at **Nag Hammadi** in Egypt in 1945) and other "Gnostic gospels" are generally dated later than the canonical Gospels and were never widely accepted by the churches. They are valuable for understanding the diversity of second-century movements, but the four canonical Gospels were the ones read across the churches from early on.

sections.heading: Reading companion
sections.content:
# Early New Testament Canon Lists Compared

*A Paideia study chart. ✓ = included / accepted; ? = disputed or uncertain; ✗ = absent or rejected; — = not mentioned.*

| Book | Marcion (c. 140) | Muratorian Fragment (trad. late 2nd c.) | Eusebius, *Church History* 3.25 (c. 325) | Athanasius, *Festal Letter* 39 (367) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Matthew | ✗ | ✓ (text lost at start) | ✓ | ✓ |
| Mark | ✗ | ✓ (text lost at start) | ✓ | ✓ |
| Luke | ✓ (edited) | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| John | ✗ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Acts | ✗ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Pauline letters (13) | 10 (no Pastorals) | ✓ 13 | ✓ | ✓ |
| Hebrews | ✗ | — | ✓ (with Paul; notes doubts in Rome) | ✓ |
| James | ✗ | — | ? disputed | ✓ |
| 1 Peter | ✗ | — | ✓ | ✓ |
| 2 Peter | ✗ | — | ? disputed | ✓ |
| 1 John | ✗ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| 2 John | ✗ | ✓ (two letters of John) | ? disputed | ✓ |
| 3 John | ✗ | ? | ? disputed | ✓ |
| Jude | ✗ | ✓ | ? disputed | ✓ |
| Revelation | ✗ | ✓ | ? "recognised" by some, "spurious" by others | ✓ |
| Apocalypse of Peter | ✗ | ? (some refuse to read it in church) | ✗ spurious | ✗ |
| Shepherd of Hermas | ✗ | ✗ for public reading (may be read privately) | ✗ spurious | ✗ (useful for catechumens) |
| Wisdom of Solomon | ✗ | ✓ (listed oddly among NT books) | — | ✗ (useful for catechumens) |

## Observations

1. **The core was settled early.** The four Gospels, Acts and the letters of Paul were widely recognised by the late second century.
2. **The debated books** were mainly the shorter general letters, Hebrews and Revelation.
3. **Athanasius** gives the first list exactly matching the 27-book New Testament, and distinguishes canonical books from those "read" for instruction (e.g. the Didache, Shepherd of Hermas) and from "apocryphal" works to be avoided.
4. The councils of **Hippo (393)** and **Carthage (397)** confirmed the 27 books for the Latin West.

*Note: The Muratorian Fragment's date is debated; a minority of scholars place it in the fourth century.*

topics.title: Manuscripts and Textual Criticism
topics.subtitle: Bible History
topics.summary: From the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Masoretic Text to Codex Sinaiticus and the papyri: how scholars reconstruct the original text of Scripture.

sections.heading: Why textual criticism?
sections.body: No original manuscript (*autograph*) of any biblical book survives. What we have are copies — thousands of them — which differ in small ways. **Textual criticism** is the discipline of comparing these copies to reconstruct the earliest attainable text. It is practised on all ancient literature; the Bible is simply its richest field.

sections.heading: The Old Testament text
sections.body:
- The **Masoretic Text** (MT) is the authoritative Hebrew text of rabbinic Judaism, carefully preserved by scribes called **Masoretes** (c. 6th-10th centuries AD) who added vowel points, accents and marginal notes (*masorah*). Its finest witnesses are the **Aleppo Codex** (c. 930) and the **Leningrad Codex** (1008), the oldest complete manuscript of the Hebrew Bible.
- The **Dead Sea Scrolls**, discovered from **1947** onward in caves near **Qumran**, include fragments of every book of the Hebrew Bible except Esther, dating from around the 3rd century BC to the 1st century AD. The **Great Isaiah Scroll** (1QIsa^a, c. 125 BC) is complete and remarkably close to the Masoretic text over a thousand years older, though the scrolls also reveal textual diversity in the Second Temple period.
- Other witnesses include the **Septuagint**, the **Samaritan Pentateuch** and the Aramaic **Targums**.

sections.heading: The New Testament text
sections.body:
The New Testament is by far the best-attested work of antiquity: about **5,800** Greek manuscripts (catalogued by the Institute for New Testament Textual Research in Münster), plus thousands of early translations (Latin, Syriac, Coptic) and quotations in the church fathers.

- **Papyri**: the earliest witnesses. **P52** (John Rylands Library), a fragment of John 18, is commonly dated to the first half of the 2nd century (some scholars prefer later). The **Chester Beatty** and **Bodmer** papyri (P45, P46, P66, P75) preserve substantial portions from around AD 200.
- **Great codices** of the 4th century: **Codex Vaticanus** (B) and **Codex Sinaiticus** (א), the latter found by **Constantin von Tischendorf** at **St Catherine's Monastery**, Mount Sinai (1844 and 1859). Sinaiticus contains the oldest complete New Testament.
- Later witnesses include **Codex Alexandrinus** (5th c.) and the many medieval **Byzantine** minuscules.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.body:
Critics weigh **external evidence** (date, quality and geographical spread of manuscripts; scholars group manuscripts into Alexandrian, Western and Byzantine text-types) and **internal evidence** (what an author was likely to write and what a scribe was likely to change). Classic rules of thumb include:

- *Lectio difficilior potior* — the **harder reading** is generally preferred, since scribes tended to smooth difficulties.
- *Lectio brevior* — the **shorter reading** is often preferred, since scribes more often added than omitted (applied with caution).
- Prefer the reading that **best explains the origin of the others**.

sections.heading: From Erasmus to today
sections.body: **Erasmus** published the first printed Greek New Testament in **1516**, based on a handful of late manuscripts; later editions became known as the **Textus Receptus**, the basis of the KJV. **Westcott and Hort** (1881) championed the older Alexandrian manuscripts. Most modern translations use the **Nestle-Aland** (NA28) / **UBS** critical text, while some scholars defend the Byzantine or Majority Text.

sections.heading: Notable variants
sections.body:
- The longer ending of **Mark (16:9-20)** is absent from Sinaiticus and Vaticanus.
- The story of the woman caught in adultery (**John 7:53-8:11**) is absent from the earliest manuscripts.
- The **Comma Johanneum** (a Trinitarian addition in 1 John 5:7-8) appears in no Greek manuscript before the late medieval period.

Scholars across the theological spectrum agree that the great majority of variants are minor — spelling, word order, or obvious slips — and that no central Christian doctrine depends on a disputed reading.

keyTerms.definition: The original manuscript of a biblical book as written by its author.
The authoritative Hebrew text preserved by medieval Jewish scribes (Masoretes).
A book with pages, which early Christians adopted in preference to scrolls.
The "received text" of the printed Greek New Testament descended from Erasmus.
The principle that the more difficult reading is more likely original.
A family of manuscripts sharing characteristic readings (Alexandrian, Western, Byzantine).

topics.title: The History of Bible Translation
topics.subtitle: Bible History
topics.summary: From the Septuagint and Jerome's Vulgate to Wycliffe, Luther, Tyndale and the King James Version, and the philosophies behind modern translations.

sections.heading: Ancient translations
sections.body: The Bible has been a translated book from the start. The **Septuagint** rendered the Hebrew Scriptures into Greek in Alexandria (3rd-2nd centuries BC). As the church spread, translations followed: the **Old Latin** (*Vetus Latina*), the **Syriac** versions culminating in the **Peshitta**, the **Coptic** versions of Egypt, and the **Gothic** Bible of **Ulfilas** (4th century), who reportedly invented an alphabet for the purpose.

sections.heading: Jerome's Vulgate
sections.body: In **382** Pope **Damasus** commissioned **Jerome** to revise the Latin Gospels. Jerome went further, translating most of the Old Testament directly from Hebrew — controversially, since many preferred the Septuagint — working in Bethlehem until around 405. His version became the **Vulgate** ("common" version), the Bible of the Western church for a thousand years; the Council of Trent declared it authentic for public use (1546).

sections.heading: Medieval and early English
sections.body: Portions of Scripture were rendered into Old English (e.g. glosses on the **Lindisfarne Gospels**, and the West Saxon Gospels). The **Wycliffe Bible** (1380s), associated with John Wycliffe and his followers, translated the whole Bible into English from the Latin Vulgate; the Constitutions of Oxford (1409) prohibited unauthorised English translations.

sections.heading: Print and Reformation
sections.body:
The **Gutenberg Bible** (c. 1455), a Latin Vulgate, was the first major book printed with movable type in Europe. Printing transformed the spread of Scripture:

- **Martin Luther** published his German New Testament in **1522** (the "September Testament"), translated from Erasmus's Greek, and the complete Bible in **1534**. Its language shaped modern German.
- **William Tyndale** produced the first printed English New Testament translated from Greek (**1526**, Worms), and portions of the Old Testament from Hebrew. Smuggled into England, it was banned and burned. Tyndale was strangled and burned near Brussels in **1536**, reportedly praying, "Lord, open the King of England's eyes." Much of his phrasing survives in later versions.
- **Miles Coverdale** produced the first complete printed English Bible (**1535**). The **Great Bible** (1539) was authorised for reading in churches.
- The **Geneva Bible** (1560), produced by English exiles, was the first English Bible with verse numbers throughout and copious study notes; it was the Bible of Shakespeare and the Pilgrims.

sections.heading: The King James Version
sections.body: Proposed at the **Hampton Court Conference (1604)** and published in **1611**, the **Authorised (King James) Version** was translated by about fifty scholars in six companies, revising earlier English versions (above all Tyndale's) against the Hebrew and Greek. It became the dominant English Bible for over three centuries. The Catholic **Douay-Rheims** (NT 1582, OT 1609-1610) was translated from the Vulgate.

sections.heading: Modern translations
sections.body:
The discovery of older manuscripts and advances in Hebrew and Greek prompted revisions: the **Revised Version** (1881-1885), the **Revised Standard Version** (1952), and many others — **NASB** (1971), **NIV** (1978), **NRSV** (1989), **ESV** (2001), **CSB** (2017). Translations sit on a spectrum:

- **Formal equivalence** ("word-for-word"): NASB, ESV, NKJV.
- **Dynamic / functional equivalence** ("thought-for-thought"), a theory articulated by **Eugene Nida**: NIV (mediating), NLT, GNT.
- **Paraphrase**: The Message.

Today, through organisations such as the United Bible Societies and Wycliffe Bible Translators, the complete Bible is available in over 700 languages, and at least some portion of Scripture in several thousand more.

sections.content:
# Bible Translation Timeline

*A Paideia study chart.*

| Date | Translation | Language | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 3rd-2nd c. BC | Septuagint (LXX) | Greek | Hebrew Scriptures translated in Alexandria; the Bible of the early church |
| 2nd c. AD | Old Latin (*Vetus Latina*) | Latin | Various early Latin versions |
| 2nd-5th c. | Syriac versions; Peshitta | Syriac | Standard Bible of Syriac-speaking churches |
| 3rd-4th c. | Coptic versions | Coptic | For Egyptian Christians |
| 4th c. | Gothic Bible | Gothic | Ulfilas, "apostle to the Goths" |
| 382-c. 405 | Vulgate | Latin | Jerome, commissioned by Pope Damasus |
| 5th c. | Armenian Bible | Armenian | Mesrop Mashtots created the Armenian alphabet |
| 10th c. | Lindisfarne Gospels gloss | Old English | Interlinear gloss by Aldred on an 8th-century Latin manuscript |
| 1380s | Wycliffe Bible | Middle English | From the Vulgate; hand-copied |
| c. 1455 | Gutenberg Bible | Latin | First major book printed with movable type in Europe |
| 1516 | *Novum Instrumentum* | Greek/Latin | Erasmus's printed Greek New Testament |
| 1522 / 1534 | Luther Bible | German | September Testament (1522); complete Bible (1534) |
| 1526 | Tyndale New Testament | English | First printed English NT from Greek |
| 1535 | Coverdale Bible | English | First complete printed English Bible |
| 1539 | Great Bible | English | First authorised English Bible for churches |
| 1560 | Geneva Bible | English | Verse numbers throughout; study notes |
| 1582 / 1609-10 | Douay-Rheims | English | Catholic translation from the Vulgate |
| 1611 | King James (Authorised) Version | English | Dominant English Bible for 300+ years |
| 1881-1885 | Revised Version | English | Used older Greek manuscripts (Westcott-Hort) |
| 1952 | Revised Standard Version | English | Revision in the KJV tradition |
| 1971 | New American Standard Bible | English | Formal equivalence |
| 1978 | New International Version | English | Mediating approach |
| 1989 | New Revised Standard Version | English | Ecumenical scholarly standard |
| 2001 | English Standard Version | English | "Essentially literal" revision of the RSV |

## Translation philosophies

- **Formal equivalence** (word-for-word): seeks to preserve wording and structure — NASB, ESV, NKJV.
- **Functional / dynamic equivalence** (thought-for-thought): seeks equivalent meaning and effect — NLT, GNT; NIV and CSB aim between the two.
- **Paraphrase**: freely restates for readability — The Message, The Living Bible.

topics.title: The Apostolic Fathers
topics.subtitle: Church Fathers
topics.summary: Clement of Rome, Ignatius of Antioch, Polycarp, the Didache, Hermas and others: the earliest Christian writings outside the New Testament.

sections.heading: Who are the Apostolic Fathers?
sections.body: The **Apostolic Fathers** are a collection of the earliest Christian writings outside the New Testament, dating roughly from **AD 70 to 150**. Some of their authors were believed to have known the apostles personally. The label was coined in the seventeenth century; the collection usually includes:

sections.heading: Clement of Rome — *1 Clement* (c. 96)
sections.body: A letter from the church at Rome to the church at Corinth, which had deposed its presbyters. It appeals for humility, order and peace, and is the earliest Christian document outside the New Testament for which we have a fairly secure date. It refers to the martyrdoms of Peter and Paul and was read publicly in some churches.

sections.heading: Ignatius of Antioch — seven letters (c. 107-110)
sections.body:
Bishop of Antioch, Ignatius wrote seven letters while being taken under guard to Rome for martyrdom: to the Ephesians, Magnesians, Trallians, Romans, Philadelphians, Smyrnaeans, and to Polycarp. Key themes:

- **Unity under the bishop**, presbyters and deacons — the earliest clear witness to the threefold ministry with a single bishop in each city.
- Strong opposition to **Docetism**: Christ "truly" was born, suffered and rose.
- The Eucharist as "the medicine of immortality" (*Ephesians* 20).
- The first known use of the phrase **"the catholic church"**: "Wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the catholic church" (*Smyrnaeans* 8).
- A passionate longing for martyrdom: "I am the wheat of God, and am ground by the teeth of wild beasts" (*Romans* 4).

sections.heading: Polycarp of Smyrna
sections.body: A disciple of the apostle John according to Irenaeus, Polycarp wrote a *Letter to the Philippians*. The **Martyrdom of Polycarp** (c. 155-160), the earliest account of a Christian martyrdom outside the New Testament, records his reply when urged to curse Christ: "Eighty and six years have I served him, and he never did me any injury: how then can I blaspheme my King and my Saviour?"

sections.heading: The Didache
sections.body: The *Didache*, or *Teaching of the Twelve Apostles*, is a short church manual (late 1st or early 2nd century). It opens with the "**Two Ways**" — the way of life and the way of death — then gives instructions on baptism (preferably in "living," running water, by pouring if necessary), fasting on Wednesdays and Fridays, praying the Lord's Prayer three times daily, the Eucharist, and testing travelling prophets. Lost for centuries, it was rediscovered by **Philotheos Bryennios** in a Constantinople manuscript in 1873 and published in 1883.

sections.heading: Others
sections.body:
- **The Shepherd of Hermas** (Rome, 2nd century): visions, mandates and parables about repentance after baptism; immensely popular, it appears in Codex Sinaiticus.
- **The Epistle of Barnabas**: a strongly allegorical reading of the Old Testament.
- **The Epistle to Diognetus**: an elegant apology describing Christians as "the soul of the world" — they live in their own countries "as sojourners."
- **Papias of Hierapolis**: known through fragments, including traditions about the origins of Mark and Matthew.

sections.heading: Why read them?
sections.body: They show the church in the generation after the apostles: its worship, organisation, moral seriousness and devotion to Christ — and the continuity and development between the New Testament and later Christianity.

keyTerms.definition: The earliest post-New Testament Christian writers, c. 70-150.

Church order with a single bishop over each city's church, attested by Ignatius.
The moral teaching contrasting the way of life with the way of death (Didache 1-6).

sections.heading: Reading companion
sections.content:
# A Reading Plan for the Church Fathers

*A twelve-week introductory plan. All texts are available free online in the public-domain Ante-Nicene and Nicene & Post-Nicene Fathers translations (for example at newadvent.org/fathers or ccel.org).*

| Week | Reading | Questions to consider |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | *The Didache* (whole) | What does early Christian worship and ethics look like? What surprises you? |
| 2 | Ignatius, *Letters to the Smyrnaeans and Romans* | Why does Ignatius emphasise the bishop? How does he view martyrdom? |
| 3 | *The Martyrdom of Polycarp*; *Epistle to Diognetus* | How do these texts describe Christians' relation to the world? |
| 4 | Justin Martyr, *First Apology* 1-12, 61-67 | How does Justin answer pagan accusations? What does Sunday worship involve? |
| 5 | Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* Book III, chs. 1-5, 18 | What are Irenaeus's tests for true teaching? What is recapitulation? |
| 6 | Tertullian, *Prescription Against Heretics* 1-20 | Why should heretics not be allowed to argue from Scripture, according to Tertullian? |
| 7 | Athanasius, *On the Incarnation* 1-25 | Why did the Word become flesh? What is the "divine dilemma"? |
| 8 | Athanasius, *On the Incarnation* 26-57 | How does the resurrection prove Christ's victory over death? |
| 9 | Gregory of Nazianzus, *Third Theological Oration* (Oration 29) | How does Gregory answer objections to the Son's divinity? |
| 10 | Basil, *On the Holy Spirit* 1-9, 16-18 | How does worship shape doctrine for Basil? |
| 11 | Augustine, *Confessions* Books I-IV | How does Augustine understand sin, desire and grace? |
| 12 | Augustine, *Confessions* Books VII-IX | What brings Augustine to conversion? What role do friends and books play? |

## Tips for reading the Fathers

1. **Read them in context.** Ask what controversy or pastoral need occasioned the work.
2. **Expect strangeness.** Their interpretive methods and cultural assumptions differ from ours — that is part of their value.
3. **Notice their love of Scripture.** The Fathers were above all biblical expositors.
4. **Read devotionally as well as critically.** Many wrote to form souls, not just to inform minds.
5. **Keep a notebook** of memorable lines and questions.

> "It is a good rule, after reading a new book, never to allow yourself another new one till you have read an old one in between."
> — C. S. Lewis, introduction to Athanasius, *On the Incarnation* (1944)

topics.title: The Apologists, Irenaeus and the Early Theologians
topics.subtitle: Church Fathers
topics.summary: Justin Martyr, Irenaeus of Lyons, Tertullian and Origen: defending the faith against pagan critics and Gnostic teachers in the second and third centuries.

sections.heading: Defending the faith
sections.body: In the second century Christians faced two challenges: hostility from Roman society and the rise of **Gnosticism**, which offered secret knowledge (*gnōsis*), despised the material world and distinguished the true God from an inferior creator. The writers who responded laid the foundations of Christian theology.

sections.heading: Justin Martyr (c. 100-165)
sections.body: A philosopher from Samaria who searched through Stoicism, Aristotelianism and Platonism before converting, Justin taught in Rome. His *First Apology* (c. 155), addressed to Emperor **Antoninus Pius**, refutes charges against Christians and gives the earliest detailed description of **Sunday worship** — readings from "the memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets," a sermon, prayers and the Eucharist (*1 Apology* 65-67). In the *Dialogue with Trypho* he argues with a Jew from the Old Testament. Justin taught that the divine **Logos** had sown "seeds" of truth (*logos spermatikos*) among all peoples, so philosophers like Socrates had glimpsed truth. He was beheaded in Rome around 165.

sections.heading: Irenaeus of Lyons (c. 130-202)
sections.body:
Raised in Smyrna, where he heard **Polycarp**, Irenaeus became bishop of Lyons after the persecution of 177. His great work **Against Heresies** (c. 180) exposes Gnostic systems, especially that of Valentinus, and answers them with:

- The **rule of faith** — the apostolic faith confessed in all the churches.
- **Apostolic succession** — the public succession of bishops in churches founded by the apostles, especially Rome, as a guarantee against secret traditions.
- The **fourfold Gospel**.
- The goodness of creation and the unity of the Old and New Testaments under one God.
- **Recapitulation**: Christ sums up and restores humanity, undoing Adam's disobedience.

His famous line: "The glory of God is a living man; and the life of man consists in beholding God" (*Against Heresies* 4.20.7).

sections.heading: Tertullian (c. 155-220)
sections.body: A brilliant, combative writer from **Carthage**, Tertullian was the first major Christian author in **Latin** and coined much of Western theological vocabulary, including *trinitas* and the formula of one *substantia* in three *personae* (*Against Praxeas*). He asked, "What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?" (*Prescription Against Heretics* 7), wary of philosophy's influence. Later in life he joined the rigorist **Montanist** movement.

sections.heading: Origen (c. 185-254)
sections.body: Head of the catechetical school in **Alexandria**, later at Caesarea, Origen was the most prolific scholar of the early church. He produced the **Hexapla**, a six-column comparison of Hebrew and Greek versions of the Old Testament; wrote commentaries and homilies on most of Scripture; composed *On First Principles*, the first systematic theology; and *Against Celsus*, a reply to a pagan critic. Tortured in the Decian persecution, he died soon after. Some speculative ideas associated with him (the pre-existence of souls, universal restoration — *apokatastasis*) were condemned in the sixth century, but his influence on biblical interpretation and spirituality was immense.

sections.heading: Also notable
sections.body: **Athenagoras** (*Plea for the Christians*, c. 177); **Theophilus of Antioch** (first to use *trias* for God, c. 180); **Clement of Alexandria** (c. 150-215), who presented Christ as the true teacher (*Paidagogos*) and Christian faith as the true philosophy; and **Hippolytus of Rome**, author of *Refutation of All Heresies*.

topics.title: Athanasius and the Cappadocian Fathers
topics.subtitle: Church Fathers
topics.summary: The champions of Nicene orthodoxy: Athanasius "against the world," Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa, and John Chrysostom.

sections.heading: Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296-373)
sections.body:
As a young deacon, Athanasius attended the **Council of Nicaea (325)** with his bishop Alexander, and in 328 became bishop of Alexandria himself. For the next 45 years he defended the Nicene faith against Arianism, enduring **five exiles** under four emperors. His steadfastness gave rise to the phrase ***Athanasius contra mundum*** — "Athanasius against the world."

His works include:

- ***On the Incarnation of the Word*** — a classic explanation of why the Word became flesh: to restore the image of God in humanity and to defeat death. "He was made man that we might be made God" (§54). C. S. Lewis wrote a famous introduction to a 1944 English translation.
- ***Orations Against the Arians*** — arguing that if the Son were a creature, he could not save us or unite us to God.
- ***Life of Antony*** — the biography that spread the monastic ideal across the empire.
- His **39th Festal Letter (367)**, listing the 27 books of the New Testament.

sections.heading: The Cappadocian Fathers
sections.body:
Three theologians from **Cappadocia** (central Anatolia) carried the Nicene cause to victory at the **Council of Constantinople (381)**:

### Basil of Caesarea, "the Great" (c. 330-379)
Bishop of Caesarea, organiser and pastor. His ***On the Holy Spirit*** defended the Spirit's full divinity, arguing from the church's worship ("glory to the Father *with* the Son *together with* the Holy Spirit"). He founded the **Basiliad**, a complex including a hospital and poorhouse, and wrote monastic rules that still guide Eastern monasticism. The *Divine Liturgy of St Basil* bears his name.

### Gregory of Nazianzus, "the Theologian" (c. 329-390)
Basil's close friend and a gifted orator. His ***Five Theological Orations*** (preached in Constantinople, 380) are classic statements of Trinitarian doctrine. He briefly presided over the Council of Constantinople. Against Apollinarius he wrote: "**What is not assumed is not healed**" (*Letter 101*). He is one of only three saints the Orthodox Church calls "the Theologian," along with John the Evangelist and Symeon the New Theologian.

### Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335-395)
Basil's younger brother, the most philosophical of the three. His works include *Against Eunomius*, the *Catechetical Oration*, and the *Life of Moses*, which presents the spiritual life as **epektasis** — endless progress into the infinite God. His *Life of Macrina* honours their elder sister, a monastic leader he called "the Teacher."

sections.heading: John Chrysostom (c. 347-407)
sections.body: Called ***Chrysostomos*** ("golden-mouthed") for his preaching, John was a priest in Antioch and from 398 archbishop of **Constantinople**. His expository homilies on Genesis, Matthew, John, Romans and other books are models of Antiochene interpretation and moral application. His denunciation of luxury among the powerful led to his deposition and death in exile. The most commonly celebrated liturgy of the Orthodox Church is the **Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom**.

sections.heading: In the West
sections.body: Contemporaries in the West included **Hilary of Poitiers** ("the Athanasius of the West," *On the Trinity*), **Ambrose of Milan** (bishop, hymn-writer, and mentor of Augustine), and **Jerome** (translator of the Vulgate).

topics.title: Augustine of Hippo
topics.subtitle: Church Fathers
topics.summary: The life, conversion and theology of the most influential Western father: the Confessions, the City of God, and the Manichaean, Donatist and Pelagian controversies.

sections.heading: Life
sections.body:
**Aurelius Augustinus** was born in **354** at **Thagaste** in Roman North Africa (modern Souk Ahras, Algeria), to a pagan father, Patricius, and a devout Christian mother, **Monica**. A brilliant student of rhetoric, he studied at Carthage, where reading Cicero's *Hortensius* awakened a love of wisdom. For nine years he followed **Manichaeism**, a dualistic religion teaching that good and evil are two eternal principles. He lived with a concubine, with whom he had a son, Adeodatus.

He taught rhetoric in Carthage, Rome and then **Milan** (384), where the sermons of Bishop **Ambrose** showed him how to read the Old Testament spiritually, and Neoplatonist writings helped him conceive of God as immaterial and of evil as privation. In a Milan garden in **386**, in anguish over his inability to give up his old life, he heard a child's voice chanting "***Tolle, lege***" ("Take up and read"). Opening Paul's letters at random, he read Romans 13:13-14 — "put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh" — and was converted. Ambrose baptised him at Easter **387**. Monica died soon after at Ostia.

Returning to Africa, he was ordained priest in Hippo Regius (391) and became bishop of **Hippo** around **395/396**, serving until his death on **28 August 430**, while the Vandals besieged the city.

sections.heading: Major works
sections.body:
- ***Confessions*** (c. 397-400): an autobiographical prayer to God — the first great spiritual autobiography of the West — opening with "You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you" (1.1).
- ***The City of God*** (413-426): written after Alaric's **sack of Rome (410)** to answer pagans who blamed Christianity. It contrasts two cities formed by two loves — the earthly city, by love of self to the contempt of God; the heavenly city, by love of God to the contempt of self (14.28).
- ***On the Trinity***: a profound meditation including psychological analogies (memory, understanding and will) for the triune God.
- ***On Christian Doctrine***: a handbook of biblical interpretation and Christian teaching.

sections.heading: Controversies
sections.body:
- **Manichaeism**: Augustine defended the goodness of creation, free will and evil as privation of good.
- **Donatism**: the North African Donatists held that sacraments administered by clergy who had lapsed in persecution were invalid, and that the true church was a pure body. Augustine argued that sacraments are valid because Christ is their true minister, and that the church is a "mixed body" of wheat and tares until the judgment.
- **Pelagianism**: against Pelagius and Julian of Eclanum, Augustine taught original sin, the bondage of the will and the necessity of grace, earning him the title **Doctor of Grace**.

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.body: Augustine shaped Western theology more than any other writer after the apostles. Both medieval Catholicism and the Protestant Reformers claimed him: Calvin quoted him constantly, and Luther was an Augustinian friar. His thought on grace, the church, the sacraments, time, memory, just war and the two cities continues to provoke reflection.

keyTerms.definition: "Take up and read" — the child's chant that prompted Augustine's conversion in 386.

sections.content:
# Augustine's *Confessions* — Study Guide

*A Paideia study aid. The* Confessions *(c. 397-400) is addressed to God throughout: a confession of sin, of faith, and of praise.*

## Outline

| Book | Period / theme | Key moments |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | Infancy and boyhood | "Our heart is restless until it rests in you"; learning to speak; hatred of Greek; schoolboy sins |
| II | Adolescence (age 16) | The theft of pears — sin loved for its own sake |
| III | Student in Carthage | Love of love; reading Cicero's *Hortensius*; joining the Manichees; Monica's tears and dream |
| IV | Teacher of rhetoric (19-28) | Death of a close friend; grief and the transience of creatures |
| V | Carthage to Rome to Milan | Disappointment with the Manichee bishop Faustus; meeting Ambrose |
| VI | Milan | Ambrose's preaching; Augustine's ambition; dismissal of his concubine |
| VII | Intellectual conversion | Neoplatonist books; God as immaterial; evil as privation of good |
| VIII | Conversion of the will | Stories of Victorinus and Antony; the garden; "Tolle, lege"; Romans 13:13-14 |
| IX | Baptism and Monica's death | Retreat at Cassiciacum; baptism by Ambrose (387); the vision at Ostia; Monica dies |
| X | Memory | Augustine's present state; the vast "fields and palaces" of memory; "Late have I loved you" |
| XI | Time | "What then is time? If no one asks me, I know"; time as a distension of the soul |
| XII | Creation | "Heaven and earth" in Genesis 1:1; legitimate diversity of interpretation |
| XIII | Creation and the Church | Allegorical reading of Genesis 1 as the life of the Church; the Sabbath rest of God |

## Discussion questions

1. Why does Augustine write his life story as a prayer addressed to God?
2. What does the pear-tree episode (Book II) reveal about the nature of sin?
3. In Book VII Augustine's intellectual problems are resolved, but he is not yet converted. Why not? What is the difference between knowing the truth and loving it?
4. What role do other people — Monica, Ambrose, Alypius, Ponticianus — play in his conversion?
5. Why do you think Augustine continues after Book IX with reflections on memory, time and creation?
6. "Late have I loved you, Beauty so ancient and so new" (X.27). How does Augustine describe his relationship to created beauty and to God?

## Further reading

- Peter Brown, *Augustine of Hippo: A Biography* (1967; rev. 2000)
- Henry Chadwick's translation of the *Confessions* (Oxford World's Classics, 1991)
- The public-domain translations by E. B. Pusey (1838) and J. G. Pilkington (1876) are freely available online.

topics.title: The Desert and the Later Fathers
topics.subtitle: Church Fathers
topics.summary: The wisdom of the desert, John Cassian, Gregory the Great, Maximus the Confessor and John of Damascus — the close of the patristic age.

sections.heading: The wisdom of the desert
sections.body:
From the late third century, thousands of men and women withdrew to the deserts of Egypt, Palestine and Syria. Their sayings, gathered in the ***Apophthegmata Patrum*** (*Sayings of the Desert Fathers*), are short, often startling stories of humility, prayer, repentance and love. A brother asked Abba Moses for a word; he replied, "Go, sit in your cell, and your cell will teach you everything." Desert mothers (*ammas*) such as **Syncletica** and **Sarah** are also remembered.

**Evagrius Ponticus** (345-399) systematised desert spirituality, analysing eight "evil thoughts" (*logismoi*) — the ancestor of the later list of seven deadly sins — and teaching on pure prayer.

sections.heading: John Cassian (c. 360-435)
sections.body: Cassian lived among the Egyptian monks and then founded monasteries near **Marseilles**. His ***Institutes*** and ***Conferences*** carried desert wisdom to the West and were prescribed reading in Benedict's Rule. His view that the beginning of faith could arise from human will was later associated with "Semi-Pelagianism."

sections.heading: Gregory the Great (c. 540-604)
sections.body: A Roman aristocrat turned monk, Gregory became pope in **590** during plague, famine and Lombard invasion. He organised relief, negotiated with invaders and sent **Augustine of Canterbury** to evangelise England (597). His *Pastoral Rule* shaped the ideal of the bishop for centuries; his *Moralia on Job* and *Dialogues* were medieval favourites. He styled himself "servant of the servants of God." With Ambrose, Augustine and Jerome he is one of the four original **Latin Doctors of the Church**.

sections.heading: Maximus the Confessor (c. 580-662)
sections.body: The greatest Byzantine theologian of the seventh century, Maximus defended the **two wills** of Christ against monothelitism, insisting that Christ's human will, freely submitting to the Father in Gethsemane, is the place where our wills are healed. For refusing to accept the imperial position he was tried, his tongue cut out and his right hand cut off; he died in exile. The **Third Council of Constantinople (680-681)** vindicated his teaching. He wrote profoundly on theosis and the cosmic Christ.

sections.heading: John of Damascus (c. 675-749)
sections.body: A monk of the monastery of Mar Saba near Jerusalem, living under Muslim rule, John wrote ***The Fount of Knowledge***, whose third part, ***An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith***, summarised Greek patristic theology and later influenced Peter Lombard and Aquinas. During the first iconoclast controversy he wrote ***Three Treatises on the Divine Images***, arguing that since the invisible God became visible in Christ, he may be depicted: "I do not worship matter, I worship the Creator of matter who became matter for my sake." He is often regarded as the last of the Greek Fathers, as **Isidore of Seville** (d. 636) is often regarded as the last of the Latin Fathers.

sections.heading: The patristic legacy
sections.body: The "age of the Fathers" is usually said to end in the seventh or eighth century. Their authority remains central for the Orthodox and Catholic churches, and the Reformers appealed to them constantly — Calvin and Luther argued that the Fathers supported reform. The twentieth-century ***ressourcement*** movement (Henri de Lubac, Jean Daniélou) and evangelical interest in "paleo-orthodoxy" (Thomas Oden) both sought renewal by returning to the Fathers.

topics.title: The Millennium and Approaches to Revelation
topics.subtitle: Eschatology
topics.summary: Amillennialism, postmillennialism, historic and dispensational premillennialism; and preterist, historicist, futurist and idealist readings of Revelation.

sections.heading: The text
sections.body: Revelation 20:1-6 describes Satan bound for "a thousand years" (Latin *mille anni*, hence **millennium**) while martyrs "came to life and reigned with Christ." How to interpret this passage — and how it relates to Christ's return — has produced four main positions. All affirm the bodily return of Christ, the resurrection and the final judgment; they differ on sequence and the nature of the thousand years.

sections.heading: The four main views
sections.body:
### Historic premillennialism
Christ returns **before** (*pre-*) a literal earthly reign of a thousand years, after which comes the final rebellion, judgment and new creation. This was the view of several early fathers, including **Papias**, **Justin Martyr** and **Irenaeus** (sometimes called *chiliasm*, from Greek *chilioi*, "thousand"). In the twentieth century it was championed by **George Eldon Ladd**. The church passes through the tribulation.

### Dispensational premillennialism
Developed by **John Nelson Darby** (1800-1882) of the Plymouth Brethren and popularised by the **Scofield Reference Bible** (1909) and later by Dallas Theological Seminary and popular books. It keeps a sharp distinction between **Israel and the church**, and typically teaches a **pre-tribulation rapture**: Christ comes secretly for the church, followed by a seven-year tribulation, then his visible return to establish a millennial kingdom centred on a restored Israel. *Progressive dispensationalism* (from the 1980s) softened some distinctions.

### Amillennialism
The thousand years is **symbolic** of the present age between Christ's first and second comings: Satan is "bound" in that the gospel goes to the nations (Matthew 12:29), and the saints reign with Christ — the departed in heaven and believers spiritually. **Augustine** (*City of God* XX) gave this view classic expression, and it became the majority position of Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and much Reformed theology. Some prefer the label "realised millennialism."

### Postmillennialism
Christ returns **after** (*post-*) a long period — the millennium, literal or symbolic — in which the gospel triumphs widely and the world is largely Christianised. It was influential among Puritans and in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries (**Jonathan Edwards**, **Charles Hodge**, **B. B. Warfield**), fuelling missionary and reform movements. It waned after the World Wars but persists, e.g. in some Reformed circles.

sections.heading: Approaches to Revelation
sections.body:
Interpreters also differ on *when* Revelation's visions are fulfilled:

- **Preterist**: mostly fulfilled in the first century — the fall of Jerusalem (70) or the Roman Empire. *Partial* preterists still expect Christ's future return; *full* preterism, which places the second coming in the past, is rejected as unorthodox by virtually all churches.
- **Historicist**: a panorama of church history from the first century to the end; popular among the Reformers, who often identified the papacy with Antichrist.
- **Futurist**: most of the book (chapters 4-22) describes events still to come; typical of dispensationalism.
- **Idealist (spiritual)**: the visions portray timeless principles of the conflict between God and evil, not specific events.

Many contemporary scholars adopt an **eclectic** approach — the visions addressed first-century churches, depict recurring patterns, and culminate in a still-future consummation.

sections.heading: A note on charity
sections.body: These views have been held by faithful Christians in every age. The Apostles' and Nicene Creeds confess only that Christ "will come again to judge the living and the dead," leaving the millennium undefined.

sections.heading: Reading companion
sections.content:
# Millennial Views at a Glance

*A Paideia study chart.*

| | Historic premillennialism | Dispensational premillennialism | Amillennialism | Postmillennialism |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Timing of Christ's return** | Before the millennium | Before the millennium (rapture before the tribulation, in most versions) | At the end of the present age (the "millennium") | After the millennium |
| **Nature of the millennium** | Literal earthly reign of Christ | Literal 1,000-year reign centred on national Israel | Symbolic of the present church age | A future golden age of gospel success (literal or symbolic length) |
| **Israel and the church** | One people of God | Distinct programmes for Israel and the church | One people of God | One people of God |
| **Tribulation** | Church passes through it | Church raptured before it (usually) | Tribulation characterises the whole age | Largely past or diminishing |
| **Outlook on history** | Mixed; decline before the end | Pessimistic for the world, hopeful for the saved | Mixed: growth of both wheat and tares | Optimistic |
| **Early / classic proponents** | Papias, Justin Martyr, Irenaeus | J. N. Darby; C. I. Scofield | Augustine; most Reformers | Puritans; Jonathan Edwards |
| **Modern proponents** | George Eldon Ladd | Charles Ryrie; John Walvoord | Anthony Hoekema; G. K. Beale | B. B. Warfield; Loraine Boettner |
| **Key emphasis** | Revelation 20 read sequentially after chapter 19 | Literal fulfilment of Old Testament promises to Israel | Revelation 20 recapitulates the church age | The Great Commission will succeed (Matthew 13:31-33) |

## Shared convictions

All four affirm:

1. The personal, visible, bodily **return of Christ**.
2. The **resurrection** of the dead.
3. The **final judgment**.
4. The eternal **new creation** in which God dwells with his people.

## Questions for discussion

1. Does Revelation 20 follow chapter 19 chronologically, or begin a new cycle of visions?
2. What does it mean for Satan to be "bound" (Revelation 20:2-3; compare Matthew 12:29)?
3. How should one's millennial view affect evangelism, social engagement and hope?

topics.title: Death, Resurrection, Judgment and New Creation
topics.subtitle: Eschatology
topics.summary: The intermediate state, the resurrection of the body, the final judgment, views of hell, purgatory, and the hope of the new heavens and new earth.

sections.heading: The shape of Christian hope
sections.body: Christian hope is not merely that souls go to heaven when they die, but that God will raise the dead and renew all creation. The creeds confess "the resurrection of the body (or of the dead), and the life everlasting."

sections.heading: Death and the intermediate state
sections.body:
Most Christian traditions teach that at death the soul is separated from the body and enters the presence of God (for the righteous) awaiting the resurrection. Paul desires "to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better" (Philippians 1:23) and to be "away from the body and at home with the Lord" (2 Corinthians 5:8). Jesus promises the dying thief, "Today you will be with me in paradise" (Luke 23:43).

A minority view, **soul sleep** (or Christian mortalism), holds that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection; it was held by some Anabaptists, by Seventh-day Adventists, and was debated during the Reformation (Calvin wrote against it in *Psychopannychia*).

sections.heading: Purgatory
sections.body: The Catholic Church teaches that those who die in God's grace but still imperfectly purified undergo **purgatory**, a final purification before entering heaven (Council of Florence, 1439; Council of Trent, 1563; *Catechism* §§1030-1032). It appeals to 2 Maccabees 12:46, 1 Corinthians 3:15 and the ancient practice of praying for the dead. Orthodox Christians pray for the dead but generally reject a defined doctrine of purgatory. Protestants reject it, holding that Christ's finished work and the believer's union with him leave no remaining satisfaction to be made.

sections.heading: The return of Christ and the resurrection
sections.body: Christ will return visibly and bodily — the **Parousia** ("presence, arrival"; Acts 1:11; 1 Thessalonians 4:16). The dead will be raised. Paul describes the resurrection body as "imperishable," "glorious," "powerful" and "spiritual" — that is, animated by the Spirit, not immaterial (1 Corinthians 15:42-44). Jesus' own resurrection body, which could be touched and eat, is the firstfruits and pattern (1 Corinthians 15:20).

sections.heading: The final judgment
sections.body: All people will stand before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10; Matthew 25:31-46; Revelation 20:11-15). Scripture speaks of judgment "according to works" (Romans 2:6) while teaching that salvation is by grace: works are typically understood as the evidence of genuine faith.

sections.heading: Hell
sections.body:
Christian theology has held several views of final punishment:

- **Eternal conscious punishment** — the majority historic view (Augustine, Aquinas, the Reformers), based on texts such as Matthew 25:46 ("eternal punishment… eternal life") and Revelation 14:11.
- **Annihilationism / conditional immortality** — the wicked are finally destroyed and cease to exist; immortality is God's gift to the redeemed (cf. Matthew 10:28; 2 Thessalonians 1:9). Held by John Stott (tentatively) and others.
- **Universalism** — all will eventually be saved. A form associated with Origen (*apokatastasis*) was condemned in the sixth century; some theologians (e.g. Gregory of Nyssa is often read this way) have expressed hope for universal restoration.

sections.heading: The new creation
sections.body: The Bible ends not with souls in heaven but with heaven coming to earth: "a new heaven and a new earth," the New Jerusalem descending, God dwelling with his people, every tear wiped away, death no more (Revelation 21-22). Romans 8:19-23 pictures creation itself "set free from its bondage to corruption." The final goal is the **beatific vision** — seeing God "face to face" (1 Corinthians 13:12; 1 John 3:2; Revelation 22:4).

keyTerms.definition: The condition of the dead between death and the resurrection.
The "arrival" or second coming of Christ.
In Catholic teaching, the final purification of those who die in grace but are not fully purified.
The view that the unrepentant are ultimately destroyed rather than punished eternally.
The "restoration of all things," associated with Origen's universalism.
The direct vision of God enjoyed by the redeemed.
