sections.heading: Reading companion
sections.content:
# The Apostles' Creed

*Traditional English text from the 1662 Book of Common Prayer (public domain).*

> I believe in God the Father Almighty,
> Maker of heaven and earth:
>
> And in Jesus Christ his only Son our Lord,
> Who was conceived by the Holy Ghost,
> Born of the Virgin Mary,
> Suffered under Pontius Pilate,
> Was crucified, dead, and buried:
> He descended into hell;
> The third day he rose again from the dead;
> He ascended into heaven,
> And sitteth on the right hand of God the Father Almighty;
> From thence he shall come to judge the quick and the dead.
>
> I believe in the Holy Ghost;
> The holy Catholick Church;
> The Communion of Saints;
> The Forgiveness of sins;
> The Resurrection of the body,
> And the Life everlasting. Amen.

## Study notes

**Origins.** A medieval legend held that each of the twelve apostles contributed one article. In fact the creed grew from the **Old Roman Creed**, a baptismal confession used in Rome by the late second or third century, which was asked in question form of candidates for baptism ("Do you believe in God the Father Almighty?…"). The text reached its present form in Gaul by around the eighth century and became the standard baptismal creed of the Western church. It is not traditionally used in the Eastern Orthodox liturgy.

**Trinitarian structure.** The creed has three articles — Father, Son and Holy Spirit — reflecting the baptismal formula of Matthew 28:19.

**"He descended into hell."** This phrase (Latin *descendit ad inferos*, "to those below") appears relatively late. It has been interpreted as Christ's truly entering the state of death (Hades, the realm of the dead), his proclamation of victory to the departed (1 Peter 3:18-20; 4:6), or — in Calvin's reading — his enduring the torments of God's judgment on the cross. Some modern versions render it "He descended to the dead."

**The last things.** The creed's final articles — "the Resurrection of the body, and the Life everlasting" — confess a bodily, not merely spiritual, hope. "From thence he shall come to judge the quick and the dead" confesses Christ's return and the final judgment.

**"The Communion of Saints."** Interpreted as the fellowship of all believers, living and departed, in Christ, and sometimes as shared participation in holy things (the sacraments).

## Questions for reflection

1. Why might a baptismal creed take the form of questions put to the candidate?
2. Which events of Jesus' life does the creed include, and what does it leave out? Why?
3. How does the bodily resurrection shape Christian ethics and care for creation?

topics.title: The Nature and Marks of the Church
topics.subtitle: Church & Sacraments
topics.summary: Biblical images of the Church, the four creedal marks, visible and invisible church, the Reformation marks, and models of church government.

sections.heading: What is the Church?
sections.body:
The New Testament word ***ekklēsia*** means an assembly "called out" — used in the Septuagint for the congregation of Israel. The Church is the people God gathers in Christ by the Spirit. Scripture describes it with rich images:

- **The people of God** (1 Peter 2:9-10), in continuity with Israel.
- **The body of Christ** (1 Corinthians 12; Ephesians 1:22-23), with Christ as head and many members with diverse gifts.
- **The temple of the Holy Spirit** (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:19-22).
- **The bride of Christ** (Ephesians 5:25-32; Revelation 19:7).
- **The household of God**, "a pillar and buttress of the truth" (1 Timothy 3:15).

sections.heading: The four marks
sections.body:
The Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed (381) confesses "**one, holy, catholic and apostolic** Church":

1. **One** — united in one Lord, one faith, one baptism (Ephesians 4:4-6).
2. **Holy** — set apart by God, and called to holiness.
3. **Catholic** — from *kath' holou*, "according to the whole": universal, possessing the fullness of the faith, for all peoples.
4. **Apostolic** — founded on the apostles' teaching (Ephesians 2:20) and, in Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican understanding, in continuity with them through **apostolic succession** of bishops.

Different traditions understand where these marks are realised: the Catholic Church teaches that the one Church of Christ "subsists in" the Catholic Church (*Lumen Gentium* 8, 1964), while recognising elements of sanctification elsewhere; Orthodoxy identifies the Church with the Orthodox communion; Protestants generally locate the marks wherever the apostolic gospel is faithfully confessed.

sections.heading: Visible and invisible
sections.body: **Augustine** distinguished the church as a "mixed body" (*corpus permixtum*) of true and false members until the final judgment. The Reformers developed the distinction between the **visible church** (all who profess the faith, with their children) and the **invisible church** (the elect of all ages, known fully only to God).

sections.heading: The Reformation marks
sections.body: Rather than locate the church by succession, the Reformers defined it by its activities. The **Augsburg Confession** (Article VII, 1530) says the church is "the congregation of saints in which the Gospel is purely taught and the Sacraments are rightly administered." The **Belgic Confession** (Article 29, 1561) adds a third mark: the exercise of **church discipline**.

sections.heading: Church government (polity)
sections.body:
- **Episcopal** — governed by bishops in succession, with priests (presbyters) and deacons: Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, many Lutherans and Methodists.
- **Presbyterian** — governed by elders (presbyters) in a hierarchy of courts: session, presbytery, synod, general assembly. Reformed and Presbyterian churches.
- **Congregational** — each local congregation is self-governing under Christ: Baptists, Congregationalists, many independent and free churches.

Each appeals to New Testament evidence: the apostles' oversight and Ignatius's early witness to bishops; the plurality of elders in Acts 14:23 and 20:17-28; and the congregation's role in discipline and decision (Matthew 18:17; Acts 6:3-6; Acts 15:22).

sections.heading: The mission of the Church
sections.body: The church exists to worship God, to build up its members, and to bear witness in word and deed — making disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:18-20). The modern **ecumenical movement**, from the Edinburgh Missionary Conference (1910) to the World Council of Churches (1948) and Vatican II's *Unitatis Redintegratio* (1964), has sought visible unity in response to Jesus' prayer "that they may all be one" (John 17:21).

sections.heading: What is a sacrament?
sections.body:
The Latin ***sacramentum*** (a soldier's oath, or something sacred) translated the Greek ***mystērion***, "mystery." **Augustine** described a sacrament as a visible sign of an invisible grace, and said, "The word is added to the element, and it becomes a sacrament" (*Tractates on John* 80.3). Traditions differ on how sacraments relate to grace:

- **Catholic** teaching holds that sacraments confer grace ***ex opere operato*** ("by the work worked") — by the power of Christ acting through the rite, not by the minister's holiness — though fruitful reception requires right dispositions.
- **Lutheran** and **Reformed** theology call sacraments "visible words" and signs and seals of God's promise, received by faith.
- Many **Baptists** and free churches prefer **ordinances** — acts of obedience commanded by Christ that proclaim and remember the gospel.

sections.heading: Seven or two?
sections.body: **Peter Lombard** (*Sentences*, c. 1150) listed seven sacraments; this was confirmed at the **Council of Florence (1439)** and the **Council of Trent (1547)**: **baptism, confirmation (chrismation), Eucharist, penance (reconciliation), anointing of the sick, holy orders and matrimony**. The Orthodox recognise the same seven "mysteries," without restricting God's mysteries to that number. The Reformers recognised **two** — **baptism** and the **Lord's Supper** — as instituted by Christ with a visible sign and gospel promise.

sections.heading: Baptism
sections.body:
All major traditions practise baptism with water in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19) and generally recognise one another's Trinitarian baptisms.

- **Infant baptism (paedobaptism)**: Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican and Methodist churches. Arguments include household baptisms (Acts 16:15, 33), continuity with circumcision as covenant sign (Colossians 2:11-12), the promise "for you and for your children" (Acts 2:39), and early testimony (Hippolytus, Origen, Cyprian).
- **Believer's baptism (credobaptism)**: Anabaptists, Baptists, Pentecostals and many evangelicals. Arguments include the New Testament pattern of repentance and faith preceding baptism (Acts 2:38; 8:12) and baptism as a personal confession of faith.
- **Mode**: immersion, pouring (affusion) or sprinkling (aspersion). The Didache already allowed pouring when running water was unavailable. Orthodox churches baptise infants by triple immersion.
- **Baptismal regeneration** — that God regenerates through baptism — is taught by Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran churches (Titus 3:5; John 3:5); most evangelicals see baptism as a sign of regeneration already received.

sections.heading: The Eucharist / Lord's Supper
sections.body:
Instituted at the Last Supper ("This is my body… this is my blood," Matthew 26:26-28; 1 Corinthians 11:23-26). Major views of Christ's presence:

1. **Transubstantiation** (Catholic): the *substance* of bread and wine is changed into the body and blood of Christ, while the *accidents* (appearances) remain. The term was used at **Lateran IV (1215)**, given Aristotelian explanation by Aquinas, and defined at **Trent (1551)**. The Mass is also understood as a re-presentation of Christ's one sacrifice.
2. **Orthodox**: a real change (*metabolē*) of the gifts through the invocation of the Spirit (*epiclesis*), affirmed as mystery without philosophical definition.
3. **Sacramental union** (Lutheran): Christ's true body and blood are present "in, with and under" the bread and wine (often mislabelled "consubstantiation," a term Lutherans reject).
4. **Spiritual real presence** (Reformed, following **Calvin**): believers truly feed on Christ's body and blood by the power of the Holy Spirit, who lifts them up to communion with the ascended Christ.
5. **Memorial** (associated with **Zwingli**): the Supper is a commemoration and proclamation of Christ's death; Christ is present by faith in the gathered community. Common among Baptists and many evangelicals.

The **Marburg Colloquy (1529)** failed to reconcile Luther ("*Hoc est corpus meum*," which he chalked on the table) and Zwingli on this point. The ecumenical document *Baptism, Eucharist and Ministry* (World Council of Churches, Lima, **1982**) explored remarkable convergences.

keyTerms.definition: "By the work worked": sacraments are effective by Christ's action, not the minister's worthiness.
Catholic doctrine that the substance of bread and wine becomes Christ's body and blood.
Lutheran teaching that Christ's body and blood are present in, with and under the elements.
The invocation of the Holy Spirit upon the gifts in the eucharistic prayer.
The baptism of infants.
A rite commanded by Christ, emphasising obedience and remembrance.

questions.prompt: Which medieval theologian's Sentences listed the seven sacraments?
questions.explanation: Lombard's Sentences (c. 1150) became the standard theology textbook.
questions.sourceReference: Baptism, the Eucharist and the Sacraments

questions.prompt: The Lutheran view that Christ's body and blood are present "in, with and under" the bread and wine is called…
questions.explanation: Lutherans generally reject the label "consubstantiation."
questions.sourceReference: Baptism, the Eucharist and the Sacraments

questions.prompt: The memorial view of the Lord's Supper is chiefly associated with…
questions.explanation: Zwingli emphasised remembrance and proclamation.
questions.sourceReference: Baptism, the Eucharist and the Sacraments

questions.prompt: The phrase "ex opere operato" means that a sacrament is effective…
options: Only if the minister is holy
By the work performed, through Christ's action
Only when received with full understanding
questions.explanation: A principle developed against the Donatist view.
questions.sourceReference: Baptism, the Eucharist and the Sacraments

questions.prompt: How many sacraments did the mainstream Reformers recognise?
questions.explanation: Baptism and the Lord's Supper, both instituted by Christ with a visible sign.
questions.sourceReference: Baptism, the Eucharist and the Sacraments

questions.prompt: The 1982 ecumenical convergence text on sacraments and ministry is known as…
questions.explanation: Baptism, Eucharist and Ministry, produced by the WCC Faith and Order Commission at Lima.

glossary.definition: A formal courtroom speech of defense or reasoned vindication of truth claims (1 Pet 3:15; Acts 22:1).
The "seminal Word" by which Justin Martyr explained fragments of moral and philosophical truth present across human cultures.
An innate human faculty or awareness of the divine implanted by the Creator (John Calvin, Institutes I.3; developed in analytic epistemology by Alvin Plantinga).

glossary.category: Historical Apologetics & the Resurrection of Jesus
glossary.definition: The apostolic heralding or core proclamation of Christ’s death, burial, resurrection, exaltation, and call to repentance.

glossary.category: Historical Apologetics & the Resurrection of Jesus
glossary.definition: Literally "standing up again"; consistently used in Jewish and early Christian Greek for bodily resurrection of the dead rather than mere survival of the soul.

glossary.category: The Problem of Evil, Suffering & Theodicy
glossary.definition: Coined by Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1710) from theos (God) and dikē (justice): the vindication of divine justice and goodness in light of evil.

glossary.category: The Problem of Evil, Suffering & Theodicy
glossary.definition: Privation or lack of a due good; the classical metaphysical doctrine that evil has no independent ontological existence apart from parasitic distortion of good.
Mercy seat / atoning sacrifice (Rom 3:25; LXX Lev 16), uniting the removal of guilt (expiation) and turning away of righteous wrath (propitiation).
Redemption price paid to emancipate captives or slaves (Mark 10:45: "to give his life as a ransom for many").
"Christ the Victor": the classic patristic view of the Cross and Resurrection as decisive triumph over sin, death, and demonic powers.
"Simultaneously righteous and a sinner": Luther’s formula for the Christian who is completely righteous in Christ before God’s judgment seat while still battling indwelling sin in this life.
Deification or divinization: transformative union with God by grace in Christ through the Holy Spirit (cf. 2 Peter 1:4), preserving the Creator–creature distinction.
"Order of salvation": the logical and theological sequence of aspects of redemption (calling, regeneration, faith, justification, adoption, sanctification, glorification; cf. Rom 8:29–30).

glossary.category: The Doctrine of the Trinity: Ousia, Hypostases & Perichoresis
glossary.definition: "Of the same essence/being": the decisive Nicene watchword affirming that the Son shares the exact undivided divine nature of the Father, contrasted with homoiousios ("of similar essence").

glossary.category: The Doctrine of the Trinity: Ousia, Hypostases & Perichoresis
glossary.definition: Distinct personal subsistence; in Cappadocian Trinitarian grammar, God is mia ousia, treis hypostaseis (one essence, three persons).

glossary.category: The Doctrine of the Trinity: Ousia, Hypostases & Perichoresis
glossary.definition: Mutual indwelling, interpenetration, and communion of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (cf. John 14:10–11).
"God-bearer" or "Mother of God," affirmed at the Council of Ephesus (431) to safeguard the personal unity of the incarnate Word from conception.
Personal union of Christ’s complete divine and human natures in the one eternal Hypostasis of God the Son.
Communication of proper attributes: attributing predicates of both the divine and human natures to the single Person of Christ.
Medieval fourfold method of biblical interpretation summarized by the couplet: Littera gesta docet, quid credas allegoria, moralis quid agas, quo tendas anagogia.
"Pattern, stamp, or mold" (Rom 5:14): real historical persons, institutions, or events in Israel’s history divinely designed to foreshadow heightened fulfillment (antitype) in Christ.
Antiochene "contemplative insight" perceiving both the immediate historical referent and the deeper Messianic horizon without erasing literal history.
Critical, disciplined drawing out of a text’s meaning from its grammar, syntax, historical setting, and literary flow (cf. John 1:18, exēgēsato).
Importing foreign presuppositions or subjective agendas into a text without contextual warrant.
"Analogy of faith" (cf. Rom 12:6): interpreting individual texts in harmony with the coherent teaching of the whole canon.

glossary.category: Martyrs, Empire & the Rise of Monasticism
glossary.definition: Originally a legal "witness" (Acts 1:8); came to designate one who seals testimony to Christ by laying down their life.

glossary.category: Martyrs, Empire & the Rise of Monasticism
glossary.definition: From koinos bios ("common life"): communal monasticism lived under a shared rule and abbot/abbess, contrasted with eremitic solitude.
Latin clause meaning "and from the Son," inserted into the Western Latin text of the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed regarding the procession of the Holy Spirit.
"First among equals": the Orthodox understanding of the Bishop of Rome’s ancient honor among the Patriarchs prior to schism.
Principle that Holy Scripture, as inspired Word of God, is the sole infallible rule of faith and practice—respecting, yet testing, creeds and councils.

Dogma affirmed at Lateran IV (1215) and Trent (1551) that in the Eucharist the whole substance of bread and wine is changed into Christ’s body and blood while outward appearances (accidents/species) remain.

glossary.category: The Hebrew Bible, Septuagint & Dead Sea Scrolls
glossary.definition: Acronym for the three divisions of the Hebrew Bible: Torah (Instruction), Nevi’im (Prophets), and Ketuvim (Writings).

glossary.category: The Hebrew Bible, Septuagint & Dead Sea Scrolls
glossary.definition: Ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures begun in Alexandria in the 3rd century BC; frequently quoted in the New Testament.

glossary.category: The Hebrew Bible, Septuagint & Dead Sea Scrolls
glossary.definition: "Tradition/transmission": the system of vowel points, accents, and marginal textual tallies created by Jewish Masoretic scholars to safeguard the exact pronunciation and consonantal integrity of the Hebrew text.
Literally a "measuring reed" or straight rod (Gal 6:16); applied to the authoritative rule of faith and the closed list of inspired books measuring all teaching.

Eusebius’s distinction between universally acknowledged NT books (Four Gospels, Acts, Paul’s Epistles, 1 Peter, 1 John) and temporarily debated books (e.g., Hebrews, James, 2 Peter, 2–3 John, Jude, Revelation) prior to final consensus.
"The more difficult reading is stronger": textual-critical principle recognizing that copyists were far more likely to smooth out awkward grammar or apparent tensions than to create them.

glossary.category: The Apostolic Fathers & Irenaeus of Lyons
glossary.definition: "Summing up under one head" (Eph 1:10): Irenaeus’s teaching that Christ retraced Adam’s story in faithful obedience to undo the Fall and bring creation to maturity.

glossary.category: The Apostolic Fathers & Irenaeus of Lyons
glossary.definition: Early heresy claiming Christ’s physical body, hunger, and crucifixion were mere phantoms or appearances rather than true human flesh (cf. 1 John 4:2–3).

glossary.category: The Apostolic Fathers & Irenaeus of Lyons
glossary.definition: "Rule of Faith": the concise Trinitarian summary of apostolic preaching taught to catechumens and used by Irenaeus and Tertullian to test Gnostic distortions.

glossary.category: Golden Age of the Fathers: East & West
glossary.definition: "Against the world": proverb honoring Athanasius’s steadfast defense of Nicene orthodoxy during decades of imperial Arian dominance.

glossary.category: Golden Age of the Fathers: East & West
glossary.definition: Love of God vs. disordered self-love—Augustine’s diagnostic key to human history, ethics, and politics in De Civitate Dei.
A token of recognition formed by fitting two halves together; ancient Christian term for a baptismal or conciliar creed uniting believers.
Distinction between Holy Scripture as the supreme "norming norm" and historic creeds/confessions as subordinate "normed norms."

glossary.category: The Seven Ecumenical Councils & Reformation Confessions
glossary.definition: Orthodox doctrine defined at Constantinople III (681) that Jesus Christ possesses two natural wills—divine and human—corresponding to his two natures.

glossary.category: The Seven Ecumenical Councils & Reformation Confessions
glossary.definition: Distinction made by John of Damascus and Nicaea II (787) between supreme sacrificial adoration due to God alone (latria) and respectful honor/veneration (proskynēsis).
